Mark an original retained product whose whole opposite support is contained in that context. A three-vertex cover of the missing graph containing that endpoint, for example $\{x,a,d\}$ when $N=\{d\}$, covers all old edges of the marked product as well. Keep one center for each other original retained product. This covers $G$ with at most $(K-1)+3=K+2$ vertices.

Otherwise one of $W,X$ is a singleton, necessarily an endpoint of its witness $cd$; rename it $c$. Every term containing $h$ vanishes on the endpoints of the other three target edges. Those edges must consequently be witnessed by
\[
 gL\vee gCM\vee q_{13}gC.
\]
If $q_{13}>0$, the safe old cubic $gC$ absorbs $gCM$, leaving two old cubics, which cannot supply three different missing witnesses. Hence $q_{13}=0$. Now the old cubic $gL$ has at most one witness and the old quartic $gCM$ at most two. All three targets force both bounds to be attained. The two quartic witnesses must be $ab$ and one path arm, say $xz$.

Quartic equality in Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors} confines the full supports of $U,V,C,M$ to the four distinct two-point transversals of $\{xz,ab\}$. The remaining path arm $xy$ is supplied by $gL$. Since $y$ lies outside that quartet, $U,V$ both contain $x$. After exchanging factors and $a,b$, the full supports are
\[
 U=\{x,a\},\quad V=\{x,b\},\quad
 C=\{z,a\},\quad M=\{z,b\}.
\]
The nonsingleton factors $U,V$ and the full cubic singleton rule give $L=\{y\}$.

Mark original retained products $P_g,P_f$ whose whole opposite supports lie respectively in the actual contexts $L=\{y\}$ and $M=\{z,b\}$. They are distinct. If the two occurrences entered the same side of one product, its nonzero opposite support would lie in $L\cap M=\varnothing$. If they entered opposite sides, their simultaneous occurrences would give a positive $gf$ coefficient, contrary to $q_{13}=0$. Keep one center for each other retained product and use the four vertices $\{y,z,b,d\}$ for the two marked products and all missing edges. The resulting full-graph cover has size at most $K-2+4=K+2$. Coincident chosen centers only lower this count.

If $M$ is zero or a positive scalar, $gCM$ is zero or an old cubic and cannot attain the two witnesses required in this last branch. Thus the argument includes every scalar and zero case. All context containments concern the full original operands, not only their restriction to $T$.
\end{proof}


\begin{lemma}[Three occurrences of two old products]\label{lem:twoproductthreeoccurrences}
Let \(G\) be finite, simple and \(C_4\)-free, with nonempty quadratic support \(H\).
Suppose that the four global missing edges induce \(P_3\sqcup2K_2\) on their endpoint set \(T\), and \(H[T]=\varnothing\).
Keep an original quadratic frame with \(K\) retained products.
Let \(g\) and \(h\) be products of at most three and at most two nonzero old homogeneous linear forms, respectively.
Consider at most three original visible insertion occurrences carrying \(g\) or \(h\), at least one of each, with their full actual old linear or scalar direct contexts and all actual pairwise cross terms.
Repeated values and repeated factors are allowed, but occurrences and original product incidences remain distinct.
If the resulting high part is safe and witnesses all four missing edges, then
\(\vc(G)\le K+2\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write the missing edges as \(xy,xz,ab,cd\), with path \(y-x-z\).
We use two original-product cover charges.
If an actual nonzero context is the full singleton \(\{w\}\), where \(w=x\) or \(w\) is an endpoint of an isolated missing edge, choose a three-vertex cover of the missing graph containing \(w\).
The context contains the complete opposite support of an original retained product.
Keep one star center for every other retained product and use the three-vertex cover for this marked product and all missing edges.
This gives at most \(K-1+3=K+2\) vertices.
Likewise, an actual full two-point context that is a transversal of \(ab,cd\), together with \(x\), gives the same charge.
All ambient old edges of the marked product are covered; no center is removed solely from information restricted to \(T\).

Boolean repetitions may pad the factor lists, without changing any original arithmetic degree.
Thus write \(g=ABC\) and \(h=DE\).
A safe old cubic \(hM_i\) has at most one missing witness, and the union for fixed \(h\) is a star.
Within the target this union has at most two edges, with the only possible double the path pair.
A safe old quartic \(gL_i\) has at most two witnesses.
If it has two, full quartic equality makes \(A,B,C,L_i\) the four distinct full transversals of their matching quartet.
In particular the three factors of \(g\) have empty common intersection.
Consequently every target witness of \(g\), or of any contribution containing \(g\), is confined to that same pair: a different target meets its quartet in at most one endpoint, which cannot lie in all three factors.

If a direct scalar context or a positive cross between two \(g\)-occurrences makes \(g\) itself safe, its old three-factor bound is one witness.
It absorbs every \(g\)-multiple, leaving at most two from the \(h\)-context star.
If the analogous event makes \(h\) safe, it has at most one witness and absorbs every mixed term.
The at most two remaining \(g\)-context terms together have at most two: either one is a double and confines both to its pair, or each has at most one.
Thus four witnesses are impossible in these cases.
We may assume all nonzero direct contexts are linear and that no repeated-high cross is present.
Let \(X=gh\) when a mixed coefficient is positive, and omit \(X\) otherwise.

We need one full-support fact for a double witness of \(X\).
A safe product of five old factor occurrences witnessing two missing matching edges has at least three occurrences whose full supports are distinct matching transversals.
Indeed, its restriction computes the matching function.
Its four maximal independent sets require four distinct rejecting classes of factors.
With five occurrences, at least three of those classes have a unique occurrence.
Each such occurrence restricts to the corresponding two-point transversal.
An extra variable in its full old support would be nonadjacent to both vertices of the complementary independent transversal, by the old-neighborhood \(C_4\) argument.
Choosing that extra variable and, in all other factors, vertices of the rejected independent transversal would violate safety.
Thus each unique occurrence has exactly its restricted two-point support.
Since \(D,E\) account for only two occurrences, at least one such full transversal belongs to \(A,B,C\).
Every \(g\)-context witness must therefore meet the matching quartet.

First take two \(g\)-occurrences and one \(h\)-occurrence, and put
\[
 G_0=gL_1\lor gL_2,\qquad H_0=hM.
\]
If either \(gL_i\) has two witnesses, all \(g\)-based contributions, including \(X\), are confined to that pair, while \(H_0\) has at most one.
Hence each \(gL_i\) has at most one.

If \(X\) has two witnesses, the full-support fact makes every \(G_0\)-witness meet their quartet.
At least one target avoids that quartet and must be supplied by \(H_0\).
The pair cannot be the two isolated edges, which would leave both path arms outside the quartet.
Thus \(H_0\) supplies the other isolated edge.
Both \(D,E\) are nonsingleton, since they meet that edge and the two \(X\)-edges.
The old-cubic singleton rule makes full \(M\) an endpoint singleton of the isolated edge, and the first cover charge applies.

Suppose \(X\) has at most one witness.
Four targets require one distinct target from each of \(gL_1,gL_2,H_0,X\).
If \(H_0\) is isolated, both \(D,E\) meet it and the distinct \(X\)-edge and are nonsingleton; again full \(M\) is an isolated endpoint singleton.
If \(H_0,X\) are the two path arms, old-neighborhood geometry forces \(x\) into both \(D,E\), so \(h(x)=1\).
Both isolated edges are then potential witnesses of \(g\).
For any independent set \(I\) of their four endpoints, safety of \(gh\) on \(I\cup\{x\}\) forces \(g(I)=0\).
Thus \(g\) computes the two-edge matching on those endpoints with at most three clauses, although four are necessary.
This is impossible.

The remaining allocation has \(H_0\) a path arm and \(X\) an isolated edge.
The forms \(D,E\) are nonsingleton, so full \(M\) is a singleton endpoint of that arm.
If it is \(x\), use the cover charge.
If it is the path leaf, the singleton rule puts \(x\) in both \(D,E\).
The other isolated edge must occur in a \(g\)-context term, so \(g\) is again potential on both isolated edges.
Safety of \(gh\), with \(h(x)=1\), gives the same impossible three-clause matching computation.
This exhausts the two-\(g\) allocation.

Now take one \(g\)-occurrence and two \(h\)-occurrences:
\[
 G_0=gL,\qquad H_0=hM_1\lor hM_2.
\]
If \(G_0\) has two witnesses, \(g\) and \(X\) are confined to that pair.
The two other targets must come from the \(h\)-star, so they are the path arms.
The pair is therefore exactly \(ab,cd\), and full quartic equality makes the actual \(L\) their two-point transversal.
Use the second cover charge.

Assume \(G_0\) has at most one witness.
If \(H_0\) has two, they are the path pair and \(h(x)=1\).
Four witnesses require both isolated edges to be potential for \(g\), through \(G_0\) and \(X\).
If \(X\) is absent this already fails by counting; otherwise safety with \(h(x)=1\) again forces a two-edge matching to have a three-clause computation.

Finally, if \(G_0,H_0\) each have at most one witness, \(X\) must have two.
A full matching transversal among \(A,B,C\) makes every \(G_0\)-witness meet its quartet.
The pair cannot be both isolated edges, since \(H_0\) could not supply both path arms outside it.
The outside target is therefore the other isolated edge, supplied by an individual \(hM_i\).
Both \(D,E\) are nonsingleton, and the singleton rule makes full \(M_i\) an endpoint of that isolated edge.
The first charge finishes the proof.

If only two occurrences are present, the unused context slot and its crosses are simply omitted in the same argument; no counted gate is added.
All charges above use nonzero actual occurrences.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Literal old and raw operands with three visible cuts]\label{prop:literaloldrawthreevisible}
Let \(G\) be a finite simple \(C_4\)-free graph, and let a positive variable-input circuit compute \(P\in\Sup(G)\).
Assume its quadratic support \(H\) is nonempty and its four global missing edges induce \(P_3\sqcup2K_2\) on their endpoint set \(T\), with \(H[T]=\varnothing\).
Keep the exact original extracted frame and its \(K\) retained multiplication nodes.
Suppose extraction and pruning delete at most three original products and exactly three original additions, all three additions visible.
Their high branches are original private-product outputs, with repetitions permitted.
Every operand in the \emph{original} private multiplication network is either a nonzero old homogeneous linear form or the raw output of an earlier private product.
Retain all original lows, degrees, full contexts, fanout and product incidences, including every pairwise occurrence cross and squares of coincident high values.
Then \(\vc(G)\le K+2\), with no restriction on retained additions or retained-product optimality.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The original three-occurrence frame is quadratic in its formal insertion symbols.
After substitution its high part therefore consists exactly of direct high-context terms and pairwise high products, including repeated-value squares.
No triple-insertion term is omitted.
The target \(P_3\sqcup2K_2\) has eight maximal independent sets and requires eight positive linear CNF clauses.

Partition the cases by the number of distinct \emph{original private-product nodes} carried by the three occurrences, not by the number of distinct Boolean values.

If there is only one such node, its literal multiplication cone uses at most three binary products and at most four old boundary occurrences.
It is a product of those old factors, up to Boolean repetitions.
The output is that product times one affine linear context, or the product itself when a repeated-high cross is positive.
Thus at most five clauses suffice, contradicting the required eight.

Suppose two original product nodes occur as highs.
If they are comparable, write their support values as \(g\) and \(gR\), where \(R\) is a product of the remaining old boundary factors.
All contributions collect into
\[
 g\bigl(P_0\lor RQ_0\bigr),
\]
with affine linear \(P_0,Q_0\); repeated-high crosses give constant terms, and a repeated earlier high may set \(P_0=1\).
A connected binary multiplication DAG on at most three nodes has at most four external boundary occurrences: six input occurrences have at least two internal uses.
After omitting Boolean repetitions, the total number of factors in \(g\) and \(R\) is at most four.
Distributing \(P_0\) over the factors of \(RQ_0\) gives at most five clauses, again impossible.
This is a support computation; original nodes and arithmetic degrees are unchanged.

If the two nodes are incomparable but share an earlier private product, the budget leaves one first quadratic product \(u\) and its two branches.
They belong to the common-ancestor chain or fork family of Lemma~\ref{lem:commonancestorpath}, including a factor \(1\) for a Booleanly absorbed raw square.
That lemma allows arbitrary insertion occurrences and excludes the target.

If their private cones are disjoint, their total product budget is at most three.
One high is a product of at most three old forms and the other of at most two.
Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductthreeoccurrences} gives the cover.
This includes distinct original nodes with equal support values: only support expressions are combined, while their original contexts and incidence charges remain distinct.

Finally, suppose three original private-product nodes occur as highs.
There are only three occurrences, so each original node occurs once.
If the original private-product DAG is an antichain, Proposition~\ref{prop:paththreevisible} applies.
If one first quadratic product is an ancestor of both other nodes, the chain/fork family of Lemma~\ref{lem:commonancestorpath} applies.
A descendant multiplied by its ancestor or by itself may remove repeated factors Booleanly, but does not change the original ancestry or gate count.

Otherwise the three-node DAG is either a join of two independent quadratic products or one dependent pair together with an independent product.
The literal join \(u=AB,v=CD,w=uv\), one occurrence each, is Proposition~\ref{prop:literaljoinpath}.
For the mixed pair, a later product \(uC\) with old linear \(C\), together with an independent quadratic product, is Proposition~\ref{prop:mixedrawthreevisible}.
If the dependent product is instead the raw square \(u^2\), its support value is \(u\); the three original occurrences satisfy Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductthreeoccurrences}, with both independent support products having at most two old factors.
This does not relabel a square as a new independent original node.

These possibilities exhaust the original literal network.
A private node receives two old boundaries, one raw ancestor and an old boundary, two independent raw ancestors, or repeated/comparable raw ancestors.
With only three private nodes these are precisely the antichain, common-ancestor, join, mixed-pair and square cases just treated.
Each case either excludes the four witnesses or gives an explicit full-graph cover with at most \(K+2\) vertices.

No affected old-plus-high operand or unresolved private-sum high is normalized by this proposition.
In particular, an original ancestry relation is never discarded and then relabeled as independent.
\end{proof}


\begin{example}[Sharpness of the two-vertex cover increment]\label{ex:literalmixedsharpness}
There is a four-cycle-free graph $G$, a nonempty quadratic subgraph $H$, and a positive variable-input circuit with $25$ gates such that
\[
 |E(H)|=14,\quad |E(G)|=18,\quad
 K=\operatorname{vc}(H)=6,\quad \operatorname{vc}(G)=8.
\]
Canonical extraction deletes exactly three multiplications and three visible additions. The four missing edges induce $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ on their endpoints, and the retained quadratic frame has its minimum $19$ gates. Thus the increment $\operatorname{vc}(G)\le K+2$ is attained in the literal mixed old/raw branch. This is a construction with $25=|E(G)|+\operatorname{vc}(G)-1$ gates; it asserts no unrestricted circuit minimum for $G$.

Take the following seventeen distinct vertices:
\[
 x,y,z,a,b,c,d,p,q,r,s,h_z,h_n,\ell_p,\ell_q,\ell_r,e.
\]
The old graph is the union of the six stars with centers and leaf sets
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
 p&x,a,\ell_p\\
 q&x,b,\ell_q\\
 r&y,b,\ell_r\\
 s&y,a\\
 h_z&z\\
 h_n&c,e
\end{array}
\]
and $G$ is obtained by adding $xy,xz,ab,cd$. Put
\[
 A=x+a,\quad B=x+b,\quad C=y+b,\quad M=y+a,\quad N=c+e,
 \qquad g=AB,\quad t=gC,\quad v=cd.
\]
The circuit computes the positive polynomial
\[
\begin{split}
 P={}&p(A+\ell_p)+q(B+\ell_q)+r(C+\ell_r)\\
    &+(s+t)M+(h_z+g)z+(h_n+v)N.
\end{split}
\]
Each named intermediate is computed once and shared as displayed; the six outer terms are joined by a binary addition tree.
\end{example}
\begin{proof}
The six centers cover $H$, while
\[
 p\ell_p,\ q\ell_q,\ r\ell_r,\ sa,\ h_zz,\ h_ne
\]
are six disjoint old edges. Hence $\operatorname{vc}(H)=6$. In $G$, the eight disjoint edges
\[
 p\ell_p,\ q\ell_q,\ r\ell_r,\ xy,\ ab,\ h_zz,\ cd,\ h_ne
\]
give a lower bound of eight. The set
$\{p,q,r,y,a,z,c,h_n\}$ covers every edge, so $\operatorname{vc}(G)=8$.

To check four-cycle-freeness, remove the three pendant leaves, the attached path $x-z-h_z$, and the separate path $d-c-h_n-e$, none of which can participate in a cycle. The remaining core has independent vertices $p,q,r,s$ with respective neighborhoods
$\{x,a\},\{x,b\},\{y,b\},\{y,a\}$, together with the disjoint edges $xy,ab$ on the other four vertices. Two different center neighborhoods intersect in at most one vertex, excluding a four-cycle with two centers. A four-cycle with one center would require a two-edge path among $x,y,a,b$ between two of its neighbors, whereas that induced graph is a matching. A four-cycle with no center is also impossible. These exhaust the possibilities. The added edges induce exactly the path $y-x-z$ and the edges $ab,cd$ on $T=\{x,y,z,a,b,c,d\}$, and $H[T]=\varnothing$.

The quadratic part of $P$ is precisely
\[
 P_H=p(A+\ell_p)+q(B+\ell_q)+r(C+\ell_r)+sM+h_zz+h_nN,
\]
the sum of the fourteen distinct old edge monomials, each with coefficient one. The remaining terms $tM,gz,vN$ have degrees four, three and three. At Boolean support level,
\[
 AB=x\vee ab,\qquad CM=y\vee ab,\qquad
 tM=xy\vee ab,\qquad gz=xz\vee abz,\qquad vN=cd\vee cde.
\]
The last two extra terms are absorbed by already present edges. Thus the Boolean support of $P$ is exactly the edge function of $G$. More explicitly, the new edges have exact two-variable-support witnesses
$x^2y^2$, $x^2z$, $a^2b^2$ and $c^2d$, respectively. Every monomial contains a $G$-edge, so $P\in\Sup(G)$ and precisely the four displayed edges are absent from the quadratic support.

The five sums $A,B,C,M,N$ and the three pendant sums use eight old additions. The six star products and the five output additions give a retained frame of six multiplications and thirteen additions, hence nineteen gates. The admitted quadratic lower bound gives
$|E(H)|+\operatorname{vc}(H)-1=14+6-1=19$, so this frame is optimal in that quadratic class.

The additional original multiplication nodes are exactly $g,t,v$. The additional additions are exactly $s+t$, $h_z+g$ and $h_n+v$. Their low inputs have degree one and their high inputs have degrees three, two and two, respectively. Canonical extraction bypasses these three visible cuts; then precisely $g,t,v$ become unused and are pruned. All old sums remain useful through their displayed stars, and every old output addition joins nonzero quadratic parts. Thus no other gate is removed. The full circuit has nine multiplications and sixteen additions, for twenty-five gates, and its deletion profile is $p=3$, $a=3$. Its high pattern is the literal dependent pair $g=AB,t=gC$ and the independent $v=cd$, each with one visible insertion and with contexts $z,M,N$. There are no pairwise insertion cross terms. The equality $\operatorname{vc}(G)=K+2$ therefore proves the stated sharpness within this exact scope.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[Essential visible cuts and original operand forms]\label{prop:essentialvisibleoperands}
Let \(G\) be finite, simple and \(C_4\)-free, and let a positive variable-input circuit compute \(P\in\Sup(G)\) with nonempty quadratic support \(H\).
Suppose its four global missing edges induce \(P_3\sqcup2K_2\) on their endpoint set \(T\), with \(H[T]=\varnothing\).
Assume that canonical extraction and pruning delete at most three products and at most three additions, and that every deleted addition is visible.
Keep the original selected frame, gate identities, minimum degrees and insertion-occurrence labels.

Then exactly three original products and three original additions are deleted, and full-current-carrier erasure cannot make any of these six gates dispensable.
Every visible high branch is the output of an original private product.
Every private-product operand is either the raw output of an earlier original private product, or an original degree-one signal having the exact arithmetic form
\[
 A+\sum_j\beta_j y_j,\qquad \beta_j\in\N,\quad \beta_j\ge0,
\]
where \(A\) is a nonzero old homogeneous linear form and the \(y_j\) are earlier original insertion occurrences, kept distinct even when their high values coincide.
No retained full quadratic carrier survives as a private-product operand or a visible high.
Original private-product ancestry is preserved by the erasure.

In particular, if every nonraw operand has all \(\beta_j=0\), the original circuit satisfies the literal old/raw and product-high hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:literaloldrawthreevisible}, without relabeling an erased dependence as independence.
No classification of the other affected-operand patterns is asserted here.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose either path arm together with the two isolated missing edges.
They form an induced missing three-edge matching on an \(H\)-independent vertex set.
Corollary~\ref{cor:threedeletedproducts} requires at least three private products, so the assumed product bound is exact.
Proposition~\ref{prop:threeproductstwosums} excludes at most two private additions with this product count and four global missing edges.
Hence the original private counts are exactly three and three.

Apply full-current-carrier erasure with the exact original selected quadratic frame fixed.
After zero branches are cleaned up, the result remains a positive variable-input circuit with the same Boolean output, the same ordinary quadratic part and the same selected frame.
It introduces no gates.
If an original private product became dispensable, the result would have at most two private products, contradicting Corollary~\ref{cor:threedeletedproducts}.
If an original private addition became dispensable, it would have at most three private products and at most two private additions, contradicting Proposition~\ref{prop:threeproductstwosums}.
Thus all six original private gates remain indispensable.
This conclusion uses the exact-frame erasure guarantee; it is not an assumption that general erasure preserves private ancestry.

For clarity, let \(\mathcal R\) be the carrier set used in that erasure: original minimum-degree-two nodes with an addition-only path to the output, including full carriers with higher terms and restored degree-two cuts.
Their addition-only output uses are protected.
An addition-only path from a degree-two node to the degree-two output cannot pass through a node with a degree-one alternative, since addition alone cannot restore the lost minimum degree.
Thus these protected paths agree with the original selected quadratic computation.

Consider a nonprotected use of a carrier \(r\in\mathcal R\).
If its recipient is a multiplication, that recipient has original minimum degree at least three: there are variable inputs and no degree-zero constants.
It is therefore a private product.
Erasing this full carrier input makes the product zero and dispensable, contradicting the preceding count.

If the recipient is an addition \(s\), examine the original degree of its other input.
When that degree is one, \(s\) is an unequal-degree cut with \(r\) as its high input.
Erasing the high bypasses \(s\), again contradicting indispensability.
When the other degree is two, \(s\) is a homogeneous degree-two addition.
It cannot be private, since every private addition is a visible unequal-degree cut.
It is therefore selected and has an addition-only path to the quadratic output, making \(r\to s\) protected.
When the other degree exceeds two, \(s\) is an unequal cut with selected low degree two.
Visibility again gives an addition-only selected output path, so \(r\to s\) is protected.
These alternatives exhaust the binary addition case.

Consequently no nonprotected carrier use can erase an original private dependence.
This argument includes the full higher-term-bearing carriers and the restored cuts; replacing them merely by their ordinary quadratic parts would not justify the conclusion.

Now inspect the high input of a visible cut.
It cannot be an input variable or an original degree-one signal, since the low has degree at least one and the high has strictly greater degree.
A retained degree-two node belongs to \(\mathcal R\), and its use as the high of a degree-one cut is the nonprotected carrier use just excluded.
An earlier private addition has original minimum degree one or two, because it is visible in the quadratic extraction.
Degree one cannot be the higher input of a cut.
A visible degree-two cut is itself a full carrier with an addition-only selected output path, so this use is excluded as well.
There is no hidden private addition under the hypotheses.
The remaining possibility is an original private-product output.
Repeated occurrences of that output remain separately labeled.

Next inspect an operand of a private multiplication.
A retained degree-two carrier or a visible degree-two cut cannot feed it.
An original wire of degree at least two that is not such a carrier must therefore be a raw private-product output: every private addition is visible of degree one or two.
All other operands have original degree one.

An original degree-one wire is obtained by additions from its nonzero ordinary degree-one part and high inputs of earlier visible cuts.
Expanding only these additive paths gives the exact arithmetic identity
\[
 A+\sum_j\beta_j y_j.
\]
The coefficients account for multiplicities and fanout.
Each \(y_j\) denotes its original insertion occurrence, even when several occurrences substitute the same private-product value.
A private product has minimum degree at least two, so the ordinary part \(A\) is precisely the nonzero homogeneous linear part.

This \(A\) is old.
For an input variable the assertion is immediate.
Otherwise the retained signal, or the selected low of the visible degree-one cut, continues to a first original retained quadratic product with a nonzero opposite linear form \(B\).
Its selected quadratic support satisfies \(AB\subseteq H\).
Choosing any variable in \(\supp(B)\) places \(\supp(A)\) in that variable's \(H\)-neighborhood.
No arbitrary new linear form from a general recursive expansion is being declared old without this selected continuation.

Finally, every possible original private ancestry path consists of raw private edges and additive degree-one paths carrying these occurrences.
A path through a full quadratic carrier would have to leave its protected addition-only output region before reaching another private product, creating one of the excluded nonprotected uses.
The remaining paths and their nonzero occurrence coefficients are unchanged.
Thus original ancestry survives, while all original lows, contexts and retained-product incidences remain fixed.

When every displayed \(\beta_j\) vanishes, each nonraw operand is literally old homogeneous linear, each high is an original private-product output, and all original ancestry and occurrence data are intact.
These are exactly the asserted hypotheses for the literal old/raw proposition.
No conclusion about unclassified nonzero-\(\beta_j\) configurations is used.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Every private product is necessary on a matching restriction]
\label{prop:matchingprivateessential}
Let a positive variable-input circuit have minimum output degree two
and nonzero squarefree quadratic part $P_2$. Fix its original
minimum-degree extraction and pruning, and suppose exactly three
original deleted gates are products. Let $S$ be six input variables
such that $P_2|_S=0$ and the Boolean output restricted to $S$ is
exactly a three-edge matching. Retained and deleted addition counts
are unrestricted.

For any one original deleted product $v$, replace its output by formal
zero at every original use, propagate zeros, bypass sums with a zero
input, and prune. The entire original extracted quadratic frame and
its selected polynomials remain unchanged, and at most two deleted
products remain. At least one of the three matching edges loses its
two-endpoint output witness. In particular the original $v$ was true
on that edge assignment. This holds separately for every such $S$;
it does not assign distinct lost edges to different products or assert
that a product is first true on an edge.

Consequently, on an induced $H$-empty four-missing target
$xy,xz,ab,cd$, each of exactly three original private products is true
on at least one of $ab,cd$, or on both $xy,xz$. More precisely, zeroing
it loses an edge in each of the matching restrictions
$\{xy,ab,cd\}$ and $\{xz,ab,cd\}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $Q$ for the polynomial after the stipulated intervention at $v$.
No selected computation reaching the original quadratic output contains
an occurrence of $v$; otherwise that original multiplication node
would belong to the extracted and pruned frame. Every retained node
has a nonzero selected polynomial and a selected route to that output.
Its selected polynomial is therefore independent of $v$ and remains
unchanged when $v$ is set to zero at all its occurrences.

Equivalently, induct through the original selected frame. Both selected
operands of a retained product or retained equal-degree addition stay
nonzero and unchanged. At an unequal-degree cut on a selected path,
the selected low part keeps its original degree and polynomial; the
high part can only keep its degree, increase it, or disappear. It
cannot become selected in place of that low part. Every retained
output route stays nonzero. Thus no retained gate is removed or
becomes private, and no higher branch becomes newly selected.
The entire original frame and the full $P_2$, including coefficients,
survive. At least $v$ disappears, no multiplication is added, and
at most two deleted products remain. The surviving $P_2\ne0$ permits
all formal-zero branches to be propagated and pruned without a
constant input in the final variable-input circuit.

Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductnormal} applies to this modified circuit:
it has minimum output degree two, the same squarefree quadratic part,
and at most two deleted products. The lemma has no graph hypothesis
and allows arbitrary deleted additions. Its whole-carrier reduction
preserves the frame and Boolean output and gives
\[
 P_2+gL+fM+\alpha g^2+\beta gf+\gamma f^2
\]
with exactly its stated linear boundaries, affine contexts and
permitted two-product forms. After restriction to $S$, the quadratic
part vanishes and Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching} forbids the
remaining template from computing the three-edge matching. This is
a local application: the global Boolean function of $Q$ need not be
an edge function, and no graph is invented from its remaining pair
witnesses.

The intervention only deletes positive monomial contributions, so
$Q\le P$ coefficientwise and in Boolean support. In particular
$Q|_S$ is still false on every matching-independent assignment.
If all three two-endpoint witnesses survived, monotonicity would
make it true on every input containing a matching edge. It would
then be exactly the matching function, contradicting the preceding
paragraph. Some matching edge therefore loses its witness. If $v$
were already false on that assignment, replacing it by zero at all
uses would change no later value in the acyclic circuit. Hence the
original $v$ was true there. Original fanout and repeated occurrences
have been treated simultaneously, without merging distinct nodes.

Apply the result separately to the six-variable sets
$\{x,y,a,b,c,d\}$ and $\{x,z,a,b,c,d\}$ of the stated path target.
They induce respectively the matchings $xy,ab,cd$ and $xz,ab,cd$,
and their quadratic restrictions vanish. If a private product is
false on both isolated-edge assignments, those witnesses cannot
change when it is zeroed. The lost witnesses must therefore be
$xy$ and $xz$, respectively, so the product was true on both.
This proves the consequence and the more precise two-restriction
assertion, without a distinct-edge or first-true conclusion.
\end{proof}



\subsubsection{Further two-insertion preparations}
\begin{proposition}[A three-clause first high with one old factor]\label{prop:threeclauseoldfactor}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, and let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$ with nonempty quadratic support $H$ and exactly four global missing edges inducing $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ on their endpoint set $T$, with $H[T]=\varnothing$. Keep an exact original two-visible-occurrence frame
\[
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf,\qquad
 g=ZD_1D_2,\qquad f=(A\vee\epsilon g)(B\vee\delta g),
\]
where $q,\epsilon,\delta\in\{0,1\}$ and $\epsilon+\delta\ge1$. The forms $Z,A,B$ are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms; $D_1,D_2$ are arbitrary linear Boolean clauses, with constants $0,1$ permitted. The contexts $L,M$ are actual compatible old linear, scalar or zero contexts. Each affected base contains the full nonzero old first low $a_0$, the product $a_0L$ is supported on $H$, and $q=1$ entails the actual inclusion $a_0\subseteq M$. Retain all original degree, occurrence, fanout and product-incidence identities; the displayed factorization does not reassign arithmetic degrees. If the safe contribution supplies all four missing witnesses, then
\[
 \operatorname{vc}(G)\le K+2,
\]
where $K$ is the original retained multiplication count.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write the targets as $xy,xz,rs,tu$. They require eight positive linear clauses, as does an induced three-edge matching. A path together with one isolated edge requires the four clauses
\[
 \{x,r\},\quad\{x,s\},\quad\{y,z,r\},\quad\{y,z,s\}.
\]
An old form cannot contain both path leaves $y,z$, since its old neighborhood center would complete a four-cycle through $x$.

Put $P=gL$. It has at most four clauses, so its target witnesses have a cover of size at most two: it cannot witness all four targets or three disjoint ones, and the only possible three-edge shape is a path plus one isolated edge. We need two full-support equality consequences. If $P$ witnesses that three-edge shape, its four restricted clauses are exactly the four displayed minimal covers. The old clauses $Z,L$ are the two small covers, so $L$ restricts to a two-point cover. If $P$ witnesses a two-edge matching, four-clause equality likewise makes the old clauses $Z,L$ two-point transversals of that matching. These statements also force $L$ to be genuinely linear.

In both cases the old clauses have exactly these \emph{full} supports. To see this, take an old uniquely rejecting clause with two-point cover $B$, and let $I$ be the complementary maximal independent set. Each vertex of $I$ has a missing neighbor in $B$. An additional clause variable $w$ outside the restricted endpoints cannot be adjacent to any vertex of $I$: its old center, the corresponding vertex of $B$, and their missing edge would form a four-cycle. The other three clauses all meet $I$, so selecting $w$ and values in $I$ would give an unsafe monomial. Thus no such $w$ exists. Center coincidences would either create a loop or make the relevant missing edge old. This proves the full-support assertions, including all outside variables.

We first show that $P$ must have a target witness. With both bases affected, $f=AB\vee g$. If $q=0$ and $P$ has none, $fM$ alone would supply all four targets but has at most seven clauses. If $q=1$, the output outside $P$ reduces to $ABM\vee g$; the old cubic or scalar-shortened product has at most one target, and the three-clause $g$ at most two. With just one base affected, rename so that $f=A(B\vee g)$. For $q=0$, the remaining $fM$ has at most five clauses; for $q=1$, absorption gives $A(BM\vee g)$, with at most seven. These also cannot supply all four. Hence $P$ has a witness. The old relation $a_0L\subseteq H$ excludes a positive scalar $L$, so $L$ is nonzero linear and meets $T$. It then forces $a_0\cap T=\varnothing$, since otherwise that old relation would give an edge or square inside the $H$-empty set $T$.

Suppose both bases are affected. For $q=1$, the output is $ABM\vee g$, already excluded. For $q=0$, it is
\[
 Q\vee g(L\vee M),\qquad Q=ABM.
\]
The second term has at most four clauses, so $Q$ must have a target. Both $A,B$ contain the outside low $a_0$, and therefore neither can be the full singleton endpoint forced by old-cubic rigidity. Thus the full actual $M$ is a singleton target endpoint. A scalar $M$ would leave a safe old quadratic with a missing witness, whose two factors must be endpoint singletons, again impossible here. Mark one original retained product whose entire opposite support lies in $M$. That singleton covers all targets of $fM$ and every old edge of the marked product. Add a cover of at most two vertices for the targets of $P$, and keep one star center for each other original product. This gives $K+2$ vertices.

Now let only $B$ be affected, so $f=A(B\vee g)$ and $a_0\subseteq B$. First take $q=0$. The output is
\[
 P\vee Q\vee gAM,\qquad Q=ABM.
\]
If $Q$ had no target, the remaining function
$g(L\vee AM)=ZD_1D_2(L\vee A)(L\vee M)$
would supply all four with at most five clauses. Thus $Q$ has a target. Its singleton factor cannot be $B$, which contains $a_0$ outside $T$. A scalar $M$ would likewise contradict the old-quadratic equality case. Hence $M$ or $A$ is a full singleton endpoint. A singleton $M$ gives the preceding original-product charge.

If $A=\{v\}$, all targets of $fM$ are incident with $v$. If $P$ witnesses three targets, its full actual $L$ is a two-point cover of that path-plus-edge shape by the equality argument above. Mark through $L$, add $v$, and keep the other $K-1$ centers, again giving $K+2$. Otherwise $P$ has at most two targets. Four witnesses then force the star at $v$ to be the two path arms and $P$ to witness both isolated edges. Matching equality confines the full old factor $Z$ to the isolated quartet. Consequently $g$ has no path witness; the two path arms would both have to come from the single old cubic $Q$, impossible.

Finally take $q=1$. Absorption gives
\[
 Y=P\vee Q\vee gA.
\]
Again $Q$ must have a target, since $g(L\vee A)$ has at most four clauses. Both $B$ and $M$ contain the outside low $a_0$, by the actual mixed identity, so the singleton endpoint factor must be $A=\{v\}$. A positive scalar $M$ is incompatible with that nonzero linear-low inclusion. All targets outside $P$ form a star at $v$. If $P$ has three targets, the full two-point $L$ charge just used gives $K+2$. Otherwise the star must be the path and $P$ the isolated matching. Full confinement of $Z$ then prevents $gA$ from supplying either path arm, leaving the old cubic $Q$ to supply both, impossible.

Zero clauses or contexts remove terms; constants and repeated $D_i$ only shorten the clause bounds or prevent equality. Every charge uses a full actual context and an original retained product. No hidden-placement normalization is inferred from the support factorization.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Two old factors before a linear preparation]\label{cor:threefactorpreparedaffected}
In the same original-frame setting, let all six forms $A,B,U,V,C,D$ be nonzero old homogeneous linear forms, and set
\[
 g=AB(U\vee V),\qquad f=(C\vee\epsilon g)(D\vee\delta g),
 \qquad\epsilon+\delta\ge1.
\]
With the same actual first-low, context and degree hypotheses, a safe contribution supplying all four missing witnesses satisfies $\operatorname{vc}(G)\le K+2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:threeclauseoldfactor} with first old factor $Z=A$ and remaining clauses $D_1=B$, $D_2=U\vee V$, renaming the two affected bases as $C,D$. All original frame data are retained.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[An old-product first high and a later linear sum]\label{prop:oldproductlaterlinearsum}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, and let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$ with nonempty quadratic support $H$ and exactly four global missing edges inducing $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ on their endpoint set $T$, with $H[T]=\varnothing$. Let
\[
 g=Z_1\cdots Z_m,\qquad 1\le m\le3,\qquad
 A=C_1\vee\cdots\vee C_s,\quad s\ge1,
\]
where all $Z_i,C_j$ and $B$ are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms. Suppose the second high has either of the forms
\[
 f=B(A\vee g)\qquad\hbox{or}\qquad f=(A\vee g)(B\vee g).
\]
Keep the exact original two-visible-occurrence contribution
\[
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf,\qquad q\in\{0,1\},
\]
with actual old linear, scalar or zero contexts $L,M$, and all original low/context, degree, occurrence, fanout and product-incidence identities. A safe $Y$ cannot supply all four missing-edge witnesses. This concerns only the displayed bounded template.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write the targets as $xy,xz,rs,tu$. An old form cannot contain both leaves $y,z$, by the four-cycle through its old center and $x$. The full target and an induced three-edge matching require eight positive linear clauses. A two-edge matching requires four. A path together with one isolated edge has the four minimal clauses
\[
 \{x,r\},\quad\{x,s\},\quad\{y,z,r\},\quad\{y,z,s\}.
\]
Any conjunctive representation of that graph needs both distinct leaf-containing clauses: a clause rejecting a maximal independent set must equal its complementary minimal cover. No old clause can supply either one. Thus a product of at most four clauses, at most one of them nonold, has at most two target witnesses. Three disjoint witnesses would require eight clauses, and the other three-edge shape requires the two distinct nonold clauses just described.

If $M$ is linear, put $Q=ABM$. It is a three-clause product and therefore has no two disjoint target witnesses. Its witnesses form a star of size at most two; a double witness is the path pair, and the old factors $B,M$ then both contain $x$. Each target of $Q$ occurs in some globally safe old cubic $C_jBM$. If $M=1$, the safe rectangle $AB$ is a star by four-cycle-freeness, again with at most two target witnesses; a double witness forces $x\in B$. Positive scalars are interpreted as $1$ only for these support identities.

If $M=0$, the contribution is $g(L\vee qB)$ in the singly affected case and $g(L\vee q)$ in the doubly affected case. It has at most four clauses and cannot supply all four targets. If $L=1$, the safe old product $g$ absorbs its other multiples and has at most one target; $Q$ has at most two. This is also impossible. We may therefore take $L$ zero or old linear and treat $M$ linear or $1$.

First let $f=B(A\vee g)$ and let $M$ be old linear. Boolean absorption gives
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 q=0:&Y=Q\vee R,\quad R=g(L\vee BM)
       =g(L\vee B)(L\vee M),\\
 q=1:&Y=Q\vee R,\quad R=g(L\vee B).
\end{array}
\]
The term $R$ has at most five or four clauses, respectively. If $Q$ has no target, $R$ would supply the eight-clause full target. If $Q$ has only one path arm, $R$ must supply an induced three-edge matching, also impossible.

If $Q$ supplies both path arms, then $B,M$ are true at $x$, and $g$ must be true on both isolated-edge assignments. For $q=0$, the positive term $gBM$ is safe; for $q=1$, the positive term $gB$ is safe. Adjoining $x$ to any independent assignment on $\{r,s,t,u\}$ therefore shows that $g$ must be false on that assignment. Its restriction would compute the two-edge matching with at most three clauses, contrary to the required four.

The remaining allocation is one isolated $Q$-witness, say $tu$. On the other five vertices, $R$ must compute the path plus $rs$. Each old $Z_i$ contains $x$, since it meets both path arms but cannot contain both leaves. For $q=1$, only the single clause $L\vee B$ could supply a leaf-containing minimal cover, whereas two are needed. For $q=0$, both such clauses must be $L\vee B$ and $L\vee M$. Neither $B$ nor $M$ can be a full singleton endpoint of $tu$: that factor would vanish on the five-vertex restriction, leaving old $L$ as one of the required leaf-containing clauses. Choose an old cubic $C_jBM$ witnessing $tu$. Old-cubic rigidity now forces $C_j$ to be a full singleton endpoint, say $t$, with $u\in B\cap M$. Since $g$ is true at $x$, the positive term $gBM$ is true on the independent pair $\{x,u\}$, a contradiction.

If $M=1$ in the singly affected case, both cross choices reduce to
\[
 Y=AB\vee g(L\vee B).
\]
The safe rectangle $AB$ has at most two targets. No target or only one path arm leaves an eight-clause restriction for the term with at most four clauses. One isolated target leaves a path plus one isolated edge, whose two leaf-containing minimal clauses cannot be supplied by the single nonold clause $L\vee B$. If $AB$ supplies both path arms, $B$ contains $x$, and safety of $gB$ forces $g$ to compute the isolated matching by the same independent-assignment argument. This is impossible with at most three clauses.

Now let both factors be affected. Then $f=AB\vee g$ and $gf=g$. If $M=1$ or $q=1$, the output reduces to $ABM\vee g$. The safe old product $g$ has at most one target, and the other term at most two, so four are impossible. Otherwise $M$ is old linear and
\[
 Y=Q\vee g(L\vee M).
\]
The second term has at most four clauses with at most one nonold clause, hence at most two targets by the preliminary observation. Four witnesses force $Q$ to supply the path pair and the second term both isolated edges. Then $M$ contains $x$. Safety of the positive term $gM$ again forces the restriction of $g$ to the isolated quartet to compute its two-edge matching, contrary to its three-clause bound.

These cases include all compatible zero and scalar contexts. Repeated factors only reduce the available distinct clauses. All restrictions were taken after global safety was established, and all Boolean identities preserve the original arithmetic degree and occurrence ledger. No more general hidden-addition classification follows.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[A quadratic high with a subproduct context]\label{prop:subproductcontext}
Let \(G\) be finite, simple and \(C_4\)-free, and let \(H\subseteq G\) be the nonempty old quadratic support.
Suppose that the four edges of \(E(G)\setminus E(H)\) induce \(P_3\sqcup2K_2\) on their endpoint set \(T\), with \(H[T]=\varnothing\).
Let \(U,V,F_1,\ldots,F_r\) be full nonzero old homogeneous linear forms, where \(1\le r\le4\), and put
\[
 g=UV,\qquad Q=\prod_{i=1}^{r}F_i.
\]
Let \(F\) be zero or a subproduct of at most three of the \emph{listed factor occurrences} of \(Q\), with the empty subproduct \(1\) permitted.
Let \(L\) be an old homogeneous linear form, zero, or \(1\).
If
\[
 Y=Q\lor g(L\lor F)
\]
is globally safe, it cannot witness all four missing edges.
Repeated listed factors are allowed, but their occurrence membership in \(F\) is retained.
This is a support statement and makes no original gate-count or normalization claim.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Write the missing edges as \(xy,xz,ab,cd\), with path \(y-x-z\).
No old form contains both path leaves \(y,z\): its old neighborhood center together with \(y,x,z\) would give a \(C_4\), while coincidence with \(x\) would make the missing arms old.

Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors} bounds the target witnesses of \(Q\) by two, and by one when \(r\le3\).
A double is an induced matching; it requires \(r=4\) and confines all four full factor supports to the four distinct two-point transversals of that matching.
The same theorem bounds a safe old quadratic or cubic by one missing witness.
A nonzero linear \(Q\) cannot itself be safe, so this degenerate case causes no exception.

If \(L=1\) or \(F=1\), the output contains the safe quadratic \(g\), which absorbs all its multiples.
Together with the at most two witnesses of \(Q\), this gives at most three.
If \(F=0\), the only other term is the safe old cubic \(gL\), or its scalar/zero shortening, again giving at most three.
We may therefore assume \(L\) is zero or old linear and \(F\) is a nonempty product of at most three listed occurrences.

Put \(R=g(L\lor F)\).
Distributing \(L\) over the factors of \(F\) gives a CNF for \(R\) with at most five linear clauses.
The target \(P_3\sqcup2K_2\) and an induced three-edge matching each require eight clauses: their eight maximal independent sets require distinct rejecting clauses.
A two-edge matching requires four.

If \(Q\) has no target witness, \(R\) would supply all four, contradicting the eight-clause bound.
If \(Q\) has just one path-arm witness, \(R\) must supply the other arm and both isolated edges, an induced three-edge matching, with the same contradiction.

Suppose \(Q\) has just one isolated witness, say \(cd\).
Then \(R\) supplies both path arms and \(ab\).
Because \(U,V\) are old, each contains \(x\): otherwise a factor meeting both arms would contain both \(y,z\).
Thus \(g(x)=1\).
Safety of \(gL\) excludes all isolated endpoints \(a,b,c,d\) from \(L\), since \(\{x,v\}\) is independent for each such endpoint \(v\).
The \(R\)-witness \(ab\) therefore implies \(F(ab)=1\).
The \(Q\)-witness \(cd\) implies \(F(cd)=1\), because \(F\) is a listed subproduct of \(Q\).

If \(F\) were true on any independent set \(I\subseteq\{a,b,c,d\}\), the safe summand \(gF\) would be true on the independent set \(I\cup\{x\}\).
Hence \(F\) is safe on those four vertices and true on both matching edges.
It computes the two-edge matching with at most three clauses, although four are necessary.
This excludes the single-isolated-witness case.

Finally suppose \(Q\) has two target witnesses.
Their full four-factor confinement also confines every factor occurrence of the nonempty subproduct \(F\).
If the witnesses are \(ab,cd\), then \(F\) vanishes on the path vertices.
Both path witnesses would have to come from the one safe old cubic \(gL\), impossible.

The remaining possibility is a path arm and an isolated edge, say \(xy,ab\).
The other two edges \(xz,cd\) induce a matching on
\[
 W=\{x,z,c,d\}.
\]
Every factor of \(F\) restricts on \(W\) to zero or the singleton \(x\), so \(F|_W\) does as well.
The full quartic \(Q\) vanishes on this restriction.
Consequently \(R|_W\) must compute that two-edge matching, but
\[
 R|_W=UV(L\lor F)|_W
\]
has at most three linear clauses.
This is the final contradiction.

All cases preserve the full old supports and the listed occurrence-subproduct relation.
No original arithmetic degree is changed by the Boolean identities.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A hidden join of two old quadratics]\label{cor:hiddenquadraticjoin}
Under the graph and old-support hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:subproductcontext}, let \(U,V,A,B,Z\) be nonzero old homogeneous linear forms and put
\[
 g=UV,\qquad h=AB,\qquad f=Z(g\lor h).
\]
Keep an exact original two-visible-cut high frame
\[
 Y=gL\lor fM\lor qgf,\qquad q\in\{0,1\},
\]
with compatible actual old linear or scalar contexts \(L,M\), including zero, and every original low/context identity, product incidence, insertion occurrence, fanout and arithmetic degree retained.
A safe \(Y\) cannot witness all four missing edges.
Only the displayed literal hidden join is asserted; neither its uninserted quadratic nor its hidden sum is identified with an old wire.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
First let \(M\) be nonzero, replacing a positive scalar by \(1\) for support evaluation.
The identity \(gf=gZ\) gives
\[
 Y=Q\lor g(L\lor F),\qquad Q=ABZM,
\]
where
\[
 F=ZM\quad(q=0),\qquad F=Z\quad(q=1).
\]
The latter case absorbs \(gZM\).
For linear \(M\), \(Q\) has four listed old factors and \(F\) uses two or one of those occurrences.
For \(M=1\), omit that factor from the list; the same subproduct relation uses fewer factors.
Proposition~\ref{prop:subproductcontext} applies.

If \(M=0\), the output is \(gL\) for \(q=0\), or \(g(L\lor Z)\) for \(q=1\).
It has at most three linear clauses and cannot compute the eight-clause target.
All calculations retain the original frame and degree labels.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A raw quadratic in a hidden preparation]\label{cor:rawquadraticpreparation}
Let \(H\) be a nonempty subgraph of a finite simple \(C_4\)-free graph \(G\).
Suppose that the four global edges outside \(H\) induce \(P_3\sqcup2K_2\) on their endpoints \(T\), with \(H[T]=\varnothing\).
Let \(U,V,A,B,C\) be nonzero old homogeneous linear forms, and let \(L,M\) be old homogeneous linear forms, zero, or \(1\).
Put
\[
 g=UV,\qquad f=AB(C\lor g),\qquad
 Y=gL\lor fM\lor qgf,\quad q\in\{0,1\}.
\]
If \(Y\) is globally safe, it cannot witness all four missing edges.
Repetitions are permitted.
In an original two-visible-frame application, \(C\lor g\) is the displayed hidden addition using raw \(g\), rather than an affected retained boundary; no classification of other hidden placements follows.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For nonzero \(M\), use \(gf=ABg\) to obtain
\[
 Y=Q\lor g(L\lor F),\qquad Q=ABCM,
\]
with
\[
 F=ABM\quad(q=0),\qquad F=AB\quad(q=1).
\]
These are subproducts of at most three listed old-factor occurrences of \(Q\).
When \(M=1\), omit its factor occurrence, giving the corresponding shorter lists.
Proposition~\ref{prop:subproductcontext} applies.

If \(M=0\), the output is \(gL\) for \(q=0\), and
\[
 g(L\lor AB)=UV(L\lor A)(L\lor B)
\]
for \(q=1\).
These have at most three or four clauses, respectively, below the target's eight.
No arithmetic degree or original gate count is inferred from these support identities.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[An unaffected linear preparation in the later high]\label{prop:unaffectedlaterpreparation}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, and let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$ with nonempty quadratic support $H$. Suppose that the four global missing edges induce $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ on their endpoint set $T$, with $H[T]=\varnothing$. Keep the original quadratic frame with $K$ retained products and the exact two-visible-occurrence contribution
\[
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf,\qquad
 g=Z_1\cdots Z_m,\quad 1\le m\le3,\qquad
 f=S(B\vee g).
\]
The $Z_i,B$ are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms, and $S$ is a nonzero linear union of old homogeneous linear forms, unaffected by the first insertion. The contexts $L,M$ are actual compatible old linear, scalar or zero contexts, and $q\in\{0,1\}$. The affected boundary $B\vee g$ and every original low/context, degree, fanout and product-incidence identity are retained. If this safe contribution witnesses all four missing edges, then $\vc(G)\le K+2$. No extra raw private boundary or normalization of other hidden placements is asserted.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write the targets as $xa,xb,cd,uv$. No old form contains both path leaves $a,b$, by the four-cycle through its old center and $x$. A safe product $SBM$, when $M$ is old linear, has at most two target witnesses: three clauses cannot witness two disjoint missing edges, and hence a double must be the path pair. Such a double forces both old forms $B,M$ to contain $x$. For $M=1$, the safe rectangle $SB$ is a star by four-cycle-freeness, with at most two targets; a double again forces $x\in B$.

The full target and an induced three-edge matching require eight positive CNF clauses. A path plus one isolated edge requires the four distinct clauses
\[
 \{x,c\},\quad\{x,d\},\quad\{a,b,c\},\quad\{a,b,d\}.
\]
In particular, any CNF computing that graph must contain two distinct leaf-containing minimal-cover clauses. An old clause cannot supply either. These assertions follow by injecting maximal independent sets into their distinct rejecting clauses, as in the preceding proofs.

For nonzero linear $M$, put $Q=SBM$. Since $gf=gS$,
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 q=0:&Y=Q\vee R,\quad R=g(L\vee SM)=g(L\vee S)(L\vee M),\\
 q=1:&Y=Q\vee R,\quad R=g(L\vee S).
\end{array}
\]
The remainder has at most five or four clauses, respectively. For $M=1$, both cross choices reduce to $Y=SB\vee g(L\vee S)$. For $M=0$, there are at most four clauses in $g(L\vee qS)$, which cannot supply the target. If $L=1$, the safe old product $g$ absorbs its multiples and has at most one missing witness, while $Q$ has at most two. Thus $L$ is zero or old linear.

For linear $M$, if $Q$ has no witness, the remainder must supply the eight-clause full target. If its only witness is a path arm, the remainder must supply an induced three-edge matching. Both are impossible. If $Q$ has only one isolated witness, say $uv$, restrict to the other five target vertices. Every old $Z_i$ contains $x$, because it meets both path arms but cannot contain both leaves. Hence $g(x)=1$.

When $q=1$, the only potentially nonold clause $L\vee S$ cannot supply the two distinct leaf-containing minimal covers. When $q=0$, those covers must be exactly $L\vee S$ and $L\vee M$. After exchanging $c,d$, their restricted supports are $\{a,b,c\}$ and $\{a,b,d\}$. Their intersection puts $L$ inside $\{a,b\}$, so $c\in S$ and $d\in M$. The $uv$ witness of $Q$ also gives an endpoint $t\in\{u,v\}$ in $M$. The positive summand $gSM$ is true on the independent triple $\{x,c,t\}$, a contradiction.

For $M=1$, the same eight-clause counts exclude zero witnesses or one path-arm witness of $Q=SB$. One isolated witness would leave a path plus an edge for $g(L\vee S)$, with only one potentially nonold clause. Thus in every surviving case $Q$ must witness both path arms.

In that case its old prefactor, $BM$ or $B$, is true at $x$. Safety of $Q$ therefore excludes all isolated endpoints $c,d,u,v$ from $S$. Restricting to those four endpoints leaves precisely $gL$ to witness their matching. This globally safe old product has at most $m+1\le4$ clauses; four are necessary. Consequently $m=3$ and $L$ is nonzero linear, and full quartic equality in Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors} confines the entire actual context $L$ to a two-point transversal of $cd,uv$.

Adjoin $x$ to that full context to obtain a three-vertex cover of all global missing edges. Mark an original retained product whose entire opposite old support is contained in $L$; the full actual context ensures such a product. The three vertices cover that product as well. Keep one center for each other original retained product. This covers $G$ with at most $(K-1)+3=K+2$ vertices. All context containments are global, and repetitions or scalar simplifications have not changed an original degree or gate count.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[A hidden quadratic join as the first high]\label{prop:quadraticjoinfirsthigh}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, and let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$ with nonempty quadratic support $H$. Suppose that its four global missing edges induce $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ on their endpoint set $T$, with $H[T]=\varnothing$. Keep the original quadratic frame and its $K$ retained products. Suppose that the exact original two-visible contribution is
\[
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf,\qquad
 g=UV\vee WX,\qquad
 f=(A\vee\epsilon g)(B\vee\delta g),
\]
where $U,V,W,X,A,B$ are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms, $q,\epsilon,\delta\in\{0,1\}$ and $\epsilon+\delta\ge1$. The actual contexts $L,M$ are compatible old linear, scalar or zero contexts. Every affected base contains the same nonzero original old first low $a_0$, with $a_0L$ supported on $H$; in particular $q=1$ implies $a_0\subseteq M$. Retain all original degrees, occurrences, fanout and product-incidence identities. If the safe contribution witnesses all four missing edges, then $\vc(G)\le K+2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write the targets as $xa,xb,cd,uv$. The first high $g=UV\vee WX$ has at most four positive linear CNF clauses. With one factor affected, rename so that $A$ is affected. Then $f=AB\vee gB$ and $gf=gB$. For linear $M$, put $Q=ABM$; the contribution is
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 q=0:&Q\vee g(L\vee BM),\\
 q=1:&Q\vee g(L\vee B).
\end{array}
\]
The second summand has at most six or five clauses. With both factors affected, $f=AB\vee g$ and $gf=g$, so the expression is $Q\vee g(L\vee M\vee q)$, with at most five clauses in the second term. Every positive summand is globally safe. For any old linear $R$, the term $gR=UVR\vee WXR$ is a union of two safe old cubics and has at most two target witnesses.

If $M=0$, at most five clauses suffice for the entire contribution, below the target's eight. If $L=1$, the safe $g$ absorbs its other multiples; its two safe old quadratics have at most two missing witnesses in total, and $Q$ has at most one. Hence scalar $L$ is excluded.

Suppose $M=1$. With both factors affected, $f$ contains $AB$, which accepts any singleton in the nonempty common low $a_0$, contradicting safety. With only $A$ affected, both choices of $q$ give
\[
 Y=AB\vee g(L\vee B).
\]
The safe old quadratic $AB$ has at most one target witness. If it has none or only a path-arm witness, the remainder would have to supply the full target or an induced three-edge matching with at most five clauses, although eight are required. Thus $AB$ witnesses an isolated edge, say $uv$. At least one of its full factors is a singleton endpoint. If $A=\{u\}$, then $a_0=\{u\}$ and the old relation $a_0L\subseteq H$ implies $L\cap T=\varnothing$. On the other five target vertices only $gB$ remains, a union of two old cubics unable to supply three targets. If $B=\{u\}$, that factor vanishes on the same restriction, leaving $gL$ and the same contradiction. This treats scalar $M$.

Now let $M$ be old linear. The safe old cubic $Q=ABM$ has at most one missing witness. Its absence would leave the full eight-clause target to at most six clauses; a path-arm witness would leave an eight-clause induced matching. Therefore $Q$ witnesses one isolated edge, say $uv$.

If the entire actual context $M$ is a singleton endpoint $t$ of that edge, mark an original retained product whose full opposite support lies in $M$. The three vertices $\{x,c,t\}$ cover all global missing edges and that marked product. Keep a center for every other original product, giving at most $K-1+3=K+2$ vertices.

Otherwise old-cubic singleton rigidity makes $A$ or $B$ a full singleton endpoint, say $u$. With both factors affected, $q=1$ is impossible because $a_0\subseteq A\cap B\cap M$ makes $ABM$ accept a singleton. For $q=0$, exchange $A,B$ so that $A=\{u\}$. Then $a_0=\{u\}$ and $L\cap T=\varnothing$. On the other five target vertices the contribution reduces to $gM$, which has at most two old-cubic witnesses rather than the required three.

With only $A$ affected, if $A=\{u\}$ then again $a_0=\{u\}$ and $L\cap T=\varnothing$. For $q=0$, the remaining function on those five vertices is $gBM$. Both old forms $B,M$ must meet the two path arms; neither contains both leaves, so each contains $x$. The safe term $ABM$ then accepts the independent pair $\{u,x\}$. For $q=1$, the remaining function is $gB$, so $x\in B$, while the actual cross identity puts $u\in M$. The same unsafe pair results. If instead $B=\{u\}$, the restriction leaves only $gL$ for either cross coefficient, again at most two old-cubic witnesses.

Every noncharged alternative is impossible. The surviving singleton-context charge proves the bound for arbitrary $K$. The proof retains all ambient old supports and original identities; it does not classify an unaffected last product or other hidden placements.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[An independent quadratic inside a later preparation]\label{prop:independentquadraticpreparation}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, and let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$ with nonempty quadratic support $H$ and exactly four global missing edges inducing $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ on their endpoints $T$, where $H[T]=\varnothing$. Keep an exact original two-visible-occurrence frame with arbitrary retained multiplication count $K$, actual old linear, scalar or zero contexts $L,M$, and every original degree, fanout, low/context and product-incidence identity. For nonzero old homogeneous linear forms $U,V,A,B,C,Z$, put
\[
 g=UV,\qquad h=AB,\qquad f=Z(C\vee h),\qquad
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf,\quad q\in\{0,1\}.
\]
If $Y$ is safe and supplies all four missing witnesses, then $\operatorname{vc}(G)\le K+2$. This is only the displayed independent-quadratic preparation; it does not normalize other hidden inputs or raw fanout.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write the targets as $xy,xz,rs,tu$ and put $P=gL$. A safe old cubic or scalar-shortened old product supplies at most one target. The full target and an induced three-edge matching need eight positive linear clauses; a path plus one isolated edge needs four.

We first give the full-context charge used here and in the following proposition. Suppose the safe function
\[
 F_0=ZM(C\vee AB)=ZM(C\vee A)(C\vee B)
\]
witnesses $xy,xz,rs$. Its restriction to those five endpoints computes precisely that three-edge graph. Four-clause equality forces its restricted clauses to be
\[
 \{x,r\},\quad\{x,s\},\quad\{y,z,r\},\quad\{y,z,s\}.
\]
A scalar $M$ leaves only three clauses, so $M$ is genuinely linear. The old forms $Z,M$ cannot contain both path leaves and are therefore the two small covers. Their full supports are these two-point sets. For example, if $M$ restricts to $\{x,r\}$ and contains an additional variable $w$, all other clauses meet the rejected independent set $\{y,z,s\}$. Safety forces $w$ adjacent to one of those three vertices. With the old center of $M$, the corresponding missing edge $xy$, $xz$ or $rs$ produces a four-cycle. Center coincidences either create a loop or make that missing edge old. Thus no outside variable is possible. The same argument applies to the other small cover.

The full actual $M$, plus one endpoint of $tu$, is a three-point cover of all missing edges. Mark an original retained multiplication whose full opposite old operand lies in $M$. Its old edges are covered, and one star center for each of the other $K-1$ original products covers the rest of $H$. This gives $K+2$ vertices. A second useful charge is immediate: if the full actual $L$ is one endpoint of an isolated missing edge, mark through $L$, add the path center and an endpoint of the other isolated edge, and keep the other $K-1$ centers.

For $q=0$, the output is $P\vee F_0$. Since $P$ has at most one target, $F_0$ supplies at least three. Its four clauses cannot supply all four targets or three disjoint edges, so it supplies exactly the path and one isolated edge. The full-context charge above proves the bound.

For $q=1$, write
\[
 Y=P\vee F,\qquad
 F=f(M\vee g)=Z(C\vee A)(C\vee B)(M\vee U)(M\vee V).
\]
The five-clause function $F$ cannot supply all four targets or three disjoint ones. Hence it supplies the path and one isolated edge, while $P$ supplies the other isolated edge, say $tu$. If the full actual $L$ is a singleton endpoint of $tu$, use the second charge. Otherwise the missing-cubic singleton rule for $UVL$ forces $U$ or $V$ to be a full singleton endpoint of $tu$. If $L=1$, the old two-factor equality case gives the same conclusion; $L=0$ cannot witness $tu$. Every witness of $gf$ then contains a $tu$ endpoint, so none of the other three required witnesses comes from $gf$. They already occur in $fM=F_0$. The first full-context charge applies.

Zero and scalar contexts either shorten the clause counts or fall in the explicitly treated singleton charge. Every removed old star is covered through its full actual context. No original gate or degree is inferred from a Boolean simplification.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A quadratic lower part together with the first high]\label{prop:quadraticlowerpartfirsthigh}
Under the same graph and exact original-frame hypotheses, let the nonzero old homogeneous linear forms $U,V,A,B,C,Z$ define
\[
 g=UV,\qquad f=Z(C\vee AB\vee g),\qquad
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf,\quad q\in\{0,1\}.
\]
A safe $Y$ supplying all four missing witnesses satisfies $\operatorname{vc}(G)\le K+2$. The displayed $AB$ may be a lower-support part rather than an original multiplication node; no gate or arithmetic degree is inferred from it.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Keep the notation $P=gL$ and $F_0=ZM(C\vee AB)$ from the preceding proof. The two full-context cover charges established there apply unchanged: three witnesses of $F_0$ give a full two-point actual $M$, and a full singleton actual $L$ at an isolated edge gives a three-point missing-edge cover.

If $q=0$, then
\[
 Y=P\vee F,\qquad F=ZM(C\vee AB\vee UV).
\]
The inner disjunction has the four clauses $C\vee A\vee U$, $C\vee A\vee V$, $C\vee B\vee U$, $C\vee B\vee V$. Thus $F$ has at most six clauses. Since $P$ has at most one target, $F$ must supply exactly the path and one isolated edge, with $P$ supplying the other isolated edge $tu$. A singleton actual $L$ at that edge gives the stated charge. Otherwise old-cubic rigidity, or the old quadratic equality case when $L=1$, forces a full singleton endpoint factor of $g$. The term $gZM$ then supplies none of the other three edge witnesses, so all three already lie in $F_0$. Its full actual $M$ gives the other charge.

If $q=1$, Boolean absorption gives
\[
 Y=(gL\vee gZ)\vee F_0.
\]
The common-cubic missing-star lemma makes the target witnesses of $gL\vee gZ$ a star with at most two edges. If $L=1$, the safe old quadratic $g$ absorbs $gZ$ and has at most one. Suppose the star has two targets. They are the two path arms; both old factors $U,V$ therefore contain $x$, since neither can contain both leaves. The old cubic $gZ$ must supply one of these arms. Its safety forces every $Z$-variable to be adjacent to $x$, and $Z$ contains the corresponding leaf, say $z$. If it contained another variable $w$, its old center and the missing edge $xz$ would give a four-cycle through $x,w$. Hence the full $Z$ is $\{z\}$. But every $F_0$ witness contains $z$, so neither isolated edge can be supplied, a contradiction.

The common part therefore has at most one target. The four-clause $F_0$ must supply the other three, which are the path and an isolated edge, since an induced three-edge matching needs eight clauses. Its full-context charge gives $K+2$. Zero terms and scalar contexts are included in the same bounds. The argument retains every actual context and all original frame data; it does not assert an additional hidden-placement classification.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[A raw shared ancestor after an unequal preparation]\label{prop:rawancestorunequalpreparation}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, and let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$ with nonempty quadratic support $H$ and exactly four global missing edges inducing $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ on their endpoints $T$, with $H[T]=\varnothing$. Keep the exact original two-visible-occurrence frame with arbitrary retained multiplication count $K$, actual old linear, scalar or zero contexts $L,M$, and all original degree, fanout, low/context and product-incidence data. For nonzero old homogeneous linear forms $U,V,Z,C,A$, put
\[
 u=UV,\qquad g=Z(C\vee u),\qquad
 f=u(A\vee\epsilon g),\qquad
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf,
 \quad \epsilon,q\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Here $u$ is the original shared raw quadratic ancestor; when $\epsilon=1$, the affected boundary retains its actual common-low identity. A safe $Y$ supplying all four missing witnesses satisfies $\operatorname{vc}(G)\le K+2$. No complete classification of original hidden placements is asserted.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write the targets as $xy,xz,rs,ab$. Boolean absorption gives $ug=uZ$ and $f=u(A\vee\epsilon Z)$. Hence
\[
 Y=Q\vee F,\qquad Q=ZCL,\qquad F=uD,
\]
where the four possibilities for the bracket $D$ are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
 \epsilon&q&D\\\hline
 0&0&ZL\vee AM\\
 0&1&ZL\vee AM\vee ZA\\
 1&0&ZL\vee AM\vee ZM\\
 1&1&Z\vee AM
\end{array}
\]
and the positive term $uZL$ is present in every case, possibly absorbed. The respective bracket CNFs are
\[
\begin{array}{l}
 (Z\vee A)(Z\vee M)(L\vee A)(L\vee M),\\
 (Z\vee A)(Z\vee M)(L\vee A),\\
 (Z\vee A)(Z\vee M)(L\vee M),\\
 (Z\vee A)(Z\vee M).
\end{array}
\]
Thus $F$ has at most six, five, five or four linear clauses. These are support identities; no displayed clause is a new original gate.

The safe old cubic $Q$, or its scalar-shortened form, has at most one target witness. The full target and any induced three-edge matching require eight positive linear clauses. Therefore four witnesses force $F$ to supply exactly the path and one isolated edge, say $rs$, while $Q$ supplies the other isolated edge $ab$. In particular $L\ne0$.

If the full actual context $L$ is a singleton endpoint of $ab$, mark an original retained multiplication whose entire opposite support lies in that singleton. Keep one old star center for each other original product, and add the path center and one endpoint of $rs$. These $K+2$ vertices cover $H$ and all four missing edges.

Assume $L$ is not such a singleton. If $L$ is old linear, the missing-cubic singleton rule for $ZCL$ forces $Z$ or $C$ to be a full singleton endpoint of $ab$. If $L=1$, the old two-factor equality case makes both $Z,C$ opposite singleton endpoints, so $Z$ is one. Suppose first that $Z$ is a full singleton endpoint of $ab$. On the endpoint set $T_0$ of the other three target edges, all $Z$-bearing terms vanish and
\[
 F|_{T_0}=(UVAM)|_{T_0}.
\]
This is a safe product of at most four old factors and cannot witness both adjacent path arms: every old factor meeting both would contain the path center and give an unsafe singleton. Hence this case is impossible.

The remaining singleton case is $C=\{a\}$, with $L$ genuinely linear and both $Z,L$ nonsingleton. The old-cubic singleton rule gives $b\in Z\cap L$. Consider the positive safe term $uZL$. If $u$ were true on any independent assignment in $T_0$, selecting $b$ from both $Z$ and $L$ would make $uZL$ true on that assignment together with $b$. This set is independent in $G[T]$, since $b$ belongs to the other isolated component. Thus $u|_{T_0}$ is false on every independent set. But $F$ contains $u$ as a factor and witnesses all three edges on $T_0$, so $u$ is true on those edge assignments. Its restriction would compute the path-plus-edge function, which requires four distinct minimal-cover clauses, whereas $u=UV$ has only two. This is impossible.

All noncharged cases have been excluded. Scalar or zero $M$, repeated factors and every $\epsilon,q$ choice are included in the bracket identities. The surviving actual singleton-$L$ charge proves the stated bound with the original $K$; no original arithmetic degree was changed by Boolean idempotence.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[Reassociating a first hidden join with old and raw operands]\label{prop:firstjoinoldraw}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$, where $G$ is finite, simple and four-cycle-free. Its nonempty quadratic support is $H$, and exactly four global missing edges induce $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ on their endpoints $T$, with $H[T]=\varnothing$. Canonical extraction and pruning delete at most three original multiplications and exactly three original additions, precisely two of them visible. Let $K$ be the original retained multiplication count.

Suppose the sole hidden addition is the original node $g=u+v$, where $u,v$ are original private multiplication outputs, possibly the same node or ancestrally related. The node $g$ itself is the high operand of the first chronological visible cut, and the second visible high $f$ is also an original private multiplication output, with repetitions allowed. Every private multiplication operand is a genuinely old homogeneous linear form or a literal raw earlier private multiplication output. In particular, no private product reads raw $g$ or an affected old-plus-high boundary. Keep all original degrees, fanout, occurrences and the complete selected quadratic frame. Then
\[
 \operatorname{vc}(G)\le K+2.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write the first visible cut as $c=a+g$ and let $d$ be the original minimum degree of its selected low $a$. Because that selected occurrence belongs to the quadratic frame, $d\in\{1,2\}$. The cut is strict, so both $u$ and $v$ have original minimum degree greater than $d$. No degree is inferred from their Boolean supports.

The selected low $a$ does not depend on raw $g$. Otherwise a path from $g$ into the selected degree-$d$ carrier would need an earlier unequal-degree addition to lower the degree or to enter that selected carrier. The first such selected entry would be an earlier visible cut. Any unselected intervening addition would be another hidden addition, whereas the only hidden addition is $g$ itself. Both alternatives contradict the original inventory. This also establishes the acyclicity needed below, even if $a$ is ancestral to $u$ or $v$.

We must check all raw uses of the shared sum before reassociating it. The node $g$ cannot feed a private product: it is a sum output, and the literal operand hypothesis excludes both raw sums and affected retained inputs. It cannot feed another hidden sum, since none exists. A new entry into a retained degree-one carrier would require another unequal-degree visible insertion. If $g$ has degree two, entry through a retained equal-degree quadratic addition would retain $g$ and its summands in the quadratic frame, contradicting their private status. If its degree is greater than two, any entry into a retained degree-at-most-two carrier requires another visible cut. The only later visible high is the specified original product $f$, not $g$; its low may depend on $c$ but cannot import raw $g$ separately without another addition. Unused occurrences have already been pruned. Thus $g$ has no useful raw consumer other than $c$.

Replace the two addition operations
\[
 g=u+v,\qquad c=a+g
\]
by the separately defined operations
\[
 c_1=a+u,\qquad c_2=c_1+v,
\]
reusing the two gate slots and redirecting every former use of $c$ to $c_2$. The preceding independence argument makes this acyclic after a topological ordering. Every original private multiplication node and every old/raw operand edge remains unchanged. The fanout argument ensures that no other useful value of $g$ has been lost.

Formal associativity gives $c_2=a+u+v=c$ as a positive polynomial, so the entire output $P$, its quadratic polynomial $P_2$, and its support $H$ are unchanged. Both new additions have actual minimum degree $d$ and strict high operands $u,v$ of larger degree. Canonical extraction therefore selects $a$ through both additions, exactly as it selected $a$ through $c$ while dropping the hidden join. The entire retained quadratic circuit and its original count $K$ remain.
