The original degree ledger is preserved as a record; the new addition degrees are computed from the explicitly new circuit, rather than assigned retrospectively to the old hidden node.

The new circuit has at most three private multiplications and exactly three visible deleted additions, with highs $u,v,f$. Repeated original nodes retain both insertion occurrences and their positive coefficient multiplicities. Every private operand is still old linear or a raw earlier private multiplication output. All actual low/context inclusions, pairwise crosses and repeated-value squares arise from the extraction of this new circuit; they are not chosen independently to fit a support formula. Proposition~\ref{prop:literaloldrawthreevisible} now applies, giving the bound with the same $G,H$ and $K$. Since the graph and retained count are unchanged, this is the conclusion for the original circuit as well.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[An unaffected first join of old quadratics]\label{cor:firstjoinoldquadratics}
Under the same graph and extraction hypotheses, suppose the first hidden high is $g=u+v$ with $u=UV$ and $v=WX$ original old-quadratic private products, the second visible high is an original old-quadratic private product $f=AB$, and every private operand is old homogeneous linear. Then $\operatorname{vc}(G)\le K+2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:firstjoinoldraw}; all its original-operand hypotheses hold with old linear inputs.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[A first hidden join of two original quadratics]\label{prop:firsthiddenquadraticjoin}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$, where $G$ is finite, simple and four-cycle-free. Let its quadratic support $H$ be nonempty, and suppose the four global missing edges induce $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ on their endpoint set $T$, with $H[T]=\varnothing$. Canonical extraction deletes at most three original products and exactly three original additions, exactly two visible. Keep the original retained product count $K$ and the exact selected frame after full-current-carrier erasure and unused off-frame pruning.

Suppose the sole surviving hidden addition is the original node $g=u+v$, with $u=UV$ and $v=WX$ original private products on nonzero old homogeneous linear operands, and $g$ itself is the first chronological visible high. The second high is unrestricted within the original budget. With all original degrees, occurrence labels, fanout and actual context identities retained, one has $\vc(G)\le K+2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write the exact two-visible contribution as $Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf$. We derive the needed input inventory from original nodes. The protected carrier set consists of all original minimum-degree-two nodes with an addition-only path to the output, including full higher-term-bearing carriers and restored degree-two cuts. Full-current-carrier erasure removes their entire nonprotected uses, not merely their ordinary quadratic parts, while preserving every protected addition-only output use. Before the first visible cut, a retained degree-one signal is old homogeneous linear. Between the two cuts its current value is an old form $A$ or an actual $A\vee g$. The first nonzero selected low $a_0$ belongs to every affected $A$, since the same retained addition paths carry it. There is no other hidden addition. Thus a private operand is old linear, an actual affected old boundary, a raw private-product output, or raw $g$. Any further useful private chain needs one of the two specified re-entries into the retained frame. This is an inventory of original signals, not a classification by equal Boolean functions.

A degree-one additive carrier cannot be a strict high, since every low has degree at least one. For completeness, even retaining the additive support alternatives $f=A\vee g$ or $f=A$ in the case analysis creates no omitted branch; here $A$ is the full old linear part. Entire restored degree-two cut carriers, including their higher terms, belong to the carrier erasure when they have addition-only output paths. For linear $M$, the ordinary quadratic term $AM$ belongs to the actual full $P_2$, and therefore to $H$; it vanishes on $T$. A positive scalar $M$ and nonzero $A$ would give a forbidden linear output term. After the old part is accounted for, the restricted contribution is respectively
\[
 g(L\vee M\vee q)\quad\hbox{or}\quad g(L\vee qA).
\]
The join $g=UV\vee WX$ has at most four clauses, and either context adds at most one. Five clauses cannot supply the target, which has eight maximal independent sets. A full retained quadratic carrier is handled by the stipulated erasure, with its selected uses protected. Thus it remains to treat raw private-product highs and raw $g$.

If $u,v$ are the same original product node, replace raw $g=u+u$ by the existing $u$ and remove the hidden addition. The Boolean output is unchanged. Since $u$ is an original private product, its uses have no degree-two path to the full quadratic output; changing its positive coefficient on those paths therefore leaves $P_2,H$ and the selected frame unchanged. The resulting circuit has at most three private products and at most two deleted additions, contrary to Proposition~\ref{prop:threeproductstwosums}. This argument identifies only the same original node, not distinct nodes with equal support values.

For distinct $u,v$, those two nodes consume two products, leaving at most one additional private multiplication. If $f=g$, the contribution is $g(L\vee M\vee q)$ and has at most five clauses. If $f=u$, absorption gives
\[
 Y=u(L\vee M\vee q)\vee vL.
\]
With no scalar term, the first part is a union of old cubics with a common quadratic factor; its missing witnesses form a star of at most two target edges. The other part has at most one. A scalar context or positive $q$ makes the first part the safe old quadratic $u$, with at most one witness, while the second still has at most one. Thus four are impossible. The case $f=v$ is symmetric. These bounds include every zero context.

If the remaining product has an affected old boundary and a raw input, the identities
\[
 u(A\vee g)=u,\qquad v(A\vee g)=v,\qquad
 g(A\vee g)=g
\]
reduce it to a case just treated. If both inputs have old bases and at least one is affected, it has the exact form
\[
 f=(A\vee\epsilon g)(B\vee\delta g),\qquad
 \epsilon+\delta\ge1.
\]
The original boundary trace supplies the common low and the actual cross identities. Proposition~\ref{prop:quadraticjoinfirsthigh} gives $\vc(G)\le K+2$.

If neither input is affected but raw $g$ occurs, the other input is old linear $C$, raw $u$, raw $v$, or raw $g$. For $f=Cg$, the output is
\[
 g[L\vee CM\vee qC].
\]
At $q=0$ it has at most six clauses, from $g(L\vee C)(L\vee M)$; at $q=1$ it has at most five, from $g(L\vee C)$. Neither supplies the eight-clause target. Products $gu,gv,g^2$ have the already treated values $u,v,g$. These are support identities with original degrees and counts held fixed.

Finally, if the remaining product has no affected input and does not read raw $g$, every private operand in the original circuit is old linear or a raw earlier private product. The first hidden join and second original-product high then satisfy Proposition~\ref{prop:firstjoinoldraw}. Its explicit reassociation retains the entire output polynomial and original $K$, and gives the required cover. This includes both-old operands, a raw ancestor times an old form, two independent raw inputs, and repeated raw inputs.

The identical-node reduction and the complete list for the single remaining product exhaust the original budget. No original product is merged merely by Boolean equality, and no higher-product hidden join or different hidden placement has been normalized.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[A hidden linear preparation before the first high]\label{prop:earlierhiddenlinearpreparation}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, and let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$ with nonempty quadratic support $H$. Suppose that its four global missing edges induce $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ on their endpoint set $T$, with $H[T]=\varnothing$. Let $K$ be the number of original retained products. Suppose that canonical extraction and pruning delete at most three products and exactly three additions, exactly two of which are visible.

Apply the full-current-carrier erasure of Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductnormal}, preserving the entire quadratic frame. Suppose that the sole surviving hidden addition is the original node
\[
                         S=U+V,
\]
where $U,V$ are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms, and that this node is an original ancestor of the first chronological visible high $g$. Keep every original degree, occurrence, fanout and actual low/context identity. Then
\[
                         \vc(G)\le K+2.
\]
This conclusion concerns the stated earlier linear preparation; it does not classify a later, nonancestral or nonlinear hidden addition.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use Boolean support notation, and write the exact two-visible contribution as
\[
                 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf,\qquad q\in\{0,1\}.
\]
The contexts are the actual old linear, scalar or zero contexts of the fixed frame. On $T$, its quadratic part vanishes. Safety and the four target witnesses would therefore make $Y|_T$ exactly the edge function of $P_3\sqcup2K_2$. Its eight maximal independent sets require eight distinct positive linear CNF clauses: a clause rejecting two such sets would also reject their union, which contains an edge. We will use the resulting eight-clause lower bound with constants and repetitions allowed.

\emph{The original boundary inventory.}
For precision, the protected set $\mathcal R$ in the carrier erasure consists of all original nodes of minimum degree two having an addition-only path to the output. It includes restored cut outputs on these quadratic paths, not merely retained multiplication nodes. Every off-frame operand occurrence leaving $\mathcal R$ is replaced by zero using its \emph{entire current value}, including all higher-degree insertion terms. The unchanged addition-only output copy absorbs the removed multiples Booleanly. No old quadratic part is subtracted from a carrier to manufacture a new high-only signal.

The complete retained circuit and its polynomial $P_2$ are unchanged. If pruning or a zero high removes a deleted addition, at most three products and two additions remain, contrary to Proposition~\ref{prop:threeproductstwosums}. Thus a circuit supplying all four witnesses retains the two visible cuts and the hidden node under consideration.

A retained degree-one carrier is an addition-only computation. Before the first visible cut it is its old homogeneous linear form. Between the two cuts its full current support is either $A$ or $A\vee g$, with $A$ its nonzero old linear part. In the affected case, the full nonzero first selected low $a_0$ is contained in $A$: the retained addition paths carrying $g$ also carry that low. Consequently the usual actual identities give $a_0L$ supported on $H$, and $q=1$ gives $a_0\subseteq M$. These statements apply whenever an affected degree-one boundary occurs, and do not turn a degree-two low into a linear one.

The hidden node $S$ cannot lie in a selected degree-one computation, since it would then have been retained. Its private appearances are raw references to $S$. There is no further hidden addition. Tracing an original private-product operand to its preceding original node therefore gives an old linear carrier, a raw earlier private product, raw $S$, or, after the first cut, an actual affected carrier $A\vee g$. Full degree-two carriers have already been erased at these uses.

Every surviving private product feeds one of the two visible highs. Otherwise its first re-entry into a nonzero selected carrier would require another visible cut; an additional off-frame sum would require another hidden addition. Remaining unused chains can be pruned. Both nonzero high inputs are original private-product outputs. Indeed, $S$ and retained degree-one carriers have actual minimum degree one and cannot be a strict high above a positive-degree selected low. An earlier visible cut output of minimum degree one has the same obstruction. If that cut output has minimum degree two, its selected route to the output is addition-only, so it and its full additive propagation belong to $\mathcal R$ and their off-frame uses are erased \emph{whole}. The second cut cannot be its own ancestor. This proves the required high and operand inventory directly from the original nodes.

Let $k$ be the number of original private products ancestral to $g$, including its root. Then $1\le k\le3$. Before the first cut their boundaries are old linear forms and the single linear preparation $S$. A connected binary multiplication DAG with $k$ products has at most $k+1$ distinct boundary nodes: with $b$ such nodes, connectivity and the $2k$ operand occurrences give $k+b-1\le2k$. Boolean idempotence removes repeated factors without changing any original node or arithmetic degree. Thus $g$ has at most $k+1$ linear clauses, one of which is $S$.

\emph{Three products before the first high.}
If $k=3$, no private product remains to process a first-cut-affected boundary. Both product highs lie in an unaffected multiplication network over old linear forms and $S$. Proposition~\ref{prop:pathpurelineargeneral} gives $\vc(G)\le K+2$, with original sharing and repeated high values retained.

\emph{Two products before the first high.}
Let $u$ be the unique proper private-product ancestor of $g$. The original relation is a product of $u$ with a linear boundary, or the square $u^2$. At the support level write
\[
                g=uW=S E F,
\]
where $W$ is linear or one after a square absorption, and $E,F$ are old linear clauses or one. The product $u$ itself has at most two linear clauses. These are support representations; an original square retains both its node and its arithmetic degree.

At most one further private product can form $f$. If $f$ is an earlier product or has no affected boundary, Proposition~\ref{prop:pathpurelineargeneral} applies. If its two operands have old bases and at least one is affected, the case where $g$ is Boolean-linear is excluded by Lemma~\ref{lem:linearfirstaffected}, padding the displayed support formula by one if needed. Otherwise $g$ is a product of at most three linear clauses with an old factor, and Proposition~\ref{prop:threeclauseoldfactor} applies. Its common-low and cross hypotheses are exactly those derived above.

It remains to consider one affected input together with a raw input. A raw $g$ factor gives $f=g(A\vee g)=g$, hence
\[
                         Y=g(L\vee M\vee q),
\]
with at most four clauses. A raw $u$ factor gives
\[
                 f=u(A\vee g)=u(A\vee W).
\]
For $q=0$ and $q=1$, respectively, the whole contribution is
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
q=0:&Y=u[WL\vee AM\vee WM]
          =u(W\vee AM)(L\vee M),\\[2pt]
q=1:&Y=u(W\vee AM).
\end{array}
\]
After distributing $W\vee AM$, these have at most five and four clauses. A raw $S$ factor gives $f=S(A\vee g)$, and the corresponding identities are
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
q=0:&Y=S[AM\vee EF(L\vee M)]
          =S(E\vee AM)(F\vee AM)(L\vee M),\\[2pt]
q=1:&Y=S(AM\vee EF).
\end{array}
\]
They have at most six and five clauses. All these bounds include zero/scalar contexts and repeated clauses, and contradict the eight-clause target. The original operand inventory exhausts the raw cases.

\emph{One product before the first high.}
Now $g=SZ$ for an old linear $Z$, or the original first product is $S^2$, with Boolean support $S$. At most two private products remain in the connected ancestry of $f$ outside $g$. They form either one final product, a two-product chain, or a repeated-input square. Accordingly $f$ has a Boolean representation by at most three boundary factors. Each factor is old linear, raw $S$, raw $g$, or an actual affected boundary $A\vee g$. Repeated use of an intermediate product does not increase this boundary count.

If no boundary is affected, use Proposition~\ref{prop:pathpurelineargeneral}. If $g$ is Boolean-linear and at least one boundary is affected, all factors are linear clauses or an affected linear clause; Lemma~\ref{lem:linearfirstaffected} excludes the target, with constant-one padding when fewer than three factors occur.

Suppose therefore that $g=SZ$ and that an affected boundary occurs. First leave aside the case of a raw $g$ factor, treated below. If a raw $S$ factor occurs, write
\[
                    f=S(A\vee\epsilon g)(B\vee\delta g),
\]
where any additional raw $S$ and any absent factor are allowed among the linear clauses or constants $A,B$. Lemma~\ref{lem:rawlinearpreparation} gives at most seven clauses. If no raw $S$ occurs, all bases are old. A two-factor representation is covered by Proposition~\ref{prop:threeclauseoldfactor}. With three factors, at least two affected boundaries are covered by Proposition~\ref{prop:pathmultipleaffected}; exactly one is covered by Proposition~\ref{prop:pathsingleaffectedzero} or Proposition~\ref{prop:pathsingleaffectedpositive}, according as $q=0$ or $q=1$. Every affected occurrence contains the same actual low $a_0$, as required. These applications retain the original factors, repetitions and incidence data.

\emph{The remaining raw-$g$ case.}
The final high $f$ is now a product of at most three boundary factors, including raw $g$ and at least one affected factor $A\vee g$. At each affected \emph{private operand use}, replace that input by a reference to the already computed original $g$. Booleanly the raw $g$ factor makes every replaced factor true whenever $f$ can be true, so the final support of $f$ is unchanged on all inputs.

This is an actual acyclic rewiring, not a relabeling of the original affected computation. The original $g$ precedes its visible cut, whereas every affected boundary follows that cut. If a changed use is in an intermediate product $h$ rather than in $f$, the two-product budget and the inventory show that every surviving use of $h$ leads to $f$, possibly twice. It cannot feed the earlier $g$, and there is no additional hidden sum or visible cut through which it could enter another output computation. Thus preservation of $f$ preserves every output use of the changed intermediate.

Only private operand occurrences are changed; all retained gates and their selected inputs remain intact. Each replaced boundary had minimum degree one, while the new raw $g$ input has degree at least two. Minimum degrees of changed private signals can only increase, so the strict visible-cut inequalities persist. No quadratic output coefficient changes: a changed contribution reaches $f$ along a product path already containing raw $g$, and hence has total degree at least three; an internal quadratic contribution altered before that raw factor reaches the output only in higher degree. The original polynomial $P_2$ and retained count $K$ are therefore unchanged. No gate has been added.

In this explicitly modified circuit both high networks are unaffected multiplication-only networks on old linear forms and the single preparation $S$, with at most three private products. Their Boolean high values and the exact output support are unchanged. Proposition~\ref{prop:pathpurelineargeneral}, applied to this modified circuit with the same $H$ and $K$, gives $\vc(G)\le K+2$ for the starting circuit as well. We do not assert that its off-frame arithmetic degrees stayed numerically equal: the proof uses their controlled increase and the unchanged quadratic frame.

The original ancestor counts $k=1,2,3$, the permitted later multiplication DAGs, all raw boundaries and all affected boundaries have now been exhausted. Each case gives the stated cover bound or contradicts the required eight clauses. This completes the specified original-branch normalization.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[A first hidden join of original private products]\label{prop:firsthiddenproductjoin}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$, where $G$ is finite, simple and four-cycle-free. Suppose the quadratic support $H$ is nonempty and the four global missing edges induce $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ on their endpoint set $T$, with $H[T]=\varnothing$. Canonical extraction deletes at most three original products and exactly three original additions, exactly two visible. Keep the original retained product count $K$ and the exact selected frame after full-current-carrier erasure and unused off-frame pruning.

Suppose the sole surviving hidden addition is the original node $g=u+v$, itself the first chronological visible high, and $u,v$ are original private-product outputs. The two input nodes may coincide or be comparable in the original ancestry, and their degrees need not be two. With every original occurrence, degree, fanout and low/context identity kept, one has $\vc(G)\le K+2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write the exact contribution of the two visible highs as
\[
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf.
\]
All support identities below keep the original arithmetic degrees unless an explicit new circuit is constructed. Before $g$ there is no earlier visible insertion and no other hidden addition. A surviving retained degree-one signal there is therefore an old homogeneous linear form. The protected set $\mathcal R$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductnormal} contains every original minimum-degree-two node with an addition-only path to the output, including full higher-term-bearing carriers and restored degree-two cuts. Erasure removes an entire operand occurrence from $\mathcal R$ to its complement, while its protected addition-only output copy remains. It never subtracts just an old quadratic part.

Consequently the surviving private-product ancestors of $u,v$ have only old homogeneous linear or raw earlier private-product operands. This follows successively along the original topological order: a further private addition is unavailable, a quadratic carrier use has been erased, and a dependence on the later $g$ would be cyclic. Thus their ancestor network is multiplication-only after its old linear boundaries.

First suppose $u=v$ as original nodes. Replace every use of $g=u+u$ by the existing $u$ and remove the hidden addition. The Boolean output and all remaining minimum degrees are unchanged. Since $u$ is private, the changed positive multiplicities occur on no degree-two route to the output; the entire $P_2$, selected frame and $K$ remain fixed. If instead $u$ is a proper original ancestor of $v$, the multiplication-only ancestry gives $P_v=P_u R$ with a positive product $R$. Booleanly $u\vee v=u$, and $\deg_{\min}v\ge3$. Replacing $g$ by $u$ is acyclic, removes only terms of degree at least three and their positive downstream multiples, and preserves the minimum degree of $g$ and every downstream node. It again fixes $P_2$ and the selected frame. The symmetric ancestor case is identical. Each construction has at most three deleted products and at most two deleted additions, contradicting Proposition~\ref{prop:threeproductstwosums}. This identifies equal original nodes or a stated ancestry relation; distinct nodes are not merged merely because their Boolean functions agree.

We may therefore assume that $u,v$ are distinct and incomparable. Let $N$ count the original private-product nodes in the union of their ancestor sets, including $u,v$. Then $N=2$ or $3$. If $N=2$, neither has an earlier private-product operand, so both are original products of old linear forms. Proposition~\ref{prop:firsthiddenquadraticjoin} applies, with the second high unrestricted, and yields the required cover.

Suppose $N=3$. All available private products now precede $g$ and the first visible cut. In particular no private product reads $g$ or a first-cut-affected boundary. If the second high $f$ is an original private-product output, Proposition~\ref{prop:firstjoinoldraw} applies directly: all original private operands are old linear or raw earlier private products, and the hidden join is the first high.

The other possible surviving high is the raw hidden node $g$. Here the original carrier alternatives require care. A first-cut output, or its addition-only propagation, of minimum degree one cannot be a strict later high above a positive-degree low. If its minimum degree is two, its full current value belongs to $\mathcal R$ through its addition-only output route, and its off-frame use has been erased in its entirety. No new residual copy of $g$ is extracted from that carrier. There is no further private sum or product after $g$. Thus a raw $g$ high is the only remaining nonzero possibility; an erased or zero high can be bypassed and pruned, giving the already excluded case with at most two deleted additions. It is harmless also to include any value having the same Boolean support as $g$ in the following support bound.

When $f$ has support $g$, absorption gives
\[
 Y=gD,\qquad D=L\vee M\vee q,
\]
where $D$ is a linear clause, scalar one or zero. We show that $g$ has a conjunctive representation by at most six positive linear clauses.

Let $w$ be the third private-product node, distinct from the incomparable $u,v$. It is ancestral to at least one of them and has old linear operands, since no earlier private product is available. If it is ancestral to only one, say $u$, then $u=wC$ for an old linear form $C$, or $u$ is the original square $w^2$. Its Boolean support is a product of at most three old linear clauses, while $v$ has two. Distributing their disjunction therefore gives at most $3\cdot2=6$ linear clauses. The square is simplified only in this Boolean expression; its original degree and node remain unchanged.

If $w$ is ancestral to both, the original products have the forms $wC$ or $w^2$, and $wE$ or $w^2$. In support notation write $u=wC'$ and $v=wE'$, where a square is represented by the scalar-one padding $C'=1$ or $E'=1$. Then
\[
 g=w(C'\vee E'),
\]
which has at most three linear clauses, including the two old factors of $w$. This introduces no scalar input into the original variable-input circuit. These two cases exhaust the three-node ancestor union.

Hence $gD$ has at most seven clauses. On $T$, the old quadratic frame is zero, while safety and the four missing-edge witnesses force $Y|_T$ to be exactly the edge function of $P_3\sqcup2K_2$. That graph has eight maximal independent sets, so its positive conjunctive representation requires at least eight clauses. The contradiction excludes the last high case. The equal-node, proper-ancestor and two incomparable-ancestor-count cases exhaust the stated hidden-join placement, proving $\vc(G)\le K+2$ with the original $K$.
\end{proof}



% SZ4-192: full mutually compared support-template proof; original occurrences fixed.
\begin{proposition}[A raw middle product with affected final inputs]
\label{prop:rawmiddleaffectedlast}
Let \(G\) be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, and let a positive
variable-input circuit compute \(P\in\Sup(G)\), with nonempty quadratic
support \(H\). Suppose there are exactly four edges outside \(H\), and
their endpoint set \(T\) satisfies \(G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2\) and
\(H[T]=\varnothing\). Keep the original quadratic frame and
its \(K\) retained multiplication nodes. Suppose the three original
private products, each with one visible insertion occurrence, are
\[
 g=UV,\qquad h=gA,\qquad
 f=(B\vee\epsilon g\vee\delta h)
   (C\vee\epsilon' g\vee\delta' h),
\]
where \(U,V,A,B,C\) are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms.
Coefficients record absence or positivity in Boolean support. Retain
the exact contribution
\[
 Y=gL\vee hN\vee fM\vee q_{12}gh\vee q_{13}gf\vee q_{23}hf .
\]
Here \(L,M\) are actual old linear contexts or zero, and \(N\) is an
actual compatible old linear, scalar, or zero context. Every
\(g\)-affected input contains the full nonzero first low \(a\), with
\(aL\) supported on \(H\); every \(h\)-affected degree-one input contains
the full nonzero second low \(b\), with \(bN\) supported on \(H\).
An input containing both highs retains both lows. All original
degrees, occurrences, fanout, cross identities, and retained-product
incidences remain fixed. If \(Y\) is safe and supplies all four missing
edge witnesses, then
\[
                         \vc(G)\le K+2 .
\]
No minimality of the retained frame is required.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Name the missing edges \(xy,xz,rs,tu\), with \(x\) the path center.
All seven endpoint symbols are distinct. We use Boolean identities
without changing any original degree or node. Since \(h=gA\) implies
\(g\), a last input has support type \(O\) (its old base), \(G\)
(its base joined with \(g\)), or \(H\) (its base joined with \(h\)).
Additional absorbed \(h\)-terms retain their original low constraints.
The case \(OO\) is Proposition~\ref{prop:mixedrawthreevisible}. Up to exchanging the last inputs, the affected cases are
\(GO,HO,GG,GH,HH\).

Put \(Q=BCM\) and write \(\lambda,\mu,\nu\) for the positivity indicators of
\(q_{12},q_{13},q_{23}\). Exact expansion gives \(Y=Q\vee gD\), with
\[
\begin{array}{c|l|c}
\text{type}&D&\text{clauses}\\ \hline
GO&L\vee AN\vee CM\vee \lambda A\vee \mu C\vee \nu AC&4\\
HO&L\vee AN\vee ACM\vee \lambda A\vee \mu BC\vee(\mu\vee\nu)AC&3\\
GG&L\vee M\vee A(N\vee\lambda\vee\nu)\vee\mu&2\\
GH&L\vee A(N\vee M\vee\lambda\vee\mu\vee\nu)\vee C(M\vee\mu)&3\\
HH&L\vee A(N\vee M\vee\lambda\vee\mu\vee\nu)\vee\mu BC&2
\end{array}
\]
For completeness, in the first row \(\lambda=1\) or \(\mu=1\) leaves at most
two clauses; otherwise \(AN\vee CM\) needs four, and adding \(AC\)
uses
\[
 AN\vee AC\vee CM=(A\vee C)(A\vee M)(N\vee C).
\]
In the second row \(\lambda=1\) leaves \(L\vee A\vee\mu BC\), with two
clauses. If \(\lambda=0,\mu=1\), the remaining quadratic terms are
\(AN\vee AC\vee BC\), with three clauses by the same identity.
If \(\lambda=\mu=0\), the expression is \(L\vee A(N\vee C(M\vee\nu))\),
again with at most three. In the third row \(\mu=1\) gives the
constant one; otherwise there are at most two clauses.
In the fourth row \(\mu=1\) gives \(L\vee A\vee C\), while
\(\mu=0,\lambda\vee\nu=1\) gives \(L\vee A\vee CM\). With all three
indicators zero, use the three-clause identity for
\(AN\vee AM\vee CM\). In the last row \(\mu=1\) gives
\(L\vee A\vee BC\), and \(\mu=0\) gives
\(L\vee A(N\vee M\vee\lambda\vee\nu)\). Zero and scalar contexts only
simplify these identities. Thus \(gD=UVD\) has at most six
positive linear clauses.

The safe old cubic \(Q\) has at most one missing witness. If it has
none, \(gD\) must compute the edge function of \(P_3\sqcup2K_2\)
after restriction to \(T\); this requires eight clauses, one for
each maximal independent set. If \(Q\)'s witness is a path arm,
restrict to the other arm and the two isolated edges. The induced
three-edge matching likewise requires eight clauses. Hence \(Q\)
witnesses an isolated edge, say \(rs\), and \(gD\) supplies
\(xy,xz,tu\).

Each of \(U,V\) meets both path arms. An old form cannot contain
both leaves \(y,z\): its old neighborhood center and \(x\) would
give a four-cycle, or would make a missing arm old. Consequently
\(x\in\operatorname{supp}U\cap\operatorname{supp}V\).
Both forms also meet \(\{t,u\}\), and hence are nonsingleton.

If the full actual \(M\) is a singleton \(\{m\}\), then \(m\) is
an endpoint of \(rs\). Mark an original retained product whose
full opposite old support is contained in \(M\), using the actual
context incidence. The set consisting of \(m,x\), and one endpoint
of \(tu\) covers that product and all missing edges. One center
for each other retained star product gives \((K-1)+3=K+2\).
We may therefore suppose that \(M\) is not a full singleton.

Fix a monomial of \(BCM\) witnessing \(rs\). The endpoint used
once is supplied by a factor whose full support is that endpoint
singleton, by old-cubic rigidity. This factor cannot be \(M\).
Renaming \(r,s\), we may take the chosen base to be \(\{r\}\);
the other base and \(M\) both contain \(s\). This chosen-witness
argument also covers cases in which both bases are singleton.

In type \(GG\), both bases contain the same nonzero first low;
in type \(HH\), both contain the same nonzero second low.
If one chosen base is \(\{r\}\), the other therefore contains
\(r\). Selecting \(r,r,s\) from the two bases and \(M\) makes
old-cubic rigidity force the full \(M=\{s\}\), a contradiction.

Consider \(GO\) or \(HO\), with affected base \(B\) and
unaffected base \(C\). First suppose \(C=\{r\}\) is the chosen
singleton. On \(T_0=\{x,y,z,t,u\}\), every contribution involving
\(f\) vanishes, leaving
\[
                         gL\vee hN\vee\lambda h .
\]
If \(\lambda=1\), the two safe old cubics \(gL,h\) supply at most two
missing edges. Hence \(\lambda=0\). The three required witnesses force
\(gL\) to supply one path arm, say \(xy\), and the old quartic
\(hN=UVAN\) to supply \(xz,tu\). In particular \(N\) is nonzero
linear. Full quartic equality gives precisely the four full
supports
\[
                \{x,t\},\quad\{x,u\},\quad\{z,t\},\quad\{z,u\}.
\]
Since \(U,V\) contain \(x\), they are the first two supports.
Old-cubic rigidity in \(UVL\) gives the full \(L=\{y\}\);
\(N\) is one of the other two supports.

Mark original retained products reached by the \(g\)- and
\(h\)-occurrences, with full opposite supports contained in
\(L,N\), respectively. The marks are distinct. On the same input
side of one product its nonzero opposite support would lie in
the empty intersection \(L\cap N\); on opposite sides the
expansion would give \(q_{12}>0\), already excluded.
The four-vertex set
\[
          \operatorname{supp}L\ \cup\ \operatorname{supp}N\
          \cup\{r\}
\]
covers both marked products and every missing edge. Centers for
the other \(K-2\) retained products give \(K+2\).

It remains in these two types to consider the chosen singleton
\(B=\{r\}\), so that \(s\in C\cap M\).
For \(GO\), the positive term \(gCM\) has a monomial supported on
the independent pair \(\{x,s\}\), a contradiction.
For \(HO\), the second low is \(\{r\}\). Since \(bN\) is
\(H\)-supported and \(H[T]\) is empty, \(N\) has no target
variable; a positive scalar \(N\) is also impossible.
The remaining terms are among
\[
 Q,\quad gL,\quad hCM,\quad \lambda h,\quad\mu gBC,\quad\mu hC,\quad\nu hC.
\]
None witnesses \(tu\). Terms \(Q,gBC\) contain \(r\). A witness
in \(gL\) or \(h=gA\), combined with \(x\in U\cap V\), would
give an unsafe independent pair. A witness in \(hC\) or \(hCM\)
would give some \(v\in\{t,u\}\cap A\); choosing \(x\) from
\(U,V\), \(v\) from \(A\), and \(s\) from \(C,M\) gives the
independent support \(\{x,v,s\}\). This excludes \(HO\).

Finally consider \(GH\), with \(B\) containing \(g\) and \(C\)
containing \(h\). Booleanly
\[
              f=BC\vee gC\vee h,\qquad gf=gC\vee h,\qquad hf=h .
\]
If the chosen singleton is \(B=\{r\}\), the positive term
\(gCM\) again contradicts safety on \(\{x,s\}\).
If it is \(C=\{r\}\), the second low makes \(N\) target-free,
while \(B,M\) contain \(s\). On \(T_0\) the contribution is
\[
                     gL\vee hM\vee(\lambda\vee\mu\vee\nu)h .
\]
A positive last indicator leaves two old cubics, insufficient
for three targets. Otherwise the required three witnesses force
the quartic \(hM\) to witness a disjoint pair among
\(xy,xz,tu\). Full equality confines \(M\) to that pair's
four endpoints in \(T_0\), contradicting \(s\in M\).

All affected types have been covered. The two actual-context
charges establish the claimed bound in the surviving cases.
The proof preserves repeated forms and coincident Boolean
values as distinct original nodes and occurrences; it asserts
no additional raw-last-input or all-visible normalization.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[A later linear preparation among three affected factors]\label{prop:laterthreefactorpreparation}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, with nonempty quadratic support $H$. Suppose there are exactly four edges outside $H$, whose endpoint set $T$ satisfies $G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$. Keep an exact original two-visible-occurrence frame
\[
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf,\qquad g=UV,\qquad S=C\vee D,
\]
\[
 f=(A\vee\alpha g)(B\vee\beta g)(S\vee\gamma g),
 \qquad q,\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\{0,1\},\quad
 \alpha+\beta+\gamma\ge1,
\]
where $U,V,A,B,C,D$ are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms. The contexts $L,M$ are the actual compatible old linear, scalar or zero contexts. Each affected factor is an actual retained or prepared boundary whose linear base contains the same nonzero old first low $a_0$; in particular $a_0\subseteq S$ when $\gamma=1$. Require the actual identities $a_0L$ supported on $H$ and, when $q=1$, $a_0\subseteq M$. Retain every original degree, occurrence, fanout, low/context and retained-product incidence identity, and let $K$ be the original retained multiplication count. If $Y$ is safe and witnesses all four missing edges, then $\vc(G)\le K+2$.

Only $S$ may be a non-old base. The display is a Boolean support identity, with no reassignment of original degrees or added gates; raw reuse of a preparation or an earlier product and arbitrary hidden placements are not normalized here.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write the missing edges as $xy,xz,ab,cd$, with seven distinct vertices and path center $x$. Put $F_0=ABS$ and $k=\alpha+\beta+\gamma$. Every positive summand below is safe. The unaffected contribution $F_0M$ has at most two missing witnesses. For a nonzero old linear $M$, it is the union
\[
 ABCM\vee ABDM,
\]
so Lemma~\ref{lem:sharedquartics} applies. A nonzero scalar $M$ leaves two old cubics, each with at most one missing witness by Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors}; zero $M$ leaves none. This bound uses full old supports and all global missing witnesses.

Consider the entire contribution apart from $gL$:
\[
 Q=f(M\vee qg),\qquad Y=gL\vee Q.
\]
It has a positive linear conjunctive representation with at most seven clauses. Indeed, each unaffected factor of $f$ contributes one clause, and each affected factor $X\vee UV=(X\vee U)(X\vee V)$ contributes two. This holds also for the single clause $X=S$. Thus $f$ has at most $3+k\le6$ clauses. If $q=0$, multiplying by $M$ adds at most one.

If $q=1$ and $M$ is scalar one, then $Q=f$. If $M=0$, let $R$ be the product of the unaffected bases among $A,B,S$, with empty product one. The support identity $f=F_0\vee gR$ gives $Q=fg=gR$, using at most $2+(3-k)\le4$ clauses. These scalar identities introduce no original constant gate. If instead $q=1$ and $M$ is genuinely linear, the factor $M\vee UV$ contributes two clauses, for a total at most $5+k$. The only possible count eight has $k=3$. Then $A,B,S,M$ all contain $a_0$ by the actual common-low identity. Choosing one vertex of $a_0$ in each factor makes the positive term $F_0M$ true on a singleton, contradicting safety. Hence $k\le2$ in that case. All zero and scalar cases are therefore included in the seven-clause bound.

On an induced vertex set, a safe monotone contribution witnessing every edge is exactly the edge function of the induced graph: it accepts every input containing an edge and no independent input. Both $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $3K_2$ have eight maximal independent sets, so their positive linear conjunctive representations need at least eight clauses.

Consequently $gL$ must have a target witness, or $Q|_T$ would contradict its seven-clause bound. By Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors}, the safe old product $gL$ has at most one missing witness, whether $L$ is linear or a nonzero scalar. Its witness cannot be a path edge. If it were $xy$, then $Q$ would witness the induced matching $xz,ab,cd$ on the other six relevant vertices, again contradicting the seven-clause bound. The case $xz$ is symmetric. Thus the unique target witness of $gL$ is an isolated edge, say $ab$.

We recall why a safe old cubic witnessing a missing edge has a full singleton factor. Every factor meets its two endpoints, while neither endpoint belongs to all three factors. Two factors therefore contain one endpoint, say $a$, and the remaining factor contains $b$ and omits $a$. Every variable $z$ in that remaining factor must be adjacent to $a$, by choosing $a$ from the first two factors. If $z\ne b$, an old center of the remaining factor and the vertices $b,a,z$ form a four-cycle; the center cannot be $a$ because $ab$ is missing. Hence the full remaining factor is $\{b\}$. For an old two-factor product witnessing a missing edge, the equality case of Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors} gives the two full endpoint singletons.

Neither $U$ nor $V$ can be singleton here. Such a singleton would be an endpoint of $ab$, and every $g$-containing term would then have at most the one target witness $ab$. But expanding $f=F_0\vee gR$ gives
\[
 Y=gL\vee F_0M\vee gRM\vee qgF_0\vee qgR.
\]
Every term except $F_0M$ contains $g$, while $F_0M$ has at most two witnesses. Four targets would be impossible. Therefore $L$ cannot be scalar, since that would make the witnessing old product $UV$ have two singleton factors. Applying the cubic singleton argument to $UVL$ now shows that the \emph{full} support of $L$ is one endpoint of $ab$, say $\{a\}$.

The actual nonzero linear context $L$ contains the full opposite support of at least one original retained quadratic multiplication node reached by this insertion. That entire retained star is covered by $a$. Choose a center for each of the other $K-1$ original retained products and add $\{a,x,c\}$. These vertices cover all old edges and all four global missing edges. They give a cover of the full graph of size at most
\[
 (K-1)+3=K+2.
\]
Repeated centers, fanout and outside old vertices do not enlarge this bound. No original node or arithmetic degree was changed by the support calculations, and the argument concerns only the stated exact preparation template.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[Earlier-high reuse after a shared first cut]\label{prop:sharedcutearlierreuse}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, with nonempty old quadratic support $H$. Suppose the four global missing edges have endpoints $T$ such that $G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$. For nonzero old homogeneous linear forms $U,V,A,B,C$, put
\[
 g=UV,\qquad h=(A\vee g)(B\vee g),\qquad
 f=h(C\vee\lambda g\vee\mu h),\qquad \lambda,\mu\ge0.
\]
Keep the exact original three-occurrence contribution
\[
 Y=gL\vee hN\vee fM\vee q_{12}gh\vee q_{13}gf\vee q_{23}hf,
 \qquad q_{ij}\ge0,
\]
with actual compatible old-linear, scalar or zero contexts and every original low/context identity. In particular, the shared first insertion has a nonzero old low $a_0\subseteq A\cap B$, $a_0L$ is old, $q_{12}>0$ implies $a_0\subseteq N$, and $q_{13}>0$ implies $a_0\subseteq M$. If $Y$ is safe, it cannot supply all four target witnesses. This is a statement about the displayed original occurrences and operands, without a classification of other insertion orders.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The calculations are Boolean support identities with the original arithmetic degrees and occurrences fixed. Replace positive coefficients by $1$ only in these identities. Write the targets as $xy,xz,ab,cd$. A safe product of at most three affine linear clauses cannot witness two disjoint targets: on their four endpoints it would compute an induced two-edge matching, which needs four clauses. Its only possible pair of target witnesses is therefore the two path arms. Consequently two such products together have at most three targets. Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors} gives the sharper bound of one missing witness for an all-old product of at most three factors. Its four-factor equality case consists of the four full, distinct transversals of an induced matching pair; any three of these supports have empty intersection.

The relation $a_0L$ old excludes a positive scalar $L$. A positive scalar $N$ would expose $AB$, which accepts a singleton from $a_0$, contrary to safety. Thus $L,N$ are old linear or zero in every safe case, while $M$ retains its compatible scalar possibilities.

If $\mu>0$, absorption gives $f=h=AB\vee g$ and $gh=g$. With
\[
 E=N\vee M\vee q_{23},\qquad
 D=L\vee q_{12}\vee q_{13}\vee E,
\]
the complete contribution is $Y=ABE\vee UVD$. These are two products of at most three affine linear clauses, so they cannot supply four targets. If $\mu=\lambda=0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:sharedcutrawchain} applies with exactly the stated original occurrences; the preceding scalar check verifies its context hypotheses.

It remains to consider $\mu=0$ and $\lambda>0$. Now
\[
 h=AB\vee g,\qquad f=ABC\vee g,\qquad gh=gf=g,\qquad hf=f.
\]
Positive $q_{12}$ is impossible, since $a_0\subseteq A\cap B\cap N$ makes the positive term $ABN$ true on a singleton. If $q_{23}>0$, absorption leaves
\[
 Y=g\vee AB(N\vee C).
\]
The first term has at most one missing witness and the second has at most two targets by the three-clause bound. If $q_{23}=0$ and $q_{13}>0$, the expression instead becomes
\[
 Y=g\vee ABN\vee ABCM.
\]
The first two terms have at most one target each. The last also has at most one: scalar or zero $M$ reduces its factor count, whereas two witnesses with linear $M$ would force full quartic equality, contradicting the nonempty intersection $a_0\subseteq A\cap B\cap M$. This excludes every positive-cross case.

Suppose all three cross coefficients are zero. Then
\[
 Y=g(L\vee N\vee M)\vee ABN\vee ABCM.
\]
If $gL$ has no target, restriction to $T$ gives
\[
 h\,[N\vee(C\vee g)M].
\]
The first factor has the four clauses $A\vee U$, $A\vee V$, $B\vee U$, $B\vee V$. The bracket has the three clauses
\[
 N\vee M,\qquad N\vee C\vee U,\qquad N\vee C\vee V.
\]
Seven clauses cannot compute the target graph, whose eight maximal independent sets require eight distinct rejecting clauses. The calculation includes scalar and zero contexts. Therefore $gL$ has a target. The old relation $a_0L$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$ then force every vertex of $a_0$ outside $T$.

The safe old quartic $ABCM$ has at most one target, since two would confine the full supports of $A,B,C,M$ to a target quartet, contrary to the outside vertex in $a_0\subseteq A\cap B$. The safe term $ABN$ has no target. Indeed, a target $vw$ would make $A,B$ nonsingleton because both contain an outside vertex, so the cubic argument in Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic} makes the full $N$ a singleton, say $\{w\}$, with $v\in A\cap B$. Choose $z\in a_0$ outside $T$. Safety requires $zw\in E(G)$. An old center of $A$, together with $v,w,z$, then forms a four-cycle: it is distinct from $w$ because $vw$ is missing. This is impossible.

Finally the safe common-factor family $gL,gN,gM$ has a missing-edge star by Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic}, hence at most two targets. If $M$ is a positive scalar, $g$ absorbs the other $g$-multiples and has at most one missing witness instead. Along with the at-most-one target of $ABCM$, this gives at most three. All coefficient, scalar and zero cases have been exhausted, with full supports and original incidences retained throughout.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[An affected dependency followed by a raw descendant]
\label{prop:oneaffectedrawdescendant}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute \(P\in\Sup(G)\), where
\(G\) is finite, simple and four-cycle-free, with nonempty quadratic
support \(H\). Suppose the four global missing edges have endpoint set
\(T\), with \(G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2\) and \(H[T]=\varnothing\).
Keep the original quadratic frame and its \(K\) retained products.
Suppose three original private products, each with one visible
insertion occurrence, have the Boolean support forms
\[
 g=UV,\qquad h=(A\vee g)B,\qquad
 f=h(C\vee\lambda g\vee\mu h),
\]
where \(U,V,A,B,C\) are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms and
\(\lambda,\mu\) record absence or positivity. Retain the exact contribution
\[
 Y=gL\vee hN\vee fM
       \vee q_{12}gh\vee q_{13}gf\vee q_{23}hf .
\]
Here \(L,N\) are actual old linear contexts or zero; \(M\) is an
actual compatible old linear, scalar or zero context. The linear
qualification on \(N\) follows from the original minimum degree two
of the strict high \(h\). The first low \(a\) is nonzero
old linear, \(a\subseteq A\), and \(aL\) is supported on \(H\).
Retain all further original low/context restrictions, degrees,
occurrences, fanout and retained-product incidences, including those
required by positive \(\lambda,\mu\).
If \(Y\) is safe and supplies all four missing witnesses, then
\[
                         \vc(G)\le K+2 .
\]
The conclusion requires no optimality of the retained frame and makes
no assertion about other affected placements.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
All calculations are Boolean support identities, with original nodes
and degrees unchanged. Put \(p,q,\rho\) for the positivity indicators
of \(q_{12},q_{13},q_{23}\), and put \(W=M\vee\rho\).
Since \(gh=gB\) and \(hf=f\), write
\[
 Y=gL\vee Q,\qquad Q=hN\vee fW\vee pgB\vee qgf .
\]
We first prove that \(Q\) has at most seven positive linear clauses.
Every old linear form is one clause, and
\[
                    X\vee UV=(X\vee U)(X\vee V)
\]
has two. Scalar or zero contexts specialize these identities and
cannot increase their clause counts.

If \(\mu=1\), then \(f=h\), \(gf=gB\), and
\[
 Q=B\bigl[(A\vee g)(N\vee W)\vee(p\vee q)g\bigr].
\]
For \(p=q=0\) this has four clauses. Otherwise it equals
\(B(A\vee g)(N\vee W\vee g)\), with five.

If \(\mu=0,\lambda=1\), then \(f=ABC\vee gB\) and \(gf=gB\).
When \(p=q=0\), distribution and absorption give
\[
              Q=B(A\vee g)(N\vee W)(N\vee C\vee g),
\]
with six clauses. Indeed its bracket after removing \(B\) expands
to \(AN\vee ACW\vee gN\vee gW\).
When \(p\vee q=1\), the bracket is \(A(N\vee CW)\vee g\), so
\[
              Q=B(A\vee g)(N\vee C\vee g)(N\vee W\vee g),
\]
with seven clauses.

If \(\mu=\lambda=0\), then \(f=hC\), \(gf=gBC\), and
\[
       Q=B\bigl[(A\vee g)(N\vee CW)\vee pg\vee qgC\bigr].
\]
For \(p=1\) this is the preceding seven-clause expression.
For \(p=q=0\) it is \(B(A\vee g)(N\vee C)(N\vee W)\),
with five clauses. For \(p=0,q=1\), it is
\[
              Q=B(A\vee g)(N\vee C)(N\vee W\vee g),
\]
with six clauses: expanding its bracket gives
\(AN\vee ACW\vee gN\vee gC\), as required.
This exhausts every coefficient choice, including \(\rho=1\)
through \(W=1\). The bound persists under every restriction of
variables.

Name the four missing edges \(xy,xz,rs,tu\), with \(x\) the path
center. Both \(P_3\sqcup2K_2\) and \(3K_2\) have eight maximal
independent sets and require eight positive linear clauses for their
edge functions. A clause cannot reject two distinct maximal
independent sets, because their union contains an edge.
A safe contribution witnessing every edge of an induced graph is
exactly that graph's edge function on its vertex set.

The safe old cubic \(gL\) has at most one missing witness.
If it has none, \(Q|_T\) contradicts the seven-clause bound.
If its witness is a path arm, remove that arm's leaf; \(Q\)
still witnesses the induced three-edge matching on the remaining
six vertices, another contradiction. Therefore \(gL\) witnesses
one isolated edge, say \(rs\). In particular \(L\ne0\) and
\(L\) meets \(\{r,s\}\).

We show that neither \(U\) nor \(V\) is a full singleton.
If one is, its vertex is an endpoint of \(rs\). Every
\(g\)-containing contribution then contains that endpoint and
cannot witness any of \(xy,xz,tu\). All three must be supplied
by the safe \(g\)-free contribution
\[
                         Q_0=ABN\vee AB(C\vee\mu)W .
\]
When \(\mu=1\), this is \(AB(N\vee W)\). Without a positive
scalar part it is the union of the two old cubics \(ABN,ABM\),
each with at most one missing witness. A positive scalar part
instead makes it the safe old quadratic \(AB\), with at most
one. Neither alternative supplies three.

Suppose \(\mu=0\). If \(\rho=1\), or if \(M\) is a positive
scalar, \(Q_0=ABN\vee ABC\), again with at most two witnesses.
If \(M=\rho=0\), only \(ABN\) remains. Thus supplying three
requires \(\rho=0\) and nonzero old linear \(M\), so
\[
                         Q_0=ABN\vee ABCM .
\]
The original minimum degree of \(h\) is two; its strict visible
cut therefore has a degree-one low, making \(N\) linear or zero.
Even if a scalar specialization were allowed, a positive scalar
\(N\) would make \(AB\) absorb every other \(g\)-free term.
The first displayed term consequently has at most one witness.
The safe quartic \(ABCM\) must have two distinct missing
witnesses. The full equality case of the old-factor theorem
makes all four full supports \(A,B,C,M\) the transversals of
their induced matching. In particular \(A\subseteq T\).

The nonzero actual low \(a\subseteq A\) therefore contains a
target vertex. Since \(gL\) witnesses \(rs\), \(L\) also contains
a target vertex. Their product \(aL\) cannot be supported on
\(H\), because \(H[T]\) is empty and \(H\) has no loops.
This contradiction excludes every singleton \(U\) or \(V\).

Full old-cubic singleton rigidity applied to \(UVL\) now forces
the actual full \(L\) to be one endpoint singleton of \(rs\);
rename it \(\{r\}\). Explicitly, selecting one endpoint twice
in a cubic witness forces every variable of the remaining
factor to be adjacent to that endpoint. Two different variables
in that old factor, together with its old neighborhood center,
would give a four-cycle; the center cannot be the opposite
endpoint because the witnessed edge is missing. Thus the factor
is a full singleton, and the nonsingleton \(U,V\) leave only
\(L\).

The actual nonzero linear context \(L\) marks an original retained
quadratic product whose entire opposite old support lies in
\(\{r\}\). That retained star is covered by \(r\). Choose a
center for each of the other \(K-1\) original retained products
and add \(\{r,x,t\}\). This set covers every old edge and all
four global missing edges, so it has size at most
\((K-1)+3=K+2\). Repeated centers and shared fanout can only
reduce the count. The proof charges actual original products
and makes no change to their degree or occurrence labels.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[An original-node inventory for all visible cuts]
\label{prop:allvisibleoriginalinventory}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$, where $G$ is finite, simple and four-cycle-free. Suppose its nonempty quadratic support is $H$, and its four global missing edges are $xy,xz,ab,cd$, with endpoint set $T$ satisfying $G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$. Keep the original extracted quadratic frame and its $K$ retained products. Suppose at most three products and three additions are deleted, every deleted addition is visible, and $\vc(G)>K+2$.

There are exactly three original private products and three original visible occurrences. With all original degrees, coefficients, occurrences, fanout and low/context incidences retained, their product network has one of the following forms. Every letter denoting an old form below is nonzero and homogeneous linear: singleton supports are allowed, and nonsingleton supports lie in an $H$-neighborhood. Boolean displays assert support identities only.

\emph{Three distinct inserted products.} Each product is inserted once. In a topological order $g,h,f$ of the original product nodes, no product operand is raw. All three original minimum product degrees are two, all selected lows have degree one, and direct contexts are old linear or zero. Write $g=UV$. The second product is $AB$, $(A\vee g)B$, or $(A\vee g)(B\vee g)$, with every indicated affected coefficient positive. For an input of $f$, let $O,G,H,J$ denote an old base with, respectively, no contribution, a positive $g$ contribution, a positive $h$ contribution, or both. Up to exchanging the two inputs, the necessary support-type table is
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
 h&\text{allowed pairs at }f\\ \hline
 AB&OG,\ OJ,\ GG,\ GH,\ GJ\\
 (A\vee g)B&OO,\ OG,\ OH,\ OJ,\ GG,\ GH,\ GJ,\ HH,\ HJ,\ JJ\\
 (A\vee g)(B\vee g)&OO,\ OG,\ OH,\ GH.
\end{array}
\]
In the first row one may also exchange the independent original nodes $g,h$ and their occurrence data. In the last row $g\Rightarrow h$ identifies $J$ with $H$ only in Boolean support; every original extra $g$ coefficient remains recorded.

\emph{Two distinct inserted products.} The inserted nodes $g,f$ are comparable, with $g$ ancestral to $f$. The third product $u$ is not inserted. There are $n$ distinct original occurrences carrying $g$ and $3-n$ carrying $f$, where $n\in\{1,2\}$. Write $g_i$ for the distinct $g$ occurrences, without copying the product node. Up to commutativity and topological ordering of independent nodes, the original network is
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{R1}:\quad &u=UV,\qquad g=uA,\qquad
 f=\Bigl(B+\sum_i\beta_i g_i\Bigr)\Bigl(C+\sum_i\gamma_i g_i\Bigr),\\
\mathrm{R2}:\quad &g=UV,\qquad u=AB,\qquad
 f=u\Bigl(C+\sum_i\delta_i g_i\Bigr),\\
\mathrm{R3}:\quad &g=UV,\qquad
 u=\Bigl(A+\sum_i\beta_i g_i\Bigr)\Bigl(B+\sum_i\gamma_i g_i\Bigr),\qquad
 f=u\Bigl(C+\sum_i\delta_i g_i\Bigr).
\end{align*}
At least one $\beta_i$ or $\gamma_i$ is positive in R1 and R3, and at least one $\delta_i$ is positive in R2. In R2 the nodes $g,u$ are independent. In R3, if both inputs of $u$ are affected, their positive index sets must be the same one-element set. Only occurrences actually earlier than a receiving input may occur in its sum. Every raw $u$ above is a literal original wire. All direct contexts and pairwise occurrence crosses, including repeated-high squares, keep their original compatibility restrictions.

In every surviving family, each private product is true on an isolated target input $ab$ or $cd$, or on both path inputs $xy,xz$. This assigns neither distinct edges nor first-true roles to products. The inventory is necessary; it does not assert realizability of the listed families or exclude them all.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Proposition~\ref{prop:essentialvisibleoperands} gives exactly three private products and three visible additions, all essential after whole-carrier erasure. Each high is an original private-product output. Each private operand is a raw earlier product or an original degree-one signal with a nonzero old base and actual earlier insertion contributions; original ancestry survives. For three distinct high occurrences the contribution is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:allvisibleinventoryframe}
 Y=gL\vee hN\vee fM\vee q_{12}gh\vee q_{13}gf\vee q_{23}hf.
\end{equation}
Every direct context has its actual old-linear, scalar or zero type. With repeated highs the same occurrence formula applies, retaining square contributions from distinct occurrences. Grouping equal Boolean values in the calculations below never merges their original nodes.

We use Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors}: a safe old cubic has at most one missing witness; a safe old quartic has at most two, and equality gives exactly the four full transversal supports of an induced two-edge matching. The cubic singleton rule and Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic} apply to full supports. The induced target $P_3\sqcup2K_2$, and either of its three-matching restrictions, require eight positive linear CNF clauses. Indeed their eight minimal vertex covers give eight distinct required clauses. An affine linear form uses at most one clause; zero or scalar specializations only shorten the bounds below. Restriction is made only after global safety has been established.

We will also use a direct original-product charge. If a degree-one selected low has a nonzero full direct context $\{v\}$, at least one original marked retained product has its complete opposite support in $\{v\}$. Choose $v$ as the center of that old star and a center for every other retained product. This covers $H$ with at most $K$ vertices including $v$. If $v$ is an isolated target endpoint, the path center and one endpoint of the other isolated edge cover the rest of the missing graph, giving $\vc(G)\le K+2$. Positivity and the full context ensure this is a charge to an original retained product, not to an arbitrarily chosen restricted factor.

\emph{The remaining raw-first affected case.}
We first establish an auxiliary calculation with the actual three distinct products
\[
 g=UV,\qquad h=B(A\vee g),\qquad f=g(C\vee h).
\]
The actual nonzero low $b_0$ of the $h$ occurrence lies in $C$, and $b_0N$ is $H$-supported. Here $L,N$ are old linear or zero, since $g,h$ have original minimum degree two; $M$ may also be scalar. Expansion of~\eqref{eq:allvisibleinventoryframe} gives
\[
 Y=Q\vee gR,\quad Q=ABN,\quad
 R=L\vee B(N\vee M\vee r)\vee C(M\vee q_{13}),\quad
 r=q_{12}\vee q_{13}\vee q_{23}.
\]
The bracket has at most four affine clauses, so $gR$ has at most six. Every displayed term is globally safe. If $Q$ has no target witness, this contradicts the full target. If its sole witness is a path arm, deleting that arm's leaf leaves a three-matching which $gR$ would have to supply, again impossible. Thus $Q$ witnesses an isolated edge, say $ab$, and $gR$ supplies $xy,xz,cd$.

Both $U,V$ contain $x$. Otherwise a factor meeting both path arms would contain $y,z$, whose old center together with $y,x,z$ gives a four-cycle; the center cannot be $x$ because $xy,xz$ are missing from $H$. Apply the cubic singleton rule to $ABN$. Singleton $N$ gives the original-product charge, so assume $N$ is nonsingleton. If $B$ is also nonsingleton, the singleton rule forces $A=\{a\}$ and $b\in B\cap N$; the positive term $UVBN$ then accepts the independent pair $\{x,b\}$, impossible. Thus $B=\{a\}$. Safety of $UVBN$ on $\{x,a\}$ forces $a\notin N$, and the $ab$ witness consequently gives $b\in N$. Set $a$ to zero. The other three targets must come from
\[
 gL\vee gC(M\vee q_{13}).
\]
If $q_{13}>0$, two safe old cubics supply at most two witnesses. Scalar or zero $M$ has the same obstruction. Otherwise the old quartic $gCM$ must supply a path arm and $cd$, while $gL$ supplies the other arm. Full quartic equality places the entire support of $C$ in $T$. Since $0\ne b_0\subseteq C$ and $b\in N$, the asserted $H$-support of $b_0N$ contradicts $H[T]=\varnothing$. Thus this case gives $K+2$ or is impossible.

The raw-raw specialization $f=gh$ with $h=B(A\vee g)$ has
\[
 Y=ABN\vee g\bigl[L\vee B(N\vee M\vee q_{12}\vee q_{13}\vee q_{23})\bigr].
\]
Its $g$ part has at most four clauses. The same ordered cubic argument applies: singleton $N$ gives the charge; with $N$ nonsingleton, nonsingleton $B$ forces the unsafe singleton-$A$ case. Hence $B=\{a\}$, safety gives $a\notin N$, and setting $a=0$ leaves only $gL$ for the other three targets. No containment in an absent $C$ is invoked.

\emph{Three distinct inserted products: exclusion of raw inputs.}
Order the original products topologically as $g,h,f$. The first is $g=UV$. If $h$ has raw $g$, its other input is old $A$, raw $g$, or old plus positive $g$. The last two possibilities give Boolean $h=g$. Every nonraw input of $f$ then has old-plus-$g$ support, and every raw input has support $g$. Grouping the two direct contexts and their square cross into affine contexts gives exactly Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching}, including its allowed dependent forms and square terms. It cannot supply a three-matching. This is an algebraic use of that lemma, not a degree-changing circuit intervention.

It remains that $h=gA$. If $f$ has no raw input, Proposition~\ref{prop:rawmiddleaffectedlast} applies with its exact once-each occurrences and compatible contexts. If $f=h(C\vee\lambda g\vee\mu h)$, zero coefficients give the literal old/raw case of Proposition~\ref{prop:literaloldrawthreevisible}; a positive coefficient gives Boolean $f=h$. The output then is $g[L\vee A(N\vee M\vee q_{12}\vee q_{13}\vee q_{23})]$, with at most four clauses overall. Raw $h$ times raw $g$ or $h$ is the same case. If $f=g(C\vee\lambda g\vee\mu h)$, positive $\lambda$ gives $f=g$; zero $\lambda,\mu$ is literal. For $\lambda=0$, $\mu>0$, the output is
\[
 g\bigl[L\vee A(N\vee M\vee q_{12}\vee q_{13}\vee q_{23})
             \vee C(M\vee q_{13})\bigr],
\]
with at most six clauses. Two raw final inputs again give support $g$ or $h$. This exhausts a raw middle product.

Now $h$ has two original degree-one inputs, so its support is $AB$, $B(A\vee g)$, or $(A\vee g)(B\vee g)$. If $f$ has raw $h$ and other input $C\vee\lambda g\vee\mu h$, the independent case is literal, Boolean $f=h$, or Proposition~\ref{prop:independentrawaffected} after symmetric renaming. A Boolean alias reduces to Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching} with affine contexts. The single- and double-affected middle cases are exactly Propositions~\ref{prop:oneaffectedrawdescendant} and~\ref{prop:sharedcutearlierreuse}.

If $f$ has raw $g$ and other input $C\vee\lambda g\vee\mu h$, a positive $\lambda$ gives Boolean $f=g$ and the same algebraic obstruction. If both coefficients vanish, $f=gC$ and $h$ are independent of each other as original product nodes; exchanging their topological names gives the already covered raw-middle/nonraw-last case of Proposition~\ref{prop:rawmiddleaffectedlast}, with unchanged occurrence data. If only $\mu$ is positive, independent $h$ gives Proposition~\ref{prop:independentrawaffected}, single-affected $h$ gives the auxiliary calculation above, and double-affected $h$ gives $f=g$ because $g\Rightarrow h$.

For two raw final inputs, a repeated input gives support $g$ or $h$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching}. The remaining value $gh$ is literal when $h$ is independent, is the separately treated raw-raw specialization when $h$ is single-affected, and equals $g$ when $h$ is double-affected. All raw inputs are excluded. Hence all three original minimum product degrees are two; their strict selected lows have degree one, and all direct contexts are linear or zero.

\emph{The nonraw type table.}
For independent $h=AB$, pair $OO$ is literal and pair $JJ$ is Proposition~\ref{prop:twocutjoinbothsides}; its linear-or-zero context hypothesis has just been proved. Exchange of the independent nodes identifies $OG$ with $OH$, $GG$ with $HH$, and $GJ$ with $HJ$. The five stated representatives remain. For single-affected $h$, the ten unordered pairs exhaust the original operand list, and the proposition makes no further exclusion.

For double-affected $h=AB\vee g$, support absorption identifies $J$ with $H$, leaving $OO$, $OG$, $OH$, $GG$, $GH$ and $HH$. Pair $HH$ is Proposition~\ref{prop:nesteddoubleaffected}, with its actual shared lows. An extra original $g$ contribution under $h$ changes no old base or required $h$-low identity.

For $GG$, write $f=CD\vee g$. Then
\[
 Y=g(L\vee N\vee M\vee q_{12}\vee q_{13}\vee q_{23})
       \vee ABN\vee CDM\vee q_{23}ABCD.
\]
If $q_{23}>0$, $g$ is safe and has at most one missing witness. The other three terms satisfy Lemma~\ref{lem:independentproducts}: the actual $h$-low lies in $M$, the $f$-low in $N$, their pair is $H$-supported, and their direct low/context products are $H$-supported. They have at most two witnesses altogether. If $q_{23}=0$ but $q_{12}$ or $q_{13}$ is positive, the safe old quadratic $g$ and two old cubics again give at most three.

If all crosses vanish, $ABN$ and $CDM$ each have at most one witness, while the missing witnesses of $gL\vee gN\vee gM$ share a vertex by Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic}. Four targets force the latter union to supply both path arms and the former cubics to supply the two isolated edges. Thus $N,M$ each contain an isolated endpoint. Both $U,V$ contain $x$, by the preceding old-center argument. A safe $UVD$ witnessing $xy$ must have full $D=\{y\}$: if $D$ also contains $w$, safety of $x^2w$ forces $xw$, and the old center of $D$ gives the forbidden cycle through $y,x,w$; $w=x$ instead gives an unsafe singleton. The analogous $xz$ context is $\{z\}$. Neither $N$ nor $M$ can supply a path arm, and the one old cubic $gL$ cannot supply both. This excludes $GG$ and proves the three rows.

\emph{Repeated inserted highs.}
With only one distinct inserted high, all other private products are its ancestors and no input can be affected by an earlier inserted high without a cycle. The network is literal old/raw and is excluded. With two inserted nodes, if they are incomparable, an affected input on any useful private route would make them comparable or create a cycle. Again the network would be literal. Thus write $g$ ancestral to $f$, and let $u$ be the uninserted third node. It is essential and must be ancestral to an inserted high. Since it has no occurrence, every use of $u$ by another private product is a literal raw input. There are exactly three ancestry positions to consider.

First suppose $u$ is ancestral to $g$. Then $u=UV$ and $g=uA$ or $u^2$. In the square case, Boolean $g=u$, and all final input forms and grouped occurrence contexts fall under Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching} with old quadratic $u$. Thus $g=uA$. If $f$ has two nonraw inputs, at least one actual $g$ coefficient is positive, since otherwise the network is literal. This is R1. If $f$ has a raw input, a positive coefficient gives support $g$ or $u(C\vee A)$; raw pairs give $u$ or $g$, and unaffected raw cases are literal. Group the actual $g$ and $f$ contexts and same-high squares into affine $\Lambda,\mathcal M$, and let $q$ be the mixed coefficient. The largest remaining expression is
\[
 u\bigl[A(\Lambda\vee\mathcal M\vee q)\vee C\mathcal M\bigr].
\]
The bracket has at most four clauses by distribution, and $U,V$ add two: the sufficient total bound is six, below eight. The $f=u$ and $f=g$ cases are shorter. No raw final input remains.

Second suppose $g,u$ are independent. They are old quadratics $g=UV,u=AB$. Essential uninserted $u$ must feed $f$ raw. The other input is raw $g/u$ or an old base with actual $g$ contributions. Raw or unaffected choices make the entire network literal, so at least one such contribution is positive. This is exactly R2.

Third suppose $g$ is ancestral to $u$, which is ancestral to $f$. Here $g=UV$. If $u$ has raw $g$, it is $gA$ or has Boolean support $g$. Since $f$ must use $u$ raw, Boolean $u=g$ gives $f=gC$ or $g$ and at most four clauses. For $u=gA$, the largest remaining output is
\[
 g\bigl[\Lambda\vee AC(\mathcal M\vee q)\bigr],
\]
with at most five clauses; affected or raw alternatives only shorten it. Hence $u$ has two nonraw inputs, with at least one positive $g$ coefficient.

The other input of $f$, besides raw $u$, cannot be raw $u$: Boolean $f=u$ then reduces the full grouped output to Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching}. Nor can it be raw $g$. If $u$ is single-affected, $gu=gB$, and the output is $g[\Lambda\vee B(\mathcal M\vee q)]$, with at most four clauses; if double-affected, $gu=g$, still shorter. Therefore the other input is an old base $C$ plus actual earlier $g$ occurrences. This gives R3 and exhausts the original recipient inputs.

Finally, if distinct occurrences $i,j$ can be chosen with $\beta_i>0$ and $\gamma_j>0$ in R3, there are two $g$ occurrences and one $f$ occurrence. Both chosen cuts precede their receiving inputs, hence precede $u$ and $f$. In support $u=AB\vee g$, so $f=ABC\vee gC$ if all $\delta_i$ vanish and $f=ABC\vee g$ otherwise. The two actual lows lie in $A$ and $B$, with their original $H$-supported context products. This is precisely Proposition~\ref{prop:doublefirsthigh}, including the repeated-high square and mixed coefficient, and is impossible. Thus the two nonempty positive index sets admit no distinct pair; they must be the same singleton. No other occurrence is discarded.

The alternatives are exhaustive by the number of distinct original inserted nodes, even when Boolean values coincide. Proposition~\ref{prop:matchingprivateessential} supplies the final isolated-edge-or-both-arms necessity, without an injective witness assignment. This proves the stated inventory and no exclusion of its remaining families.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[An independent raw middle product with repeated highs]\label{prop:independentrawmiddlecover}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, and let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$ with nonempty squarefree quadratic support $H$. Suppose the four global missing edges are $xy,xz,ab,cd$, their endpoint set $T$ induces $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ in $G$, and $H[T]=\varnothing$. Keep the exact original quadratic frame with $K$ retained products. After whole-current-carrier erasure and pruning, suppose exactly three original products and three original additions are private, all additions are visible, and the literal product inputs are
\[
 g=UV,\qquad u=AB,\qquad
 f=u\Bigl(C+\sum_i\delta_i g_i\Bigr),
\]
with nonzero old homogeneous linear $U,V,A,B,C$, independent original products $g,u$, and at least one positive $\delta_i$. The original product $u$ is not inserted. Exactly $n\in\{1,2\}$ original insertion occurrences carry $g$, and the other $3-n$ carry $f$; only actually earlier occurrences $g_i$ can enter the displayed input. Retain all coefficients, selected lows, contexts, fanout and original node and degree labels.

Then $\vc(G)\le K+2$. More precisely, the four target witnesses require $n=1$, zero total mixed $g/f$ occurrence coefficient, three degree-one selected lows, and zero coefficients pairing distinct occurrences of the same high. Both high values restricted to $T$ must be unsafe. These conclusions do not assert realizability of the remaining allocation or normalize other affected networks to this syntax.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Put $v=uC$, so at support level $f=v\vee ug$. Write $L_i$ for the actual direct contexts of the $g$ occurrences and $M_j$ for those of the $f$ occurrences. Their unions $L=\bigvee_iL_i$ and $M=\bigvee_jM_j$ are notation only and need not be old forms. The first high has original minimum degree two, so its selected lows have degree one and its contexts are old linear or zero. The second high has original minimum degree three; its contexts may initially also be scalar. The exact original three-occurrence expansion on $T$ is
\[
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee p g\vee q ug\vee r f.                 \tag{*}
\]
Here $p,r$ collect distinct-occurrence pairs with the same high, and $q$ collects the mixed pairs. The support identities $g^2=g$, $f^2=f$, $gf=ug$ do not merge original nodes or occurrences. A same-occurrence diagonal coefficient is zero because its nonzero degree-one selected low would otherwise contribute a positive square to $P_2$; a degree-two low has only an addition-only continuation. Thus no original term is silently omitted.

Every positive summand is safe on $T$, and $Y$ equals its edge function. Restricted old supports remain old relative to their original ambient $H$-centers, even when those centers lie outside $T$. We may therefore apply the old-factor bounds to restricted safe terms. Full global supports will be used explicitly for the final retained-product charge.

We record two consequences of those bounds. A safe union $ABCD_1\vee ABCD_2$ of quartics sharing three old factors has at most two missing witnesses. Indeed, if one term has two, full four-factor equality makes its supports the four distinct transversals of an induced matching. The shared three supports have empty common intersection and lie on those four vertices. A new edge meeting all three cannot have an endpoint outside that set, and the induced matching admits no new edge inside it. If each term has at most one the bound is immediate. A scalar context makes the cubic absorb its extensions; zero contexts are omitted. Also, the witnesses of safe cubics $UVL_i$ lie in one star. On this target there are at most two, and two must be $xy,xz$.

An individual old form meeting both path arms contains $x$: otherwise it contains $y,z$, and its old center together with $x$ gives a four-cycle. That center cannot be $x$, since the path arms are missing from $H$. This observation includes singleton forms.

\emph{Neither high is safe.}
If $g$ were safe on $T$, adding it to the output would preserve the target and absorb all its multiples. For $r>0$ the target would become $g\vee uC$, with at most two witnesses. For $r=0$ it would become $g\vee uCM$, with at most three by the shared-quartic bound. Both are impossible. Hence $g$ is unsafe and $p=0$.

If $f$ were safe, adding it similarly gives
\[
 Y=Q\vee R\vee S,\qquad Q=ug,\quad R=uC,\quad
 S=\bigvee_i gL_i.
\]
Here $Q$ has at most two missing witnesses, $R$ at most one, and $S$ at most two in one star. If $Q$ has at most one, all four witnesses force $S$ to supply both path arms and $R,Q$ the two isolated edges. Thus $U,V$ both contain $x$, while $u$ is true on both isolated edges. Safety of $ug$, after setting $x=1$, makes the two-clause product $u$ restricted to the isolated vertices a safe function witnessing both disjoint edges. It would equal their edge function, which needs four positive clauses.

If $Q$ has two witnesses, $U,V,A,B$ are the four full transversals of their induced matching. Any new $S$ edge must attach at $U\cap V$. If this intersection is empty there is none; otherwise write it $\{z\}$. The complementary pair has $A\cap B=\{z'\}$, where $zz'$ is a matching edge. Every new $R$ edge must attach at $z'$. Two new $S$ edges, or one new $S$ edge and one distinct new $R$ edge, together with $zz'$ would create a connected three-edge subgraph or a triangle in the target. Neither occurs in $P_3\sqcup2K_2$. Since $R$ itself has at most one witness, at most one new edge can accompany $Q$'s two. Again four are impossible.

Thus $f$ too is unsafe. Consequently $r=0$, no positive scalar $M_j$ is possible, and every selected low has degree one: a degree-two low at an $f$ cut would give a nonzero scalar addition-only direct context exposing $f$. All individual contexts are now old linear or zero.

\emph{A positive mixed coefficient is impossible.}
Suppose $q>0$. Its $ug$ term absorbs all $ugM_j$, so
\[
 Y=S\vee R\vee Q,\qquad
 S=\bigvee_i gL_i,\quad R=uC\bigvee_jM_j,\quad Q=ug.
\]
The shared-quartic bound gives at most two witnesses for $R$. Moreover
\[
 R\vee Q=u\bigl[C(\bigvee_jM_j)\vee g\bigr]
\]
has at most six positive affine clauses: four for the disjunction of two two-clause products and two for $u$. If $S$ has no witness, this contradicts the target's eight-clause bound. If its only witness is a path arm, removing that leaf leaves a three-matching supplied by the same six-clause expression, again impossible.

If $S$ has both path witnesses, $g(x)=1$, and the other expression must witness both isolated edges. Thus $u$ is true on both. Safety of $ug$ with $x=1$ again forces a two-clause representation of a two-edge matching, a contradiction.

It remains that $S$ has just one isolated witness, say $ab$. The factor $u$ is common to every term supplying $xy,xz,cd$, so both $A,B$ contain $x$. Thus $u(x)=1$. Since $g$ is true on $ab$, safety of $ug$ forces both $U,V$ to omit $x$: if one contained $x$, an endpoint of $ab$ in the other would give an unsafe independent pair. If $Q$ witnessed $xy$, both $U,V$ would therefore contain $y$. Some context $L_i$ witnessing $ab$ contains an endpoint $e$ of that edge; then the independent pair $\{y,e\}$ makes $gL_i$ true. This excludes $xy$, and the same argument excludes $xz$. If $Q$ witnessed $cd$, restricting $g$ to the isolated vertices and adjoining $x$ would make it a safe two-clause function witnessing both $ab,cd$, also impossible. Consequently $R$ must supply all three of $xy,xz,cd$, contradicting its two-witness bound. This excludes every positive mixed coefficient for both occurrence allocations.

\emph{Zero mixed coefficient, two first-high occurrences.}
Now $q=0$. First take $n=2$, so $M$ is a single old context and
\[
 Y=S\vee u(C\vee g)M.
\]
The second term has at most five clauses. The same eight-clause restrictions exclude zero $S$ witnesses or one path witness.
