If $S$ supplies both arms, $g(x)=1$ and $uM$ is true on both isolated edges. Safety of $ugM$ with $x=1$ would make the three-clause product $uM$ equal the two-edge matching, impossible.

Therefore $S$ has one isolated witness, say $ab$, while the other term supplies $xy,xz,cd$. Its common old factors $A,B,M$ all contain $x$. Singleton safety gives $C(x)=g(x)=0$. The old form $C$ cannot contain both path leaves. If it contained neither, $g$ would witness both arms, forcing $g(x)=1$. Hence, after exchanging $y,z$, we have $z\in C$, $y\notin C$, and $g$ witnesses $xy$. The safe quartic $uCM$ witnesses $xz$ but cannot also witness $cd$: four-factor equality has only two transversals containing $x$, whereas its three distinct equality factors $A,B,M$ contain $x$. Thus $ugM$ witnesses both $xy$ and $cd$.

On each independent pair $\{x,c\}$ and $\{x,d\}$, the factors $A,B,M$ are true. One of $U,V$ must reject each pair. The same one cannot reject both, because both factors meet $cd$. Rename them so that $U$ rejects $\{x,c\}$ and contains $y,d$, while $V$ rejects $\{x,d\}$ and contains $y,c$. Since $S$ witnesses $ab$, choose $e\in U\cap\{a,b\}$. The independent set $\{x,c,e\}$ then makes $A,B,M$ true at $x$, $V$ true at $c$ and $U$ true at $e$, contradicting safety of $ugM$. Thus $n=2$ is impossible.

\emph{One first-high occurrence and the original cover charge.}
For $n=1$, $S=gL$ is one safe old cubic and $M=M_1\vee M_2$. The second term $u(C\vee g)M$ still has at most five clauses. The previous restrictions therefore force $S$ to witness an isolated edge, say $ab$.

If the full global $L$ is a singleton endpoint of $ab$, its original degree-one cut incidence marks a retained product whose complete opposite selected support is that singleton. Choose this endpoint, $x$, and one endpoint of $cd$. These three vertices cover all missing edges and the entire marked retained star. Choosing one center for every other original retained product gives
\[
 \vc(G)\le(K-1)+3=K+2.
\]
This uses the full global context and an actual original product; it does not charge a restricted support or a hypothetical replacement frame.

Otherwise $L$ is nonsingleton. The full old-cubic singleton rule for $UVL$ witnessing $ab$ forces one of $U,V$ to be a full singleton endpoint of $ab$. Set both $a,b$ to zero, so $g$ vanishes. The remaining $xy,xz,cd$ must be supplied by
\[
 uC(M_1\vee M_2).
\]
The old common factors $A,B,C$ all meet both path arms and therefore contain $x$. Each nonzero individual $M_j$ omits $x$ by safety and cannot contain both leaves by oldness. Thus one context supplies $xy$ and the other $xz$, and both are needed. Whichever supplies $cd$ also supplies a path arm. Its quartic would have two witnesses with three full equality factors $A,B,C$ containing $x$, although only two of the four distinct transversals contain $x$. This contradiction leaves only the full singleton-context case and its $K+2$ bound. All zero contexts and repeated support values were included throughout.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Two affected inputs after a repeated cubic high]
\label{prop:bothaffectedrepeatedcubic}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and $C_4$-free, and let a positive variable-input
circuit compute $P\in\operatorname{Sup}(G)$ with nonempty squarefree quadratic
support $H$. Suppose its four global missing edges are $xy,xz,ab,cd$, their
endpoint set $T$ induces $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ in $G$, and $H[T]=\varnothing$.
Preserve the exact original quadratic frame, its arbitrary number $K$ of
retained products, all original minimum degrees, full current protected
carriers, operand incidences, fanout, insertion labels and coefficients.
After whole-current-carrier erasure and pruning, suppose exactly three
original products and three original additions are private, all the additions
are visible, and the literal private products are
\[
 u=UV,\qquad g=uA,\qquad
 f=\Bigl(B+\sum_i\beta_i g_i\Bigr)
   \Bigl(C+\sum_i\gamma_i g_i\Bigr),
\]
where $U,V,A,B,C$ are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms, with singleton
supports allowed. The node $u$ is not an inserted high. Exactly $n\in\{1,2\}$
distinct original insertion occurrences carry $g$, and the remaining $3-n$
carry $f$. Both displayed sums have a positive coefficient and use only
actually earlier $g$ occurrences; the two sums may use the same or different
occurrences. All contexts, lows and occurrence-pair coefficients are the
actual ones. Then the circuit cannot supply all four missing witnesses,
independently of $K$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
All support identities below are Boolean identities. They do not identify
original nodes or occurrences or change their original minimum degrees.
We first note that a globally safe product
\[
 F_1F_2F_3D                                             \tag{*}
\]
of three old homogeneous linear forms and an arbitrary nonnegative affine
linear form $D$ witnesses at most two of the four target edges. Indeed, any
three target edges either form an induced three-edge matching or consist of
both path arms and one isolated edge. In the first case, restriction to their
six endpoints makes the expression a positive CNF with at most four clauses.
Safety and all three edge witnesses would make it exactly the matching edge
function, which requires eight clauses. To recall the counting argument,
every maximal independent set must falsify a clause, and a clause cannot be
false on two distinct maximal independent sets: their union contains an edge.
An $r$-edge matching has $2^r$ maximal independent sets.

In the second case, say the witnessed edges are $xy,xz,ab$, each $F_i$ meets
both path arms and therefore contains $x$. Otherwise it contains both $y,z$,
and its old $H$-center gives a four-cycle with $x$. Thus $F_1F_2F_3$ is true
on $\{x\}$. The $ab$ witness forces either a positive constant in $D$ or an
endpoint of $ab$ in its support. The expression then accepts $\{x\}$ or an
independent pair $\{x,a\}$ or $\{x,b\}$, contradicting safety. This proves
$(*)$, including zero and constant-factor boundaries.

Write $I$ for the $n$ original $g$ occurrences and $J$ for the $m=3-n$
original $f$ occurrences. Since the original minimum degrees of $g$ and $f$
are respectively three and two, the direct $g$ contexts $L_i$ are compatible
old homogeneous linear forms, scalars or zero, whereas every direct $f$
context $M_j$ is old homogeneous linear or zero. Keep the occurrence symbols
separate in the exact frame and substitute their high values only afterward.
The private contribution is
\[
 Y=\bigvee_{i\in I}gL_i\ \vee\!\bigvee_{j\in J}fM_j
       \vee\alpha g^2\vee\beta gf\vee\gamma f^2,       \tag{1}
\]
where the three coefficient flags collect the actual occurrence-pair terms.
A same-occurrence diagonal is absent because its nonzero degree-one low
would give a diagonal monomial in squarefree $P_2$; a degree-two low cannot
participate in a quadratic product. Squares from distinct occurrences with
the same high are retained. In particular $\alpha=0$ if $n=1$, and
$\gamma=0$ if $m=1$. All summands are globally safe, and on $T$ the
quadratic frame vanishes, so $Y$ must witness all four targets.

Both affected inputs have the support of their old base joined with $g$.
Consequently
\[
 f=(B\vee g)(C\vee g)=BC\vee g.
\]
Set $Q=BC$. Since $g\le f$, equation (1) becomes
\[
 \begin{split}
 Y&=gW\vee QZ,\\
 W&=\bigvee_iL_i\vee\bigvee_jM_j\vee\alpha\vee\beta\vee\gamma,\\
 Z&=\bigvee_jM_j\vee\gamma.                           
 \end{split}\tag{2}
\]
Here $W$ is affine linear and need not be old. Every displayed summand in
(2) is a safe support subfunction of $Y$. In particular every $gM_j$ and
$BCM_j$ is safe, through the corresponding original term $fM_j$.
By $(*)$, $gW=UVAW$ has at most two target witnesses.

If $Z$ has a positive constant, $QZ=BC$ is a safe old quadratic and has at
most one missing witness. If $m=1$ and $Z$ has no constant, $QZ=BCM_1$ is a
safe old cubic or zero, again with at most one missing witness. Neither case
can give four witnesses. Thus the whole $n=2,m=1$ case is excluded, with all
its same-high squares and mixed coefficients. The only remaining case has
$n=1,m=2,\gamma=0$ and
\[
 QZ=BCM_1\vee BCM_2.
\]
Each nonzero summand is a safe old cubic and has at most one missing witness.
The common-cubic-star bound puts the missing witnesses of their union in one
star. To cover four targets together with $gW$, this union must therefore
supply exactly $xy,xz$, while $gW$ supplies $ab,cd$.

Both old supports $B,C$ meet both path arms, so both contain $x$. A context
$M_j$ supplying the $xy$ witness must omit $x$, by safety of $BCM_j$, and
therefore contains $y$. The corresponding $gM_j$ is safe. Restrict
$g=UVA$ to $\{a,b,c,d\}$. If an independent assignment there made $g$ true,
adjoining $y$ would make $gM_j$ true on an independent subset of $T$, a
contradiction. Hence this restriction of $g$ is safe for the two-edge
matching. It is true on both edges because $gW$ witnesses them. Positivity
then makes it exactly that matching edge function. But it has at most three
linear clauses, whereas two independent edges require four. This final
contradiction treats all remaining actual coefficients and contexts.

The argument uses full global supports before each specified restriction.
It applies equally when the affected inputs use the same earlier occurrence,
different earlier occurrences or overlapping coefficient sets. It does not
classify a single-affected input pair or any other private product network.
\end{proof}

% Complete224 inserted after full mutual comparison; original staged text preserved.
\begin{proposition}[A single affected input after a repeated cubic high]
\label{prop:singleaffectedrawcubiccover}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$, where $G$ is finite,
simple and four-cycle-free. Let its nonempty squarefree quadratic support be
$H$, and let its four global missing edges be $xy,xz,ab,cd$, with
$G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$ on their endpoints. Preserve the
full original quadratic frame and its arbitrary retained product count $K$.
After whole-current-carrier erasure and pruning, suppose exactly three
original products and three original additions are private, all three
additions visible, and the literal private products are
\[
 u=UV,\qquad g=uA,\qquad f=C\Bigl(B+\sum_i\beta_i g_i\Bigr),
\]
where $U,V,A,B,C$ are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms, singleton supports
allowed. The node $u$ is not an inserted high. Exactly $n\in\{1,2\}$ distinct
original insertion occurrences carry $g$; the other $3-n$ carry $f$. At least
one $\beta_i$ is positive, and only actually earlier $g$ occurrences enter
the displayed input. The $C$ input is the stipulated unaffected old form.
Keep every original minimum degree, occurrence, coefficient, fanout, selected
low, context and retained-product incidence. Then
\[
 \vc(G)\le K+2.
\]
No retained optimality or additional order of the insertion occurrences is
assumed. Repeated forms and wires are allowed.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
All following identities are support identities; original nodes, minimum
degrees and counts remain fixed. We use the bound proved at the start of
Proposition~\ref{prop:bothaffectedrepeatedcubic}: a safe product of three old
linear forms and an arbitrary nonnegative affine linear context witnesses
at most two target edges. A restriction preserves oldness with the original
ambient $H$-centers, so the same bound applies on an indicated induced subset
of $T$. Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors} gives at most one missing witness
for an old quadratic or cubic and at most two for an old quartic, with its
full-support equality description. The target and a three-matching each
require eight positive CNF clauses; a two-matching requires four.

Put $m=3-n$, and keep all occurrence symbols separate until substituting
their high values. The original minimum degrees of $g$ and $f$ are three
and two. The exact private contribution is
\[
 Y=\bigvee_{i=1}^{n}gL_i\ \vee\!\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}fM_j
      \vee p g^2\vee qgf\vee r f^2,
 \qquad g=UVA,\quad f=BC\vee gC.
\]
Here $L_i$ is its actual compatible old linear, scalar or zero context, and
$M_j$ is old linear or zero. The flags $p,q,r$ collect actual distinct-occurrence
pair coefficients; $p=0$ if $n=1$, and $r=0$ if $m=1$. Same-occurrence
diagonals vanish because a nonzero degree-one low squared would give a
diagonal in squarefree $P_2$, while a degree-two low cannot enter a retained
quadratic product. Squares from distinct occurrences are still present in
this display. All positive summands are globally safe, and the quadratic
frame vanishes on $T$.

Neither high is safe even on $T$. If $g$ were safe there, it would have at
most one target witness by the old cubic bound. Every $g$-containing term
has witnesses among that one edge. The other witnesses lie in the at most
two old cubics $BCM_j$; if $r>0$, they instead lie below the single safe old
quadratic $BC$. Thus there are at most three target witnesses. It follows
that $g$ is unsafe, so $p=0$ and every nonzero scalar $L_i$ is excluded.
If $f$ were safe on $T$, the whole output would lie below the safe function
\[
 f\vee g\Bigl(\bigvee_iL_i\Bigr)
   =BC\vee g\Bigl(C\vee\bigvee_iL_i\Bigr).
\]
Its first term has at most one target witness and its second at most two by
the affine-context bound. This is again impossible. Hence $f$ is unsafe and
$r=0$ as well. A degree-two selected $g$ low would have a nonzero scalar
continuation, already excluded. All selected lows therefore have degree one,
and every nonzero $L_i,M_j$ is a full actual old linear context.

Write $L=\bigvee_iL_i$ and $M=\bigvee_jM_j$. These unions are linear or zero;
they need not be old or original wires. Since $gf=gC$ in support,
\[
 Y=gL\vee BCM\vee gCM\vee qgC.                         \tag{1}
\]
If $q>0$, this becomes $g(L\vee C)\vee BCM$. The first term has at most two
target witnesses. Each $BCM_j$ is an old cubic with at most one, and their
union has its witnesses in one star by Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic}.
Four targets therefore force $m=2,n=1$, with $BCM$ witnessing both path arms
and the first term witnessing $ab,cd$. Both old supports $B,C$ meet both
path arms and hence contain $x$: otherwise one contains $y,z$, whose old
center makes a four-cycle with $x$. The positive term $gC$ is safe. If an
independent assignment on $\{a,b,c,d\}$ made $g$ true, adjoining $x$ would
make $gC$ true on an independent subset of $T$. Thus $g$ restricted to those
four vertices is safe and witnesses both matching edges. Its three clauses
cannot represent that four-clause edge function. Consequently $q=0$.

We record the original-product charge used below. Suppose a full nonzero
actual context $D$, one of the $L_i,M_j$, is contained in a three-vertex
cover $Z$ of all four global missing edges. Mark the original retained
products reached by that insertion along selected linear routes. At least
one is marked. Positivity puts the full opposite selected operand of each
marked product in $\supp(D)$, so $Z$ covers all old edges supplied by every
marked product. Add one old-star center for each unmarked retained product.
If $s\ge1$ distinct products were marked, this covers all of $G$ with at
most $(K-s)+3\le K+2$ vertices. The mark is a set of original products;
sharing, repeated centers and coefficients do not duplicate the charge.

For $q=0$, equation (1) is
\[
 Y=g(L\vee CM)\vee BCM.                                \tag{2}
\]
The first term has at most five clauses: the three old clauses of $g$ and
the clauses $L\vee C$, $L\vee M$. Let $E$ be the target witness set of
$BCM$. The common-cubic bound gives $|E|\le2$, and if equality holds then
$E=\{xy,xz\}$. If $E$ is empty, the first term alone safely witnesses all
four edges, contradicting the eight-clause bound. If $E$ is just one path
arm, say $xy$, restrict to $\{x,z,a,b,c,d\}$. The first term safely witnesses
the three-matching there, again contradicting the eight-clause bound. No
assertion that every higher-support term of $BCM$ vanishes is needed: the
edge witnesses and safety suffice. Two cases remain.

If $E=\{xy,xz\}$, then $m=2,n=1$ and $B,C$ contain $x$. A context witnessing
$xy$ contains $y$, while choosing $x$ from both $B,C$ gives the monomial
$x^2y$. The full singleton certificate in Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic} makes
that context exactly $\{y\}$. The other witnessing context is exactly
$\{z\}$. Thus the terms $gCM_j$ witness neither isolated edge. The sole
direct $g$ context $L_1=L$ must supply both $ab,cd$. Full four-factor equality
for the globally safe old quartic $UVAL$ makes its factors the four distinct
transversals of those two edges, without outside vertices. The full actual
$L$ is therefore one endpoint of $ab$ together with one endpoint of $cd$.
Adding $x$ gives a three-cover of all missing edges containing $L$, and the
original-product charge proves the bound. No claim that $B$ or $C$ is a full
singleton has been used.

Finally suppose $E=\{cd\}$, after exchanging isolated edges. The first term
of (2) must witness $xy,xz,ab$, so every old factor of $g$ contains $x$ and
$g(\{x\})=1$. Choose $j$ such that $BCM_j$ witnesses $cd$. The full $C$
cannot be a singleton: it would be an endpoint of $cd$, so all $fM_k$ would
fail on $xy,xz,ab$, leaving three witnesses to $gL$, contrary to its two-edge
affine-context bound. If the full $M_j$ is a singleton, it is $c$ or $d$.
Together with $x$ and one endpoint of $ab$ it lies in a three-cover of the
four missing edges, and the original-product charge applies.

Otherwise $C,M_j$ are both nonsingleton old supports. In a witnessing cubic
monomial on $cd$, the factor supplying the once-chosen endpoint must be a
full singleton by Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic}. It can only be $B$. Relabel so
$B=\{c\}$ and $d$ is chosen from both $C,M_j$. Then $gCM_j$ is true on
$\{x,d\}$, since $g(\{x\})=1$. This is an independent pair in the induced
target and contradicts safety. Zero contexts cannot be the witnessing
$M_j$, so they cause no omitted case.

Every coefficient and witness allocation has now been covered. In each
possible case a full original context gives the stated global cover,
including every ambient old edge. The argument removes this exact
single-affected R1 family; it does not classify the nonraw three-high table,
R3 or other original private networks.
\end{proof}

% Complete226 inserted after full mutual comparison; original staged text preserved.
\begin{proposition}[The complete repeated R3 cover bound]
\label{prop:repeatedRthreecover}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$, where $G$ is
finite, simple and four-cycle-free, its squarefree quadratic support $H$ is
nonempty, and its four global missing edges are $xy,xz,ab,cd$. On their
endpoints assume $G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$.
Keep the exact original frame with arbitrary retained product count $K$.
Suppose its three private products and three visible private additions have
the original R3 form
\[
 g=UV,\qquad
 u=\Bigl(A+\sum_i\beta_i g_i\Bigr)
   \Bigl(B+\sum_i\gamma_i g_i\Bigr),\qquad
 f=u\Bigl(C+\sum_i\delta_i g_i\Bigr).
\]
Here $U,V,A,B,C$ are full nonzero old homogeneous linear forms, with
singletons allowed. There are $n\in\{1,2\}$ distinct original insertion
occurrences of $g$ and $m=3-n$ of $f$, and none of $u$. At least one of
$u$'s inputs is affected. If both are affected, their positive index sets
are the same one-element set. Every displayed coefficient is nonnegative,
and only actually earlier occurrences can feed an input. Preserve all
original minimum degrees, occurrence labels, coefficients, fanout,
low/context identities and retained-product incidences. Then
\[
 \vc(G)\le K+2.
\]
No retained optimality or additional ordering of cuts is assumed.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
All identities below concern Boolean supports; the original product minimum
degrees remain $2,2,3$. Write $Q=ABC$. If only one input of $u$ is affected,
exchange $A,B$ so it is the first. Depending on whether any $\delta_i$ is
positive, the full support of $f$ is $ABC\vee gBC$ or $ABC\vee gB$.
If both inputs are affected, it is $ABC\vee gC$ or $ABC\vee g$.
Thus uniformly
\[
 f=Q\vee gD,\qquad D\in\{BC,B,C,1\}.                 \tag{1}
\]
The expression $D$ is an empty product or a subproduct of at most two
\emph{listed factor occurrences} of $Q$. Repeated old forms are permitted.
The original restriction on the two affected index sets is retained;
(1) does not assert a broader circuit normalization.

Let $L_i$ be the actual direct context of the $i$th $g$ occurrence and
$M_j$ that of the $j$th $f$ occurrence. The former is old homogeneous linear
or zero, since its selected low has degree one. The latter is old linear,
scalar or zero as allowed by its actual low degree. The exact occurrence
frame is
\[
 Y=\bigvee_i gL_i\vee\bigvee_j fM_j
       \vee p g^2\vee qgf\vee r f^2.                 \tag{2}
\]
The nonnegative coefficients $p,q,r$ collect only actual distinct-occurrence
terms. In particular $p=0$ for $n=1$ and $r=0$ for $m=1$. A same-occurrence
diagonal would put the square of a nonzero linear low into squarefree
$P_2$; a quadratic low cannot enter a retained quadratic multiplication.
Distinct repeated-high squares are still present in (2). Every positive
summand is globally safe. Since the old frame vanishes on $T$, $Y$ must
witness all four target edges. Also $gf=gD$ in support, because $D$ is a
subproduct of $Q$.

We use the old-factor bound and its full-support equality case from
Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors}, and the cubic singleton/common-star facts
of Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic}. Old quadratics and cubics have at most one
missing witness; an old quartic has at most two, an induced matching. At
four-factor equality the full supports are the four distinct transversals,
with no outside vertices. The induced path target and an induced
three-matching each need eight positive affine CNF clauses; an induced
two-matching needs four. These counts follow by assigning a different
falsified clause to each maximal independent set. A valid clause cannot be
false on two such sets, whose union contains an edge. Zero factors and
constant clauses only reduce the bound.

An old support meeting both $xy$ and $xz$ contains $x$. Otherwise it
contains $y,z$, and its $H$-center with $x$ creates a four-cycle; that center
cannot be $x$ because both edges are missing from $H$. All centers in this
proof are ambient centers, even after a restriction to $T$.

\emph{Two facts about the common old prefix.}
First, the safe union $QM_1\vee QM_2$ has at most two missing witnesses
when each nonzero $M_j$ is old linear. If neither quartic has two, this is
immediate. Otherwise four-factor equality confines the three common
supports $A,B,C$ to three distinct transversals of a two-matching on $W$.
Their common intersection is empty. A witness of the other quartic must
meet all three. A pair using a vertex outside $W$ could do so only if its
other vertex lay in that empty intersection; within $W$ only the same two
edges exist. A positive scalar constituent of $M_1\vee M_2$ instead makes
$Q(M_1\vee M_2)=Q$, which has at most one witness. The bound therefore
holds for every compatible union of at most two contexts.

Second, suppose this union witnesses two edges whose endpoints $W$ induce
$2K_2$, and all nonzero $M_j$ are old linear. Then the \emph{full} supports
$A,B,C$ are three distinct two-point transversals of those edges. Here is
the required rigidity argument, including vertices outside $W$.
Each prefix factor meets both edges and so avoids at most one of their
four independent transversals. Some transversal $I$ is accepted by all
three factors. Safety forces every $M_j$ to avoid $I$. The two witnesses
force the union of the contexts to contain both vertices of $J=W\setminus I$.
Each other transversal $I'$ meets $J$ and is accepted by an actual context.
It must therefore be rejected by $Q$. The three prefix factors reject
these three transversals one each, and the rejecting factor's restriction
to $W$ is $W\setminus I'$.

Fix such a factor $F$ and a context accepting $I'$. If $z\notin W$ belonged
to $F$, it would be nonadjacent to each $t\in I'$. Indeed $F$ contains the
missing-edge mate $s$ of $t$ and the vertex $z$. Its old center $h$ would
give the four-cycle $h,s,t,z$ if $zt$ were an edge. All four vertices are
distinct: $h=t$ would make the missing edge $st$ old, and simplicity
excludes the remaining coincidences. Thus $I'\cup\{z\}$ is independent,
but satisfies $QM_j$ by choosing $z$ in $F$ and elements of $I'$ in every
other factor. This contradicts safety. Hence $F=W\setminus I'$ in full.
Doing this for all three rejecting factors proves the assertion. It does
not assert that the contexts themselves are confined.

\emph{Remove exposed highs and bound both contributions.}
The high $g$ is unsafe even on $T$. If it were safe there, its old quadratic
bound would give at most one target witness; every $g$-containing term of
(2) could supply only that edge. The remaining $QM_j$ supply at most two
by the first prefix fact. If $r>0$, the exposed $Q$ dominates those terms
and has at most one. In either event at most three targets are witnessed.
Therefore $p=0$.

If $r>0$, then $m=2,n=1$, and the exposed $f$ absorbs all its direct and
cross terms. The full support becomes
\[
 Y=Q\vee g(L_1\vee D).
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:subproductcontext} applies with the three listed
factors of $Q$, their subproduct $D$ (including the empty product), and
the one actual old-linear-or-zero $L_1$. It excludes all four targets.
Thus $r=0$ as well.

Put $L=\bigvee_i L_i$, $M=\bigvee_j M_j$. These unions need not be old
supports or available wires. The former is linear or zero, the latter
affine or zero. Equation (2) now gives
\[
 Y=QM\vee R,\qquad R=g[L\vee D(M\vee q)].             \tag{3}
\]
The terms $QM,gL,gDM$, and $gD$ when $q>0$, are globally safe. In particular
$gD$ is not assumed safe when $q=0$. If $D$ has $d\le2$ listed factors,
the bracket in (3) has at most $d+1$ linear clauses: $L$ joined to each
factor of $D$, and $L\vee M\vee q$. Hence $R$ has at most $d+3\le5$ clauses.

The first prefix fact bounds $QM$ by two target witnesses. We claim that
$R$ also has at most two in a putative four-witness output. Three of its
targets cannot include one path arm and both isolated edges, since that
induced three-matching needs eight clauses. Thus the only possible triple
is $xy,xz,ab$, after relabeling. Then $U,V$ contain $x$, so $g(\{x\})=1$.
Safety of $gL$ excludes every isolated endpoint from $L$, and $cd$ must be
witnessed by $QM$.
For $q>0$, the $ab$ witness forces $D$ true there, and $QM$'s $cd$ witness
forces $D$ true there too. Since $gD$ is safe, adjoining $x$ to an independent
accepted assignment of $D$ on the isolated vertices shows that this
restriction of $D$ is safe. It witnesses both isolated edges with at most
two clauses, a contradiction. For $q=0$ the identical argument applies to
$DM$: it is true on both edges, is safe after adjoining $x$, and has at
most $d+1\le3$ clauses. The necessary bound is four. This includes $D=1$
and all affine or zero contexts.

Consequently $QM$ and $R$ each witness exactly two targets, with disjoint
witness sets. A positive scalar constituent of $M$ would give $QM=Q$ and
at most one witness. Every nonzero actual $M_j$ is therefore now a full
old homogeneous linear context.

\emph{The two prefix-context witnesses are a matching.}
Suppose $QM$ witnesses $xy,xz$. Each individual old quartic has matching
witnesses, so $m=2,n=1$. All of $A,B,C$ contain $x$. If $QM_j$ witnesses
$xy$, then $M_j$ contains $y$ and not $x$. For each $w$ in its full support,
the monomial $x^3w$ forces $xw\in E(G)$. Any $w\ne y$ and the old center
of $y,w$ now form a four-cycle with $x$; the center cannot be $x$ because
$xy\notin H$. Thus the full context is exactly $\{y\}$. The other is
exactly $\{z\}$.
If $q=0$, $M$ vanishes on both isolated edges, which would then both be
witnesses of the sole safe old cubic $gL_1$. This is impossible. If $q>0$,
$D(\{x\})=1$ (also for the empty product), and $g$ is true on both isolated
edges since $R$ witnesses them. Safety of $gD$ and adjoining $x$ make the
restriction of $g$ to the isolated vertices a safe two-matching expression
with two clauses, again impossible. Thus the two $QM$ witnesses are an
induced matching.

\emph{Find a full actual context in a three-cover.}
Let $W$ be their endpoints. The second prefix fact makes the full $A,B,C$
three distinct transversals contained in $W$.
If $D=1$, unsafety of $g$ forces $q=0$, and $R=g(L\vee M)$. Every actual
constituent of $L,M$ is now old linear. The common-cubic lemma makes $R$'s
two target witnesses the path arms, leaving the isolated edges to $QM$.
Then $U,V$ contain $x$. A context $M_j$ witnessing an isolated edge contains
an isolated endpoint $e$, but the safe positive term $gM_j$ is true on the
independent pair $\{x,e\}$, a contradiction.

Suppose $D$ is nonempty. Its factors are full supports contained in $W$,
so it vanishes on an edge disjoint from $W$. Such a target of $R$ must be
witnessed by an actual $gL_i$.
If the two $QM$ witnesses are $ab,cd$, both path arms are disjoint from $W$.
One old cubic cannot witness both, so $n=2,m=1$. Full quartic equality for
$QM_1$ makes the full $M_1$ a transversal consisting of one endpoint of
each isolated edge. Together with $x$ it lies in a three-cover $Z$ of all
four global missing edges.

The other matching case is $xy,ab$, after relabeling. The remaining $cd$
is disjoint from $W$ and must be witnessed by an actual $UVL_i$.
Since $R$ also witnesses $xz$, both $U,V$ meet that edge. Neither is a full
singleton endpoint of $cd$. In a witnessing cubic monomial on $cd$, the
factor supplying the once-chosen endpoint is a full singleton. It must
therefore be $L_i$, equal to $\{c\}$ or $\{d\}$ in full. This actual context
lies in the three-cover consisting of that endpoint, $x$, and one endpoint
of $ab$. These are all matching pairs among the four targets.

In each surviving case a full nonzero actual context $D_0$, one of $L_i$
or $M_j$, is contained in such a three-cover $Z$. Its selected low has
degree one: this is automatic for $g$, and for $f$ follows from its linear
rather than scalar context. At least one original retained multiplication
is reached from the insertion along selected linear paths, since the
context is nonzero and the selected output quadratic. Choose one.
Positivity puts its entire opposite old operand inside $\supp(D_0)$.
Thus $Z$ covers every old edge supplied by that original product.
Each other retained product supplies a star: its selected supports are
disjoint by squarefree $P_2$, and two nonsingleton sides would form a
four-cycle. Choose one center for each of the other $K-1$ original products.
Those centers together with $Z$ cover $H$ and all four global missing edges,
hence $G$, with at most $(K-1)+3=K+2$ vertices. Sharing and repeated centers
only decrease this count. No rewritten factor, restricted context or
new product has been charged. This proves the stated complete R3 cover
bound, leaving the other original-node and numerical possibilities open.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The original two-visible hidden-node inventory]\label{prop:twovisiblehiddeninventory}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, and let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$ with nonempty quadratic support $H$. Suppose its four global missing edges have endpoint set $T$, with $G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$. Canonical extraction and pruning delete exactly three original products and three original additions, exactly two of the latter visible. Let $K$ be the original retained multiplication count. Apply whole-current quadratic-carrier erasure and off-frame pruning, retaining the selected frame and all original degree, occurrence, fanout and low/context identities. Write $P^\ast$ for the polynomial of this current erased/pruned circuit; its Boolean output and entire quadratic part agree with those of $P$.

If $\vc(G)>K+2$, the unique surviving hidden addition $S$ is essential and has exactly one of the following descriptions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Its original inputs are a degree-one signal $A+\beta g$ and a raw original private-product output $u$ of minimum degree at least two. Here $A$ is nonzero old homogeneous linear, $g$ is the first visible high, and $\beta\ge0$ vanishes unless that first insertion is ancestral to the input. Thus $S$ has original degree pattern $(1,d)$ with $d\ge2$. It is a proper ancestor of a visible product high and cannot itself be a strict visible high. Repeated or shared raw ancestors are permitted.
\item The node $S=u+v$ is itself the second visible high, with raw original private-product operands $u,v$, and its visible parent's selected low has degree one. After pruning, $S$ has no other surviving use. Reassociating that parent from $a+(u+v)$ to $(a+u)+v$ gives an all-visible circuit with the same current polynomial $P^\ast$, quadratic frame and support $H$, retained count $K$, and no new product. The three high occurrences are the original first high, $u$ and $v$; coincident nodes or values remain distinct occurrences.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, two original degree-one inputs to the hidden addition are excluded. Two private-product inputs are excluded except for the exact second-high reassociation in the second alternative. Neither remaining alternative is asserted to be impossible, and no complete all-visible classification is assumed.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
We keep original minimum degrees throughout the support calculations. The one arithmetic reassociation is identified explicitly at the end.

\emph{Essentiality and boundary types.}
Use only the whole-current carrier stage of Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductnormal}: a protected carrier includes a restored degree-two cut on an addition-only output path, and its entire current value is erased at an off-carrier use. No old quadratic part is subtracted from that value. If a deleted addition became dispensable, Proposition~\ref{prop:threeproductstwosums} would exclude the remaining at-most-three-product/two-addition circuit. If a private product became dispensable, Lemmas~\ref{lem:twoproductnormal} and~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching}, restricted to one path arm and the two isolated edges, would exclude the resulting three-matching function. The selected frame still supplies every old edge and positivity preserves safety. Thus all six private gates, in particular $S$, remain essential.

Write the exact two-visible contribution as
\[
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf,\qquad q\in\{0,1\},
\]
with the actual old linear, scalar or zero contexts and their original identities. On $T$ the selected quadratic carrier vanishes, so $Y|_T$ is precisely the edge function of $P_3\sqcup2K_2$. Its eight maximal independent sets require eight distinct positive linear clauses: a clause false on two distinct such sets would remain false on their union, which contains an edge. In particular, a representation with at most seven clauses is impossible. Constants and zero contexts cannot increase a clause count.

An original-node induction now supplies the boundary types. Before the first visible cut a degree-one boundary is old homogeneous linear. Afterwards its full current form is $A+\beta g$, with $A$ the nonzero old selected linear part and $\beta=0$ unless the first occurrence is ancestral. Oldness follows from its selected continuation to an original quadratic product with a nonzero opposite linear input. A restored degree-one cut belongs to this family; a restored degree-two cut is an entire protected carrier. All other surviving off-frame nodes are the three original private products and $S$. Hence a visible high is a private-product output or $S$, and the two operands of $S$ are degree-one signals or raw private-product outputs. A zero operand would make $S$ dispensable. An original degree-one signal cannot be a strict visible high.

\emph{Two degree-one inputs.}
If $S$ is ancestral to the first high, both inputs are old and Proposition~\ref{prop:earlierhiddenlinearpreparation} applies. Otherwise put
\[
 S=R\vee\gamma g,\qquad R=C\vee D,\quad \gamma\in\{0,1\},
\]
at support level, with $C,D$ old. Each affected boundary retains the genuine first low. The first high is a multiplication-only old-boundary network; let $k$ be the number of its distinct original private-product ancestors, including itself. Then $k=1$ or $2$: the essential later degree-one $S$ must reach a distinct product high $f$.

For $k=1$, write $g=UV$. At most two further private products produce $f$, so their support has at most three boundary factors after removal of repeated factors only. The possible boundaries are old or actual affected old wires, the raw prepared wire $S$, and raw $g$. If a raw $g$ occurs, then on $g=1$ every affected factor becomes $1$, and
\[
 f=gF,\qquad Y=g\bigl[L\vee F(M\vee q)\bigr],
\]
where $F$ has at most two linear-clause factors. This gives at most five clauses.

If raw $g$ does not occur, repeated uses of $S$ reduce to one support factor. With no affected coefficient, Proposition~\ref{prop:pathpurelineargeneral} applies. With two remaining factors, the affected-preparation alternatives are exactly Proposition~\ref{prop:oldproductlaterlinearsum}, and the opposite affected placement is Proposition~\ref{prop:unaffectedlaterpreparation}. With three factors, one prepared base and two old bases, any affected coefficient gives Proposition~\ref{prop:laterthreefactorpreparation}. Their common-low hypotheses are inherited from the actual original occurrences. These cases include a square of an intermediate product, because repetition changes the support list but not the original ledger.

If only the prepared factor remains, $f=R$ is again the unaffected case. For $f=R\vee g$, and more generally for $g$ with $r\le3$ old factors, the exact identities are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 q=0:&\quad Y=g(L\vee M)\vee RM=(g\vee RM)(L\vee M),\\
 q=1:&\quad Y=g\vee RM.
 \end{aligned}
\]
They use at most $2r+1\le7$ or $2r\le6$ clauses. This treats a repeated prepared wire without reducing its original arithmetic degree.

For $k=2$, let $h=UV$ be the first product. Then $g=hZ$ with $Z$ old, or $g=h^2$; in support the latter permits $Z=1$. The sole remaining product $f$ has raw $S$ as an input. An old/affected other input or a second $S$ is covered by the preceding two-factor and repeated-factor cases, now with $r\le3$. For the raw $g$ input, $f=g(R\vee\gamma g)$ gives either $f=g$, or
\[
 Y=g\bigl[L\vee R(M\vee q)\bigr],
\]
with at most five clauses. For raw $h$, the exact support expression is
\[
 Y=h\bigl[ZL\vee RM\vee\gamma ZM\vee qZR\vee q\gamma Z\bigr].
\]
For $(\gamma,q)=(0,0)$ the bracket is the union of two two-clause products, with at most four clauses. For $(0,1)$ it is
$(Z\vee M)(R\vee ZL)$, with at most three. For $(1,0)$ it is $Z(L\vee M)\vee RM$, with at most four. For $(1,1)$ it is $Z\vee RM$, with at most two. Adding the two factors of $h$ leaves at most six. Thus all degree-one/degree-one hidden inputs are excluded, including shared raw ancestors and repeated products.

\emph{One input of each type.}
If just one input has degree one, the boundary induction gives exactly $A+\beta g$ and a raw private product $u$ of degree at least two. The hidden sum has degree one, so cannot be a strict high. Since it is essential, its surviving route must reach a visible product high. A selected degree-one trace reaching this unequal $S$ would make it a visible deleted cut, contrary to its hidden status; an off-frame whole quadratic carrier has been erased. Thus it is a proper ancestor as asserted in the first alternative. No further exclusion of this family is used.

\emph{Two product inputs, neither being the second-high case.}
Write $S=u+v$. Coincident inputs, or inputs related by a raw multiplication-only descent, permit a support bypass by the smaller-degree ancestor: the descendant implies the ancestor and their sum has the ancestor's original minimum degree. This preserves the selected frame and Boolean output and makes an addition dispensable, contradicting Proposition~\ref{prop:threeproductstwosums}. This absorption is not inferred from ancestry through an affected degree-one boundary. If $S$ is the first high itself, Proposition~\ref{prop:firsthiddenproductjoin} applies.

Suppose $S$ is neither visible high. Its useful output passes through a private product $w$ before reaching a high. The distinct nodes $u,v,w$ exhaust the private-product budget.

First let the first high be $w$. Before that cut, all private boundaries are old or raw. After the preceding absorption, $u=AB$ and $v=CD$ are independent old quadratics, and
\[
 w=(u\vee v)Z,\qquad Z\in\{\text{an old form},u,v,S\}.
\]
The second high is $u,v$ or $w$. For repeated high $w$, the output is $w(L\vee M\vee qw)$, with at most six clauses: $u\vee v$ has four clauses, and an old $Z$ adds one; the raw choices only shorten this count. For second high $u$ and old $Z$, the output is
\[
 vZL\vee u(ZL\vee M\vee qZ).
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:subproductcontext} applies with $Q=vZL$, quadratic $u$, old context $M$, and the listed subproduct $ZL$ for $q=0$ or $Z$ for $q=1$. Scalars omit a factor; if $Q=0$, the remaining expression has at most five clauses directly. The second-high $v$ case is symmetric. For $Z=u$ or $v$, the first high reduces in support to one of those quadratics, so the repeated-high bound or Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching} applies. For $Z=S$, the first high has support $S$ and the second-high $u$ expression is
\[
 vL\vee u(L\vee M\vee q).
\]
Use Proposition~\ref{prop:subproductcontext} with $Q=vL$ and subproduct $L$ when $q=0$; for $q=1$ its other context may be $1$. Zero $Q$ is again immediate. These are pure algebraic applications, with no exchange of chronological low identities.

Now let the first high be $u$, the $v$ case being symmetric. Raw comparability is already excluded. Thus $u=UV$ is old quadratic and
\[
 v=(A\vee\varepsilon u)(B\vee\delta u),\qquad S=u\vee AB,
\]
with actual old/affected boundaries. The third product $w=SZ$ must be the second high, and $Z$ is an old/affected boundary $C\vee\eta u$, or raw $u,v,S$. For old $C$, Corollary~\ref{cor:hiddenquadraticjoin} applies. For $Z=C\vee u$, one has $w=u\vee ABC$ and
\[
 Y=ABCM\vee u(L\vee M\vee q),
\]
which is Proposition~\ref{prop:subproductcontext} with the occurrence-subproduct $M$, using context $1$ when $q=1$. Scalars and zero $M$ are included. For $Z=u$, the repeated high has a short clause representation. For $Z=v$, $w=v$ in support and the displayed $u,v$ form is exactly Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching}; this does not change the original gate count or degree of $w$. For $Z=S$, use the same subproduct argument with $Q=ABM$. This exhausts the original product-input placements in which $S$ is neither high.

\emph{A second-high hidden join has no other use.}
The only remaining placement is that $S$ is the second visible high. If it had another surviving use, that use would pass through a private product $w$ and reach the first high; a return to $S$ would be a cycle. Again $u,v,w$ exhaust the products. Before the first cut, coincident or raw comparable inputs are removed as above, and otherwise $u,v$ are independent old quadratics. The first high is $w=SZ$, with $Z$ old, $u$, $v$ or $S$, and
\[
 Y=S\bigl[ZL\vee M\vee qZ\bigr].
\]
For old $Z$, the bracket has at most two clauses, giving at most six with $S$. For raw $u$ or $v$, it has at most three clauses when $q=0$ and two when $q=1$, giving at most seven. For $Z=S$, the support is $S(L\vee M\vee qS)$ and at most five clauses suffice. Thus no such additional use survives. Fanout from the visible parent remains unrestricted; the claim concerns the hidden node $S$ itself.

\emph{The second selected low and exact reassociation.}
Its selected low has original degree one or two. If it had degree two, both $u,v$ would have degree at least three. Apart from already removed raw comparable or coincident inputs, two such products within a three-product budget must share the remaining initial old quadratic $h=UV$ as a raw operand. Indeed two old or affected degree-one inputs would give degree two. Thus $u=hA$ and $v=hB$, allowing a raw $h$ in place of either degree-one boundary.

If the first high is $h$, every affected $h$-boundary becomes $1$ on $h=1$, as does a raw $h$ factor. Hence $S=hR$ for a positive linear clause $R$ or $1$, and
\[
 Y=h\bigl[L\vee RM\vee qR\bigr]
\]
has at most four clauses. If the first high is $u$, write $u=hX$ with $X$ old or $1$. The other product is $h(B\vee\beta u)$, or has raw $h$ as its second operand. Combining it with $u$ gives $S=hR$, with $X\le R$ and $R$ a positive linear clause or $1$. In particular, this explicitly includes ancestry through the affected boundary; it does not assert $S=u$. Now
\[
 Y=h\bigl[XL\vee RM\vee qXR\bigr].
\]
For $q=0$ the bracket has at most four clauses, and for $q=1$ it is $X\vee RM$, with at most two. Thus at most six suffice. The first-high $v$ case is symmetric. The remaining raw descendant is the previously excluded raw-comparability case. A degree-two selected low is therefore impossible.

The surviving parent is $a+(u+v)$ with $\deg(a)=1$ and $\deg(u),\deg(v)\ge2$. The hidden node has no other surviving use, so rewire these same two addition nodes to compute
\[
 a+(u+v)=(a+u)+v.
\]
This is an exact arithmetic identity. Both new additions are visible strict degree-one cuts and select the same original low contribution. The full current polynomial $P^\ast$, every other surviving use, the selected quadratic frame and $K$ are unchanged; no product is added. This last arithmetic reassociation does not claim that the preceding carrier erasure preserved the higher terms of the pre-erasure polynomial $P$. Together with the original first cut they give three visible deleted additions, retaining $g,u,v$ as occurrences even when nodes or values coincide. This proves the second alternative.

The two alternatives have different original minimum degrees and are disjoint. The original input types and all possible placements have been exhausted; only the asserted unequal hidden family or exact transfer to an all-visible circuit remains.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[An old factor after an earlier unequal preparation]\label{prop:earlierunequaloldfactor}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, and let a positive
variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$ with nonempty quadratic
support $H$. Suppose exactly four edges are missing from $H$, their
endpoint set $T$ satisfies $G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$, and $H[T]=\varnothing$.
Canonical extraction and pruning delete exactly three original products
and three original additions, exactly two additions being visible.
Keep the original quadratic frame and its $K$ retained products.

After whole-current-carrier erasure and off-frame pruning, suppose the
unique hidden addition and the first chronological visible high have
the literal surviving original-node inputs
\[
 u=UV,\qquad S=C+u,\qquad g=SZ,
\]
where $U,V,C,Z$ are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms and $u,g$ are
distinct original product nodes. Each identity specifies the two actual
input wires; it is not merely a factorization of a Boolean function.
Repeated forms and wires, positive coefficient multiplicities, and all
original degrees, occurrences, fanout, low/context and product-incidence
identities are retained. There is no further restriction on the third
private product or second visible high. Then
\[
 \vc(G)\le K+2.
\]
This does not classify a first high $S*S$, a preparation with a longer
raw-product input, or another unequal-hidden placement.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Assume $\vc(G)>K+2$. Use the whole-current-carrier erasure with the exact
original frame preserved: every nonprotected use of an original
minimum-degree-two carrier having an addition-only output route is
erased as a whole, including higher terms and restored degree-two cuts.
No old quadratic part is subtracted from a current carrier. If a private
product disappeared, Corollary~\ref{cor:threedeletedproducts} would be
contradicted on either path arm together with the two isolated edges.
If a private addition disappeared, Proposition~\ref{prop:threeproductstwosums}
would be contradicted. Thus all three original private products and
additions survive. Temporary zeros are removed, and the nonzero
unchanged $P_2$ leaves a variable-input circuit.

\emph{The actual boundary inventory.}
Write $f$ for the third original product. It cannot be a surviving
ancestor of $u,S,g$ through $U,V,C,Z$: those actual input values are
homogeneous linear, whereas a positive product contributes degree at
least two. This concerns the stipulated current original wires, not a
general ancestry-preservation assertion for erased branches.
The first high has original degree two, so its strict visible cut is
$c_1=a+g$ with a nonzero old degree-one low $a$.
The hidden $S$ cannot lie on a selected degree-one path, for that would
make its selected low occurrence visible. Before $c_1$ a retained
linear signal is therefore old homogeneous linear; between the two
visible cuts it has the form
\[
 A+\alpha g,\qquad \alpha\ge0,
\]
where $A$ is a nonzero old homogeneous linear form and
$\alpha>0$ implies $a\subseteq A$. This follows by tracing its retained
addition-only computation: there is no other hidden sum and no earlier
visible insertion. A raw use of $S$ cannot acquire an additional
private sum, and whole quadratic carriers have already been erased
at their nonprotected uses.

The second visible high must be $f$. A useful path from $f$ must enter
the selected frame through a visible cut; an equal-degree quadratic
entry would instead retain that product. It cannot enter through $S$
or $c_1$, since neither their stipulated high inputs nor the old first
low depend on $f$. There is no other private sum or product to carry
$f$ into a different high. A degree-one retained carrier cannot be a
strict high, and a retained quadratic carrier has no surviving
nonprotected use. Hence the second cut has the original $f$ as high,
even if its Boolean value agrees with another original node.
In particular that cut cannot be an ancestor of $f$.

Consequently each actual operand of $f$ is either a retained or
first-cut degree-one value $A+\alpha g$, or a raw reference to $S,u,g$.
These four types exhaust the original inputs; no new factorization or
reordering of the cuts is used. The two-occurrence frame is
\[
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf,\qquad q\in\{0,1\},
\]
with actual old-linear or zero $L$ and compatible old-linear, scalar or
zero $M$. The first low satisfies $aL\subseteq H$, and $q=1$ implies
the actual inclusion $a\subseteq M$. Every affected base contains the
same $a$. A same-occurrence square in a retained product would put the
nonzero low square in $P_2$, which is impossible. Distinct high nodes
with equal Boolean values still retain their separate occurrences
and cross term.

The contribution $Y$ is globally safe and supplies all four missing
witnesses, so $Y|_T$ is the path-plus-two-edge function. It needs eight
positive linear clauses. In Boolean notation only,
\[
 S=(C\vee U)(C\vee V),\qquad g=ZS;
\]
thus $S$ has at most two clauses and $g$ at most three, including the old
factor $Z$. These identities do not change the original degrees of
$u,S,g$. Zero or scalar contexts only simplify the clause bounds below.

\emph{Two degree-one operands.}
Suppose $f=(A\vee\alpha g)(B\vee\beta g)$, with positive coefficients
replaced by their support indicators. If $\alpha+\beta>0$,
Proposition~\ref{prop:threeclauseoldfactor} applies with
$D_1=C\vee U$ and $D_2=C\vee V$. Its old factor $Z$ and every genuine
affected-base/first-low identity are present, giving $\vc(G)\le K+2$.
If $\alpha=\beta=0$, apply Proposition~\ref{prop:independentquadraticpreparation}
with its quadratic high equal to our $f=AB$, its internal old quadratic
equal to $u$, and its prepared high equal to our $g$. Its two formal
high labels and actual contexts are exchanged; that support statement
has no chronological ordering condition on the two labels. No physical
cut is moved. It again gives the required bound.

\emph{One raw operand and one degree-one operand.}
For $f=u(A\vee\alpha g)$,
Proposition~\ref{prop:rawancestorunequalpreparation} applies directly,
including the actual common-low identity when $\alpha>0$.
For $f=S(A\vee\alpha g)$, use $Sg=g$. At $\alpha=0$,
\[
 Y=S[ZL\vee AM\vee qZA].
\]
The bracket has at most four clauses when $q=0$; when $q=1$ it equals
$(Z\vee A)(Z\vee M)(L\vee A)$.
At $\alpha>0$, one has $f=SA\vee g$ and $gf=g$, so
\[
 Y=S[Z(L\vee M\vee q)\vee AM].
\]
Its bracket has at most four clauses. Both cases give at most six
clauses in total, a contradiction.
For $f=gA$,
\[
 Y=g[L\vee A(M\vee q)]
\]
has at most five clauses. For $f=g(A\vee g)=g$, the expression
$g(L\vee M\vee q)$ has at most four. These are support calculations,
not mergers of original product nodes.

\emph{Both operands raw.}
The six unordered pairs from $S,u,g$, including repeated wires, remain.
For $(S,S)$, $f$ is Booleanly $S$ and
\[
 Y=S[M\vee Z(L\vee q)],
\]
with at most four clauses. The pairs $(S,g)$ and $(g,g)$ make $f$
Booleanly $g$, yielding $g(L\vee M\vee q)$, again at most four clauses.
For $(u,g)$, use $uS=u$ to obtain
\[
 Y=Z[CL\vee UV(L\vee M\vee q)].
\]
Inside the bracket, a product of two linear clauses is joined to a
product of three. Distributivity gives at most six clauses there,
and the external $Z$ gives at most seven, still a contradiction.

Finally, $(S,u)$ and $(u,u)$ make $f$ Booleanly $u$, and
\[
 Y=ZCL\vee u[M\vee ZL\vee qZ].
\]
If $L=0$, at most three clauses suffice. Otherwise let $Q=ZCL$ with
its three listed old factor occurrences. At $q=0$ put $F=ZL$, a
subproduct of the listed $Z,L$ occurrences; at $q=1$ put $F=Z$.
Then $Y=Q\vee u(M\vee F)$, and
Proposition~\ref{prop:subproductcontext} excludes all four witnesses.
Repeated forms preserve the specified occurrence membership. The
actual scalar or zero $M$ is allowed in that proposition.

All ten unordered pairs of the four original operand types have now
been treated. Each is impossible or gives $\vc(G)\le K+2$. No additional
gate was introduced, no original square was reassigned a lower
arithmetic degree, and no context was replaced by a restricted-support
surrogate. The conclusion concerns only the stated literal original
$u,S,g$ branch.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A squared unequal preparation]\label{prop:squaredunequalpreparation}
Let $N$ be either $3K_2$ or $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ on its full vertex set $T$. Work with Boolean supports of nonnegative homogeneous linear forms on $T$, allowing zero forms. Put
\[
 u=UV,\qquad s=C\vee u.
\]
Let $f$ be the product of two operands, each equal to $u$, $s$, or $A\vee\alpha s$, where the two linear bases $A$ and the flags $\alpha\in\{0,1\}$ may differ. Repeated operands are allowed. For arbitrary nonnegative affine linear Boolean forms $L,M$, including $0,1$, and $q\in\{0,1\}$, the expression
\[
 Y=sL\vee fM\vee qsf
\]
cannot equal the edge function of $N$.

Consequently, let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$, where $G$ is finite, simple and four-cycle-free, with nonempty squarefree quadratic support $H$ and exactly four global missing edges. Suppose there are exactly three original private products and three original private additions, exactly two visible, and an induced set $T$ with $H[T]=\varnothing$ and $G[T]$ one of the two stated target graphs. After whole-current-carrier erasure and off-frame pruning preserving the original selected quadratic frame, the sole hidden addition and first visible high cannot have the literal surviving inputs
\[
 u=UV,\qquad S=C+u,\qquad g=S*S,
\]
where $U,V,C$ are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms, $u,g$ are distinct original products, and both input occurrences of $g$ are the same original $S$ wire. This excludes the exact branch with arbitrary third product and second visible high, independently of the retained count $K$. It does not classify longer raw inputs to $S$, a different first-high product, or arbitrary unequal hidden sums.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A product of $k$ affine linear Boolean forms has at most $k$ positive CNF clauses. A matching of $m$ edges requires at least $2^m$: each valid clause meets every edge pair and can reject at most one of the $2^m$ maximal independent transversals. In particular two edges require four clauses and three require eight. It suffices to prove the local assertion for $3K_2$, because setting one path leaf to zero in $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ preserves all operand types and leaves a three-matching. Restricted homogeneous forms may vanish, as permitted in the statement.

If $C=0$, then $s=u=UV$ and the allowed $f$ operands give exactly the linear, affected, raw and repeated-raw forms of Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching}. Its affine-context obstruction applies, including vanishing bases and all $q$ cases.

Suppose $C\ne0$. If $L=0$, factor
\[
 Y=f(M\vee qs).
\]
Each of the two $f$ operands has at most two clauses:
\[
 s=(C\vee U)(C\vee V),\qquad
 A\vee s=(A\vee C\vee U)(A\vee C\vee V),
\]
and raw $u$ also has two. The final factor $M\vee qs$ has at most two. Thus six clauses suffice, contradicting the three-matching target. Zero, unit and repeated factors do not increase this count.

Now $L\ne0$. The positive term $CL$ is safe. A positive constant in $L$ would accept a singleton from $C$, so $L$ has no constant. Choose $c\in\supp(C)$, and let $d$ be its matching mate. Every variable in $L$ must be $d$, or $CL$ accepts a singleton or an independent pair. Conversely every variable in $C$ must be $c$. Hence, at support level,
\[
 C=c,\qquad L=d,\qquad s=c\vee u.
\]
Call the other matching edges $ab,ef$. The term $ud$ is safe. On the restriction $c=0,d=1$, the resulting two-clause product $u$ is a subfunction of the two-edge matching on $a,b,e,f$. It cannot witness both remaining edges, since then positivity and safety would make it that matching, which requires four clauses. By monotonicity, $u$ is therefore false on at least one of the original edge pairs with $c=d=0$, say $ef$.

On that pair $s=L=0$, so $fM$ must supply the witness. Neither input of $f$ can be raw $u$ or raw $s$, since both vanish there. Both inputs must be nonraw forms $A\vee\alpha s$. Restrict instead to $c=1,d=0$. Now $s=1,L=0$, each such input becomes an affine linear form or $1$, and
\[
 Y=f(M\vee q)
\]
has at most three clauses. The target on $a,b,e,f$ is still the two-edge matching, requiring four. This proves the complete local assertion, including all scalar, zero and flag choices.

For the circuit consequence use only the general whole-carrier stage of Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductnormal}: protect the full current value of every original minimum-degree-two node with an addition-only output path, including restored cut outputs, and erase the entire current carrier on its off-frame uses. This preserves Boolean output, $P_2$ and the original selected frame. No higher part is subtracted separately. If a private product became dispensable, Corollary~\ref{cor:threedeletedproducts} on an induced three-matching would give a contradiction. If a private addition became dispensable, Proposition~\ref{prop:threeproductstwosums} would contradict the four global missing edges. Thus all three products and additions remain essential.

The stipulated old homogeneous forms $U,V,C$ and literal input chain $u,S,g$ leave no entry for the third private product as a surviving ancestor. The two inputs of $g$ are already the stipulated $S$ wire. A visible high is a private-product output in this particular current circuit: a degree-one signal cannot be a strict high; $S$ has minimum degree one; full quadratic carriers and restored degree-two cut outputs have been erased on such uses; and there is no other private addition. Retained higher-degree nodes cannot belong to the degree-two selected frame. The second high must therefore be the third product, denoted $f$. Otherwise that product would have to feed $u,S,g$ or another private route into a visible cut to be useful, all excluded by the literal input wires and the exhausted gate budget. A direct equal-degree selected quadratic entry would retain it; a higher entry is itself a visible cut. Repetition of $u$ or $g$ as the second high would consequently leave the third product dispensable.

The original minimum degree of $g=S*S$ is two, so its first selected low has degree one. A selected degree-one trace reaching the unequal $S$ would make $S$ a visible deleted cut, contrary to its hidden status. With no other hidden addition, every retained degree-one additive path feeding $f$ therefore has exact form $A+\alpha g$, with a nonzero old homogeneous linear selected part $A$. A raw occurrence of $S$ inside such a retained sum would expose $S$; an extra private sum would exceed the three-addition budget. Raw $u$ has no insertion occurrence, so cannot enter a degree-one retained signal without a further visible cut. The second cut cannot precede its own high. After whole-carrier erasure the complete original list of possible $f$ inputs is consequently
\[
 \text{raw }u,\quad\text{raw }S,\quad\text{raw }g,
       \quad A+\alpha g.
\]
All original coefficients, degrees, occurrences, fanout and low/context incidences remain fixed.

Expand the selected frame in its two original insertion symbols. Its old part is $P_2$, and the other terms are $gL\vee fM\vee qgf$. Diagonal terms are excluded by squarefreeness of $P_2$, not merely by the number of symbols: fanout of a degree-one selected low into both sides of a retained product would also contribute its nonzero square to $P_2$, including a positive diagonal monomial. A degree-two low cannot enter a retained quadratic multiplication at all. Thus both diagonal coefficients vanish; all distinct-occurrence cross data remain.

At Boolean support level only, both raw $S$ and raw $g$ have value $s=C\vee UV$, while raw $u$ has value $u$. Their different original nodes, degrees and input occurrences are not identified. The displayed original-input list gives exactly the local algebraic operand list, and actual direct contexts are compatible linear, scalar or zero forms. On $T$, the old $P_2$ vanishes and the remaining function is the edge function of $G[T]$. The local assertion contradicts this. No retained-count estimate or more general hidden-input normalization is used.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[An alias first high in an unequal preparation]\label{prop:unequalaliasfirst}
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph without a four-cycle, and let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$ with nonempty squarefree quadratic support $H$ and exactly four edges outside $H$. Suppose an $H$-independent vertex set $T$ induces either $3K_2$ or $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ in $G$. Keep the exact original selected quadratic frame. Suppose exactly three original products and three original additions are private, exactly two of the additions being visible.

After full-current quadratic-carrier erasure and pruning, suppose the sole hidden addition has literal surviving inputs
\[
 u=UV,\qquad S=C+u,
\]
where $U,V,C$ are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms and $u$ is an original private product. Suppose the first visible high is a second distinct original product with literal inputs
\[
 g=Su\qquad\text{or}\qquad g=u^2,
\]
where the two occurrences in $u^2$ are the same original wire. Then this branch is impossible. The third private product and the second visible high are initially unrestricted. The conclusion allows arbitrary retained counts, a first selected low of degree two, all compatible scalar or zero contexts, fanout and repeated operands. All original node, degree, occurrence and low/context data are retained; the Boolean identity $g=u$ does not change the original minimum degree three or four of $g$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Choose an induced three-edge matching $R\subseteq T$: for the path shape use either path arm and the two isolated edges. In both cases $H[R]$ is empty. Full-current carrier erasure, as proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductnormal}, preserves the Boolean output, the exact quadratic part $P_2$ and the entire original selected frame. Its protected set includes every original minimum-degree-two node having an addition-only output path, including restored cuts and full carriers with higher terms. Erase the entire current values only on their nonprotected uses.

All three private products remain useful, since losing one would contradict Corollary~\ref{cor:threedeletedproducts} on $R$. All three private additions also remain useful: otherwise Proposition~\ref{prop:threeproductstwosums} would apply to the unchanged nonempty $H$ and four global missing edges. These are statements about the actual erased and pruned circuit, before any Boolean alias is used.

Call the remaining private product $f$, and the two visible cuts $t_1,t_2$ in their original topological order, with first high $g$. No surviving path from $f$ can enter the homogeneous linear inputs $U,V,C$: positivity and the minimum degree at least two of a product exclude such a contribution. The stipulated literal inputs therefore exclude every surviving path from $f$ to $u,S,g$. This does not assert that erasure generally preserves an ancestry relation on a removed carrier route.

We next identify the second high, rather than assuming it is $f$. A useful private product must reach the selected frame through an unequal-degree cut. Direct entry into a selected degree-one position is impossible; an equal-degree entry into a selected quadratic addition would select and retain the product. The node $f$ cannot enter through the fixed $S$ or the fixed high $g$. It cannot enter the selected low of $t_1$ without being retained or passing through an earlier unequal cut; the only earlier private addition available for that purpose would be $S$, which cannot depend on $f$. Thus $f$ must reach the high of $t_2$. There is no later private product on this route, since neither $u$ nor $g$ depends on $f$, and no intervening private addition is available. A retained degree-one node cannot carry $f$ before a cut. A retained quadratic carrier cannot provide an alternative: an equal-degree selected route would retain $f$, a higher-degree entry would be another private cut, and off-carrier uses have been erased. Hence the second high is exactly the original node $f$. In particular $t_2$ is not ancestral to its own high, and the second high cannot instead repeat $u$ or $g$ or be an unresolved sum.

The selected low of $t_1$ has degree one or two. If it has degree one, its current value is an old homogeneous linear form $a$. A selected degree-one trace reaching $S=C+u$ would select $C$ and make $S$ visible, contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore before $f$ every retained degree-one boundary has the form
\[
 E=A+\lambda g,\qquad \lambda\ge0,
\]
where $A$ is its nonzero old selected linear form; a positive coefficient records an actual path from the first insertion. There is no separate raw-$u$ contribution without another unequal cut, no direct selected $S$ contribution while $S$ remains hidden, and no contribution from $t_2$ before its own high $f$. Fanout changes only the coefficient.

If the first selected low instead has degree two, the full output of $t_1$ is a protected quadratic carrier: its selected route to the quadratic output contains only additions. Its entire off-carrier uses have been erased, so it cannot supply an operand of $f$. The retained degree-one boundaries before $f$ are then unaffected old forms, and the displayed formula has $\lambda=0$. Raw fanout from the different node $g$ remains possible. The insertion through $t_1$ has a scalar direct context; its quadratic low is never relabeled as linear.

This gives the complete actual operand census for $f$. An operand cannot be a retained quadratic carrier, whose off-carrier use is erased. An input variable or retained degree-one source is of type $E$ above. Among private additions only the literal $S$ is a further source: a linear $t_1$ is already included in $E$, a quadratic $t_1$ is unavailable, and $t_2$ cannot precede $f$. The only earlier private product sources are the raw nodes $u,g$. Thus each operand is one of
\[
 A+\lambda g,\qquad S=C+u,\qquad u,\qquad g.
\]
Separate linear boundaries may have different bases and coefficients, and all ten unordered pairs, including repeated sources, are covered. Actual chronology can remove possibilities from this list but cannot add a source type. When $g=u^2$, usefulness additionally requires $f$ to read $S$, since $S$ has no other surviving exit; this refinement is not needed below.

Give the two original visible occurrences independent high symbols before substituting their dependencies. The exact output frame is
\[
 P_2+gL+fM+qgf,
\]
with the actual nonnegative affine direct contexts $L,M$ and nonnegative cross coefficient $q$. A degree-two selected low contributes only a scalar direct context and has no retained-product cross term. For a degree-one insertion, using its own occurrence in both operands of a retained product would put the square of its nonzero selected low in the squarefree $P_2$, so no same-occurrence square occurs. This argument keeps all distinct-occurrence cross terms and the full current carriers; it does not discard a higher term merely because its quadratic part vanishes.

Now, only in Boolean supports, put $b=UV$. Both stipulated high expressions satisfy
\[
 (C\vee b)b=b,\qquad b^2=b.
\]
The four possible operand types of $f$ consequently become $A\vee\lambda b$, $C\vee b$, $b$, and $b$. Their products belong to the six forms of Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching}: two ordinary or affected linear factors, a raw $b$ times an ordinary or affected factor, or $b^2$. Zero recursive coefficients, repeated factors and positive scalar multiples are included. In particular two raw $S$ inputs remain an allowed affected-product representation; no original degree is reset by simplifying its support.

Restrict outside $R$ to zero. The original $P_2$ vanishes and the output must be the three-edge matching function. It now has a support representation
\[
 bL+tM+qbt,
\]
where $t$ is one of those six forms and the restricted ordinary linear forms may vanish. Lemma~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching}, with its optional square coefficients zero and its arbitrary affine contexts, gives a contradiction. This is an algebraic support application: the original circuit still has the three distinct products $u,g,f$, with their original degrees and occurrences. No gate is merged or recounted. The argument never uses an optimality assumption on the retained frame.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A raw cubic beside an unequal preparation]\label{prop:rawcubicunequalpreparation}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\operatorname{Sup}(G)$, where $G$ is finite, simple and four-cycle-free. Let its nonempty quadratic support be $H$, and suppose its four global missing edges are $xy,xz,ab,cd$, on an endpoint set $T$ with $G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$. Keep the original quadratic frame and its $K$ retained products. Suppose exactly three original products and three original additions are deleted, exactly two additions are visible, and after whole-current-carrier erasure and pruning the unique hidden addition and first chronological visible high have the literal original input wires
\[
 u=UV,\qquad S=C+u,\qquad g=uA,
\]
where $U,V,C,A$ are nonzero old homogeneous linear forms and $u,g$ are distinct original private products. Repeated forms and wires are allowed. There is no further hypothesis on the third product or second high, and no extra ordering of $S$ relative to the first visible cut. No such circuit exists, for any retained multiplication count $K$.
All original minimum degrees, occurrences, coefficients, fanout and low/context incidences remain fixed; no optimality of the retained circuit is assumed.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
We first derive the complete original input list. Every private product is indispensable: losing one in a frame-preserving reduction contradicts Lemmas~\ref{lem:twoproductmatching} and~\ref{lem:twoproductnormal} on an induced three-matching inside $T$. Every private addition is indispensable by Proposition~\ref{prop:threeproductstwosums}. Whole-current-carrier erasure protects the full current values of original minimum-degree-two nodes with addition-only output paths, including restored cut outputs, and erases their off-frame occurrences entirely. It does not subtract only their quadratic parts.

Let $f$ be the third private product. The literal old inputs $U,V,C,A$ and the specified wires of $u,S,g$ leave no surviving entry for $f$ into those nodes. The hidden $S$ has minimum degree one. It cannot itself be a strict high, and any selected degree-one trace reaching it makes $S$ a visible deleted unequal cut, contrary to its hidden status. The same observation excludes its entry into a selected low or retained linear addition path. No other hidden sum is available, and off-frame quadratic-carrier uses are erased. Since $S$ is indispensable, it must therefore feed a private product directly; the fixed inputs of $u,g$ leave only $f$. Thus a literal input of $f$ is $S$.

A surviving useful path from $f$ must first enter the quadratic frame through a visible high. An equal-degree selected entry would retain the product; a higher-degree additive entry is a cut. There is no remaining private node that can carry $f$ to $u,S,g$, and protected carrier escapes have been erased. The first high is the specified $g$, so the second high must be $f$. If it instead repeated $u$ or $g$, the third product would have no surviving use. These are statements about original nodes, not about possible coincidences of their Boolean values.

The other input of $f$ is now raw $u$, raw $g$, raw $S$, or a retained degree-one value. A selected degree-one boundary has nonzero old baseline $B$ and can carry only the earlier visible insertion $g$; an uncut $S$ term would make $S$ visible, and a further private sum is unavailable. Thus its full value is $B+\alpha g$, with $\alpha\ge0$. If the first selected low has degree two, its whole cut-output carrier is erased off-frame, so only $\alpha=0$ is possible. In particular we never replace such a low by a linear one. The complete list is
\[
 f=Su,\qquad f=Sg,\qquad f=S^2,\qquad
 f=S(B+\alpha g).
\]
It allows repeated wires and every compatible temporal order.

The exact two-symbol frame gives, in Boolean support,
\[
 P_2\vee gL\vee fM\vee qgf,\qquad q\in\{0,1\},
\]
with the actual old linear, scalar or zero direct contexts $L,M$. Individual insertion-square coefficients vanish because a degree-one selected low feeding both sides of a retained product would produce a positive diagonal square in $P_2$; a degree-two low cannot feed such a product. This uses squarefreeness of $P_2$, not merely the number of insertion symbols. On $T$, $P_2$ vanishes, so the globally safe contribution
\[
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf
\]
must witness all four targets.

An old full support meeting both $xy$ and $xz$ contains $x$. Otherwise it contains both $y,z$, whose old $H$-center together with $x$ gives a four-cycle; the center cannot be $x$ because both path arms are missing from $H$. We also use the eight-clause lower bound for $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and for an induced three-matching. Safe summands that witness every edge on either restriction must equal its edge function there, by positivity and monotonicity.

For $f=Su$, Boolean absorption gives $f=u$ and
\[
 Y=u\bigl[AL\vee M\vee qA\bigr].
\]
For $q=0$ the bracket is $(A\vee M)(L\vee M)$, and for $q=1$ it is $A\vee M$. Including $U,V$ gives at most four clauses. For $f=Sg$, $f=g$ and $Y=g(L\vee M\vee q)$ likewise has at most four clauses. Both contradict the eight-clause target bound.

For $f=S^2$, Booleanly $f=S$. Put $L'=L\vee q$ and $D=AL'\vee M$. Since $CM$ implies $D$,
\[
 Y=uD\vee CM=(u\vee CM)D.
\]
The first factor has the four clauses
\[
 (U\vee C)(U\vee M)(V\vee C)(V\vee M),
\]
and $D=(A\vee M)(L'\vee M)$ has at most two. Thus there are at most six clauses, again impossible. These identities include scalar and zero contexts and retain all distinct original product nodes and degrees.

It remains to take $f=S(B+\alpha g)$. Let $\epsilon$ record whether $\alpha>0$. Since $ug=g$, positive expansion and Boolean absorption yield
\[
 Y=Q\vee R,\qquad Q=BCM,\qquad R=uF,
\]
where
\[
 F=AL\vee BM\vee\epsilon AM\vee qAB\vee\epsilon q A.
\]
Every displayed positive term is globally safe. The following identities hold with all zero and scalar contexts:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|l|c}
\epsilon&q&F&\text{clauses}\\ \hline
0&0&(A\vee B)(A\vee M)(L\vee B)(L\vee M)&4\\
0&1&(A\vee B)(A\vee M)(B\vee L)&3\\
1&0&(A\vee B)(A\vee M)(L\vee M)&3\\
1&1&(A\vee B)(A\vee M)&2.
\end{array}
\]
Including $U,V$, $R$ has at most six clauses. The original minimum degree of this $f$ is two, so its selected low has degree one and its actual context $M$ is old homogeneous linear or zero. Consequently the safe old cubic $Q$, when nonzero, has at most one missing witness by Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors}.

If $Q$ has no target witness, $R$ supplies the whole eight-clause target. If its one witness is a path arm, deleting that arm's leaf leaves an induced three-matching supplied entirely by $R$, again requiring eight clauses. Hence $Q$ must witness an isolated edge, say $ab$, and $R$ supplies $xy,xz,cd$. Both $U,V$ meet the path arms, so both contain $x$.

Suppose first that $B$ is a full singleton. Its $ab$ witness places it at one endpoint, say $a$. Set $a=b=0$ and every variable outside $\{x,y,z,c,d\}$ to zero. All $B$ terms disappear and the remaining contribution is
\[
 g(L\vee\epsilon M\vee\epsilon q).
\]
If $\epsilon q=1$, this is the safe old cubic $g$. Otherwise it is one safe old quartic or the union $gL\vee gM$ of two safe quartics sharing the three old factors $U,V,A$. Lemma~\ref{lem:sharedquartics} bounds their union by two missing witnesses. A scalar-one context makes the cubic absorb its extension, and a zero context is omitted. None of these cases can supply the required $xy,xz,cd$.

If instead $M$ is a full singleton endpoint of $ab$, the same restriction leaves
\[
 g(L\vee qB\vee\epsilon q).
\]
Exactly the same cubic/shared-quartic bound gives at most two missing witnesses and the same contradiction.

It remains that neither $B$ nor $M$ is a full singleton. Choose a cubic monomial of $BCM$ witnessing $ab$. Its once-selected endpoint must be supplied by $C$, since the missing-cubic singleton argument in Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic} would otherwise make $B$ or $M$ a singleton. Thus, after exchanging $a,b$, the full support of $C$ is $\{a\}$ and $b\in B\cap M$. But the safe summand $uBM$ then contains $x^2b^2$, supported on the independent pair $\{x,b\}$. This is impossible. The three alternatives exhaust all singleton configurations, and all original input types have now been excluded.
\end{proof}

% Complete220 admitted after the separately saved full mutual comparison.
\begin{proposition}[An independent quadratic first high beside an unequal preparation]\label{prop:independentquadraticfirst}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$, where $G$ is finite, simple and four-cycle-free. Let the nonempty quadratic support be $H$, and let its four global missing edges be $xy,xz,ab,cd$, with $G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$ on their endpoint set $T$.
