boundary. The remaining actual source types are precisely
\[
 g=tA=UVA,\qquad g=t^2,                             \tag{1}
\]
of minimum degrees three and four, respectively, with full nonzero old
linear $A$. There is no further private sum, cut or product to form another
input. Repeated old forms are allowed, and the raw $t$ input is an actual
wire, not merely a Boolean factor.

Let $f$ be the product after $S$. It receives $S$ literally and is the second
visible high. There is no other useful downstream private exit; repeating
$g$ or $t$ at the second cut would leave $f$ unused. An equal-degree
selected product entry would retain both the product and its $S$ trace.
Thus $t,g,f$ are distinct original nodes and the inserted highs are $g,f$.
An available retained degree-one boundary has full value $D+\delta g$,
where $D$ is a full nonzero old selected part and $\delta\ge0$. The only
possible earlier insertion is $c_1$. If it has not yet occurred, then
$\delta=0$. If $\delta>0$, the actual route forces $a_0$ to have degree
one and $\operatorname{supp}(a_0)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(D)$.
If $a_0$ has degree two, every such boundary is unaffected.
Neither uninserted $t$ nor hidden $S$ can enter its selected trace without
another cut. Oldness of $D$ follows from its own selected quadratic
continuation, not from arbitrary unions; no separate $D$ wire is inferred.

The entire literal last-input list is therefore
\[
 f=Sg,\qquad St,\qquad S^2,\qquad S(D+\delta g).      \tag{2}
\]
There is no distinct raw-$u$ case, since $u=g$ as original nodes.
Keep repeated $S$ inputs and every actual cut order. The exact occurrence
contribution is
\[
 Y=gL\vee fM\vee qgf,\qquad q\in\{0,1\}.             \tag{3}
\]
It is globally safe and supplies all four targets on $T$.
The individual $L$ is old homogeneous linear or zero when $a_0$ has degree
one, and scalar or zero when it has degree two. The context $M$ has its
compatible old-linear, scalar or zero type. In the square and nonraw cases
of (2), the original minimum degree of $f$ is two, so $M$ is old linear
or zero. Same-occurrence diagonals are absent by squarefree $P_2$ and
the original low degrees. The distinct-occurrence coefficient $q$ is kept.
If $a_0$ has degree two, then $q=0$, since it cannot meet another
positive-degree selected low in a retained quadratic product.

\emph{Three old factors with an affine context.}
We need the following elementary bound. If $W=UVA$ consists of full old
linear factors, and $F$ is any affine linear form, not necessarily old,
then a safe $WF$ has at most two target witnesses.
It has at most four affine linear CNF clauses. A triple consisting of
one path arm and both isolated edges is an induced three-matching, which
needs eight clauses. The only other triple has both path arms and an
isolated edge. If both arms are witnessed, each old factor contains $x$:
otherwise it contains $y,z$, whose $H$-center forms a four-cycle with $x$.
That center cannot be $x$, since the arms are missing from $H$.
Thus $W(\{x\})=1$. A positive constant in $F$ would make $WF$ true on
the independent singleton $\{x\}$. Otherwise its isolated-edge witness
requires an endpoint $e$ in $F$, making $WF$ true on the independent
pair $\{x,e\}$. Both are impossible. Zero $F$ supplies no witness.

We also use Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors}: safe old quadratics and
cubics have at most one missing witness, and a safe old quartic at most
two. The path target and an induced three-matching require eight positive
affine linear CNF clauses, and an induced two-matching requires four.
Each maximal independent set must falsify a different valid clause.
These restricted counts use safety and all edge witnesses, not a claim
that higher redundant monomials vanish. In particular two old linear
factors with an affine context have at most three clauses and cannot
witness two disjoint targets.

\emph{The original square source $g=t^2$.}
First suppose $a_0$ has degree one. Replace every actual use of $g$ by
the existing earlier wire $t$, and remove $g$. Their Boolean supports
agree. This is an actual node removal, not a change to the original
degree of a surviving $g$.
At $c_1$ the selected low remains the same degree-one form and $t$ remains
a strict high of degree two. Every inserted $t$ contribution acquires a
positive-degree operand before the selected quadratic output, so has
output degree at least three. Every other $g$ route goes through $S$ and
$f$ or directly into $f$, also adding a positive degree. The hidden sum
keeps exactly its linear part $C$.
A square or nonraw $f$ keeps minimum degree two; $Sg$ after replacement
has minimum degree three, above either possible original selected low,
and $St$ has minimum degree three. Thus $P_2,H$ and the entire selected
frame, including $K$, are unchanged, as is Boolean output. At most two
private products remain, contradicting the cited matching obstruction.

Now suppose $a_0$ has degree two. Then $L$ is scalar or zero, $q=0$, and
every retained degree-one input of $f$ has $\delta=0$.
Use the support identity $g=t$ while keeping its original minimum degree
four; no deletion is attempted.
For $f=Sg$ or $St$, support $f=t$ gives
$Y=t(L\vee M)$ with at most three affine clauses.
For $f=S^2$,
\[
 Y=tL\vee CM\vee tM.
\]
A positive scalar $L$ exposes $t$ and absorbs $tM$, leaving two safe old
quadratics with at most two witnesses. With $L=0$, the old cubic $tM$
and quadratic $CM$ still have at most two altogether.
For $f=SD$,
\[
 Y=tL\vee CDM\vee tDM.
\]
A positive scalar $L$ absorbs $tDM$, leaving an old quadratic and an old
cubic. With $L=0$, the cubic $CDM$ and quartic $tDM$ have at most three
witnesses. None supplies four. This exhausts the source-square case,
keeping its two first-low degrees separate.

\emph{The raw cubic source: raw and square final inputs.}
Now $g=tA=UVA$ is the actual old cubic of minimum degree three, and $L$
retains its actual old-linear, scalar or zero type.
For $f=Sg$, support $f=g$ gives
$Y=g(L\vee M\vee q)$ with at most four affine clauses.
For $f=St$, support $f=t(C\vee A)$ and $gf=g$ give
\[
 Y=t\bigl[A(L\vee M\vee q)\vee CM\bigr].             \tag{4}
\]
The bracket is a disjunction of two products of affine linear forms,
hence has at most four clauses; the two old factors of $t$ add at most
two. Six clauses cannot supply the target. Both scalar contexts, zero
contexts and every $q$ are included without changing an original degree.
For $f=S^2$, $M$ is old linear or zero and
\[
 Y=g(L\vee M\vee q)\vee CM.                         \tag{5}
\]
The first safe term has at most two witnesses by the three-old-factor
bound, and the safe old quadratic $CM$ has at most one. Four witnesses
are impossible, including when $L$ is a positive scalar.

\emph{Every nonraw final input for the cubic source.}
Let $f=S(D+\delta g)$. Its original minimum degree is two, and $M$ is
old linear or zero. A positive $\delta$ requires an actually earlier
degree-one first insertion; no order is imposed when $\delta=0$.
For $\delta>0$, Boolean absorption gives $f=CD\vee g$ and $gf=g$, so
\[
 Y=g(L\vee M\vee q)\vee CDM.                        \tag{6}
\]
The first safe term has at most two witnesses, and the old cubic $CDM$
at most one. This excludes every permitted context and cross flag.

For $\delta=0$, write
\[
 Y=Q\vee R,\qquad Q=CDM,\qquad
 R=g\bigl[L\vee D(M\vee q)\bigr],\quad g=UVA.        \tag{7}
\]
The positive terms $Q,gL,gDM$, and $gD$ when $q>0$, are globally safe.
The old cubic $Q$ has at most one witness. The bracket in $R$ is
$(L\vee D)(L\vee M\vee q)$, so $R$ has at most five affine clauses.
If $Q$ has no witness, $R$ supplies the eight-clause whole target.
If $Q$ has only a path-arm witness, deleting that arm's leaf leaves
the eight-clause induced three-matching supplied by $R$.
Both are impossible. Thus $Q$ witnesses an isolated edge, say $ab$,
and $R$ supplies $xy,xz,cd$.

Each full old factor $U,V,A$ then meets both path arms and contains $x$
by the old-center argument above. Hence $g(\{x\})=1$.
Safety of $gL$ excludes a positive constant and every isolated endpoint
from $L$. In particular $L$ vanishes on $cd$.
Safety of $gDM$ also says that $D$ and $M$ cannot both contain an isolated
endpoint $e$, since the independent pair $\{x,e\}$ would satisfy it.

Choose a cubic monomial of the safe $CDM$ witnessing $ab$.
Its factor supplying the once-chosen endpoint has full singleton support,
by Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic}.
If the full actual $M$ is a singleton, it is an endpoint of $ab$.
It lies in the three-cover consisting of that endpoint, $x$ and an
endpoint of $cd$, and gives the original-product charge below.

Otherwise $M$ is nonsingleton. If $D$ were a full singleton endpoint
of $ab$, it would vanish on $cd$; since $L$ also vanishes there,
$R=g[L\vee D(M\vee q)]$ could not witness $cd$.
This rules out that singleton case independently of $q$.
The remaining singleton is therefore $C$. Relabel so $C=\{a\}$.
Both $D$ and $M$ are now nonsingleton. In the chosen cubic witness the
once-chosen endpoint cannot come from either, since its supplying old
factor would then be a full singleton. Thus $C$ supplies $a$ once and
$D,M$ both supply $b$. This puts $b$ in their full intersection, making
the safe $gDM$ true on the independent pair $\{x,b\}$, a contradiction.
All possibilities have been exhausted.

Consequently the zero-$\delta$ branch is impossible or supplies a full
singleton actual $M$ in a three-cover. Zero $M$ was already excluded by
the five-versus-eight-clause argument, and any positive scalar $L$ was
explicitly excluded by safety when $g(\{x\})=1$. No affected-$C$ overlap,
extra cut order or selected-part wire has been introduced.

\emph{The global original-product charge.}
Every surviving branch either invokes the exact old-source proposition
or has a nonzero full individual actual $M$ in a three-vertex cover $Z$
of all four global missing edges. In the latter case the original
minimum degree of $f$ is two, so its selected low has degree one.
Following the insertion along selected degree-one paths reaches at least
one original retained quadratic product, because the actual linear
context is nonzero at a selected quadratic output.
Mark each distinct reached product once. Positivity of the original frame
places its full opposite old selected operand in
$\operatorname{supp}(M)$, not just its restriction to $T$.
Hence $Z$ covers all old edges supplied by every marked product.
Each unmarked retained product is a star: squarefree $P_2$ forces
disjoint selected supports, and two nonsingleton sides would form a
four-cycle. Choose one center per unmarked original product.
Together with $Z$ they cover all of $H$ and all four global missing
edges, including ambient vertices outside $T$. For $s\ge1$ distinct
marked products, the number of vertices is at most
\[
 K-s+3\le K+2.
\]
Repeated paths, centers and products do not duplicate the charge.
No Boolean factor or rewritten expression is counted as an original node.

The old-quadratic case and the two derived source types in (1) exhaust
the initially unrestricted source. Every last input in (2), both
source-square first-low degrees, every actual cut order and compatible
context or mixed coefficient has been treated. The conclusion concerns
only the source that is the same original first-high node with unaffected
old input $C$. It leaves different-source cases, other hidden orders,
all-visible patterns, matching attachments and the numerical row outside
its scope.
\end{proof}

% Complete checked transcription; original proof versions remain archived.
\begin{proposition}[An unaffected linear input with an arbitrary raw source]
\label{prop:generalunaffectedpreparationcover}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and $C_4$-free, and let a positive variable-input
circuit compute $P\in\operatorname{Sup}(G)$ with nonempty squarefree quadratic
support $H$. Suppose its four global missing edges are $xy,xz,ab,cd$, their
endpoint set $T$ induces exactly $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ in $G$, and $H[T]$ is empty.
Preserve the original selected quadratic frame and its arbitrary number $K$
of retained multiplication nodes. After whole-current-carrier erasure and
pruning, suppose exactly three original products and three original additions
are private, exactly two of the latter visible, and the unique hidden addition
has literal inputs
\[
 S=C+u,
\]
where $C$ is an actual full unaffected nonzero old homogeneous linear input
wire and $u$ is a raw original private-product output of minimum degree at
least two. The source inputs, its private ancestry, the first and second
visible highs, and the placement of $S$ are otherwise unrestricted.
Keep all original nodes, input and insertion occurrences, minimum degrees,
coefficients, fanout, selected lows and paths, full contexts and retained-product
incidences, including repeated inputs and coincident Boolean values of distinct
nodes. Keep every compatible old-linear, scalar or zero context and every
actual mixed coefficient. Then
\[
 \vc(G)\le K+2.
\]
No minimum-retained-count hypothesis or additional cut ordering is required.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Reduction to a derived original census.}
Write $g$ for the first visible high. If $u$ has two actual unaffected old
homogeneous linear inputs, Proposition~\ref{prop:literalunequalpreparationcover}
applies. If $u=g$ as an original node, use
Proposition~\ref{prop:sourceisfirsthigh}; if $g$ is a proper surviving original
ancestor of $u$, use Proposition~\ref{prop:unaffectedancestralpreparation}.
These alternatives use the literal hypotheses of those propositions and
preserve the same original frame and $K$. We prove that all remaining
possibilities are impossible.

The hidden $S$ has minimum degree one and cannot itself be a strict high.
A useful route from $S$ must traverse a private product after $S$: an
addition-only selected linear route would expose $S$, and an off-frame full
quadratic carrier is erased as a whole. With no other hidden sum, the first
such product, denoted $f$, has $S$ as an actual raw input. It is distinct from
$u$ and every source ancestor.

Every surviving strict high in this setting is a private-product output.
A retained linear value is not strict above a positive-degree low; a full
current degree-two selected carrier has no surviving off-frame use; and no
extra nonlinear private sum is available. An earlier visible-cut output of
minimum degree one is not strict. If its minimum degree is two, its selected
quadratic trace to the output is addition-only, so its \emph{entire current
value} belongs to the protected carrier set and is erased on an off-frame
use as another high. This also excludes additive retained carrier wrappers;
no subtraction of only an old quadratic part is used.

If $u$ had no proper private-product ancestor, no surviving visible-cut
influence could enter it without importing a private high ancestor, while
$S$ is later. Its actual full input wires would be unaffected old homogeneous
linear forms, a case already covered. Thus there is a proper surviving private
ancestor $v$ of $u$. The distinct nodes $v,u,f$ exhaust the three-product
budget. Since the first high $g$ is neither $u$ nor a source ancestor in the
remaining case, $g=f$. The first-high node is therefore after $S$, and both
visible cuts are after the source network. No affected boundary is available
to that network or to $f$. There are no other private ancestors, intermediate
products or later products. Consequently the complete literal lists are
\[
 v=UV,\qquad u=vA\ \text{or}\ v v,\qquad
 f=Sv,\ Su,\ SS\ \text{or}\ SD,
 \qquad h\in\{v,u,f\},
\]
where $h$ is the second visible high and $U,V,A,D$ are full nonzero old
homogeneous linear inputs when present. A linear wrap carrying $S$ would make
$S$ visible; another private sum or an intervening private product is
unavailable. Repetitions remain original occurrences. The original source minimum degrees are
respectively three and four; the original minimum degrees of $SS,SD,Sv,Su$ are respectively
two, two, three, and four or five. This order is derived only for the residual
census, not imposed on the whole proposition. The argument uses surviving
paths while preserving the original labels of any erased ancestry.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The exact frame and support notation.}
Let $L$ be the full actual context of the first insertion $f$, and $M$ that
of the second insertion $h$. In Boolean support,
\[
 Y=fL\lor hM\lor qfh,\qquad q\in\{0,1\}.
\]
If $h=f$, the two insertion occurrences are still distinct and their cross
$qf^2$ is retained. Same-occurrence diagonals are excluded by squarefree $P_2$
for degree-one lows and by original degree for degree-two lows. The contexts
are old homogeneous linear or zero for a degree-one selected low, and scalar
or zero for a degree-two low. In particular $L$ is linear or zero for
$f=SS,SD$, and $M$ is linear or zero for $h=v$. Positive $q$ forces both lows
linear and gives the full actual inclusion
\[
 \operatorname{supp}\ell\subseteq\operatorname{supp}M,
 \qquad \ell L\text{ is supported on }H,
\]
where $\ell$ is the first selected low. Every displayed positive summand is
globally safe. These types and incidences are inherited from the original
frame, not recomputed after a support identity.

Put $B_0=UV$. For support calculations write $u=B_0A$, with $A=1$ only as a
formal Boolean placeholder when the literal source is $v v$. This does not
supply a unit wire, remove a product or change that source's original degree
four. The four supports of $f$ are
\[
 B_0(C\lor A),\qquad B_0A,\qquad C\lor B_0A,
 \qquad (C\lor B_0A)D.
\]
An old support cannot contain both leaves $y,z$, by the old-center and
$C_4$ argument. Thus if a multiple of $B_0$, or of $u$, witnesses both path
arms, each of its nonunit old prefix factors contains $x$, and the prefix is
true on $\{x\}$.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Target bounds and an isolated-witness allocation.}
The whole target and an induced three-edge matching require eight positive
affine CNF clauses; an induced two-edge matching requires four. Indeed each
maximal independent set needs a distinct falsified valid clause. A globally
safe old quadratic or cubic has at most one missing witness, and safe old
quartics or quintics have at most two, which form an induced matching.
Full quartic equality confines all four full factors to the four distinct
two-point transversals. For a safe old cubic witnessing a missing edge, a
factor supplying the once-selected endpoint is a full singleton. In
particular, if two factors are nonsingletons, the third is that singleton
and the opposite endpoint belongs to both other supports. These are the full-support bounds of Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors}
and Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic}, applied before restriction.

Suppose $Y=Q\lor R$ supplies all four targets, $Q$ has at most one target,
and $R$ has at most seven affine clauses. Then $Q$ supplies an isolated
edge, say $ab$, and $R$ supplies $xy,xz,cd$. Otherwise $R$ supplies the entire
eight-clause target, or deleting the leaf of a path-arm-only witness of $Q$
leaves an eight-clause three-matching in $R$. Higher redundant terms of $Q$
need not vanish for this witness argument.

We also use the following full singleton-guard observation. If a prefix
$B_0$ is true on $\{x\}$ and $B_0M$ is globally safe, an old linear guard $M$
cannot meet an isolated endpoint. If it supplies $xy$, its full support is
$\{y\}$: another support vertex $w$ requires $xw$ by safety, while the
old $H$-center of $M$, together with $x,y,w$, gives a $C_4$. Coincident
vertices either make $xy$ old or require a loop. The safety premise belongs
to $B_0M$, not to $B_0$ alone.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Second high equal to the last product.}
For $h=f$,
\[
 Y=f(L\lor M\lor q).
\]
The four displayed supports of $f$ have at most $3,3,3,4$ affine clauses,
and the guard adds at most one. The counts decrease when $A=1$. Thus this
case has at most five clauses, including all scalar or zero contexts and
the repeated-high cross, and is impossible.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Second high equal to the source.}
For $h=u$, the cases $f=Su$ and $f=Sv$ give respectively
\[
 u(L\lor M\lor q),\qquad
 B_0\bigl[A(L\lor M\lor q)\lor CL\bigr],
\]
with at most four and six affine clauses. For $f=SS$,
\[
 Y=CL\lor u(M\lor L\lor q).
\]
The first term is a safe old quadratic and the second has at most four
clauses. The isolated-witness allocation makes $CL$ witness $ab$ and the
source multiple witness both path arms and $cd$. Hence $u(\{x\})=1$.
Since $L$ meets $ab$, positive $uL$ is true on an independent pair
$\{x,e\}$ with $e\in\{a,b\}$, a contradiction.

For $f=SD$,
\[
 Y=CDL\lor u\bigl[M\lor D(L\lor q)\bigr].
\]
The old cubic has at most one target and the second term at most five
clauses. Again the first witnesses $ab$ and the second both arms and $cd$,
so $u(\{x\})=1$. If $q=1$, safe $uD$ is true on $\{x,e\}$ for an $ab$
endpoint in $D$. If $q=0$, safety of $uM$ excludes a positive scalar and all
isolated endpoints from $M$; consequently $cd$ must be witnessed by $uDL$.
Both $D,L$ meet $ab$ and $cd$ and are nonsingletons. The cubic singleton
certificate for $CDL$ forces, after relabeling, full $C=\{a\}$ and
$b\in\operatorname{supp}D\cap\operatorname{supp}L$. Then $uDL$ is true on
independent $\{x,b\}$. This contradiction includes the support placeholder
$A=1$ and every actual scalar or zero context. No reversal of original cut
order has been made.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Second high equal to the raw ancestor: raw last operands.}
Let $h=v$, so $M$ is old linear or zero. For $f=Su$ and $f=Sv$ respectively,
\[
 Y=B_0\bigl[M\lor A(L\lor q)\bigr],\qquad
 Y=B_0\bigl[M\lor(C\lor A)(L\lor q)\bigr].
\]
In either case the bracket has at most two affine clauses and $U,V$ add two.
Thus at most four clauses occur, including $A=1$, either cross flag and all
compatible scalar $L$. Both cases are impossible.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Second high equal to the raw ancestor: the literal square.}
For $h=v,f=SS$, the actual $L$ is old linear or zero and
\[
 Y=Q\lor R,\qquad Q=CL,\qquad
 R=B_0\bigl[M\lor A(L\lor q)\lor qC\bigr].
\]
The remainder has at most four clauses: at $q=0$ its bracket is $M\lor AL$,
and at $q=1$ it is $M\lor A\lor C$. Hence $Q$ supplies $ab$, $R$ supplies
$xy,xz,cd$, and $B_0(\{x\})=1$. Full $C,L$ both meet $ab$. Positive $q$
exposes safe $B_0C$, contradicting an independent pair $\{x,e\}$ with an
$ab$ endpoint $e$ in $C$.

At $q=0$, $R=B_0M\lor B_0AL$. Safety of $B_0M$ excludes isolated endpoints
from $M$, so it supplies at most one path arm and no isolated target.
If $A=1$, the other term is an old cubic with at most one target, already
insufficient. Otherwise it is an old quartic with at most two matching
targets. Thus $B_0M$ supplies one arm and $B_0AL$ the other arm, say $xy$,
and $cd$. Full quartic equality confines $U,V,A,L$ to $\{x,y,c,d\}$.
In particular the full $L$ misses $a,b$, contradicting the required $CL$
witness. The equality is applied to full ambient factors, not only their
restrictions to the target.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Second high equal to the raw ancestor: an old last input and zero cross.}
Let $h=v,f=SD,q=0$. Both $L,M$ are old linear or zero, and
\[
 Y=Q\lor R,\qquad Q=CDL,\qquad
 R=B_0\bigl[M\lor ADL\bigr].
\]
The cubic $Q$ has at most one target; $R$ has at most five affine clauses,
with a smaller bound for $A=1$. The allocation gives the isolated $ab$ to
$Q$ and $xy,xz,cd$ to $R$. Thus $B_0(\{x\})=1$, $M$ misses isolated
endpoints, and $B_0M$ has at most one target, a path arm. The safe product
$B_0ADL$ has at most five old factors and at most two matching witnesses.
It must supply the other arm, say $xy$, and $cd$.

Full $D,L$ each meet $ab$ and $cd$, so both are nonsingletons. The cubic
singleton certificate gives
\[
 \operatorname{supp}C=\{a\},\qquad
 b\in\operatorname{supp}D\cap\operatorname{supp}L.
\]
Put $W=\{x,y,c,d\}$. Set the target vertex $b$ to one and all vertices
outside $W\cup\{b\}$ to zero, leaving $W$ free. The induced-target
hypothesis makes $b$ nonadjacent to every vertex of $W$. Full $D,L$ are now
constantly true. Safety of the original positive summand $UVADL$ implies
that the remaining product
\[
 (UVA)\big|_{b=1,\ \text{all other vertices outside }W=0}
\]
is safe for the two-matching $xy,cd$. It witnesses both edges, because the
original witnesses remain true after the monotone substitution. This is a
product of at most three affine clauses, or two if $A=1$, contradicting the
four-clause lower bound. The restricted clauses are not claimed to be old
homogeneous input wires; no gate is removed or charged by the substitution.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{A common-prefix bound.}
If $F_1,F_2,F_3,N_1,N_2$ are old nonzero homogeneous linear forms and both
$F_1F_2F_3N_1$ and $F_1F_2F_3N_2$ are globally safe, their union has at most
two missing target witnesses. If each quartic has at most one, this is
immediate. Otherwise one has two matching witnesses. Full quartic equality
makes the three common prefix factors full distinct transversals of that
matching, whose common intersection is empty. A target of the other quartic
cannot have an endpoint outside the matching quartet, because its other
endpoint would need to meet all three full factors. Inside the quartet the
only edges are the same matching pair. Thus there is no new witness. If one
guard is the Boolean constant one, the exposed safe old cubic absorbs the
other term and has at most one target. Zero terms decrease the bound.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Second high equal to the raw ancestor: an old last input and positive cross.}
For $h=v,f=SD,q=1$, support absorption gives
\[
 Y=Q\lor R,\qquad Q=CDL,\qquad
 R=UV\bigl[M\lor D(C\lor A)\bigr].
\]
The bracket equals $(M\lor D)(M\lor C\lor A)$, so $R$ has at most four
clauses. Again $Q$ supplies $ab$, $R$ supplies $xy,xz,cd$, and
$UV(\{x\})=1$. Write
\[
 R=UVM\lor UVD(C\lor A).
\]
For actual old $A$, the second term is the union of two safe quartics with
the three common full factors $U,V,D$, hence has at most two targets by the
preceding bound. For $A=1$ it exposes a safe cubic with at most one. Safe
$UVM$ has at most one target and no isolated witness. To supply the three
required targets, it must therefore witness one path arm; in particular the
$A=1$ possibility is excluded. The full singleton-guard observation makes
its actual context $M$ the singleton leaf, say $\{z\}$.

The positive actual mixed coefficient joins the two original selected
linear occurrences at a retained quadratic multiplication. Therefore the
full nonzero first low $\ell$ lies in full $M$, and $\ell L$ is supported
on $H$. Thus $\operatorname{supp}\ell=\{z\}$. Since $H[T]$ is empty and
$P_2$ is squarefree, $L$ contains no vertex of $T$: another vertex would
give an old edge inside $T$, and $z$ would give a forbidden diagonal.
Consequently $CDL$ cannot supply $ab$, a contradiction. This original
opposite-context inclusion is used only at positive cross; the zero-cross
case used its separate independent assignment.

All twelve residual last-product/second-high combinations, both original
source degrees, all compatible scalar or zero contexts, repeated inputs and
cross flags have been exhausted. They are impossible. Every original circuit
in the proposition therefore lies in one of the three initial exact cover
theorems, which gives $\vc(G)\le K+2$ for the same retained frame and count.
Their full ambient retained-product charges apply because these are the four
\emph{global} missing edges. No optimality of $K$, new gate, changed degree or
additional cut order has been introduced.
\end{proof}

% Complete checked consequence; mathematical frontier already counted at review30.
\begin{corollary}[The two-visible path case reduces to an all-visible circuit]
\label{cor:twovisiblepathreduction}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and $C_4$-free, and let a positive variable-input
circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$ with nonempty squarefree quadratic support $H$.
Suppose its four global missing edges are $xy,xz,ab,cd$, their full endpoint
set $T$ induces exactly $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ in $G$, and $H[T]=\varnothing$.
Keep the original selected quadratic frame and its arbitrary retained
multiplication count $K$. In the whole-current-quadratic-carrier-erased and
off-frame-pruned setting, suppose exactly three original products and three
original additions are private, exactly two additions visible. Preserve all
original nodes, operand and insertion occurrences, minimum degrees,
coefficients, fanout, selected lows and paths, full contexts and
retained-product incidences. Write $P^\ast$ for this current polynomial;
its Boolean output and entire quadratic part agree with those of $P$.

If $\vc(G)>K+2$, the unique surviving hidden addition is the second visible
high $S=u+v$, with raw original private-product operands $u,v$. Its visible
parent's selected low $a$ has original minimum degree one, and $S$ has no
other surviving use. The exact arithmetic reassociation
\[
 a+(u+v)\longmapsto(a+u)+v
\]
therefore gives an all-visible circuit with the same current polynomial
$P^\ast$, quadratic frame, support $H$ and retained count $K$, using no new
product. The three high insertion occurrences are the original first high,
$u$ and $v$; coincident original nodes or Boolean values remain distinct
occurrences. Two additions replace two additions.

Equivalently, every circuit in this two-visible family either satisfies
$\vc(G)\le K+2$ or has this precise all-visible arithmetic representative.
No optimality of $K$ is assumed.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Assume $\vc(G)>K+2$ and apply
Proposition~\ref{prop:twovisiblehiddeninventory} to the same original frame.
Its first alternative gives the literal hidden inputs
\[
 S=R+u,\qquad R=A+\beta g,\qquad \beta\ge0,
\]
where $g$ is the first visible high, $A$ is nonzero old homogeneous linear,
and $u$ is a raw original private product of minimum degree at least two.
The displayed value of $R$ is its full current polynomial, collected along
actual retained addition-only paths from the first insertion; it is not a
Boolean support replacement.

If $\beta>0$, $R$ is the actual affected degree-one boundary of
Proposition~\ref{prop:generalaffectedpreparationcover}, with selected old
part $A$. That theorem permits $A$ to be unavailable as a separate wire and
imposes no additional source ancestry, degree, high or cut-order restriction.
All original counts, full contexts and retained-product incidences are those
of the present circuit. It gives $\vc(G)\le K+2$, a contradiction.

If $\beta=0$, use the existing input wire $R$ itself, whose full value is
$A$, as the input $C$ of
Proposition~\ref{prop:generalunaffectedpreparationcover}. The inventory's
only possible surviving visible influence on this boundary is the first
insertion, along its actual retained degree-one paths. Positivity makes any
surviving contribution have positive coefficient; hence none survives when
$\beta=0$. Thus $R$ is an actual full unaffected nonzero old homogeneous
linear input in the stipulated current setting. No new wire for a selected
part is supplied, and no original degree is changed by a support identity.
The raw source $u$ and every other original datum satisfy that proposition's
unrestricted source hypotheses. It again gives $\vc(G)\le K+2$ for the same
$K$, a contradiction. This argument concerns surviving input occurrences;
it does not reclassify any historical erased path.

The two coefficient cases exhaust the inventory's unequal-input
alternative. Its second alternative therefore holds, including the
single-use condition for $S$ and the original minimum-degree-one low $a$.
Associativity of addition gives the displayed equality of full arithmetic
polynomials. Since $S$ has no other surviving use, replacing these two
addition nodes changes no other contribution, and all fanout of the old
parent receives the identical polynomial. The operands are already
available, so the replacement is acyclic and leaves all product nodes
untouched.

Both raw operands have original minimum degree at least two. Each new sum
therefore selects the same degree-one low contribution $a$, first against
$u$ and then against $v$. Both cuts are visible; the original first visible
cut remains. The checked reassociation in
Proposition~\ref{prop:twovisiblehiddeninventory} consequently preserves the
quadratic frame, its entire quadratic part, $H$ and the same $K$. Repeated
highs remain separate insertion occurrences: even when $u=v$, the arithmetic
identity keeps both contributions rather than collapsing them by Boolean
idempotence. There is no claim that the two addition DAGs are identical.
The polynomial preserved exactly is the current $P^\ast$, not the higher
terms of the original unerased $P$.
\end{proof}

% Complete checked original-author-route transcription; no main-file mutation.
% Exact bounded statement only.  This result alone does not exclude the full all-visible family.
\begin{proposition}[Two target potentials and seven zero-cross reductions]
\label{prop:nonrawsevenzerocross}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$, where $G$ is
finite, simple and four-cycle-free.  Suppose its nonempty quadratic support
is $H$, and its four global missing edges are $xy,xz,ab,cd$, with endpoint
set $T$ satisfying $G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$.
Keep the exact original extracted quadratic frame and its arbitrary
retained-product count $K$.  Suppose there are exactly three original
private products and three private additions, all additions are visible,
and the three highs are the three distinct original product nodes, each
inserted once.  Every private-product operand has original minimum degree
one, with its nonzero old homogeneous linear base and its actual earlier
insertion contributions.  Preserve all original nodes, occurrences,
degrees, coefficients, selected lows and paths, fanout, full contexts and
retained-product incidences.  Boolean identities below change none of
these data.

Each original private product is true on at least two distinct target-edge
assignments.  This does not assign different targets to different products
or assert a unique witness or a first-true product.

Order the product nodes topologically as $g,h,f$, write $g=UV$, and write
the exact three-occurrence contribution as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nonrawsevenframe}
 Y=gL\vee hN\vee fM\vee q_{12}gh\vee q_{13}gf\vee q_{23}hf,
 \qquad q_{ij}\in\{0,1\}.
\end{equation}
Here a coefficient records whether its actual coefficient is absent or
positive; $L,N,M$ are the full original direct contexts.  If all three
$q_{ij}$ are zero, then $\vc(G)\le K+2$ in each of the following exact
original operand configurations:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|l}
 &h&f\\ \hline
1&AB&(C\vee g)D\\
2&AB&D(C\vee g\vee h)\\
3&AB&(C\vee g)(D\vee g)\\
4&AB&(C\vee g)(D\vee g\vee h)\\
5&(A\vee g)B&CD\\
6&(A\vee g)(B\vee g)&CD\\
7&(A\vee g)(B\vee g)&(C\vee g)D.
\end{array}
\]
All base forms in this table are full nonzero old homogeneous linear
forms, repetitions are allowed, and every displayed affected input is an
actual original operand with the indicated positive occurrence
coefficients and its original low/context identities.  No other operand
configuration or positive-cross allocation is excluded by this table.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
We give the full original-context argument.  A term is \emph{safe} if each
of its monomials contains a $G$-edge.  Every positive summand of the output
is safe.  On a target edge assignment, a safe term is true precisely when
it has that missing edge as an exact support.  By
Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors}, an old cubic has at most one missing
witness; an old quartic has at most two, and equality fixes its four full
factor supports to the four distinct transversals of the corresponding
induced two-edge matching, with no extra vertices.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Original contexts and a selected-continuation anchor.}
Every private product has original minimum degree two, so its selected
low has degree one.  The selected frame is quadratic in the three
independent insertion symbols.  An individual squared symbol would
repeat a variable from its nonzero old low in the quadratic part,
contradicting squarefreeness.  This gives
\eqref{eq:nonrawsevenframe}.  The contexts are old homogeneous linear
forms and are globally nonzero: follow the selected continuation from
the original visible cut to its first retained multiplication; the
complete nonzero opposite homogeneous factor appears in its direct
context.  A context may restrict to zero on $T$.

Write $a_0,b_0,c_0$ for the nonzero old homogeneous parts of the three
selected lows.  Then $a_0L,b_0N,c_0M$ are supported on $H$-edges.  An
affected base receiving $g$ contains $a_0$, and one receiving $h$ contains
$b_0$.  If $q_{12}>0$, then $a_0\subseteq N$, $b_0\subseteq L$, and
$a_0b_0$ is supported on $H$-edges; the analogous facts hold for the other
pairs.  Here and below containment of forms means containment of
supports.  These identities come from the same original retained
product occurrence that produces the cross coefficient.

More precisely, let $W$ be an actual original degree-one operand
carrying insertion $i$, let $E$ be its full homogeneous base, and let
$L_i$ be that occurrence's full context.  There is a nonzero old form $B$
such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nonrawsevenanchor}
 EB\text{ is supported on }H\text{-edges},\qquad B\subseteq L_i.
\end{equation}
Indeed, $W$ is not an input variable.  It is a retained linear addition
or a restored visible cut on the original selected frame.  Follow its
selected degree-one continuation to the first retained multiplication,
and take $B$ to be the entire ordinary degree-one part of the opposite
input.  Positivity puts $EB$ in the quadratic part; the same selected
addition-only route carries insertion $i$ to that product and puts $B$
in its direct context.  Later visible cuts on this route preserve the
earlier occurrence through their low paths.  The original low $a_i$ is
contained in $E$.  Choosing any $k\in\supp(B)$ gives $Ek$, $a_ik$, and
$a_iL_i$ supported on $H$-edges, with $k\in L_i$.
This anchor belongs to an actual operand, not to an algebraically
introduced old form.  Full-carrier erasure preserves the selected
degree-one paths used here; no new selected gate is required.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{A two-product support bound.}
Let $X=UV$ and let a second nonraw product have support
\[
 Z=AB,\qquad Z=B(A\vee X),\qquad\text{or}\qquad Z=AB\vee X.
\]
Suppose $XL\vee ZN\vee qXZ$ is safe and has the applicable actual
nonzero old contexts, low identities, and anchors just proved.  It has
at most two missing witnesses.  We check all cases.
For $Z=AB$, zero $q$ gives two old cubics.  For positive $q$, apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:independentproducts} to the two old quadratics, their
actual contexts and the two low forms: the required mixed inclusions
and old products are exactly the positive-cross identities.
For $Z=B(A\vee X)$ and $q=0$, the terms are $XL,ABN,XBN$.
Choose $k\in L$ from \eqref{eq:nonrawsevenanchor} for the actual
$A\vee X$ operand.  Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:independentproducts} to
$UV$ and $BN$, with contexts $L,A$ and low forms $a_0,k$.
Its inclusions are $a_0\subseteq A$ and $k\subseteq L$; its required
old products are $a_0k,a_0L,kA$, all verified by that anchor.
For positive $q$, absorption gives $XL,ABN,XB$; the actual cross puts
$a_0$ in $N$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:relatedcubics}, with $a_0$ in
$A\cap N$ and $a_0L$ old, gives the same bound.
For $Z=AB\vee X$ and $q=0$, use
Lemma~\ref{lem:relatedcubics} on $XL,XN,ABN$, since the first low
lies in both affected bases $A,B$.  For positive $q$, the term $X$ is
safe and absorbs its multiples, leaving $X\vee ABN$; each term has
at most one missing witness.  This exhausts the cases.  The identity
$(A\vee X)(B\vee X)=AB\vee X$ is used only for support; it does
not change the original degree or counted node.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Two potentials for each original product.}
Override one original private high by zero in all its uses and recompute
its descendants in their original order.  This only removes positive
contributions, so the remaining subexpression is safe.  It is a
support-counting device, not a newly charged circuit.
If $g$ is overridden, the surviving $h$ has its old quadratic base and
$f$ is one of the independent, single-affected or double-affected forms
in $h$.  The original $b_0,N$, actual recipient anchors and $q_{23}$
identities are unchanged homogeneous data.  The two-product bound
therefore gives at most two surviving targets.  Overriding $h$ leaves
the corresponding pair $g,f$ with their original anchors and $q_{13}$
data; overriding $f$ leaves $g,h$ with $q_{12}$.  The same bound applies.
Thus every override loses at least two of the four target assignments.
On an assignment on which the original overridden high was zero,
topological induction says that overriding it and recomputing changes
no value.  Each lost target therefore makes that original high true.
This proves the asserted two distinct potentials, without assigning
disjoint sets or first-true roles to different products.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{One- and two-context cover charges.}
Let $D$ be a nonzero actual direct context.  At least one original
retained product marked by that occurrence has its entire opposite
homogeneous support contained in $D$.  If a three-vertex cover $S$ of
the global missing set contains $D$, then $S$ covers that product's old
edges.  Choose one star center for each of the other retained products.
Every retained product is a squarefree quadratic star, since two
disjoint nonsingleton factors would create a four-cycle.  The resulting
cover of all of $G$ has size at most $(K-1)+3=K+2$.

If two nonzero full direct contexts $D,E$ are disjoint and contained in
$T$, they mark different original retained products.  If the two
occurrences entered the same factor of one product, its full nonzero
opposite support would lie in $D\cap E$.  If they entered opposite
factors, both homogeneous factors would lie in $T$, producing an
$H$-edge in $T$ or a square.  Both are impossible.  An individual
occurrence cannot enter both sides, by its old-low square.  Hence a
four-vertex cover $S$ of the missing set containing $D\cup E$ gives
the cover bound $(K-2)+4=K+2$.  In particular, a singleton context at
$x$ or at an isolated-edge endpoint gives the first charge, and the
contexts $\{y\},\{z\}$ give the second, with
$S=\{y,z,a,c\}$.  Fanout and further marked products only improve
these estimates.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Two consequences under $\vc(G)>K+2$.}
For a fixed old quadratic $X$, a family of safe cubics $XD_i$ with
actual direct contexts has at most one target in its union.  Otherwise
Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic} makes its two targets $xy,xz$.
Both factors of $X$ contain $x$: an old support meeting both arms while
omitting $x$ contains $y,z$, whose old center creates a four-cycle
with $x$ or makes a missing arm old.  Thus $X$ is true on $x$ alone.
Safety puts every vertex of a witnessing context among the neighbors
of $x$.  An old context containing the missing neighbor $y$ or $z$
cannot contain a second such neighbor, since its old center would
again create a four-cycle or make the missing edge old.  The full
witnessing contexts are therefore $\{y\}$ and $\{z\}$, contradicting
the two-context charge.

We also need the following full-support singleton observation.  If a
safe old cubic $XD$ witnesses $e$ while its quadratic $X$ is true on a
disjoint target $e'$, both factors of $X$ meet two disjoint endpoint
pairs.  Neither is singleton.  In a cubic witness monomial one
endpoint is repeated twice; safety and oldness force the remaining
factor to be the singleton opposite endpoint.  Indeed, a second
vertex in that factor would be another neighbor of the repeated
endpoint and, together with its old center, create a four-cycle or
make the missing edge old.  Hence the full $D$ is a singleton
endpoint of $e$.

Suppose now that safe cubics $XD,ZD$ with the same actual direct
context witness different targets $e_1,e_2$.  Under the contrary
cover inequality, $X$ cannot be true on a third target $e_3$.
If $e_3$ is disjoint from $e_1$, the singleton observation makes
$D$ a singleton endpoint common to $e_1,e_2$.  Thus those edges
are the two path arms and $D=\{x\}$, which gives a cover charge.
If $e_3$ is adjacent to $e_1$, they are the two arms.  Both factors
of $X$ contain $x$, so the preceding oldness argument makes $D$
the singleton leaf of $e_1$.  It cannot meet the different target
$e_2$, which is isolated.  These exhaust the possibilities; the same
conclusion holds with $X,Z$ interchanged.

We now prove the seven table entries, assuming $\vc(G)>K+2$ and all
three actual cross coefficients zero.  All expanded terms are safe.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Entry 1.}
The actual $C/L$ anchor bounds $gL\vee CDM\vee gDM$ by two missing
witnesses, by the single-affected case of the two-product bound.
The remaining old cubic $ABN$ adds at most one.  Four targets are
impossible.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Entry 2.}
Put $Q=CDM$, $X=gDM$, and $Z=hDM$.  The actual $g$- and
$h$-recipient anchors for the same base $C$ bound each of
$gL\vee Q\vee X$ and $hN\vee Q\vee Z$ by two witnesses.
If $Q$ witnesses a target, the two bundles overlap and have at most
three in their union.  Suppose $Q$ witnesses none.

If $X$ has two targets, full quartic equality confines $U,V,D,M$
to their matching quartet and makes them the four distinct
transversals.  The first bundle has no target outside that pair.
A new target of $Z$ must use the same quartet vertex in both
$D,M$; if their intersection is empty it cannot exist.  Distinct
transversals intersect in at most one vertex.  Among the four
targets, the only possible edge incident to the quartet but outside
the pair is the other path arm.  Thus a new target of $Z$ forces
the confined pair to be a path arm and an isolated edge, and can
add only the other arm.  The final target must come from $hN$
on the other isolated edge.  The old quadratic $h$ is also true on
the new arm through $Z$; these two edges are disjoint.  The
singleton observation makes full $N$ an isolated endpoint, giving
the one-context cover charge.  If $Z$ has two targets, interchange
$g,L,X$ with $h,N,Z$.

Otherwise $X,Z$ each have at most one target.  Four targets force
$gL,hN,X,Z$ to witness four different edges.  If either direct
cubic witnesses an isolated edge, its quadratic is also true on
the distinct target of its mixed quartic, necessarily disjoint.
Its full context is a singleton isolated endpoint, giving the
charge.  In the remaining allocation $gL,hN$ witness the two arms
and $X,Z$ the isolated edges.  The same observation makes $L,N$
singleton endpoints of their respective arms.  A singleton $x$
gives the first charge; otherwise they are the different leaves
$y,z$ and give the two-context charge.  Entry 2 is exhausted.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Entry 3.}
Booleanly $f=CD\vee g$, so
$Y=gL\vee gM\vee ABN\vee CDM$.  The first two safe cubics
have at most one target by the actual-context common-quadratic
consequence.  Each remaining old cubic adds at most one.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Entry 4.}
Booleanly $f=CD\vee g\vee Ch$, so
$Y=gL\vee gM\vee hN\vee CDM\vee hCM$.
The first two terms have at most one target.  The actual base $D$
receives $h$; its low and anchor in $N$ apply the single-affected
two-product bound to $hN,CDM,hCM$, using quadratics $h,CM$ and
contexts $N,D$.  These terms have at most two targets.  The total
is at most three.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Entry 5.}
The original $A/L$ anchor applies the two-product bound to
$gL\vee hN=gL\vee ABN\vee gBN$, giving at most two targets.
The old cubic $CDM$ adds at most one.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Entry 6.}
Booleanly $h=AB\vee g$, so
$Y=gL\vee gN\vee ABN\vee CDM$.
The actual-context common-quadratic family $gL,gN$ has at most
one target; the other two old cubics add at most two.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Entry 7.}
Here $Y=gL\vee gN\vee ABN\vee CDM\vee gDM$.
The actual $C/L$ anchor bounds $gL\vee CDM\vee gDM$ by two;
the actual-context family $gL,gN$ has at most one target.
If $gL$ witnesses a target, $gN$ adds no new one, and the preceding
bundle together with $ABN$ has at most three.
Suppose $gL$ has none.  If $gN\vee ABN$ has at most one target,
adding the at-most-two-target bundle $CDM\vee gDM$ again gives
at most three.  Otherwise $gN$ and $ABN$ witness different targets.
Apply the shared-context consequence to quadratics $g,AB$ and
actual context $N$.  Every target on which $g$ is true lies among
those two.  In particular $gDM$ adds no third target, and $CDM$
adds at most one.  This exhausts the final entry.

All seven cases contradict $\vc(G)>K+2$.  Repeated forms cannot
evade full quartic equality, which itself forces distinct supports
when two witnesses occur.  Positive multiplicities and target-zero
restrictions cause no change to any full original anchor or cover
charge.  Part (A) allowed positive crosses; the seven exclusions
used their stated zero-cross hypothesis.  No unlisted configuration
or full all-visible conclusion follows from this proposition.
\end{proof}

% Complete author-route transcription after full mutual comparison.
% Original proof and all exposure/correction records remain separate.
\begin{proposition}[Unsafe nonraw highs and a split affected cell]
\label{prop:nonrawunsafehighsplit}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute \(P\in\Sup(G)\), where
\(G\) is finite, simple and four-cycle-free.  Its nonempty squarefree
quadratic support is \(H\), and its exactly four global missing edges are
\[
 J=E(G)\setminus E(H)=\{xy,xz,ab,cd\}.
\]
Their endpoint set \(T\) satisfies \(G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2\) and
\(H[T]=\varnothing\).  Let \(K\) be the number of original retained
multiplications.  Suppose there are exactly three original private
multiplications and three original private additions, all additions
visible.  The insertion highs are the three distinct original private
product nodes, each inserted once.  Every private operand has original
minimum degree one and consists of a nonzero old homogeneous linear
base together with its compatible earlier insertion contributions.
Here a singleton support is allowed as an old form; every nonsingleton
old support lies in an \(H\)-neighborhood.  Keep the exact original
selected frame, all nodes, minimum degrees, coefficients, selected lows
and paths, full contexts, fanout and retained-product incidences.

Then every original private-high Boolean function is globally unsafe:
it is true on some independent set of \(G\).  Consequently, if a high
\(v_k\) Booleanly implies both \(v_i\) and \(v_j\), where \(i\ne j\) are
original insertion occurrences, their actual pair coefficient
\(q_{ij}\) is zero.  The index \(k\) may equal \(i\) or \(j\), and
coincident Boolean values do not identify original nodes.  These two
conclusions hold for arbitrary \(K\), without a contrary cover
inequality.

Moreover, the entire original cell
\[
 g=UV,\qquad h=(A\vee g)(B\vee g),\qquad
 f=(C\vee g)(D\vee h\vee\varepsilon g),\qquad
 \varepsilon\in\{0,1\},
\]
has \(\vc(G)\le K+2\).  The six displayed base forms are full nonzero
old homogeneous linear forms, with repetitions allowed.  The two
inputs of \(h\) and the first input of \(f\) are actual boundaries
carrying the first insertion; the second input of \(f\) actually
carries the \(h\)-insertion and retains its optional additional
\(g\)-contribution.  All actual pair coefficients are initially
unrestricted.  The displayed Boolean notation records support only;
it changes no original arithmetic degree, coefficient incidence or
counted gate.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{A two-product support bound.}
We first prove a fact for any finite four-cycle-free graph \(G\) and
nonempty quadratic support \(H_0\); no four-target shape is needed.
Consider a circuit with two private products having minimum-degree-one
operands, one visible degree-one cut for each product, and no other
private addition.  Preserve its actual selected frame.  With one
independent symbol for each insertion, its exact contribution beyond
the quadratic part is
\[
 gL\vee fM\vee qgf,
\]
where \(L,M\) are the nonzero old homogeneous linear contexts and there
is no individual square.  The first product is \(g=UV\).  The second
has one of the three Boolean forms
\[
 f=AB,\qquad f=B(A\vee g),\qquad f=AB\vee g.
\]
All forms here are old relative to the actual \(H_0\).

We spell out the actual anchor needed in the affected cases.  If a
retained or restored degree-one operand with full homogeneous base
\(A\) receives \(g\), follow its selected addition-only continuation
to the first retained multiplication.  Its opposite nonzero
homogeneous support \(D_0\) satisfies
\[
 AD_0\text{ is supported on }H_0,\qquad D_0\subseteq L.
\]
For any \(k\in D_0\), the singleton form \(\{k\}\) is old.  The
nonzero first low \(a_0\) lies in \(A\), and the three products
\(a_0L,\ a_0k,\ kA\) are supported on \(H_0\).
These are original-node statements, not choices made after restricting
the variables.

The six possibilities are as follows.  Each listed product is safe,
by positivity of the full output.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If \(f=AB\) and \(q=0\), there are just the two old cubics
\(UVL,ABM\), each with at most one missing witness by
Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors}.
\item If \(f=AB\) and \(q>0\), the terms are
\(UVL,ABM,UVAB\).  The actual cross identities put the first low in
\(M\), the second low in \(L\), and make their product, as well as
each low times its own direct context, \(H_0\)-supported.
Lemma~\ref{lem:independentproducts} therefore bounds their missing
witness union by two.
\item If \(f=B(A\vee g)\) and \(q=0\), the terms are
\(UVL,ABM,UVBM\).  Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:independentproducts} to the old products \(UV,BM\),
contexts \(L,A\), and low forms \(a_0,\{k\}\).  The inclusions
\(a_0\subseteq A\), \(\{k\}\subseteq L\) and the old products
\(a_0L,kA,a_0k\) were established above.  The union has at most two
missing witnesses.
\item If \(f=B(A\vee g)\) and \(q>0\), Boolean absorption gives
\(UVL,ABM,UVB\).  The actual cross puts \(a_0\) in \(M\); hence
\(a_0\subseteq A\cap M\), while \(a_0L\) is \(H_0\)-supported.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:relatedcubics} to the common pair \(U,V\),
contexts \(L,B\), and remaining factors \(A,M\).  Again the union
has at most two.
\item If \(f=AB\vee g\) and \(q=0\), the terms are
\(UVL,UVM,ABM\).  The same original first low lies in \(A\cap B\),
and its product with \(L\) is \(H_0\)-supported.
Lemma~\ref{lem:relatedcubics} gives at most two missing witnesses.
\item If \(f=AB\vee g\) and \(q>0\), the mixed term makes \(g\)
itself safe and absorbs all its multiples.  The remaining union is
the safe old quadratic \(g\) and the old cubic \(ABM\), each with
at most one missing witness.
\end{enumerate}
Thus at most two edges of \(G\) lack quadratic witnesses in \(H_0\).
Absent private gates or terms only reduce these counts.  This fact
uses full old supports and actual contexts globally and assumes
neither an optimal retained count nor a cover inequality.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Every original private high is unsafe.}
Suppose an original high \(v\) were safe.  Add a new output addition
\(P+v\), reusing the same original product node \(v\).  The Boolean
output remains the graph function.  Both inputs of this new addition
have minimum degree two, so the canonical quadratic extraction keeps
both of them and retains the new addition.  This minimum-degree
assertion does not say that their full ordinary polynomials are
homogeneous.

Bypass the unique original visible cut \(c_v\) carrying \(v\) through
its actual selected low.  The node \(v\) is upstream of \(c_v\) and
does not change.  Every contribution removed from the other output
branch is a positive multiple of the unchanged \(v\), and the new
direct summand \(v\) Booleanly absorbs it.  Thus the resulting
positive variable-input circuit still computes the same graph
function; no formal zero input remains in the physical circuit.

This bypass changes no old ordinary quadratic monomial.  The cut
has minimum degree one, its higher input has minimum degree two,
and every path from the cut output to the output encounters a
multiplication: an addition-only path would carry a forbidden
linear monomial to the output.  Therefore a contribution from its
high to the old output has ordinary degree at least three.  The
original selected low paths and retained frame stay intact.

Let \(E,F\) be the full homogeneous linear parts of the two original
inputs of \(v\).  They are old relative to the original \(H\), and
the quadratic component of \(v\) is \(EF\).  The new quadratic
support is exactly
\[
 H'=H\cup\operatorname{supp}_{\mathrm{edges}}(EF).
\]
Safety of \(v\) makes \(EF\) a safe old quadratic: all its quadratic
monomials are edges of \(G\), with no square.
Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors} bounds its missing witnesses by one.
Consequently at least three edges of \(G\) remain outside \(H'\).
The auxiliary quadratic support is nonempty and lies in the same
four-cycle-free graph, and its output polynomial belongs to
\(\Sup(G)\).

In the auxiliary extraction \(v\) is a retained quadratic product,
directly below the new retained output addition.  The two other
original private products are not selected through \(v\)'s inputs:
those inputs have minimum degree one, and their earlier private
highs occur on the high sides of strict degree-one cuts, which
selection bypasses.  The original selected frame still survives
through the old output.  The cut \(c_v\) is gone; the other two cuts
remain on their selected low paths and remain visible, unless
harmless unused-node pruning removes them.  No private addition
was added.  Bypassing \(c_v\) preserves every other private
operand's minimum degree one and its nonzero homogeneous base.

There is no surviving raw use of the now-retained \(v\) in a private
operand: such uses were excluded in the original nonraw frame,
and the bypass removes its insertion route.  Each other high keeps
its one original insertion occurrence.  Thus the auxiliary circuit
has at most two nonraw private products and two visible cuts.
Its full contexts and bases are old relative to its actual
\(H'\), by their selected continuations.  The two-product bound
just proved allows at most two edges outside \(H'\), contradicting
the at-least-three count.

This proves the first assertion for arbitrary original \(K\).
The auxiliary quadratic support is explicitly \(H'\), not \(H\);
the newly retained product \(v\) is never charged as though it
belonged to the original \(K\).

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Actual pair coefficients.}
If \(q_{ij}>0\), positivity makes the actual product \(v_iv_j\)
safe.  If \(v_k\) implies both factors, it implies this safe product
and is safe itself, contrary to the preceding assertion.  Hence
\(q_{ij}=0\).  This keeps the original occurrence indices even when
two Boolean values coincide.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Two charges against the original frame.}
Return now to the original \(H,K\).  A nonzero actual direct linear
context \(N\) contains an entire opposite homogeneous support of an
original retained quadratic product.  If the full support of \(N\)
lies in a three-vertex cover \(S\) of \(J\), then \(S\) covers that
retained product.  Add one center for each of the other \(K-1\)
retained stars to obtain
\[
 \vc(G)\le (K-1)+3=K+2.
\]
The retained products are stars because \(G\) is four-cycle-free.

If two nonzero actual contexts \(N,M\) are disjoint and both lie
in \(T\), their marked retained products are distinct.  Otherwise,
entry through the same side would put a nonzero opposite support
in \(N\cap M\); entry through opposite sides would put both
homogeneous factors of one retained product in \(T\), contradicting
\(H[T]=\varnothing\) or squarefreeness.  If \(N\cup M\) lies in a
four-vertex cover \(S\) of \(J\), cover these two products with \(S\)
and all other retained products with their centers.  Then
\[
 \vc(G)\le (K-2)+4=K+2.
\]
All marked products and full supports are original; neither charge
uses the auxiliary circuit.

In particular, a singleton actual context at \(x\), or at an
isolated-edge endpoint, gives the first charge.  Singleton contexts
at \(y\) and \(z\) give the second charge.  It follows that, under
\(\vc(G)>K+2\), a fixed old quadratic \(g\) has at most one target
among the safe cubics \(gL,gN,gM\).  Indeed,
Lemma~\ref{lem:commoncubic} makes two distinct targets a star, hence
the two path arms.  Oldness forces \(x\) into both factors of \(g\).
The missing-cubic singleton argument in that lemma, applied to
the repeated \(x\), forces the two full witnessing contexts to be
\(\{y\},\{z\}\), and the second charge applies.

We shall also use the following full-support observation.  If old
forms \(A,B\) have a common nonzero support and the safe cubic
\(ABN\) witnesses a missing edge, then \(N\) is a singleton
endpoint of that edge.  When both \(A,B\) are nonsingleton this is
the missing-cubic singleton rule.  Otherwise, say \(A=\{u\}\),
their common support puts \(u\) in \(B\), so \(AB\) is true on
\(\{u\}\).  A missing witness makes \(N\) contain a missing neighbor
of \(u\), while safety puts every element of \(N\) among the
neighbors of \(u\) and excludes \(u\).  A second element of the
old support \(N\), together with its old center, would give a
four-cycle, or make the missing edge old.  Thus the full \(N\),
not merely its restriction to \(T\), is the required singleton.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The entire double/split cell.}
The nonzero original first low \(a_0\) lies in \(A,B,C\).  The
nonzero original \(h\)-cut low \(b_0\) lies in \(D\), and \(b_0N\)
is supported on \(H\).  The optional extra \(g\)-contribution does
not change these actual identities.  Booleanly,
\[
 h=AB\vee g,\qquad f=CD\vee ABC\vee g.
\]
Thus \(g\) implies both \(h,f\), and the coefficient conclusion
forces all three actual \(q_{12},q_{13},q_{23}\) to vanish.  This
is a deduction, not an assumed zero-cross normalization.
The exact remaining contribution is
\[
 Y=gL\vee gN\vee gM\vee ABN\vee CDM\vee ABCM.
\]
Assume \(\vc(G)>K+2\).  The common-\(g\) cubic family supplies at
most one target altogether, and each of \(ABN,CDM\) supplies at
most one.  Put \(Q=ABCM\).  By
Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors}, this safe old quartic has at
most two missing witnesses, and two must form an induced matching.

Suppose first that \(Q\) has two target witnesses.  The full-support
equality case of Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors} makes
\(A,B,C,M\) the four distinct two-point transversals of their
endpoint quartet.  If these witnesses are the two isolated
edges, \(M\) together with \(x\) lies in a three-cover of \(J\),
and the first original-context charge applies.  If they are a
path arm and an isolated edge and \(M\) contains the path center,
adjoin one endpoint of the remaining isolated edge to obtain
the same charge.

In the only case not already charged, rename the pair as
\(xy,ab\) and write \(M=\{y,a\}\), exchanging isolated endpoints
if necessary.  Any term containing \(M\) can witness only these
two targets.  Therefore
\[
 gL\vee gN\vee ABN
\]
must supply both \(xz\) and \(cd\).  Its first two terms together
supply at most one, so \(ABN\) supplies one of them.
Since \(A,B\) share \(a_0\), the full-support observation makes
\(N\) a singleton endpoint.  A witness \(cd\) gives an isolated
singleton context and the first charge.  For a witness \(xz\),
\(N=\{x\}\) gives the first charge; if \(N=\{z\}\), it is disjoint
from \(M=\{y,a\}\), and their union lies in the four-cover
\(\{y,z,a,c\}\).  The second charge applies.  Thus every
two-witness case for \(Q\) contradicts the assumed cover inequality.

Finally suppose \(Q\) has at most one target.  Four targets force
the common-\(g\) family, \(ABN\), \(CDM\), and \(Q\) to supply
four different targets.  Again \(N\) is a full singleton endpoint.
An isolated endpoint or \(x\) gives the first charge, so, after
exchanging path leaves, \(ABN\) witnesses \(xy\) and
\(N=\{y\}\).  The remaining three edges \(xz,ab,cd\) form a
matching; in particular the different witnesses of \(CDM\) and
\(Q\) are disjoint.

Both \(C\) and \(M\) meet each of these disjoint endpoint pairs,
because they occur in both products.  Neither is a singleton.
The missing-cubic singleton rule for safe \(CDM\) therefore forces
the full \(D\) to be a singleton endpoint of its target.  But
the actual recipient base \(D\) contains the nonzero old low
\(b_0\).  The actual old product \(b_0N\), with \(N=\{y\}\), would
then give an \(H\)-edge wholly inside \(T\), or an old square.
Both are impossible.

This proves \(\vc(G)\le K+2\) for the stated cell with arbitrary
original \(K\) and all actual initial cross coefficients.  The
argument preserves full ambient supports and all original
occurrences.  It does not normalize another cell, a hidden
addition, or a repeated-high family.
\end{proof}

% Complete original-author-route transcription after full mutual comparison.
% The four double-affected-middle cells only; no main-file mutation.
\begin{proposition}[The complete double-affected-middle row]
\label{prop:doubleaffectedmiddlerow}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$, where $G$ is
finite, simple and four-cycle-free.  Suppose its nonempty ordinary
quadratic support is $H$, and its four global missing edges are
$xy,xz,ab,cd$, with endpoint set $T$ satisfying
$G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$.
Keep the exact original selected quadratic frame and its arbitrary
retained-product count $K$.  Suppose there are exactly three original
private products and three original private additions, all additions
are visible, and the three highs are the three distinct original
private-product nodes, each inserted once.  Every private-product input
has original minimum degree one, with its nonzero old homogeneous linear
base and its actual available earlier insertion contributions.
Preserve every original node, degree, occurrence, coefficient, selected
low and path, fanout, full context and retained-product incidence.

Order the product nodes topologically as $g,h,f$.  Suppose
\[
 g=UV,\qquad h=(A\vee g)(B\vee g),
\]
and, up to interchanging the two final input sides, $f$ has one of the
following original operand types:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:doublemiddleforms}
\begin{array}{c|l}
1&f=CD,\\
2&f=(C\vee g)D,\\
3&f=C(D\vee h\vee\varepsilon g),\\
4&f=(C\vee g)(D\vee h\vee\varepsilon g),
\end{array}
\qquad \varepsilon\in\{0,1\}.
\end{equation}
The six base forms are full nonzero old homogeneous linear forms and
may repeat.  Each affected factor is its actual original operand, with
its compatible positive occurrence coefficients and all original
low/context identities.  The optional extra $g$ coefficient remains
recorded even when Boolean absorption removes it from a displayed
value.  Keep the complete actual contribution
\begin{equation}\label{eq:doublemiddleframe}
 Y=gL\vee hN\vee fM\vee q_{12}gh\vee q_{13}gf\vee q_{23}hf,
 \qquad q_{ij}\in\{0,1\},
\end{equation}
where a coefficient records absence or positivity of its actual
occurrence coefficient, and all three coefficients are initially
unrestricted.  The contexts are the full original old linear direct
contexts with their selected lows and mixed identities.
If $Y$ is globally safe and supplies all four target witnesses, then
$\vc(G)\le K+2$.
This excludes the entire double-affected-middle row; it does not
classify the independent-middle or single-affected-middle rows.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every support identity below is Boolean and changes no arithmetic
minimum degree, original gate or occurrence.  In particular, ordering
product nodes does not impose an unproved order on unrelated cuts.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The exact frame and target potentials.}
Every original private product has minimum degree two, since its two
inputs have minimum degree one.  Its selected low therefore has degree
one.  The independent-symbol selected frame has the form
\eqref{eq:doublemiddleframe}; an individual squared insertion symbol
would give a square from its nonzero old low in the quadratic part.
All three full contexts $L,N,M$ are old homogeneous linear forms and
are globally nonzero.  Indeed, follow a visible cut on a selected
linear continuation to its first retained quadratic product; the
entire opposite nonzero homogeneous factor occurs in that direct
context.  A context may nevertheless vanish on $T$.

Let $a_0,b_0,c_0$ be the nonzero old homogeneous parts of the three
selected lows.  Then $a_0L,b_0N,c_0M$ are supported on $H$-edges.
The two actual inputs of $h$ receive $g$, so
$a_0\subseteq A\cap B$.  An actual input base receiving $h$ contains
$b_0$.  Positive pair coefficients retain their original mixed-low
and retained-product identities.  Here containment of forms means
containment of supports; no base is assumed to be an available
standalone circuit wire.

Proposition~\ref{prop:nonrawsevenzerocross} applies to these three
original nodes: each of $g,h,f$ is true on at least two distinct target
edge assignments.  We use only that potential statement, without
assigning different targets to different nodes.  In particular the old
quadratic $g$ is not globally safe, since
Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors} allows a safe old quadratic at most
one missing witness.  Booleanly $h=AB\vee g$, so $gh=g$.  Safety of the
positive output therefore forces
\begin{equation}\label{eq:doublemiddleqzero}
 q_{12}=0.
\end{equation}
This uses no general unsafe-high assertion about the other nodes.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Actual selected anchors and original cover charges.}
Let an actual degree-one operand with full old homogeneous base $E$
receive insertion $i$.  Follow its selected additive continuation to
its first retained quadratic product, and let $B_0$ be the entire
opposite homogeneous input.  Then $EB_0$ is supported on $H$-edges and
$B_0$ is contained in the full context $L_i$ of that occurrence.  The
homogeneous selected low of occurrence $i$ is contained in $E$.
This is the actual selected-path argument of
\eqref{eq:nonrawsevenanchor}; it does not assert an anchor for an
algebraically invented base.

A nonzero actual direct context contains the entire opposite factor
of at least one original retained product.  If a three-vertex cover
$W$ of the four global missing edges contains that full context, it
covers the whole support of the marked retained product.  Choose one
center for each other original retained product.  This gives a cover
of $G$ with at most $(K-1)+3=K+2$ vertices.  Each retained product is a
squarefree quadratic star: overlapping factors give a square, and two
disjoint nonsingleton factors give a four-cycle.

For two disjoint nonzero full contexts contained in $T$, the marked
retained products are different.  If both occurrences entered the same
side of one product, its nonzero opposite factor would lie in their
empty intersection.  If they entered opposite sides, both old factors
would lie in $T$, giving an $H$-edge there or a square.  Hence, if their
union is contained in a four-vertex cover of the missing edges, that
cover and centers for the other $K-2$ products give $K+2$.
Repeated centers only lower these bounds.  In particular, an actual
full singleton context at $x$ or any isolated-edge endpoint incurs the
first charge.  Full singleton contexts $\{y\},\{z\}$ incur the second,
using the target cover $\{y,z,a,c\}$.

For the rest of the proof suppose, to the contrary, that
$\vc(G)>K+2$.  Thus an actual singleton context at a target vertex can only be a path
leaf, and two actual singleton contexts cannot be the two different
leaves.  All these charges use the full ambient $H$ and the original
retained count $K$.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Two full-support singleton facts.}
First let $X=EF$ be an old quadratic true on at least two target
assignments, and suppose the safe old cubic $XD$ witnesses a target
$e$.  Then the \emph{full} support of $D$ is a singleton endpoint of
$e$.  The quadratic $X$ is true on $e$ and on another target $e'$.
If the two targets are disjoint, both $E,F$ meet two disjoint endpoint
pairs and are nonsingleton.  The old-cubic singleton argument then
forces $D$ to be the full singleton.  To recall that argument, a cubic
witness repeats one endpoint; safety forces every vertex of the factor
used for the other endpoint to neighbor the repeated endpoint.  If
that old factor had another vertex, its old center would create a
four-cycle with the missing edge, unless that edge were already in
$H$.  Thus this factor is a full singleton, and it cannot be either
of the two nonsingleton factors $E,F$.

If $e,e'$ are adjacent, they are the two path arms.  An old support
meeting both arms but omitting $x$ contains $y,z$; its old center and
$x$ then make a four-cycle, or make an arm old.  Thus both $E,F$
contain $x$.  Safety of $XD$ puts every vertex of $D$ among neighbors
of $x$, excludes $x$ itself, and puts the missing leaf of $e$ in $D$.
A second vertex of $D$, its old center and $x$ would again give a
four-cycle or make the missing arm old.  Thus $D$ is the full singleton
leaf.  This covers every possible second target, including outside
vertices in all full supports.

Second, suppose old $A,B$ share the nonzero form $a_0$, and safe $ABN$
witnesses a missing edge.  Then full $N$ is a singleton endpoint.  If
$A,B$ are nonsingleton, use the same cubic singleton argument.  Otherwise,
say $A=\{t\}$; their common support puts $t$ in $B$, so $AB$ is true
on $t$ alone.  A missing witness puts a missing neighbor of $t$ in $N$,
and safety puts every vertex of $N$ among neighbors of $t$.  A second
vertex and the old center of $N$ give the same forbidden four-cycle.
Thus again $N$ is the full singleton.  These statements concern full
supports, not just their restrictions to $T$.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The entire direct contribution.}
The two target potentials of $g$ and the first singleton fact show
that any target of $gL$ makes full $L$ an endpoint singleton.  Under
the contrary cover inequality it must be $y$ or $z$.  Hence $gL$ has
at most one target, a path arm.  Each target of
$hN=ABN\vee gN$ similarly makes full $N$ an endpoint singleton:
use the second fact for $ABN$ and the first for $gN$.  Thus $hN$ also
has at most one target, a path arm.  If $gL$ and $hN$ have different
targets, their full contexts are the two different leaves, contradicting
the two-product charge.  Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:doublemiddledirect}
 D_0=gL\vee hN\quad\hbox{has at most one target, a path arm.}
\end{equation}

We shall also use the following extension.  If an additional safe
cubic $XM$ has an old quadratic $X$ with two target potentials and
$M$ is an actual full direct context, then every target of $XM$
makes $M$ a full singleton path leaf.  Adding $XM$ to $D_0$ still
gives at most one target, since different arms would provide two
actual opposite-leaf contexts.  We use this only for $X=f=CD$ in the
first final form and for $X=g$ in the fourth.  An arbitrary old operand
is not thereby declared an actual direct context.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Shared-factor confinement.}
Suppose all target witnesses outside a family come from at most one
path arm, and every term of the family contains two specified old
factors $E,F_0$.  If one safe old quartic in the family witnesses two
targets, full equality in Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors} confines
both $E,F_0$ to the four endpoints $W$ of that induced matching.
Every target of every term in the family must meet $W$.
If the matching consists of the two isolated edges, $W$ has no path
vertex, so the family has no arm and its complement supplies at most
one.  If it consists of one arm and one isolated edge, the other
isolated edge is disjoint from $W$; neither the family nor its outside
arm contribution supplies that edge.  These are all induced two-edge
matchings among the targets.  Thus either situation contradicts four
target witnesses.

Only full quartic equality is used here.  We have not confined an
arbitrary safe context to a target quartet.  The family may contain
additional terms with any other factors, provided the same two old
factors occur in every term.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Mandatory factors and bare cubic crosses.}
For the second final form let $E=D$, and for the third let $E=C$.
This is a mandatory old factor of $f$, so every contribution containing
$f$ contains $E$.  By \eqref{eq:doublemiddleqzero}, every other
contribution belongs to $D_0$ and has only a path-arm target under the
contrary inequality.

Suppose a positive actual cross makes $gE$ safe and that cubic has a
target witness.  The first singleton fact makes full $E$ a singleton
endpoint.  Since $f$ has two distinct target potentials and every
monomial of $f$ contains $E$, this singleton must be $x$, the only
vertex incident to two target edges.  Then all $f$-containing terms
have only path-arm targets, as does $D_0$.  Neither isolated target
is supplied, a contradiction.  Therefore such a present bare cubic
$gE$ has no target witness.

In the third final form the same conclusion holds for a present safe
cubic $ABE$: the second singleton fact applies since $A,B$ share
$a_0$, and the mandatory-factor argument again forces $E=x$ and
misses both isolated edges.  Positive multiples of a target-free term
are target-free.  These assertions are made only when the actual
positive cross makes the bare cubic safe; no ordinary degree is
changed or inferred from them.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{First final form: $f=CD$.}
Using $h=AB\vee g$ and \eqref{eq:doublemiddleqzero}, the contribution
is the direct union $gL\vee hN\vee fM$ together with the present
members of
\[
 Q=gCD,\qquad R=ABCD.
\]
More precisely, $q_{13}$ gives $Q$ and $q_{23}$ gives $Q\vee R$.
Both are safe old quartics when present.  The original high $f=CD$
has two target potentials, so the extension of
\eqref{eq:doublemiddledirect} shows that the entire direct union has
at most one target, a path arm.

If neither present quartic has two targets, they contribute at most
two further targets, for a total at most three.  If either has two,
full quartic equality confines both $C,D$ to its matching quartet.
Both quartics share these two factors, so shared-factor confinement,
with the direct arm contribution outside, rules out four targets.
This includes zero and positive values of every original coefficient.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Second final form: $f=(C\vee g)D$.}
Here $f=CD\vee gD$ in support, and
\[
 gf=gD,\qquad hf=gD\vee ABCD.
\]
If $q_{13}=q_{23}=0$, the contribution is
$D_0\vee CDM\vee gDM$.  The old cubic $CDM$ has at most one target.
If the old quartic $gDM$ has at most one, the total is at most three.
If it has two, full $D,M$ are confined to their matching quartet.
The remaining family $CDM\vee gDM$ shares $D,M$, so shared-factor
confinement with $D_0$ outside rules out four targets.

If $q_{13}$ or $q_{23}$ is positive, the bare cubic $gD$ is safe.
The mandatory-factor argument makes it target-free, as is its multiple
$gDM$.  For $q_{23}=0$, only $D_0$ and $CDM$ can supply targets,
at most two.  For $q_{23}>0$, the additional term is the safe old
quartic $R=ABCD$.  If it has at most one target the total is at most
three.  If it has two, full $C,D$ are confined and the remaining
family $CDM\vee R$ shares those factors; shared-factor confinement
again applies.  No actual cross has been dropped without its exact
Boolean absorption or an explicitly proved target bound.
