\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Third final form: $f=C(D\vee h\vee\varepsilon g)$.}
The optional original coefficient is still recorded.  Since $g$
implies $h$, the support identities are
\[
 f=CD\vee ABC\vee gC,\qquad
 gf=gC,\qquad hf=ABC\vee gC.
\]
If $q_{23}>0$, both $gC$ and $ABC$ are safe, and the mandatory-factor
argument makes both target-free.  Their multiples $gCM,ABCM$ have no
target either.  Only $D_0$ and $CDM$ remain, with at most two targets.

If $q_{23}=0$ and $q_{13}>0$, the safe bare $gC$ and its multiple
$gCM$ are target-free.  The remaining terms are $D_0,CDM,Q=ABCM$.
If $Q$ has at most one target there are at most three.  If it has two,
full $C,M$ are confined, and the family $CDM\vee Q$ shares those
factors.  Shared-factor confinement rules out four targets.

It remains to consider $q_{13}=q_{23}=0$, when
\begin{equation}\label{eq:doublemiddlethirdzero}
 Y=D_0\vee CDM\vee ABCM\vee gCM.
\end{equation}
If either quartic has two targets, full $C,M$ are confined.  Every term
after $D_0$ shares $C,M$, so shared-factor confinement applies.
Suppose instead that both quartics have at most one target.  Four
targets then force $D_0$ to supply one arm and each of
$CDM,ABCM,gCM$ to supply a different remaining target.  Those three
remaining targets are the other arm and the two isolated edges,
a matching of size three.

Both $C$ and $M$ meet all three of these disjoint endpoint pairs,
since they occur in each of the three terms; neither is singleton.
The old-cubic singleton rule for $CDM$ therefore forces full $D$ to
be a singleton endpoint $t$ of its witnessed target.  The actual
$h$-recipient base $D$ contains the nonzero homogeneous low $b_0$,
so $b_0=\{t\}$.  Since $b_0N$ is supported on $H$ and $t\in T$,
the condition $H[T]=\varnothing$ forces $N$ to have no target vertex.
Thus $hN$ has no target and the required arm of $D_0$ comes from $gL$.

The singleton fact and the cover charge make full $L$ the singleton
leaf of that arm.  Each of the two actual inputs of $h$ receives $g$.
Apply the selected-continuation anchor to $A$ and separately to $B$.
Their nonzero opposite old factors lie in $L$ and hence have that
singleton leaf as their full support.  Both $A$ times the leaf and
$B$ times the leaf are supported on $H$.  Since the leaf lies in $T$
and $H[T]=\varnothing$, both $A$ and $B$ have empty restriction to
$T$; a repeated leaf would give a forbidden square.  This contradicts
the required target witness of $ABCM$.  The argument used the
selected anchors of actual operands, not algebraic substitutes for
circuit wires, and did not infer a degree from absorption of the
optional coefficient.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Fourth final form: $f=(C\vee g)(D\vee h\vee\varepsilon g)$.}
Booleanly
\[
 h=AB\vee g,\qquad f=CD\vee ABC\vee g.
\]
Thus $g$ implies both $h$ and $f$, and every pair product $gh,gf,hf$
contains the globally unsafe $g$ as a Boolean subfunction.  Positivity
and safety force all three actual pair coefficients to vanish.
This uses only the first old quadratic and its two target potentials.
The contribution becomes
\[
 Y=D_0\vee gM\vee CDM\vee ABCM.
\]
The safe cubic $gM$ has an actual direct context.  The extension of
\eqref{eq:doublemiddledirect} shows that $D_0\vee gM$ has at most
one target, a path arm.  The old cubic $CDM$ has at most one and the
old quartic $Q=ABCM$ has at most two.  If $Q$ has at most one, the
total is at most three.  If it has two, full $C,M$ are confined, and
the family $CDM\vee Q$ shares those factors.  Its outside contribution
is the at-most-one arm already established, so shared-factor
confinement again rules out all four targets.  Both original values
of $\varepsilon$ have been covered.

The four cases exhaust exactly \eqref{eq:doublemiddleforms}.  Every
initial actual pair coefficient was retained until it was individually
forced to zero or its term was shown target-free.  No original node
was merged, no gate was created by expansion, no minimum degree was
changed, and no optimality of the retained frame was assumed.  The
contradiction to four global target witnesses proves $\vc(G)\le K+2$
for the entire stated row and arbitrary original $K$.
\end{proof}


% Complete manuscript transcription of whole-author SZ4-231, Part A.
% Source: paper3_all_visible_three_product_cover_author_complete_v1.md
% Source SHA256: 4dd0069e874a68c67f43563cb604175fd5736189c1bf02f2aa0a362c7d091e3f
% The statement follows the exact unchanged clean statement. Historical
% save/exposure/readback paragraphs remain in the immutable source and metadata.
\begin{proposition}[The entire all-visible three-product family]
\label{prop:allvisiblethreeproductcover}
Let $G$ be finite, simple and four-cycle-free, and let a positive
variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$. Let $H$ be its nonempty
squarefree ordinary quadratic support, and suppose its exactly four global
missing edges are $xy,xz,ab,cd$. On their full endpoint set $T$, suppose
$G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$. Keep the exact original
selected quadratic frame and its arbitrary retained multiplication count
$K$; retained addition counts and optimality are unrestricted.

Suppose canonical minimum-degree extraction and pruning delete exactly
three original multiplication nodes and exactly three original addition
nodes, and every deleted addition is visible. Preserve every original
node and operand wire, minimum degree, insertion occurrence, coefficient,
fanout, selected low and path, full direct context, pairwise occurrence
coefficient and retained-product incidence. Then
\[
\vc(G)\le K+2.
\]
Initially there is no restriction on private-product ancestry, raw or
affected operands, repeated inputs, which original product supplies a
visible high, repetition of high values or high nodes across the three
distinct insertion occurrences, or any compatible scalar or zero context.
Coincident Boolean values do not identify original product nodes or
insertion occurrences. Actual same-high and distinct-high cross terms,
with their original degree and low compatibility, remain part of the data.
A Boolean support identity supplies no new wire, changes no original
degree and does not itself delete a counted node. Any actual reduction
preserves the Boolean function, ordinary $P_2$, $H$ and the exact original
selected frame and $K$. Whole-current-carrier erasure, where used, retains
original labels and uses its exact preservation and survival arguments.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
No Boolean identity below creates an original wire, resets an ordinary
minimum degree, copies or merges an original product or insertion, or
deletes a counted gate. Every retained-product charge is made against the
actual original frame. Formal auxiliary products and clauses are support
expressions only. All original zero or positive coefficient distinctions
are preserved until their necessary zero conditions are proved under the
contrary inequality.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{A. Exact original inventory and completed background branches.}
Assume for contradiction that $\vc(G)>K+2$. Apply
Proposition~\ref{prop:allvisibleoriginalinventory} in its exact scope:
finite four-cycle-free $G$, nonempty $H$, the induced $H$-empty four global
target edges, the fixed original frame, at most three private products and
additions, and all private additions visible. Our counts are exactly
three, so its count hypotheses hold. That proposition already includes
the original high and operand essentiality, original matching-restriction
product necessity and the full original-node and raw-input census. We use
its conclusion without rebuilding or expanding the counted circuit.

The resulting necessary alternatives are as follows.

\emph{Three distinct inserted original products, once each.}
In a topological order $g,h,f$ of the product nodes, every input has
original minimum degree one and is nonraw, with a nonzero old homogeneous
base and its actual available earlier insertion contributions. All
product minimum degrees are two, and selected lows have degree one.
Direct contexts are old linear or zero as stated by the inventory. In
the complete original positive variable-input frame they are globally
nonzero: following each selected degree-one visible path to its first
original retained product places that whole nonzero opposite factor in
its direct context. A restriction to $T$ can be zero. Write $g=UV$.
The three rows and their exact necessary final input types are
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
 h & \text{final input types}\\ \hline
 AB & OG,\ OJ,\ GG,\ GH,\ GJ\\
 (A\vee g)B & OO,\ OG,\ OH,\ OJ,\ GG,\ GH,\ GJ,\ HH,\ HJ,\ JJ\\
 (A\vee g)(B\vee g) & OO,\ OG,\ OH,\ GH.
\end{array}
\]
Here $O,G,H,J$ mean an old base plus, respectively, no earlier high,
$g$, $h$, or both, with all indicated coefficients positive and all
actual input and cut availability retained. Exchanges of input sides or
independent product names occur only where the inventory permits them,
carrying their entire original occurrence data. In the double row a
displayed $H$ can include an additional original $g$ coefficient; the
Boolean implication $g\Rightarrow h$ absorbs its value only, not its
recorded occurrence.

\emph{Two distinct inserted original products $g,f$, with $g$ ancestral
to $f$.}
The third original product $u$ is not inserted. There are $n$ original
occurrences carrying $g$ and $3-n$ carrying $f$, where $n=1$ or $2$,
and the exact original families are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 R1:\quad &u=UV,\qquad g=uA,\qquad
 f=\Bigl(B+\sum_i\beta_i g_i\Bigr)
   \Bigl(C+\sum_i\gamma_i g_i\Bigr);\\
 R2:\quad &g=UV,\qquad u=AB\ \text{independent},\qquad
 f=u\Bigl(C+\sum_i\delta_i g_i\Bigr);\\
 R3:\quad &g=UV,\qquad
 u=\Bigl(A+\sum_i\beta_i g_i\Bigr)
   \Bigl(B+\sum_i\gamma_i g_i\Bigr),\qquad
 f=u\Bigl(C+\sum_i\delta_i g_i\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
The stated nonzero affected coefficients, original availability and
shared-index restriction in the both-affected $R3$ preparation are part
of the inventory's conclusion. Every $g_i$ denotes an original insertion
occurrence, not a copied product. All direct contexts, pairwise crosses
and same-high squares retain their actual degree and low compatibility.
Earlier alternatives with fewer inserted nodes or raw three-distinct-high
inputs have already been excluded by the inventory itself. This step
asserts no additional exhaustive census.

The whole $R2$ family is excluded by
Proposition~\ref{prop:independentrawmiddlecover}, which covers both
occurrence allocations and all compatible actual coefficients for
arbitrary $K$. The both-affected and single-affected parts of $R1$ are
excluded, respectively, by
Propositions~\ref{prop:bothaffectedrepeatedcubic} and
\ref{prop:singleaffectedrawcubiccover}, again with both occurrence
allocations, full context and low identities, and arbitrary $K$.
The original $R3$ family, including one- or both-affected preparation,
optional later original $g$ occurrences and both allocations, is excluded
by Proposition~\ref{prop:repeatedRthreecover}. Each gives
$\vc(G)\le K+2$ in the exact original family supplied by the inventory.
Matching these statements needs no gate merging, erased-dependency
relabeling or retained optimality.

The double-middle row is excluded by
Proposition~\ref{prop:doubleaffectedmiddlerow}. Its exact scope permits
$h=(A\vee g)(B\vee g)$ and all four actual final types
\[
 CD,\qquad (C\vee g)D,\qquad
 C(D\vee h\vee\varepsilon g),\qquad
 (C\vee g)(D\vee h\vee\varepsilon g),\quad
 \varepsilon\in\{0,1\},
\]
with arbitrary $K$ and all three initial cross coefficients. These are
precisely the remaining four double-row types, including the optional
original $g$ coefficient that the inventory's $H$ notation absorbs at
the level of support. The full original low and context data agree.
This gives the required cover contradiction in that row; it makes no
assertion about a wider Boolean display.

It remains to prove the independent and single-middle rows. Parts B and C
below supply their complete derivations. Both use the two-target-potential
necessity of Proposition~\ref{prop:nonrawsevenzerocross} within its
original-frame scope. Part C also uses the global unsafety of the three
original highs from Proposition~\ref{prop:nonrawunsafehighsplit}, in the
exact nonraw distinct-high setting; its scope does not require the
contrary cover inequality. The exact original conditions have just been
derived from Proposition~\ref{prop:allvisibleoriginalinventory}.
Old-factor, cubic, independent- and related-two-product, and
original-context facts are used only in their stated scopes, with the
low and anchor remappings explicitly given below.


% Complete manuscript transcription of whole-author SZ4-231, Part B.
% The independent-middle derivation is retained inline in full. No reference
% to the separately checked independent-middle proposition replaces a case.
\medskip\noindent\textbf{B. Complete independent-middle derivation.}
The row hypotheses are those of Part A, with $h=AB$ and the five listed
final forms. The following argument proves that row directly.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B1. Original frame and notation.}
The target set is $J=\{xy,xz,ab,cd\}$; its endpoint set $T$ induces
$P_3\sqcup2K_2$, and $H[T]=\varnothing$. These are the four global
missing edges. The retained-product count $K$ is the arbitrary original
one. There are exactly three original private products and three private
additions, all additions visible; the three distinct original high nodes
are inserted once each. Every original product input has minimum degree
one and a nonzero old homogeneous linear base with its actual earlier
insertion contributions.

Write $g=UV$ and $h=AB$ for the two independent original old quadratics.
The five final-input forms are
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
 OG & f=(C\vee g)D,\\
 OJ & f=D(C\vee g\vee h),\\
 GG & f=(C\vee g)(D\vee g),\\
 GH & f=(C\vee g)(D\vee h),\\
 GJ & f=(C\vee g)(D\vee g\vee h).
\end{array}
\]
All six full old forms are nonzero; repetitions are allowed. The exact
output contribution is
\begin{equation}
 Y=gL\vee hN\vee fM\vee qgh\vee rgf\vee shf.
 \label{eq:allvisibleindependentframe}
\end{equation}
Here $q=q_{12}$, $r=q_{13}$ and $s=q_{23}$ record the actual absence or
positivity of the original cross coefficients. None is initially assumed
zero. The full actual direct contexts $L,N,M$ are old linear and globally
nonzero: following each selected degree-one visible continuation to its
first original retained product puts that product's complete nonzero
opposite homogeneous factor in the context. A context may restrict to
zero on $T$.

Let $a_0,b_0,c_0$ be the nonzero old homogeneous parts of the selected lows
of $g,h,f$. Then $a_0L,b_0N,c_0M$ are supported on $H$. A base of an
actual $g$-recipient operand contains $a_0$; an actual $h$-recipient
contains $b_0$. Positive $q$ gives
\begin{equation}
 a_0\subseteq N,\qquad b_0\subseteq L,\qquad
 a_0b_0\text{ is supported on }H.
 \label{eq:allvisibleindependentmixed}
\end{equation}
Positive $r$ gives $a_0\subseteq M$, $c_0\subseteq L$, and $a_0c_0$
old. Positive $s$ gives $b_0\subseteq M$, $c_0\subseteq N$, and
$b_0c_0$ old. These are original occurrence and retained-product
identities, not consequences of a changed circuit. Product topological
order is not an assumed order on unrelated cuts.

For a safe positive support expression $F$, write $\mathcal W(F)$ for
its set of target witnesses in $J$. A private high need not be safe;
write $\mathcal P(g),\mathcal P(h),\mathcal P(f)$ for the target edge
assignments on which the respective Boolean high is true.
Proposition~\ref{prop:nonrawsevenzerocross} gives, in this exact setting,
\begin{equation}
 |\mathcal P(g)|\ge2,\qquad |\mathcal P(h)|\ge2,\qquad
 |\mathcal P(f)|\ge2.
 \label{eq:allvisibleindependentpotential}
\end{equation}
This makes no exclusive, injective or first-true allocation. A safe old
quadratic has at most one missing witness, so neither $g$ nor $h$ is
globally safe. An old cubic has at most one missing witness; an old
quartic has at most two, and equality fixes its four full supports to
the four distinct two-element transversals of the corresponding induced
matching. Every use below retains full old neighborhoods and outside
variables. We continue under the contrary inequality $\vc(G)>K+2$;
that inequality is not an extra hypothesis of the proposition.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B2. Full-support singleton rules.}
A safe old cubic witnessing a missing edge $uv$ has a full singleton
factor at one endpoint. Choose a witness monomial, say $u^2v$, and the
factor that supplied the single $v$. Replacing that choice by any $w$
in its full support gives $u^2w$. Safety excludes $w=u$ and forces
$uw\in E(G)$. The factor is old and contains the missing neighbor $v$
of $u$. If it had another vertex $w$, its old $H$-center $p$ would
differ from $u$, since $uv$ is not old. Then $u,v,p,w$ would be four
distinct vertices of a four-cycle. Thus that entire factor is $\{v\}$.
The argument also handles the other orientation and repeated old factors.

We need an amplified version. If an old quadratic $X=EF$ is true on two
targets and the safe expression $XB$ witnesses one target, then full
$B$ is a singleton endpoint and $X$ contains the square of the other
endpoint. If both $E,F$ are nonsingleton, the preceding unique-endpoint
factor must be $B$, giving both assertions. If one factor is a singleton
$t$, both target potentials contain $t$, so $t=x$ and they are the two
path arms. The other old support meets both arms; if it omitted $x$, it
would contain $y,z$, and its old center would make a four-cycle with $x$
or make an arm old. Hence $X$ contains $x^2$. Safety of $XB$ excludes
$x$ from $B$; its missing-arm witness and the old-center argument force
full $B$ to be the corresponding leaf singleton. This includes two
singleton factors and full outside vertices.

In particular, a target of $gL$ or $hN$ makes that full actual context
an endpoint singleton, and the quadratic contains the opposite square.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B3. Actual-context charges and anchors.}
Each retained product in the original quadratic frame is a squarefree
quadratic star. Overlap of its two nonzero linear factors gives a square;
two disjoint nonsingleton factors give a four-cycle. Choosing one center
per original retained product therefore covers $H$, with repeated
centers only improving the count.

If a full nonzero actual context lies in a three-vertex cover of the four
global missing edges, mark an original retained product whose full
opposite factor lies in that context. Those three vertices cover the
entire marked product as well. Centers for the other $K-1$ products give
$K+2$. Thus, under the contrary inequality, an actual singleton context
at a target vertex can only be $y$ or $z$; $x$ and all isolated endpoints
give this charge.

Two full actual contexts $\{y\}$ and $\{z\}$ mark distinct retained
products. At a common product, the same-side alternative has empty
nonzero opposite-factor intersection. Opposite sides would put an
$H$-edge in $T$, or give a square. The four-cover $\{y,z,a,c\}$, plus
centers for the other $K-2$ products, gives $K+2$. Thus two different
actual leaf contexts are impossible under the contrary inequality.

By B2, each of $gL,hN$ has at most one target, a path arm. Different
targets would yield the two opposite leaf contexts. Consequently
\begin{equation}
 D_0=gL\vee hN\quad\text{has at most one target, which is a path arm.}
 \label{eq:allvisibleindependentdirect}
\end{equation}

For any actual recipient operand with old base $E$ carrying insertion
$i$, follow its selected degree-one continuation to its first retained
product. Its whole nonzero opposite old factor $R$ lies in the full
context $L_i$, and $ER$ is supported on $H$. The selected low $a_i$ is
contained in $E$. Choosing $k\in R$ gives $Ek,a_i k,a_iL_i$ supported
on $H$ and $k\in L_i$. This actual-path anchor is not assumed for an
invented algebraic base.

We use Lemma~\ref{lem:independentproducts} in the following exact form.
Safe old-quadratic terms $XL,ZM,XZ$ together have at most two missing
witnesses if nonzero old lows $\alpha\subseteq M$ and
$\beta\subseteq L$ satisfy $\alpha L,\beta M,\alpha\beta$ supported
on $H$. In the auxiliary applications below, a product such as $CM$ is
an algebraic support expression, not a counted original gate.

We use Lemma~\ref{lem:relatedcubics} in its exact form: for nonzero old
$U,V,L,D,E,F$, if a nonzero old $a\subseteq E\cap F$ has $aL$ old,
then safety of $UVL,UVD,EFD$ gives at most one missing witness in the
first two terms together and at most two in all three. Every remapping
below identifies its actual low, recipient or mixed-coefficient source.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B4. A safe last-high subfamily cannot supply all four targets.}
Define the actual positive subfamily
\begin{equation}
 Y_0=D_0\vee f(M\vee rg\vee sh).
 \label{eq:allvisibleindependentlastfamily}
\end{equation}
We show that $Y_0$ cannot witness all four targets under the contrary
cover inequality, irrespective of the actual value of $q$. This does
not delete $q$'s original gate or coefficient:
\eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentlastfamily} is a safe positive subfamily
of the original $Y$, using all original data and the potential necessity
\eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentpotential} from that original circuit.

If a safe expression $Z$ has a conjunctive normal form with at most seven
positive linear clauses, then $D_0\vee Z$ cannot witness all four.
If $D_0$ has no target, restrict to $T$, where the graph function of
$P_3\sqcup2K_2$ needs eight clauses, one for each distinct minimal
vertex cover. If $D_0$ has one arm, restrict to the endpoints of the
other arm and the two isolated edges, an induced three-edge matching
requiring eight clauses. The expression $Z$ must be true on each of
those edges, and global safety makes it zero on every independent set,
so its restriction equals that graph function. Zero or scalar
restrictions only shorten the conjunctive normal form. This is support
algebra, not a new physical circuit.

For $Z=f(M\vee rg\vee sh)$, the last factor uses at most four linear
clauses, or at most two if $r,s$ are not both positive. If both are zero,
it uses one. The five $f$ forms have, respectively, $3,5,4,4,6$ clauses;
these explicit counts follow from $g=UV,h=AB$ by distributing
disjunction over the two-factor conjunctions.

The $OG$ cell has $3+4\le7$ clauses for every $r,s$, so it is excluded.

The $OJ$ cell has $5+2\le7$ clauses except when $r=s=1$. In that case
$gf=gD$ and $hf=hD$ are safe bare old cubics. If either witnesses a
target, B2 makes full $D$ an endpoint singleton. Since $D$ is a
mandatory factor of $f$ and $f$ has two target potentials, $D$ must be
$x$. Every $f$-containing contribution then has only arm targets, as
does $D_0$, and $Y_0$ misses both isolated edges. Thus, in a four-target
realization of $Y_0$, both crosses must be target-free. The remaining
$fM$ has at most six clauses, again impossible with $D_0$.

In $GG$, $g\Rightarrow f$; positive $r$ would make $g$ itself safe,
contrary to \eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentpotential}. Hence $r=0$,
and $4+2\le6$ clauses exclude the cell for either $s$.

The $GH$ cell has $4+2\le6$ clauses unless $r=s=1$; B5 below proves
that remaining case.

In $GJ$, again $g\Rightarrow f$, forcing $r=0$. If $s=0$, $fM$ has
$6+1=7$ clauses. B6 proves the positive-$s$ case.

These reductions neither assume nor erase $q$. The exceptional positive
last-cross cases below use only terms already contained in $Y_0$.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B5. The $GH$ last-high subfamily when $r=s=1$.}
For $f=(C\vee g)(D\vee h)$, the exact Boolean expansions
$gf=gD\vee gh$ and $hf=hC\vee gh$ absorb their $M$-multiples, giving
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 Y_0&=A_g\vee A_h\vee Q\vee R,\\
 A_g&=gL\vee gD,\qquad A_h=hN\vee hC,\qquad
 Q=CDM,\qquad R=gh.
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:allvisibleindependentGH}
\end{equation}
The term $R$ is safe because the two actual positive last-high crosses
supply it, even if $q=0$. Every displayed term is safe.

The actual $g$-recipient $C$ contains $a_0$, and positive $r$ puts
$a_0$ in $M$. With $a_0L$ old,
Lemma~\ref{lem:relatedcubics}, applied using the pair $C,M$, shows
$|\mathcal W(A_g)|\le1$ and $|\mathcal W(A_g\vee Q)|\le2$.
Similarly, the actual $h$-recipient $D$ and positive $s$ give
$b_0\subseteq D\cap M$ and $b_0N$ old, so
$|\mathcal W(A_h)|\le1$ and $|\mathcal W(A_h\vee Q)|\le2$.

The actual $C/L$ anchor gives
$|\mathcal W(gL\vee hC\vee R)|\le2$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:independentproducts}: choose $k$ in the whole opposite
factor inside $L$, so $Ck,a_0k,a_0L$ are old, and apply the lemma to
old quadratics $g,h$, contexts $L,C$, and lows $a_0,k$. The actual
$D/N$ anchor similarly gives
$|\mathcal W(hN\vee gD\vee R)|\le2$.

If $R$ has two targets, these two bundles confine all four cubics
$gL,hN,gD,hC$ to that target pair. The old cubic $Q$ adds at most one,
so $Y_0$ has at most three.

If $R$ has at most one target, all four targets would force
$A_g,A_h,Q,R$ to supply four different single targets. If $gD$ supplies
$A_g$'s target, B2 makes full $D$ an endpoint singleton. The different
target of $Q$ also contains $D$, so these are the two path arms and
$D=\{x\}$. Then $A_h$ and $R$ must supply the isolated targets.
The expression $A_h$ cannot obtain its isolated target from $hN$,
whose full singleton isolated context would give $K+2$. If it obtains
that target from $hC$, B2 makes full $C$ an isolated endpoint singleton,
so $Q$ cannot be a path arm. This is a contradiction. The argument when
$hC$ supplies $A_h$'s target is symmetric. If neither bare cubic
supplies its respective target, the actual terms $gL$ and $hN$ supply
two distinct arms, forcing opposite full leaf contexts and $K+2$.
Thus $Y_0$ never supplies four targets in this case.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B6. The $GJ$ last-high subfamily when $s=1$.}
Here $r=0$, $f=CD\vee g\vee Ch$, and $hf=Ch\vee gh$.
Absorption gives
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 Y_0&=A_g\vee A_h\vee Q\vee R,\\
 A_g&=gL\vee gM,\qquad A_h=hN\vee hC,\qquad
 Q=CDM,\qquad R=gh.
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:allvisibleindependentGJ}
\end{equation}
All terms are safe, and the $h/f$ cross supplies $R$. The two actual
$g$-recipient bases $C,D$ contain $a_0$, and $a_0L$ is old.
Lemma~\ref{lem:relatedcubics} gives $|\mathcal W(A_g)|\le1$ and
$|\mathcal W(A_g\vee Q)|\le2$. Actual $D$ receiving $h$ and positive
$s$ give $b_0\subseteq D\cap M$ and $b_0N$ old; the same lemma gives
$|\mathcal W(A_h)|\le1$ and $|\mathcal W(A_h\vee Q)|\le2$.
The actual $C/L$ anchor gives
$|\mathcal W(gL\vee hC\vee R)|\le2$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:independentproducts}, as in B5.

If $R$ has two targets, full $U,V,A,B$ are the four distinct two-point
transversals of its induced matching. If the pair is $ab,cd$, neither
old quadratic has a path-arm potential; $A_g,A_h$ are confined to that
pair, and $Q$ adds at most one. Otherwise relabel the pair as $xy,ab$.
The only possible target outside that pair for $g$ or $h$ is $xz$, and
at most one quadratic can be true there: both its full factors must be
the two $x$-transversals, leaving the other quadratic the two
$y$-transversals. The bundle with $R$ already confines $gL,hC$ to the
pair. If $gM$ supplies the extra arm, $g$ contains $x^2$ and full
$M=\{z\}$ by B2; then $Q$ cannot witness $cd$. If $hN$ supplies it,
full $N=\{z\}$. The actual $h$-recipient $D$ has its full nonzero
opposite factor inside $N$; hence $Dz$ is old, and $H[T]=\varnothing$
forces $D$ to have empty target restriction. The term $Q$ then has no
target. In every alternative the four targets cannot all be covered.

If $R$ has at most one target, four targets would force $A_g,A_h,Q,R$
to give distinct single targets. If $hC$ supplies $A_h$'s target, B2
makes full $C$ an endpoint singleton $v$. The actual $g$-recipient $C$
contains $a_0$, so $a_0=\{v\}$; $a_0L$ old and $H[T]=\varnothing$
force $L$ to contain no target vertex. Thus $A_g$'s target comes from
$gM$. Under the contrary cover inequality, its actual full context $M$
is a singleton path leaf, so $Q$, which contains $M$, cannot have a
different target from $gM$. If $hC$ has no target, $A_h$'s target comes
from actual $hN$, and $A_g$'s different target comes from actual $gL$
or $gM$. Two different leaf contexts again give $K+2$. This completes
B4 for all five forms and every $r,s$.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B7. Consequences for the first independent cross.}
The whole original contribution is $Y=Y_0\vee qR$, with $R=gh$.
Since $Y$ witnesses all four targets and B4 says that $Y_0$ cannot do so,
$q$ must be positive, and $R$ must have a target witness not already
supplied by $Y_0$. In particular, $R$ is globally safe and nonempty on
at least one target. As a safe old quartic it has at most two.

Because $q$ is positive, the actual low and context identities
\eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentmixed} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:independentproducts} give
\begin{equation}
 |\mathcal W(gL\vee hN\vee R)|\le2.
 \label{eq:allvisibleindependentbase}
\end{equation}
We first exclude two targets of $R$, then analyze its only possible
single target. At no point is $q$ deleted from the original circuit.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B8. Two targets of $R$ are impossible.}
Suppose $R$ has two targets.
Equation~\eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentbase} confines both direct cubics
to that pair. Full $U,V,A,B$ are the four distinct transversals of its
matching quartet $W$.

If the pair is $ab,cd$, both $g,h$ are false on both path arms. On those
assignments each nonraw final input reduces to its homogeneous old base.
Every cross with the last high vanishes there. Only $CDM$ can supply
the two arms, contrary to the old-cubic bound.

Otherwise relabel the pair as $xy,ab$. Both $g,h$ are false on $cd$, so
the safe old cubic $CDM$ must witness $cd$. The other arm $xz$ must be
supplied outside the confined direct contribution. At most one of $g,h$
can be true on $xz$: its two factors must both contain $x$ and consume
the two $x$-transversals. If neither is true, only $CDM$ can supply
$xz$ as well, which is impossible. Let $\kappa$ name the unique
original high true on $xz$, and let $\lambda$ name the other.
The high $\kappa$ owns the two $x$-transversals and contains $x^2$;
$\lambda$ owns the two $y$-transversals and contains $y^2$.
The latter high and its cross with $f$ are false on $xz$, so only $fM$
or a present $\kappa f$ can supply that arm.

Count the actual final input operands receiving $\kappa$.

\emph{Zero.} Both final inputs reduce to $C,D$ on $xz$. The $fM$
route would make $CDM$ witness both $xz$ and $cd$. A present
$\kappa f$ route supplying $xz$ contains the safe term $\kappa CD$.
Thus $C,D$ meet both disjoint pairs $xz,cd$ and are nonsingleton.
The missing witness of the old cubic $CDM$ forces full $M$ to be an
isolated endpoint singleton, and the actual-context charge gives $K+2$.

\emph{One.} Write that input as $E\vee\kappa\vee\text{optional }\lambda$
and the other as $F\vee\text{optional }\lambda$. The homogeneous cubic
$EFM$ witnesses $cd$. If $fM$ supplies $xz$, it cannot use $EFM$,
which already witnesses $cd$; the safe term $\kappa FM$ must supply
it. Both $F,M$ meet $xz$ and $cd$, so neither is singleton. The cubic
$EFM$ witness forces full $E=\{t\}$, an endpoint of $cd$. Since
$E$ is an actual recipient of $\kappa$, its original nonzero selected
low is $\{t\}$. Positive $q$ puts that low in the full direct context
of $\lambda$. The safe $\lambda$-direct term then contains $y^2t$,
which is unsafe on $T$. This is a contradiction.

If $\kappa f$ supplies $xz$, its support is
$\kappa F\vee\text{optional }\kappa\lambda$. The high $\lambda$
is false there, so the safe bare cubic $\kappa F$ must witness $xz$.
B2 forces full $F=\{z\}$. But $F$ must meet $cd$ for $EFM$ to
witness $cd$, a contradiction.

\emph{Two.} We have $\kappa\Rightarrow f$. A positive
$\kappa f$ coefficient would make the unsafe $\kappa$ itself safe,
which is impossible by its two target potentials. Thus $fM$ must
supply $xz$. Since $CDM$ already supplies $cd$ and $\lambda$ is
false on $xz$, the safe term $\kappa M$ supplies the arm. Full
$M=\{z\}$, incompatible with the $CDM$ witness on $cd$.

This exhausts the two original final operands. The names $\kappa$ and
$\lambda$ merely designate one or the other independent original node;
no original ancestry, coefficient or gate is relabeled or removed.
Therefore $R$ cannot have two target witnesses.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B9. Opposite endpoint squares force an actual direct witness.}
We use an original-cross observation for the single-target case.
Suppose $R=gh$ witnesses a target $uv$, $g$ contains $u^2$, and
$h$ contains $v^2$. Choose $k$ in nonzero $a_0$ and $\ell$ in
nonzero $b_0$. By \eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentmixed},
$k\in N$, $\ell\in L$, and $k\ell$ is an $H$-edge. Safety of
$gL$ gives $u\ell\in E(G)$ and $\ell\ne u$; safety of $hN$
gives $vk\in E(G)$ and $k\ne v$. Also $k\ne\ell$.

If $k=u$, the actual safe term $hN$ contains $v^2u$ and witnesses
$uv$. If $\ell=v$, actual $gL$ witnesses $uv$. If neither
coincidence occurs, $u,\ell,k,v$ are four distinct vertices, and
$u\ell,\ell k,kv,vu$ form a four-cycle. Hence one of the two direct
terms must witness $uv$. The argument also applies after exchanging
$g,h$. It does not assume $k,\ell$ are outside $T$; the coincidence
alternatives are essential and have been retained explicitly.

In particular, opposite squares on an isolated target are impossible
under the contrary cover inequality, since B3 permits no isolated
direct target. On a path target they put that $R$ target in $D_0$,
and hence in $Y_0$.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B10. Classifying a single target of $R$ by potential assignments.}
We now know that $R$ has exactly one target $e$. The Boolean identity
$R=gh$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal P(g)\cap\mathcal P(h)=\{e\}.
 \label{eq:allvisibleindependentintersection}
\end{equation}
Each potential set has at least two members. Choose an extra target
for each high; by \eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentintersection}, those
extras must be different.

First let $e$ be a path arm, say $xy$. If one high, say $g$, also
has $xz$, both its old factors contain $x$ by the old-neighborhood
two-arm observation, so $x^2$ occurs in $g$. The other high $h$
cannot have $xz$ by \eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentintersection};
therefore it has an isolated target, say $ab$. Each factor of $h$
meets $ab$. Neither factor can contain $x$: choosing $x$ from that
factor, an isolated endpoint from the other, and $x^2$ from $g$ would
make $R$ unsafe. Since both factors must meet $xy$, both contain
$y$. Thus $h$ contains $y^2$.

If neither high has $xz$, their extra potentials are the two different
isolated edges, say $g$ has $ab$ and $h$ has $cd$. Suppose an
endpoint $t$ of $xy$ occurs in some factor of $g$ and in some factor
of $h$. Choose $t$ from those factors, a vertex of $ab$ from the
other $g$ factor, and a vertex of $cd$ from the other $h$ factor.
The chosen variables form an independent set on $T$, contradicting
safety of $R$. Thus the unions of the $xy$-endpoints appearing in
the two pairs of factors are disjoint. Each pair's two factors meet
$xy$, so one pair contains $x$ in both factors and the other contains
$y$ in both. Again the highs have opposite endpoint squares.

B9 therefore places the sole $R$ target $xy$ in $D_0\subseteq Y_0$.
Since $Y=Y_0\vee R$ has all four witnesses, $Y_0$ then has all four,
contrary to B4. This excludes a path-arm single target.

Now let $e$ be an isolated edge, relabeled $ab$. If one high has
$cd$ as an additional potential, the other cannot have $cd$ by
\eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentintersection} and must have a path arm.
If an endpoint $t$ of $ab$ occurred in a factor of each high,
selecting $t$ twice and a variable from each other's extra edge would
give an independent set: $cd$ and the path arm are disjoint and have
no cross edge on $T$, and neither meets an $ab$ endpoint by a
$G$-edge. Safety again forces the two $ab$-endpoint unions to be
disjoint, giving opposite squares at $a,b$. By B9 there would be an
isolated direct target, which is impossible.

Thus neither high has $cd$. Their extra potentials must be the two
different path arms; neither can have both by
\eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentintersection}. After exchanging $y,z$,
the exact remaining potential sets are
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal P(g)=\{ab,xy\},\qquad \mathcal P(h)=\{ab,xz\}.
 \label{eq:allvisibleindependentexception}
\end{equation}
Neither high has $cd$ as a target potential, and neither contains
$x^2$, since that would make it true on both arms. The amplified
singleton fact in B2 now shows that neither actual direct cubic can
have a target: an allowed direct target would have a full leaf context
and force $x^2$ in its high. Thus $D_0$ has no targets, consistently
with the sole target $ab$ of $R$.

All potential conclusions concern only the four specified target
assignments. We have not confined the full supports of $U,V,A,B$ in
the one-target case.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B11. Full direct contexts avoid the other isolated endpoints.}
Under \eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentexception}, $L$ contains neither
$c$ nor $d$. Suppose, for example, that $c\in L$. Restrict $g$ to
the four variables $W=\{a,b,x,y\}$. Each of its two restricted old
factors is nonzero, since $g$ is true on both $ab$ and $xy$. The
polynomial $(g|_W)c$ is a positive subexpression of globally safe
$gL$. By the induced target hypothesis, $c$ is adjacent in $G$ to
no vertex of $W$. Thus every monomial of $g|_W$ itself must already
contain a $G$-edge. It is a globally safe old quadratic on $W$
witnessing the two missing edges $ab,xy$, contrary to the old-factor
bound. The argument for $d$ is identical.

Using $W=\{a,b,x,z\}$ and $hN$ similarly shows that $N$ contains
neither $c$ nor $d$. Restricting an old factor preserves its
old-neighborhood property, or makes it singleton, and the resulting
polynomial is safe on the full graph $G$ because all its variables
lie in $W$. No new circuit or retained frame is created.

Positive $q$ and \eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentmixed} now imply that
both $a_0,b_0$ avoid $c,d$. Consequently, an actual final input base
receiving either earlier insertion cannot be a full singleton $\{c\}$
or $\{d\}$: it contains the corresponding nonzero original low.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B12. The final missing edge forces an impossible old cubic.}
On $cd$, both $g,h$ are false by
\eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentexception}. Thus the complete
contribution \eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentframe} reduces there to
$CDM$: all direct terms and all crosses with $g$ or $h$ vanish, and
each affected final operand reduces to its old base. Hence the safe
old cubic $CDM$ witnesses $cd$.

By the full singleton rule in B2, at least one of $C,D,M$ is the
full singleton $\{c\}$ or $\{d\}$. If it is $M$, this is an actual
full context at an isolated endpoint, and the original retained-product
charge gives $K+2$, contrary to the inequality.

If it is an affected base $C$ or $D$, B11 contradicts its actual
nonzero low inclusion. In $GG,GH,GJ$, both final bases are affected,
so all alternatives are already excluded. In $OG$ or $OJ$, the only
unaffected base is $D$, a mandatory factor of the entire original
high $f$. If full $D=\{c\}$ or $\{d\}$, $f$ can be true only on
the single target $cd$, contrary to its two distinct target potentials
in \eqref{eq:allvisibleindependentpotential}. Thus the final two forms
are excluded as well.

This uses actual full supports, actual original low inclusions, the
global four-edge list and the original context charge. It requires
neither an optimal $H$-cover nor a conjectured singleton outside
context, and does not assume $C$ or $D$ was an available isolated wire.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{B13. Independent-row conclusion.}
The last-high subfamily argument, the full-quartic two-target case and
the single-target analysis exhaust every possible actual $q$ and safe
$R$ witness count. Every $r,s$ and each of the five original final
forms is included. Therefore $\vc(G)>K+2$ is impossible in the
independent-middle row. The full derivation above is retained inline.


% Full original-author Part C transcription, C1--C14, by operator_k.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Part C. The complete single-affected-middle row.}
We now treat all ten actual final pairs and all actual coefficients.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C1. Exact original frame and contrary inequality.}
Use the full hypotheses and the original nonraw, three-distinct-high
inventory. Work under $\vc(G)>K+2$. The target edges are
$J=\{xy,xz,ab,cd\}$; their seven endpoints $T$ induce
$P_3\sqcup2K_2$, and $H[T]=\varnothing$. These are the four global
missing edges. All selected lows, input wires and degrees, occurrences,
fanout, cross coefficients, old neighborhoods and retained-product
incidences remain fixed.
Write the first two original highs as
\[
 g=UV,\qquad h=(A\vee g)B,
\]
with full nonzero old homogeneous linear $U,V,A,B$.
The third high $f$ has two original minimum-degree-one nonraw inputs,
with full nonzero old bases $C,D$. Their unordered types are
\[
\begin{array}{c|l@{\qquad}c|l}
\mathrm{OO}&CD&\mathrm{OG}&(C\vee g)D\\
\mathrm{OH}&(C\vee h)D&\mathrm{OJ}&D(C\vee g\vee h)\\
\mathrm{GG}&(C\vee g)(D\vee g)&\mathrm{GH}&(C\vee g)(D\vee h)\\
\mathrm{GJ}&(C\vee g)(D\vee g\vee h)&\mathrm{HH}&(C\vee h)(D\vee h)\\
\mathrm{HJ}&(C\vee h)(D\vee g\vee h)&\mathrm{JJ}&(C\vee g\vee h)(D\vee g\vee h).
\end{array}
\]
This is the admitted necessary original-input inventory. Every displayed
positive contribution is actual; zero and positive coefficients are not
reclassified by support absorption.
The original contribution is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:allvisiblesingleframe}
 Y=gL\vee hN\vee fM\vee qgh\vee rgf\vee shf,
\end{equation}
where $q=q_{12},r=q_{13},s=q_{23}$ record original absence or positivity.
The forms $L,N,M$ are the full actual old homogeneous linear contexts.
They are globally nonzero: a selected degree-one visible path reaches
an original retained quadratic product, whose whole nonzero opposite
old factor lies in the direct context. They may restrict to zero on $T$.

Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the nonzero old homogeneous parts of the
selected lows. The products $\alpha L,\beta N,\gamma M$ are supported
on $H$. A base receiving $g$ contains $\alpha$; a base receiving $h$
contains $\beta$. Thus $\alpha\subseteq A$. Positive $q$ gives
$\alpha\subseteq N$, $\beta\subseteq L$, and $\alpha\beta$ old.
Positive $r$ gives $\alpha\subseteq M$, $\gamma\subseteq L$, and
$\alpha\gamma$ old. Positive $s$ gives $\beta\subseteq M$,
$\gamma\subseteq N$, and $\beta\gamma$ old. These are original
occurrence identities.
For every actual $g$-recipient base $E$, its original selected
continuation supplies a nonzero old opposite factor $R_E\subseteq L$
with $ER_E$ old. In particular there is a vertex $k\in L$ with $Ek$
old. We call this the $E/L$ anchor. It is not assumed for an arbitrary
algebraically introduced base. When $r>0$, $M$ also has such an anchor:
choose $k$ in the nonzero $\gamma\subseteq L$, since $\gamma M$ is old.

Proposition~\ref{prop:nonrawsevenzerocross} supplies at least two
separate target potentials for each original $g,h,f$ under the contrary
inequality. This is not an exclusive or first-true witness assignment.
Part (A) of Proposition~\ref{prop:nonrawunsafehighsplit} makes every
original high globally unsafe in this original all-visible setting;
we use this when $h$ implies $f$. The first high $g$ is already unsafe
by its two potentials and the old-quadratic bound.
For any support expression $W$, write $\mathcal P(W)$ for the set of
target edge assignments on which it is true. If $W$ is safe these are
its missing witnesses. Every positive summand of
\eqref{eq:allvisiblesingleframe} is safe.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C2. Full-support and actual-cover preliminaries.}
A nonzero old form cannot contain both $y,z$: its $H$-neighborhood
center and the target edges $xy,xz$ would form a four-cycle. A safe
product of two old forms has at most one missing witness; a safe old
cubic has at most one, and a safe old quartic has at most two. In the
last equality case, its four full supports are the four distinct
two-point transversals of the induced matching formed by its witnesses.

A safe old cubic witnessing a missing $uv$ has a full singleton endpoint
factor. Choose a witness $u^2v$. In the factor supplying the unique $v$,
an extra support vertex $w$ would give $u^2w$; safety forces $uw$.
The old center differs from $u$, since $uv\notin E(H)$, and gives the
four-cycle $u,v,\text{center},w,u$ unless $w=v$. Repetitions and outside
vertices are included.
For the amplified rule, suppose an old quadratic $X=EF$ is true on at
least two targets and safe $XJ_0$ witnesses one. Then the full old
$J_0$ is an endpoint singleton, and $X$ contains the opposite square.
If $E,F$ are nonsingleton, the preceding rule puts the singleton in
$J_0$. If one is a singleton $t$, both potentials are incident to $t$,
so $t=x$ and they are the two arms. The other old factor contains $x$,
since otherwise it contains both $y,z$. Thus $X$ contains $x^2$, and
the same safety and old-center argument makes $J_0$ the missing leaf
singleton.

Each original retained product is a squarefree quadratic star:
overlapping factors give a square, and two disjoint nonsingleton factors
give a four-cycle. One chosen center per original retained product
covers $H$. If a full actual context lies in a three-vertex cover of the
four global missing edges, mark an original retained product whose
full opposite factor lies in that context. The three-cover covers the
whole marked star; centers for the other $K-1$ products give $K+2$.
Hence an actual singleton context at a target vertex can only be $y$ or
$z$ under the contrary inequality.

We also use the following \emph{final-edge test}. Suppose $g,h$ are both
false on an isolated target $cd$, and $\alpha,\beta$ avoid $c,d$.
There every direct or cross term involving $g$ or $h$ vanishes, and
both inputs of $f$ reduce to their old bases. The safe old cubic $CDM$
must therefore witness $cd$. Its full singleton endpoint factor cannot
be $M$, whose actual context gives $K+2$. It cannot be an affected base,
since that base contains its corresponding nonzero $\alpha$ or $\beta$.
If it is an unaffected base, that entire original input is a singleton
endpoint of $cd$ and is mandatory in $f$, contrary to $f$'s two target
potentials. Thus these hypotheses are incompatible with four witnesses.
More generally, avoidance is needed only for the particular lows
entering the actual final bases.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C3. Two witnesses in the middle direct quartic.}
Put $Q=ABN$ and $R=gBN$, so $hN=Q\vee R$, with both terms safe.
Suppose $R$ has two witnesses. Its full $U,V,B,N$ are the four distinct
transversals of a missing matching.
If the matching is $\{ab,cd\}$, actual full $N$ is an isolated-edge
transversal; adjoining $x$ gives a three-cover containing $N$, hence
$K+2$. Otherwise rename the matching $\{xy,ab\}$. If $N$ contains $x$,
adjoining an endpoint of $cd$ again gives a three-cover. The only
uncharged possibility is $N=\{y,a\}$ or $N=\{y,b\}$.

All four factors then lie in $W=\{x,y,a,b\}$. In particular $g,h$ are
both false on $cd$, since the mandatory $B$ has no $c,d$. Also $A$
avoids $c,d$. Indeed, if $c\in A$, the safe summand $cBN$ would make
$BN$ safe on $W$, because $c$ is adjacent to no vertex of $W$. Yet both
$B,N$ meet $xy$ and $ab$, giving a safe old quadratic with two missing
witnesses. The same argument excludes $d$ from $A$. Thus
$\alpha\subseteq A$ avoids $c,d$. Since $N$ contains a target vertex
and $\beta N$ is old, $\beta$ has no target vertex. The final-edge test
excludes $cd$. Therefore $R$ has at most one target in any putative
counterexample. This is full-support quartic equality; no confinement
is inferred from a one-witness quartic.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C4. A two-target fork obstruction.}
Suppose $g=UV$ has at least two target potentials and $gL$ is safe.
Let $E,F,J_0$ be full nonzero old forms, with
\[
 (E\vee g)FJ_0=EFJ_0\vee gFJ_0
\]
safe. Suppose $gFJ_0$ has at most one target, $E$ has an $E/L$ anchor
(some $k\in L$ has $Ek$ old), and $J_0$ cannot be a singleton target
vertex. Then the displayed expression has at most one target.
If it had two, its old cubic would witness $e_0$ and $gFJ_0$ a different
$e_1$. Both $F,J_0$ meet both edges. The high $g$ is false on $e_0$;
otherwise the second term also witnesses $e_0$, giving it two targets.

First suppose $F,J_0$ are nonsingleton. The cubic singleton rule makes
full $E=\{t\}$ for an endpoint of $e_0=tw$. Both $F,J_0$ contain $w$:
a witness using $t$ in one of those factors and $w$ uniquely in the
other would make the latter a full singleton. Hence safe $gFJ_0$
contains Boolean $gw$ as a positive subexpression. Both potentials of
$g$ lie outside $e_0$.
If $e_0$ is isolated, restrict $g$ to the other five target vertices.
The vertex $w$ has no edge to that set, so safety of $gw$ makes the
restriction a safe old quadratic. Both potentials survive, a
contradiction.
If $e_0=xy$ and $w=y$ is the leaf, $g$ cannot have both isolated
potentials, by the same restriction in safe $gy$. Thus $g$ is true on
$xz$ and an isolated edge. Since it is false on $xy$, one old factor
omits $x,y$ and contains $z$. The other meets the isolated edge.
Choosing $z$, an isolated endpoint from the other factor, and $y$
makes $gy$ true on an independent set, a contradiction.
If $e_0=xy$ and $w=x$ is the center, $g$ again cannot have both isolated
potentials, so it is true on $xz$ and an isolated edge. The amplified
singleton rule applied to safe $gx$ gives $z^2$ in $g$. Since
$E=\{y\}$, its anchor gives $k\in L$ with $yk\in E(H)$; safety of
$gL$ gives $zk\in E(G)$. The vertex $k$ differs from $x,y,z$:
$xy\notin E(H)$, $H$ has no loops, and $gL$ cannot contain a singleton
$z$. Thus $y,k,z,x$ form a four-cycle.

If $F$ is singleton, the two targets are the two arms and $F=\{x\}$;
$J_0$ is nonsingleton by hypothesis. Rename the cubic target $xy$ and
the quartic target $xz$. Old $J_0$ meets both arms and hence contains
$x$. Safety of $ExJ_0$ excludes $x$ from $E$, and its $xy$ witness puts
$y$ there. The witness $yx^2$ makes full $E=\{y\}$. Safe $gxJ_0$
contains $gx$ because $x\in J_0$; its $xz$ witness forces $z^2$ in $g$,
and the same $E/L$ anchor gives the four-cycle. These exhaust all
possible singleton factors and prove the obstruction.
If $J_0$ is an actual context, the same argument works under the
contrary inequality without an a priori nonsingleton premise. Its only
possible singleton meeting two target edges is $x$, whose original
product charge gives $K+2$; no other singleton meets two target edges.
Apply the obstruction to $E=A,F=B,J_0=N$, using C3 and the actual
$A/L$ anchor. We obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:allvisiblesinglemiddlebound}
 |\mathcal P(hN)|\le1.
\end{equation}
All auxiliary expressions here are support expressions, not newly
counted private products.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C5. The middle direct term has no isolated witness.}
Suppose the sole middle-direct witness is $ab$. Since $N$ is actual,
it is not a full endpoint singleton. Since $h$ has two target
potentials and $B$ is mandatory, $B$ is not such a singleton either.
A singleton outside $ab$ could not witness $ab$.
If $Q=ABN$ witnesses $ab$, nonsingleton $B,N$ make full $A=\{a\}$,
after exchanging endpoints, and both $B,N$ contain $b$ by the
unique-endpoint argument of C4. Safe $R$ contains $gb$.
Restricting $g$ to $W=T\setminus\{a,b\}$, where $b$ has no neighbors,
shows that $g$ has at most one potential outside $ab$. Since $A=\{a\}$,
$h$ outside $ab$ is just $gB$. The union of potentials of $g,h$ has at
most two target edges. Both highs are false on each of the other two,
so \eqref{eq:allvisiblesingleframe} forces the same safe old cubic
$CDM$ to witness both, impossible. Thus $Q$ has no $ab$ target and
$R$ alone witnesses it.

All four full factors $U,V,B,N$ are nonsingleton. For $U,V$, this
follows from $g$'s $ab$ potential and another target disjoint from it;
for $B$, from the analogous potentials of $h$; for $N$, from its actual
context charge. A quartic witness with three copies of one endpoint
and one of the other would make the unique-endpoint factor a full
singleton by the same old-center argument. A singleton monomial is
unsafe. Thus exactly two factor occurrences contain $a$, exactly two
contain $b$, and none contains both. This concerns only their
restrictions to $\{a,b\}$, not their full supports.

If $U,V$ contain the same endpoint, say $a$, then $B,N$ both contain
$b$. Again $gb$ is safe and gives at most one potential outside $ab$.
Safety of $ABN$, using $b\in B\cap N$, forces $A[T]\subseteq\{a\}$;
$Q$'s lack of an $ab$ witness excludes $a$ too. Thus $A[T]$ is empty,
and $h$'s potentials are a subset of $g$'s. Two other target edges
are left to the one old cubic $CDM$, impossible.
We may therefore name endpoints so that $U,B$ contain only $a$ and
$V,N$ only $b$ on this pair. Let $W=T\setminus\{a,b\}$.
Since $V,N$ contain $b$, which has no neighbor in $W$, safety of $R$
forces the product $(U|_W)(B|_W)$ to be safe. Both factors are nonzero:
$g$ has an extra target, and $h$ has one with mandatory $B$.
A safe old quadratic on $G[W]=P_3\sqcup K_2$ has both restricted
supports singleton endpoints of one edge $uv$. Indeed its factors are
disjoint and every cross pair is an edge; the only possible
nonsingleton complete bipartite side would contain both leaves $y,z$,
forbidden for an old form. Hence
\[
 U|_W=\{u\},\qquad B|_W=\{v\},\qquad uv\in E(G[W]).
\]
Also $A$ avoids $a,b$. If it contained $a$, safe $ABN$ would have an
$a^2b$ witness forcing $N$ singleton; if it contained $b$, it would
force $B$ singleton. Safety of $Q$, using $b\in N$, makes
$(A|_W)(B|_W)$ safe. Thus $A|_W$ is either empty or consists of
neighbors of $v$ in $W$; when $uv$ is a path edge, it in particular
avoids $c,d$.

Every $g$ potential outside $ab$ is incident to $u$, and every $h$
potential outside $ab$ is incident to $v$, because these restricted
factors are singletons. If $uv=cd$, their combined potentials lie in
$\{ab,cd\}$, leaving both arms to $CDM$, impossible. If $uv$ is a path
edge, their combined potentials omit $cd$. Then $A$, and hence
$\alpha$, avoid $c,d$. The actual $N$ contains $b$, and $\beta N$ old
makes $\beta[T]$ empty. The final-edge test excludes $cd$.
These exhaust $W$. Consequently $hN$ has no isolated target; together
with \eqref{eq:allvisiblesinglemiddlebound}, it has at most one target,
always a path arm.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C6. At most one arm from the two direct terms.}
If $gL$ has a target, amplification and its actual-context charge give,
after exchanging leaves, full $L=\{y\}$ and $x^2$ in $g$.
The actual $A/L$ anchor makes $Ay$ old, so $A[T]$ is empty since
$H[T]=\varnothing$. Thus $h=gB$ on $T$.
Restricting safe $gy$ to the four isolated vertices makes the
restricted $g$ a safe old quadratic. At least one isolated edge, say
$cd$, is false on $g$ and hence on $h$. Also $\alpha\subseteq A$
avoids $c,d$. If $hN$ had a target, $N$ would contain a target vertex,
forcing $\beta[T]$ empty from $\beta N$ old. The final-edge test would
exclude $cd$. Hence $hN$ is target-free whenever $gL$ has a target.
We have proved
\begin{equation}\label{eq:allvisiblesingledirect}
 D_0=gL\vee hN\quad\text{has at most one target, a path arm.}
\end{equation}

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C7. A safe raw cross forces the middle factor.}
Suppose $gB$ is globally safe. We first show that it has a target.
If it had none, $B$ would avoid all endpoints of every potential of
$g$. The raw part $gB$ would have no target, so $h$'s potentials would
be those of $AB$, disjoint from $g$'s. Since each high has at least two
potentials, these would partition the four edges into two pairs.
Moreover $g$ could have no square at a target vertex. A square $u^2$
and any target vertex $v$ in mandatory $B$ would, by safety, require
$uv$ to be a target edge; it would then be a target of $gB$, contrary
to the assumption. Such a $v$ exists because $h$ has two potentials.
In particular $g$ cannot have both arms, since old forms meeting both
force $x^2$.

If $g$ has both isolated potentials, $h$ has both arms and old $B$
must contain $x$. Safety of $gx$ makes $g$, restricted to the isolated
vertices, safe with two missing witnesses, impossible.
Otherwise rename the partition so that $g$ has $xy,ab$ and $h$ has
$xz,cd$. The form $B$ avoids $x,y,a,b$ and must contain $z$ for $h$'s
$xz$ potential. Thus $gz$ is safe. On $xy$ the two old factors of $g$
meet $x,y$, and one contains $y$. The other meets $ab$. Choosing $y$,
an $ab$ endpoint from the other factor, and $z$ gives an independent
true assignment, a contradiction. This exhausts the partition.

Thus safe $gB$ has a target. Amplification makes full $B$ an endpoint
singleton. Since it is mandatory in the two-potential $h$, it is
$B=\{x\}$. The unique target of $gB$ is one arm, say $xy$, and $g$
contains $y^2$. At least one isolated edge, say $cd$, is false on $g$:
safe $gx$ restricted to the isolated vertices is a safe old quadratic.
It is false on $h$ too, since $h$ has mandatory $B=\{x\}$.
These consequences use only full old factors, original potentials
and safety.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C8. The actual first-middle cross vanishes.}
If $q>0$, Boolean $gh=gB$ is safe. By C7, $B=\{x\}$, $g$ contains
$y^2$, and both $g,h$ are false on an isolated edge $cd$.
The actual mixed identity gives $\alpha\subseteq A\cap N$.
The safe summand $ABN$ contains $x\delta^2$ for every
$\delta\in\alpha$, so $\alpha$ avoids all isolated target endpoints.
Also $\beta\subseteq L$, and safety of $gL$ with $y^2$ makes $L$,
and hence $\beta$, avoid every isolated endpoint. The final-edge test
contradicts the four witnesses. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:allvisiblesinglefirstcrosszero}
 q=0.
\end{equation}
This is a derived restriction on the actual coefficient, not deletion
of an original gate.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C9. Seven-clause reductions and the remaining list.}
Put $F=f(M\vee rg\vee sh)$. By C6--C8, $Y=D_0\vee F$, with $D_0$
having at most one target, a path arm. If $F$ has a CNF with at most
seven positive linear clauses, $Y$ cannot witness all four. If $D_0$
has no target, restrict to $T$: safe $F$ would equal the four-edge
graph function there, which needs eight clauses. If $D_0$ has an arm,
restrict to the other arm and the two isolated edges, an induced
three-matching also requiring eight. This is the minimal-vertex-cover
count; zero restrictions can only shorten a CNF.

The high $g$ has two clauses and $h=(A\vee g)B$ has three. Since
$g\vee h=g\vee AB$, their disjunction has at most four. Consequently
$M\vee rg\vee sh$ has one clause when both coefficients vanish,
at most two when only $r$ is positive, at most three when only $s$
is positive, and at most four when both are positive.
The ten forms of $f$ have respectively
$2,3,4,5,4,5,6,6,7,8$ clauses, in the order of C1.
If $g$ implies $f$, positive $r$ would make $g$ safe, so $r=0$ for
GG, GJ and JJ. If $h$ implies $f$, positive $s$ would make the globally
unsafe original $h$ safe, so $s=0$ for HH, HJ and JJ, by
Proposition~\ref{prop:nonrawunsafehighsplit}(A). All original occurrence
coefficients remain recorded.
The seven-clause bound immediately excludes the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item OO and OG for every $r,s$;
\item GG, since $r=0$ and its count is at most $4+3$;
\item OH unless $r=s=1$;
\item OJ when $s=0$;
\item GH when $s=0$;
\item GJ when $s=0$, with $r=0$ already;
\item HH when $r=0$, with $s=0$ already.
\end{itemize}
The exact remaining list is OH with $r=s=1$; OJ with $s=1$ and either
$r$; GH with $s=1$ and either $r$; GJ with $s=1,r=0$; HH with
$r=1,s=0$; HJ with $s=0$ and either $r$; and JJ with $r=s=0$.
Parts C10--C13 cover all of them, without a coefficient or occurrence
normalization.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C10. The mandatory-factor families OH and OJ.}
When every last-high contribution has a common old factor $D$, that
factor meets three pairwise-disjoint target edges: $D_0$ leaves at
least the induced three-matching consisting of the other arm and the
two isolated edges. Hence $D[T]$ has at least three vertices.
In particular $D$ is not singleton, and a safe old quartic containing
it cannot have two targets, since full quartic equality would make its
full support a two-point transversal. This observation applies only
to the actual displayed mandatory factor.

For OH with $r=s=1$, $f=(C\vee h)D$. The exact expansions
$hf=hD$ and $gf=gCD\vee gBD$, with absorption of $fM$ terms, give
\[
 F=hD\vee(M\vee g)CD.
\]
Both terms are safe. The first is $(A\vee g)BD$. Its raw quartic
$gBD$ has at most one target, and $A$ has its actual $A/L$ anchor.
Apply the C4 fork obstruction with $J_0=D$ to bound this term by one.
For the second term, $gCD$ has at most one target; its base $M$ has an
$M/L$ anchor, since $r>0$ gives nonzero $\gamma\subseteq L$ with
$\gamma M$ old. Apply that obstruction with $E=M,F=C,J_0=D$.
Thus the last-high family has at most two targets but must supply a
three-matching, a contradiction.

For OJ with $s=1,r=0$, $f=D(C\vee g\vee h)$. The identities
$g\vee h=g\vee AB$ and $hf=hD$ give
\[
 F=hD\vee(C\vee g)DM.
\]
All terms have mandatory $D$, whose target restriction has at least
three vertices, so each relevant quartic has at most one target.
The first term is bounded by the $A/L$ anchor; the second by the
actual $C/L$ anchor, since $C$ receives $g$ in the J input.
The fork obstruction with $(E,F,J_0)=(A,B,D)$ and $(C,M,D)$ bounds
each by one, a contradiction.
If $r=s=1$ in OJ, $gf=gD$ absorbs its multiples, leaving
\[
 F=ABD\vee CDM\vee gD.
\]
The first two old cubics have at most one target each. A target of
safe $gD$ would make full $D$ singleton by amplification, contrary to
its three matching incidences. Hence $F$ again has at most two targets.
This completes both mandatory-factor families.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C11. GH and GJ with a positive $h/f$ cross.}
In GH, $hf=hC\vee gB=ABC\vee gB$. Thus $s>0$ makes $gB$ safe.
The same identity holds in GJ after absorption:
$f=CD\vee g\vee ABC$ and $hf=ABC\vee gB$.
In both cases C7 gives $B=\{x\}$, a target leaf square in $g$, and
an isolated $cd$ false on both $g,h$.
The safe old cubic $ABC$, with $B=\{x\}$, has both $A,C$ containing
the original $\alpha$, since both are actual $g$-recipient bases.
It therefore contains $x\delta^2$ for every $\delta\in\alpha$,
so $\alpha$ avoids all isolated target endpoints.

For GJ, both final bases $C,D$ receive $g$, and neither is a full
singleton endpoint of $cd$. On $cd$, the last high reduces to $CD$,
so the safe cubic $CDM$ witnesses $cd$. Its singleton factor cannot
be $C$ or $D$, while an actual singleton $M$ gives $K+2$.
This contradiction includes every actual extra $h$ contribution in
J; no new low is assumed for a removed Boolean term.
For GH, $C$ receives $g$ and $D$ receives $h$. Positive $s$ gives
$\beta\subseteq M$, and the actual recipient gives $\beta\subseteq D$.
Again $CDM$ witnesses $cd$. Full $C$ cannot be an endpoint singleton,
since it contains nonzero $\alpha$ avoiding $cd$, and full $M$ cannot
be one because of its actual charge. If full $D=\{c\}$, its nonzero
$\beta$ equals $\{c\}$, so $c\in M$. The witness must put $d\in C$;
choosing $d$ from $C$ and $c$ from both $D,M$ forces full $C=\{d\}$
by the unique-endpoint cubic rule, the same contradiction.
The opposite endpoint is identical. This handles $r=0$ and $r=1$
together, since the required $h/f$ terms and positive-$s$ identities
are present in both.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C12. HH and HJ with a positive $g/f$ cross.}
For HH, $f=CD\vee h$ and $s=0$. Positive $r$ gives
$gf=gCD\vee gB$, so $gB$ is safe. Part C7 gives $B=\{x\}$,
a target leaf square, say $y^2$, in $g$, and an isolated $cd$ false
on both highs. Both $C,D$ receive $h$ and contain $\beta$.
Safety of $gCD$ forces $y$ adjacent to every $\delta\in\beta$,
from the monomials $y^2\delta^2$. Thus $\beta$ avoids the isolated
vertices. On $cd$, the required old cubic is $CDM$. Neither $C$ nor
$D$ is a full endpoint singleton because both contain $\beta$;
$M$ is not one by its actual charge. This is a contradiction.
For HJ, $s=0$ and $f=CD\vee h\vee gC$. Positive $r$ gives
\[
 gf=gB\vee gC.
\]
Again C7 applies. The actual $C$-recipient contains $\beta$, and
safety of $gC$ with $y^2$ in $g$ forces $\beta$ to avoid all isolated
vertices. Both final bases $C,D$ receive $h$ and contain $\beta$.
The same $CDM$ singleton argument excludes the isolated edge false
on $g,h$, proving HJ with positive $r$.
Every deduction retains the actual original coefficients. No step
assumes a new $\beta$ or a merged occurrence after support absorption.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C13. HJ without crosses, and JJ.}
For HJ with $r=s=0$,
\[
 F=fM=(A\vee g)BM\vee(D\vee g)CM.
\]
The displayed $M$ is a common actual factor of every last-high term.
Since $D_0$ has at most one arm, $F$ must witness a three-matching.
Therefore $M$ meets its three disjoint edges and has at least three
target vertices. Each safe old quartic $gBM,gCM$ has at most one
target, because two would make its full $M$ a two-point transversal.
The first term satisfies the C4 fork obstruction with
$E=A,F=B,J_0=M$, using the actual $A/L$ anchor. The second satisfies
it with $E=D,F=C,J_0=M$: $D$ is an actual $g$-recipient in J and has
its $D/L$ anchor. Each term has at most one target, so their union
cannot supply a three-matching. This auxiliary factorization creates
no physical gates and charges no invented product.

Finally consider JJ. The implications $g\Rightarrow f$ and
$h\Rightarrow f$ force $r=s=0$. Boolean absorption gives
\[
 f=CD\vee g\vee AB,\qquad F=CDM\vee gM\vee ABM.
\]
If $gM$ has a target, amplification makes actual $M$ a full endpoint
singleton. Its original-product charge excludes the center and the
isolated endpoints, so it is a path leaf. The entire $F$ then has
at most that single arm, and $D_0$ has at most one arm, insufficient.
If $gM$ has no target, the old cubics $CDM,ABM$ have at most two in
union; adding $D_0$ still gives at most three. JJ is impossible too.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{C14. Completion of the single-middle row.}
Every one of the ten actual nonraw final-input pairs and every original
$q,r,s$ has been covered. Under $\vc(G)>K+2$, the fixed original
single-affected-middle frame cannot witness all four global targets.
Thus the entire row satisfies $\vc(G)\le K+2$ for arbitrary original
$K$. The complete direct-term, safe-raw-cross and fork arguments are
given in C1--C13; none is imported from an incomplete partial or a
pending checker route.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{D. The whole all-visible family.}
The original-node inventory is exhaustive under the contrary inequality.
Its repeated-high $R1,R2,R3$ alternatives contradict their exact

Proposition~\ref{prop:doubleaffectedmiddlerow} in exactly the stated
original-input scope. Its independent-middle and single-middle rows

pattern remains. Therefore
\[
 \vc(G)\le K+2
\]
for the entire original all-visible three-product, three-addition family
in the statement.

The initial allowance of arbitrary compatible scalar or zero contexts,
raw or affected operands, repeated inputs, repeated original highs and
coincident Boolean values is discharged only through the exact inventory
of Proposition~\ref{prop:allvisibleoriginalinventory}. In the surviving
distinct-high rows, original minimum-degree-two highs and selected
degree-one paths justify the nonzero full old linear contexts used in the
proof. Their target restrictions may be zero throughout. Original nodes
and occurrences are never identified by Boolean aliases. Every
full-support restriction or clause count is a support argument and does
not become a counted physical reduction. Every cover charge uses the
fixed original $K$ and the fact that the four listed edges are all global
missing edges, so retained-star centers plus the stated missing-edge
cover really cover $G$. Isolates and outside context vertices are
retained wherever the full-support proofs use them.

This conclusion concerns the stated all-visible family only. It asserts
no hidden-addition normalization, matching-attachment result, other
outside shape, empty-$H$ result, numerical-row closure or general circuit
optimum. The exact scope of each component statement is unchanged.
\end{proof}
