% Complete author-route transcription of the fully compared independent-middle result.
% Stage preparer: foundation. This is transcription, not an additional fresh proof.
\begin{proposition}[The complete independent-middle row]
\label{prop:independentmiddlerow}
Let a positive variable-input circuit compute $P\in\Sup(G)$, where $G$ is
finite, simple and four-cycle-free. Suppose its nonempty ordinary
quadratic support is $H$, and its four global missing edges are
$xy,xz,ab,cd$. Their endpoint set $T$ satisfies
$G[T]=P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$.
Keep the exact original selected quadratic frame and its arbitrary
retained-product count $K$.
There are exactly three original private multiplication nodes and three
original private addition nodes, all three additions visible. The three
highs are the three distinct original private-product nodes, each
inserted once. Every original private-product input has minimum degree
one, with its nonzero old homogeneous linear base and its actual
available earlier insertion contributions. Preserve every original node,
degree, occurrence, coefficient, selected low and path, fanout, full
direct context and retained-product incidence. A product topological
order does not impose an order on unrelated cuts.

Let the first two original products be independent old quadratics
$g=UV$ and $h=AB$. Up to interchanging the final input sides and exchanging
the two independent highs together with their exact original data,
suppose the third product has one of the following original operand forms:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:independentmiddleforms}
\begin{array}{c|l}
\mathrm{OG}&f=(C\vee g)D,\\
\mathrm{OJ}&f=D(C\vee g\vee h),\\
\mathrm{GG}&f=(C\vee g)(D\vee g),\\
\mathrm{GH}&f=(C\vee g)(D\vee h),\\
\mathrm{GJ}&f=(C\vee g)(D\vee g\vee h).
\end{array}
\end{equation}
All six full old homogeneous linear forms $U,V,A,B,C,D$ are nonzero,
and repetitions are permitted. Each affected factor is its actual
original operand with the indicated compatible positive occurrence
coefficients, including all original low/context identities. Coefficients
record only absence or positivity for Boolean support; no ordinary
degree, gate deletion or node identification is inferred from Boolean
idempotence or absorption. An old base need not be an available standalone
wire.
Keep the complete exact three-occurrence contribution
\begin{equation}\label{eq:independentmiddleframe}
Y=gL\vee hN\vee fM\vee qgh\vee rgf\vee shf,
\qquad q,r,s\in\{0,1\},
\end{equation}
where $q,r,s$ record the actual cross coefficients, initially
unrestricted, and $L,N,M$ are the full actual old homogeneous linear
direct contexts. Retain all original selected-low, mixed-low,
full-context and retained-product-incidence identities.
If $Y$ is globally safe and supplies all four target witnesses, then
$\vc(G)\le K+2$. This excludes the five displayed independent-middle
forms; it does not classify the single-affected-middle row or close the
numerical saving row.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every support identity in this proof is Boolean. It neither merges
original nodes nor resets an ordinary degree, creates a gate by expansion,
or assumes that an algebraically introduced old form is available as an
original wire. All original lows, coefficients, selected paths, full
contexts and retained-product incidences remain fixed.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{1. Original data and the contrary assumption.}
Write $J=\{xy,xz,ab,cd\}$. The actual contexts $L,N,M$ are globally
nonzero: following each selected degree-one visible continuation to its
first original retained product puts that product's complete nonzero
opposite homogeneous factor in the context. A context may restrict to
zero on $T$.
Let $a_0,b_0,c_0$ be the nonzero old homogeneous parts of the selected
lows of $g,h,f$. The products $a_0L,b_0N,c_0M$ are supported on $H$.
An actual $g$-recipient base contains $a_0$, and an actual $h$-recipient
base contains $b_0$. A positive $q$ gives
\[
 a_0\subseteq N,\qquad b_0\subseteq L,\qquad a_0b_0
 \text{ supported on }H.
\]
A positive $r$ gives $a_0\subseteq M$, $c_0\subseteq L$ and
$a_0c_0$ supported on $H$; a positive $s$ gives $b_0\subseteq M$,
$c_0\subseteq N$ and $b_0c_0$ supported on $H$.
These are full-support inclusions from original occurrences and retained
products, not identities of a changed circuit.

For a safe expression $F$, let $\mathcal W(F)$ be its target-witness set
in $J$. A private high need not be safe; let $\mathcal P(g)$,
$\mathcal P(h)$ and $\mathcal P(f)$ be the target edge assignments on
which each high is true. Suppose for contradiction that $\vc(G)>K+2$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:nonrawsevenzerocross} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:independentmiddlepotentials}
 |\mathcal P(g)|\ge2,\qquad |\mathcal P(h)|\ge2,
 \qquad |\mathcal P(f)|\ge2.
\end{equation}
There is no exclusive, injective or first-true allocation in this
necessity. A safe old quadratic has at most one missing witness, so
neither $g$ nor $h$ is globally safe. An old cubic has at most one missing
witness, while an old quartic has at most two. Equality for a quartic
fixes its four \emph{full} supports to the four distinct two-element
transversals of the corresponding induced matching, by
Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors}. Full old neighborhoods and outside
variables are retained in every application.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{2. Full-support singleton rules.}
A safe old cubic witnessing a missing edge $uv$ has a full singleton
factor at one endpoint. Choose a witness monomial, say $u^2v$, and the
factor supplying the single $v$. Replacing that choice by any $w$ in its
full support gives $u^2w$. Safety excludes $w=u$ and forces $uw\in E(G)$.
The factor is old and contains the missing neighbor $v$ of $u$. If it had
another vertex $w$, its old $H$-center $p$ would differ from $u$, since
$uv\notin E(H)$. The four distinct vertices $u,v,p,w$ would form a
four-cycle. Thus the entire factor is $\{v\}$. The other orientation
and repeated old factors are included.

We need the amplified version. If an old quadratic $X=EF$ is true on
two targets and the safe cubic $XB$ witnesses one target, then the full
$B$ is an endpoint singleton and $X$ contains the square of the other
endpoint. If both $E,F$ are nonsingleton, the unique-endpoint factor just
identified must be $B$, giving both assertions. If one is a singleton
$t$, both target potentials contain $t$, so $t=x$ and they are the two
path arms. The other old support meets both arms. If it omitted $x$, it
would contain $y,z$, and its old center would form a four-cycle with $x$
or make an arm old. Hence $X$ contains $x^2$. Safety of $XB$ excludes
$x$ from $B$; its missing-arm witness and the old-center argument force
the full $B$ to be the corresponding leaf singleton. This also includes
two singleton factors and full outside vertices.
In particular, a target of $gL$ or $hN$ makes that full actual context
an endpoint singleton, and its quadratic contains the opposite square.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{3. Original context charges and anchors.}
Every retained product in the original quadratic frame is a squarefree
quadratic star. Overlap of its two nonzero linear factors gives a square;
two disjoint nonsingleton factors give a four-cycle. Thus one chosen
center per original retained product covers $H$, with repeated centers
only improving the count.
If a full nonzero actual context lies in a three-vertex cover of the
four global missing edges, mark an original retained product whose full
opposite factor lies in that context. Those three vertices cover the
entire marked product as well. Centers for the other $K-1$ products give
$K+2$. Under the contrary inequality, an actual singleton context at a
target vertex can therefore only be $y$ or $z$; $x$ and each isolated
endpoint give this charge.

Two full actual contexts $\{y\}$ and $\{z\}$ mark distinct retained
products. If the marked product and side were the same, the nonzero
opposite factor would lie in their empty intersection. Opposite sides
of one product would put an $H$-edge in $T$, or give a square. The
four-cover $\{y,z,a,c\}$ and centers for the other $K-2$ products give
$K+2$. Hence two different actual leaf contexts are impossible. By the
amplified singleton rule, each of $gL,hN$ has at most one target, a path
arm; different targets would give the two opposite leaf contexts.
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:independentmiddledirect}
 D_0=gL\vee hN\quad\text{has at most one target, a path arm.}
\end{equation}

For any actual recipient operand with old base $E$ carrying insertion
$i$, follow its selected degree-one continuation to its first retained
product. The whole nonzero opposite old factor $B_i$ lies in the full
context $L_i$, and $EB_i$ is supported on $H$. The selected low $a_i$
is contained in $E$. Choosing $k\in B_i$ gives $Ek$, $a_i k$ and
$a_iL_i$ supported on $H$, with $k\in L_i$. This is the actual-path
anchor proved in Proposition~\ref{prop:nonrawsevenzerocross}; it is not
postulated for an invented algebraic base.

We use Lemma~\ref{lem:independentproducts} in its exact form: safe
old-quadratic terms $XL,ZM,XZ$ have at most two missing witnesses in
union if nonzero old lows $\alpha\subseteq M$ and
$\beta\subseteq L$ satisfy $\alpha L$, $\beta M$ and
$\alpha\beta$ supported on $H$. Auxiliary expressions such as $CM$
are support products, not counted original gates.
We also use Lemma~\ref{lem:relatedcubics}: for nonzero old
$U,V,L,D,E,F$ and a nonzero old $a\subseteq E\cap F$ with $aL$
supported on $H$, safety of $UVL,UVD,EFD$ gives at most one missing
witness in the first two together and at most two in all three.
Each use below specifies its actual low, recipient or mixed-coefficient
source.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{4. The safe last-high subfamily.}
Define the actual positive subfamily
\begin{equation}\label{eq:independentmiddlesubfamily}
 Y_0=D_0\vee f(M\vee rg\vee sh).
\end{equation}
We first show that $Y_0$ cannot witness all four targets under the
contrary inequality, irrespective of $q$. This does not delete $q$'s
original gate or coefficient. It is a safe positive subfamily of $Y$,
using all the original data and the potential necessity
\eqref{eq:independentmiddlepotentials} from that original circuit.

If a safe expression $Z$ has a positive linear CNF with at most seven
clauses, then $D_0\vee Z$ cannot witness all four. If $D_0$ has no
target, restrict to $T$: the graph function of $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ needs
eight clauses, one for each distinct minimal vertex cover. If $D_0$
has one arm, restrict to the endpoints of the other arm and the two
isolated edges, an induced three-edge matching that also needs eight
clauses. The expression $Z$ must be true on each of those edges, while
global safety makes it zero on every independent set. Monotonicity
therefore makes its restriction exactly that graph function. Zero or
scalar restrictions can only shorten the CNF. This is support algebra,
not a new physical circuit.

For $Z=f(M\vee rg\vee sh)$, the last factor has at most four linear
CNF clauses, or at most two unless both $r,s$ are positive, and one
when both vanish. The five forms of $f$ have respectively
$3,5,4,4,6$ clauses, obtained by distributing disjunction over the two
factors of $g=UV$ and $h=AB$.
Thus OG has $3+4\le7$ clauses for every $r,s$.
OJ has $5+2\le7$ except when $r=s=1$. In that exception,
$gf=gD$ and $hf=hD$ are safe bare old cubics. A target of either makes
full $D$ an endpoint singleton by part 2. Since $D$ is a mandatory
factor of $f$ and $f$ has two target potentials, it must be $D=\{x\}$.
Every $f$-containing contribution then has only arm targets, as does
$D_0$, so $Y_0$ misses both isolated edges. Therefore both crosses are
target-free in any proposed four-target $Y_0$ configuration. The
remaining $fM$ has at most six clauses, again impossible with $D_0$.

In GG, $g$ implies $f$. A positive $r$ would make $g$ itself safe,
contrary to its two target potentials. Hence $r=0$, and $4+2\le6$
clauses suffice for either $s$. GH has $4+2\le6$ unless $r=s=1$;
part 5 treats that exception. GJ likewise forces $r=0$. If $s=0$,
$fM$ has $6+1=7$ clauses; part 6 treats $s=1$.
These reductions neither assume nor erase $q$. The exceptional cases
use only terms already contained in $Y_0$.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{5. The GH exception with $r=s=1$.}
For $f=(C\vee g)(D\vee h)$, the identities
$gf=gD\vee gh$ and $hf=hC\vee gh$ absorb their $M$-multiples and give
\[
 Y_0=A_g\vee A_h\vee Q\vee R,\qquad
 A_g=gL\vee gD,\quad A_h=hN\vee hC,\quad Q=CDM,\quad R=gh.
\]
The two actual positive last-high crosses supply $R$, even if $q=0$.
Every displayed term is safe.
The actual $g$-recipient $C$ contains $a_0$, and $r>0$ puts $a_0$
in $M$. Since $a_0L$ is supported on $H$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:relatedcubics} with the pair $C,M$ gives
$|\mathcal W(A_g)|\le1$ and $|\mathcal W(A_g\vee Q)|\le2$.
Similarly the actual $h$-recipient $D$ and $s>0$ give
$b_0\subseteq D\cap M$, with $b_0N$ supported on $H$, so
$|\mathcal W(A_h)|\le1$ and $|\mathcal W(A_h\vee Q)|\le2$.

The actual $C/L$ anchor also gives
$|\mathcal W(gL\vee hC\vee R)|\le2$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:independentproducts}. Choose $k$ in the whole opposite
factor inside $L$; then $Ck,a_0k,a_0L$ are supported on $H$. Apply the
lemma to quadratics $g,h$, contexts $L,C$, and lows $a_0,k$.
The actual $D/N$ anchor similarly gives
$|\mathcal W(hN\vee gD\vee R)|\le2$.
If $R$ has two targets, these two bounds confine all four cubics
$gL,hN,gD,hC$ to that pair; $Q$ adds at most one. Thus $Y_0$ has at most
three targets.

If $R$ has at most one, four targets would force $A_g,A_h,Q,R$ to
supply four different single targets. Suppose $gD$ supplies the target
of $A_g$. Part 2 makes full $D$ an endpoint singleton. The different
$Q$ target also contains $D$, so they must be the two path arms and
$D=\{x\}$. Then $A_h$ and $R$ must supply the isolated targets.
The isolated target of $A_h$ cannot come from $hN$, because its actual
full singleton isolated context would give $K+2$. If it comes from
$hC$, full $C$ is an isolated endpoint singleton by part 2, making a
path-arm target of $Q$ impossible. The argument when $hC$ supplies the
target of $A_h$ is symmetric. If neither bare cubic supplies its
respective target, the actual $gL,hN$ supply two different arms, forcing
opposite full leaf contexts and $K+2$. This proves the GH exception.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{6. The GJ exception with $s=1$.}
Here $r=0$, $f=CD\vee g\vee Ch$, and $hf=Ch\vee gh$.
Absorption gives
\[
 Y_0=A_g\vee A_h\vee Q\vee R,\qquad
 A_g=gL\vee gM,\quad A_h=hN\vee hC,\quad Q=CDM,\quad R=gh.
\]
All terms are safe, and the $h/f$ cross supplies $R$.
The two actual $g$-recipient bases $C,D$ contain $a_0$, with $a_0L$
supported on $H$. Lemma~\ref{lem:relatedcubics} gives
$|\mathcal W(A_g)|\le1$ and $|\mathcal W(A_g\vee Q)|\le2$.
The actual $h$-recipient $D$ and $s>0$ give
$b_0\subseteq D\cap M$, with $b_0N$ supported on $H$, so the same lemma
gives $|\mathcal W(A_h)|\le1$ and
$|\mathcal W(A_h\vee Q)|\le2$.
As in part 5, the actual $C/L$ anchor gives
$|\mathcal W(gL\vee hC\vee R)|\le2$.

If $R$ has two targets, the full $U,V,A,B$ are the four distinct
transversals of its induced matching. If the pair is $ab,cd$, neither
old quadratic has a path-arm potential. Both $A_g,A_h$ are confined to
the pair and $Q$ adds at most one. Otherwise rename the pair $xy,ab$.
The only possible target outside it for $g$ or $h$ is $xz$, and at most
one quadratic can be true there: both its factors must be the two
$x$-transversals, leaving the other quadratic the two $y$-transversals.
The bound involving $R$ already confines $gL,hC$ to its pair.
If $gM$ supplies the extra arm, $g$ contains $x^2$ and full $M=\{z\}$
by part 2, so $Q$ cannot witness $cd$.
If $hN$ supplies that arm, full $N=\{z\}$. The actual $h$-recipient
$D$ has its full nonzero opposite factor inside $N$, so $Dz$ is
supported on $H$. Since $H[T]=\varnothing$, $D$ has empty target
restriction and $Q$ has no target. Four targets are impossible in
every alternative.

If $R$ has at most one, four targets would force $A_g,A_h,Q,R$ to
supply four different single targets. Suppose $hC$ supplies the target
of $A_h$. Full $C$ is an endpoint singleton $v$ by part 2. Since the
actual $g$-recipient $C$ contains $a_0$, we have $a_0=\{v\}$.
The old product $a_0L$ and $H[T]=\varnothing$ make $L[T]$ empty, so
the target of $A_g$ must come from $gM$. Its actual full context $M$
is a singleton path leaf under the contrary inequality. The term $Q$
containing that leaf cannot have a different target from $gM$.
If $hC$ has no target, the target of $A_h$ comes from actual $hN$, and
the different target of $A_g$ comes from actual $gL$ or $gM$.
Two different actual leaf contexts again give $K+2$.
This completes part 4 for all five forms and every $r,s$.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{7. The first independent cross.}
The full contribution is $Y=Y_0\vee qR$, where $R=gh$.
Since $Y$ supplies all four and $Y_0$ cannot, $q$ is positive and $R$
has a target not supplied by $Y_0$. In particular $R$ is globally safe
and has at least one, but at most two, targets.
The actual positive-$q$ identities and
Lemma~\ref{lem:independentproducts} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:independentmiddlecrossbound}
 |\mathcal W(gL\vee hN\vee R)|\le2.
\end{equation}
We exclude two targets of $R$ and then its only possible single target.
At no point is $q$ deleted from the original circuit.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{8. Two targets of $R$.}
Suppose $R$ has two targets. Bound~\eqref{eq:independentmiddlecrossbound}
confines both direct cubics to that pair, and the full $U,V,A,B$ are
the four distinct transversals of its matching quartet.
If the pair is $ab,cd$, both $g,h$ are false on both path arms. Each
nonraw final operand reduces to its old base on those assignments, and
every cross with the last high vanishes. Only $CDM$ can supply the two
arms, contrary to the old-cubic bound.

Otherwise rename the pair $xy,ab$. Both $g,h$ are false on $cd$, so
safe $CDM$ must witness $cd$. The other arm $xz$ must be supplied outside
the confined direct contribution. At most one of $g,h$ is true on $xz$:
its factors must both contain $x$ and consume the two $x$-transversals.
If neither is true, only $CDM$ can supply $xz$ as well, impossible.
Let $\kappa$ name the unique original high true on $xz$, and $\lambda$
the other. The first owns the two $x$-transversals and contains $x^2$;
the second owns the two $y$-transversals and contains $y^2$.
The high $\lambda$ and its cross with $f$ are false on $xz$.
Thus only $fM$ or a present $\kappa f$ can supply that arm.
Count the \emph{actual} final operands receiving $\kappa$.

\emph{Zero recipients.}
Both final operands reduce to $C,D$ on $xz$. An $fM$ route would make
$CDM$ witness both $xz$ and $cd$.
A present $\kappa f$ route supplying $xz$ contains the safe term
$\kappa CD$. Hence both $C,D$ meet the disjoint pairs $xz,cd$ and are
nonsingleton. The missing witness of $CDM$ forces full $M$ to be an
isolated endpoint singleton, and the original-context charge gives
$K+2$.

\emph{One recipient.}
Write that input as $E\vee\kappa\vee\varepsilon\lambda$ and the
other as $F\vee\delta\lambda$, where $\varepsilon,\delta\in\{0,1\}$
retain the actual optional incidences. The old cubic $EFM$ witnesses
$cd$. If $fM$ supplies $xz$, it cannot use $EFM$, already witnessing
$cd$; the safe term $\kappa FM$ must supply it. Both $F,M$ meet $xz$
and $cd$, so neither is singleton. The cubic singleton rule forces
full $E=\{t\}$ for an endpoint $t$ of $cd$. Since $E$ is an actual
recipient of $\kappa$, its original nonzero selected low is $\{t\}$.
Positive $q$ puts that low in the full direct context of $\lambda$.
The safe $\lambda$-direct term then contains $y^2t$, which is unsafe
on the independent pair $\{y,t\}\subset T$.
If instead $\kappa f$ supplies $xz$, its support is
$\kappa F\vee\delta\kappa\lambda$. Since $\lambda$ is false there,
the safe bare cubic $\kappa F$ must witness $xz$. Part 2 forces full
$F=\{z\}$, but $F$ must meet $cd$ for $EFM$ to witness $cd$.
This is again impossible.

\emph{Two recipients.}
The high $\kappa$ implies $f$. A positive actual $\kappa f$ coefficient
would make the unsafe $\kappa$ safe, contrary to its two target
potentials. Thus $fM$ supplies $xz$. The old $CDM$ already supplies
$cd$, and $\lambda$ is false on $xz$, so the safe support term
$\kappa M$ supplies that arm. Full $M=\{z\}$ by part 2, contradicting
the $CDM$ witness on $cd$. In particular Boolean absorption of the
positive square term here makes no assertion about an original degree.

These exhaust the two original final operands. The symbols $\kappa$
and $\lambda$ merely name one or the other independent original node;
no original ancestry, coefficient or gate is removed. Thus $R$ cannot
have two targets.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{9. Opposite squares and an actual direct witness.}
Suppose $R=gh$ witnesses $uv$, with $u^2$ in $g$ and $v^2$ in $h$.
Choose $k$ in nonzero $a_0$ and $l$ in nonzero $b_0$.
The positive-$q$ identities put $k\in N$, $l\in L$ and $kl\in E(H)$.
Safety of $gL$ gives $ul\in E(G)$ and $l\ne u$; safety of $hN$ gives
$vk\in E(G)$ and $k\ne v$. Also $k\ne l$.
If $k=u$, actual $hN$ contains $v^2u$ and witnesses $uv$.
If $l=v$, actual $gL$ witnesses $uv$.
If neither coincidence occurs, $u,l,k,v$ are four distinct vertices,
and $ul,lk,kv,vu$ form a forbidden four-cycle.
Hence one of the actual direct terms witnesses $uv$.
The argument is symmetric in $g,h$ and makes no assumption that $k,l$
are outside $T$: the coincidence alternatives are essential.
Opposite squares on an isolated target are therefore impossible under
the contrary inequality, because an isolated direct witness gives the
context charge. On a path target they put that target into $D_0$, and
hence into $Y_0$.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{10. A single target of $R$.}
We now know that $R$ has exactly one target $e$. Its global safety and
$R=gh$ imply
\begin{equation}\label{eq:independentmiddleintersection}
 \mathcal P(g)\cap\mathcal P(h)=\{e\}.
\end{equation}
Each potential set has at least two members. Choose one extra target
for each high; they are different by
\eqref{eq:independentmiddleintersection}.
First suppose $e$ is a path arm, say $xy$.
If one high, say $g$, also has $xz$, both its old factors contain $x$
by the old-neighborhood two-arm observation, so $g$ contains $x^2$.
The other high $h$ cannot have $xz$ and hence has an isolated target,
say $ab$. Each of its factors meets $ab$. Neither can contain $x$:
choosing $x$ from that factor, an isolated endpoint from the other,
and $x^2$ from $g$ would make $R$ unsafe. Both factors must meet $xy$,
so both contain $y$, and $h$ contains $y^2$.

If neither high has $xz$, their extra potentials are the two different
isolated edges, say $ab$ for $g$ and $cd$ for $h$.
If an endpoint $t$ of $xy$ occurs in a factor of each high, choose $t$
from those factors, a vertex of $ab$ from the other $g$ factor, and a
vertex of $cd$ from the other $h$ factor. These variables form an
independent set in $T$, contradicting safety of $R$.
Thus the unions of the $xy$ endpoints appearing in the two factor
pairs are disjoint. Each pair's two factors meet $xy$, so one pair
contains $x$ in both factors and the other contains $y$ in both.
Again the highs have opposite endpoint squares.
Part 9 puts the sole target $xy$ of $R$ into $D_0\subseteq Y_0$.
Then $Y=Y_0\vee R$ having all four witnesses would imply that $Y_0$
has all four, contrary to part 4. This excludes a path-arm single
target.

Now suppose $e$ is isolated, renamed $ab$. If one high has $cd$ as an
extra potential, the other cannot have $cd$ and must have a path arm.
If an endpoint $t$ of $ab$ occurred in a factor of each high, choose
$t$ twice and a vertex from each of the other factors' extra edges.
These choices form an independent set: $cd$ and the chosen path arm
are disjoint with no cross edge in $G[T]$, and neither is adjacent to
an $ab$ endpoint. Safety therefore forces the two $ab$-endpoint unions
to be disjoint, giving opposite squares at $a,b$. Part 9 would then
give an isolated direct target, impossible.

Consequently neither high has $cd$. Their extra potentials must be
the two different path arms; neither high can have both, by
\eqref{eq:independentmiddleintersection}. After exchanging $y,z$, the
exact remaining potential sets are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:independentmiddleremainingpotentials}
 \mathcal P(g)=\{ab,xy\},\qquad
 \mathcal P(h)=\{ab,xz\}.
\end{equation}
Neither has a $cd$ potential or contains $x^2$, since that square would
make it true on both arms. The amplified singleton rule now shows that
neither actual direct cubic has a target: an allowed direct witness
would have a full leaf context and force $x^2$ in its high.
Thus $D_0$ has no targets. These conclusions concern only the four
specified target assignments. They do not confine the full supports of
$U,V,A,B$ in this single-target case.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{11. Full contexts avoid the other isolated endpoints.}
Under \eqref{eq:independentmiddleremainingpotentials}, $L$ contains
neither $c$ nor $d$. Suppose, for example, that $c\in L$.
Restrict $g$ to $W_0=\{a,b,x,y\}$. Its two restricted old factors are
nonzero, since it is true on both $ab$ and $xy$.
The polynomial $(g|_{W_0})c$ is a positive subexpression of globally
safe $gL$. The vertex $c$ is adjacent to no vertex of $W_0$ in $G[T]$.
Every monomial of $g|_{W_0}$ must therefore already contain a $G$-edge.
This is a globally safe old quadratic on $W_0$ witnessing the two
missing edges $ab,xy$, contrary to Proposition~\ref{prop:oldfactors}.
The same argument excludes $d$.
Using $W_0=\{a,b,x,z\}$ and $hN$ similarly shows that $N$ contains
neither $c$ nor $d$.
Restriction preserves the old-neighborhood condition, or makes a
factor singleton; the restricted polynomial is safe in the full graph
because all its variables lie in $W_0$. No circuit or retained frame
is created.
Positive $q$ now puts the full $a_0$ in $N$ and the full $b_0$ in $L$,
so both lows avoid $c,d$. An actual final base receiving either earlier
insertion therefore cannot be a full singleton $\{c\}$ or $\{d\}$:
it contains the corresponding nonzero original low.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{12. The final missing edge.}
On $cd$ both $g,h$ are false. Thus the complete contribution
\eqref{eq:independentmiddleframe} reduces to $CDM$: the direct terms
and every cross with $g$ or $h$ vanish, and every affected final operand
reduces to its old base. The safe old cubic $CDM$ witnesses $cd$.
Part 2 makes at least one of the full $C,D,M$ a singleton $\{c\}$ or
$\{d\}$. If it is $M$, the original context charge gives $K+2$.
If it is an affected base $C$ or $D$, part 11 contradicts its actual
nonzero low inclusion. Both bases are affected in GG, GH and GJ,
exhausting their alternatives. In OG and OJ, the only unaffected base
is $D$, a mandatory factor of the entire original $f$. If it is a full
singleton $\{c\}$ or $\{d\}$, $f$ can be true on only the one target
$cd$, contrary to \eqref{eq:independentmiddlepotentials}. Thus these
last two forms are also impossible.
This argument uses full original supports, the global four-edge list
and original-context charges. It requires neither an optimal $H$-cover
nor a conjectured singleton outside context, and does not assume that
$C$ or $D$ was an isolated available wire.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{13. Completion.}
The safe last-high-subfamily argument, the full-quartic two-target case
and the single-target analysis exhaust every actual $q$ and every
possible witness count of safe $gh$. All $r,s$ and all five original
final operand forms were included. The assumption $\vc(G)>K+2$ is
therefore impossible. This proves the exact conclusion for arbitrary
original $K$, without asserting the unclassified single-affected-middle
row, a complete all-visible normalization or numerical-row closure.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The remaining four-witness possibility]\label{cor:fourresidualfinal}
Let $G$ be finite and four-cycle-free. For a circuit below the star count with exactly four missing quadratic witnesses and nonempty quadratic support $H$, write $d=\vc(G)-\vc(H)$, let $D$ be the deleted-gate count, and let $e$ be the extracted circuit's excess over $|E(H)|+\vc(H)-1$. The only remaining necessary numerical possibility is
\[
 d=3,\qquad D=6,\qquad e=0,
\]
and the six deleted gates must be three products and three additions.

The quadratic remainder is optimal. The outside graph of a minimum $H$-cover cannot contain an induced four-edge matching. The exceptional outside graphs $P_4\sqcup K_2$ and $K_3\sqcup K_2$ are excluded. The outside shape $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ is also excluded. Hence the remaining outside shape is $3K_2$ with isolated vertices, and at least two cuts are visible.

For the path shape, Corollary~\ref{cor:twovisiblepathreduction} takes every remaining two-visible saving candidate to an all-visible arithmetic representative, preserving the current erased/pruned polynomial $P^\ast$, the selected quadratic frame, $H$ and its retained count $K$. Proposition~\ref{prop:allvisiblethreeproductcover} excludes the entire resulting all-visible three-product, three-addition family, including arbitrary private ancestry, raw or affected operands, repeated insertion occurrences and every compatible cross allocation. It gives $\vc(G)\le K+2$ without requiring retained optimality. In the saving row $K=\vc(H)$ and $\vc(G)=K+3$, so the cover bound is a contradiction. No original product node is identified merely because Boolean values coincide.

On the remaining three-matching shape, Proposition~\ref{prop:matchingattachmentleafgate} gives its exact necessary attachment condition whenever an original deleted $1+1$ addition exists: a unique crossing attachment center has nonempty full old outside leaf support contained in a partial matching transversal, and a matched attachment endpoint requires its mate in that support. This condition does not settle arbitrary hidden input degrees or the full matching-attachment family. The numerical saving row and unrestricted Boolean problem remain open.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:maxfour} removes the maximal-gain row from Corollary~\ref{cor:fourmissingledger}. For retained product and addition counts $K,A$, write
\[
 e=(K-\vc(H))+(A-(|E(H)|-1)).
\]
Both summands are nonnegative by the separate quadratic bounds. Proposition~\ref{prop:gainthreesix} removes $d=3,D=5,e=0$ and the $e=1$ allocation $K=\vc(H)$, $A=|E(H)|$. The other $e=1$ allocation has $K=\vc(H)+1$, $A=|E(H)|-1$. Corollary~\ref{cor:gainthreeprofile} reduces that allocation to two private products and three additions, and Proposition~\ref{prop:gainthreefiveprivate} excludes it. This removes the whole $d=3,(D,e)=(5,1)$ row.

For cover gain two with $D=5,e=0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:oneproductcover} excludes at most one private product, because $K=\vc(H)$; Proposition~\ref{prop:oneadditionall} excludes at most one private addition. Proposition~\ref{prop:threeproductstwosums} excludes the three-product/two-addition allocation. In the remaining two-product/three-addition case, Proposition~\ref{prop:allvisibletwocover} excludes three visible cuts. With two visible cuts, Corollary~\ref{cor:hiddenunequalany} excludes a hidden unequal-degree sum; Proposition~\ref{prop:hiddenequalpure} makes the equal-degree alternative pure old-linear, and Propositions~\ref{prop:independentlinearglobal} and~\ref{prop:dependentlinearglobal} exclude its two ancestry alternatives. With one visible cut, Proposition~\ref{prop:onevisibletwocover} gives $\vc(G)\le K+1=\vc(H)+1$. Thus the entire cover-gain-two row is excluded.

In the remaining $d=3,D=6,e=0$ row, $K=\vc(H)$. Proposition~\ref{prop:gainthreeproducts} requires at least three deleted products without an addition-count restriction. At most one deleted addition is excluded by Proposition~\ref{prop:oneadditionall}. The only allocations were therefore $(p,a)=(3,3)$ and $(4,2)$. Proposition~\ref{prop:fourproductstwosumscover} gives $\vc(G)\le K+2$ for the latter, contrary to $\vc(G)=K+3$. Hence only three products and three additions remain.

Corollary~\ref{cor:fourdeletedproducts} excludes an outside induced four-edge matching in this three-product allocation. On either exceptional outside graph, Proposition~\ref{prop:hiddenlinearnecessary} requires a hidden original $1+1$ addition. At least one cut is visible; Proposition~\ref{prop:onevisibleexceptional}, Corollary~\ref{cor:allvisibleexceptional}, and Proposition~\ref{prop:twovisibleexceptional} exclude respectively one, three and two visible cuts. Proposition~\ref{prop:onevisibleindependentsets} excludes one visible cut on either remaining outside shape: $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ and $3K_2$ with isolates each have eight maximal independent sets, and their outside vertex sets are $H$-independent. Proposition~\ref{prop:paththreevisible} excludes nonancestral products when all cuts are visible, and Proposition~\ref{prop:pathpurelineargeneral} excludes its exact two-visible unaffected linear-preparation template for arbitrary cross coefficient, each by the contradiction $\vc(G)\le K+2$. Lemmas~\ref{lem:pathproductunion} and~\ref{lem:commonancestorpath} exclude their stated product--union and common-ancestor support templates. Proposition~\ref{prop:literaljoinpath} excludes its literal-join profile. On the outside shape $3K_2$ with isolates, Proposition~\ref{prop:matchingattachmentleafgate} requires a unique crossing attachment center with nonempty full old outside leaf support contained in a partial matching transversal whenever an original deleted $1+1$ addition exists. If the attachment endpoint is matched, its mate must belong to that support; all other centers fail the partial-transversal test. Proposition~\ref{prop:matchinglinearsum} is its stated narrower consequence. No conclusion about other hidden input degrees is inferred. Propositions~\ref{prop:pathmultipleaffected}--\ref{prop:pathsingleaffectedpositive} exclude their prepared-high templates with affected old base boundaries. Lemmas~\ref{lem:rawlinearpreparation} and~\ref{lem:linearfirstaffected} exclude their exact shared raw-preparation and affected linear-first-high templates. Propositions~\ref{prop:doublefirsthigh}, \ref{prop:sharedcutrawchain} and~\ref{prop:sharedcutearlierreuse} exclude their bounded double-insertion, shared-cut/raw-chain and earlier-high-reuse templates, and Proposition~\ref{prop:mixedrawthreevisible} excludes the literal dependent pair plus independent product with one occurrence each. Proposition~\ref{prop:literaloldrawthreevisible} now excludes every all-visible literal old/raw network on the induced $P_3\sqcup2K_2$ target, including repeated highs. Proposition~\ref{prop:essentialvisibleoperands} gives the original-node operand forms and preserves private ancestry; hence at least one affected coefficient must be positive. Propositions~\ref{prop:nesteddoubleaffected}, \ref{prop:twocutjoinbothsides} and~\ref{prop:independentrawaffected} exclude their precise affected configurations. Propositions~\ref{prop:rawmiddleaffectedlast} and~\ref{prop:oneaffectedrawdescendant} give the cover contradiction for their respective raw-middle/affected-final-input and single-affected/raw-descendant families, and Proposition~\ref{prop:laterthreefactorpreparation} does so for its exact later three-factor linear preparation. Proposition~\ref{prop:matchingprivateessential} additionally makes every original private product indispensable on each induced three-matching restriction. On the path target each is therefore true on an isolated missing edge or on both path arms; no distinct-edge or first-true assignment is inferred. These conclusions preserve the original retained-product count. Proposition~\ref{prop:allvisibleoriginalinventory} exhausts the original all-visible product and occurrence patterns. Proposition~\ref{prop:independentrawmiddlecover} then excludes its R2 family, including both repeated-high allocations and every actual cross coefficient, by the original full-context cover bound $\vc(G)\le K+2$. Proposition~\ref{prop:bothaffectedrepeatedcubic} excludes the both-affected part of R1 for either repeated-high allocation and every actual cross coefficient. Proposition~\ref{prop:singleaffectedrawcubiccover} gives $\vc(G)\le K+2$ for its single-affected part, retaining the full actual context and original-product charge. Both apply without retained optimality. Thus R1 is entirely excluded in this saving row. Proposition~\ref{prop:repeatedRthreecover} gives $\vc(G)\le K+2$ for the entire R3 family, including both repeated-high allocations, one or both affected middle inputs, every later coefficient and all compatible actual contexts. Its full common-prefix rigidity and original-product charge use no retained optimality. Hence all two-distinct-inserted-product alternatives are excluded. At this intermediate inventory stage, only the finite nonraw table with three distinct highs remains; the whole-family exclusion below removes that table without altering its earlier complete component proofs. For two visible cuts on the induced path target, Corollary~\ref{cor:twovisiblepathreduction} now applies because the saving row has $\vc(G)=K+3$. It starts from the exact original hidden-node inventory of Proposition~\ref{prop:twovisiblehiddeninventory}. In its unequal-input alternative the actual degree-one boundary has full value $R=A+\beta g$. If $\beta>0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:generalaffectedpreparationcover} applies to the actual affected boundary, allowing $A$ to be only a selected old part rather than an available wire. Both permit an arbitrary raw original private-product source and give $\vc(G)\le K+2$ for the same frame and $K$. The earlier literal, squared, alias, cubic, source-first and ancestral-source results remain complete prerequisites at their stated original-input hypotheses.

Only the second-high hidden join from the inventory remains. Its unique surviving use and original degree-one selected low permit the exact reassociation $a+(u+v)=(a+u)+v$. The current polynomial $P^\ast$, selected quadratic frame and retained count are preserved, every product node is unchanged, and the original first high, $u$ and $v$ remain distinct insertion occurrences even if some nodes or values coincide. This is a permitted arithmetic change to the two addition nodes; it is not an identification of the two addition DAGs or a claim that carrier erasure preserved every higher term of the original $P$. To apply Proposition~\ref{prop:allvisiblethreeproductcover}, let $C$ be the chosen minimum $H$-cover and suppose its outside shape is $P_3\sqcup2K_2$, with possible isolated vertices. The four outside edges are absent from $H$ because $C$ covers $H$. Since there are exactly four global missing edges, these outside edges are the whole missing set. The full repeated-high proofs, seven zero-cross reductions, global unsafe-high argument, split-cell proof and complete double-middle proof remain at their exact original hypotheses. The present corollary does not transfer that conclusion to the other outside shape: the general $3K_2$ attachment configurations and the numerical saving row remain open.
\end{proof}



\section{A disjunction count permitting conjunction gates}
The following lemma is the counting ingredient needed after circuit transposition. It is stated for ordinary Boolean circuits and is independent of inverse-semiring terminology.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:orsums}
Let $S_1,\ldots,S_r$ be nonempty subsets of a finite input set $Y$, with $|S_i\cap S_j|\le1$ for $i\ne j$. A monotone Boolean circuit with these $r$ designated outputs
\[
 h_i(y)=\bigvee_{u\in S_i}y_u
\]
has at least $\sum_{i=1}^r(|S_i|-1)$ disjunction gates. Conjunction gates, shared wires and constants zero and one are permitted.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a wire $g$, let
\[
 A(g)=\{u\in Y:g(1_{\{u\}})=1\}.
\]
Fix $S=S_i$, and let $b_S$ be the input equal to zero on $S$ and one outside $S$. Call a wire \emph{false} when $g(b_S)=0$. Monotonicity implies that a false wire has $A(g)\subseteq S$, since $1_{\{u\}}\le b_S$ for $u\notin S$.

Process the gates in their original order, maintaining a partition of $S$, initially into singletons. We maintain that for every processed false wire, its set $A(g)$ is empty or is contained in one part. False variable inputs have singleton sets and a false constant has the empty set. At a false conjunction gate, at least one operand is false, and $A(g)$ is contained in that operand's set. No change to the partition is needed. At a false disjunction gate both operands are false, and $A(g)$ is their union. If their nonempty sets lie in different parts, merge these two parts; otherwise make no change. This preserves the invariant and makes at most one merge at that gate. A merge gate is false on $b_S$ and is true on at least two distinct singleton inputs from $S$.

The designated output $h_i$ is false on $b_S$ and has $A(h_i)=S$. Thus all elements of $S$ must belong to one part at the end, requiring at least $|S|-1$ merges. Finally a merge gate for $S_i$ cannot also be a merge gate for $S_j$: being false on both complementary assignments forces its singleton set into $S_i\cap S_j$, whereas a merge requires that set to have at least two elements. The gates counted for distinct outputs are disjoint. Summing proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\section{The one-sided Boolean count}
This section proves Theorem~\ref{thm:onesided}, including the role of degree in the transposition.

Trim the circuit to the gates feeding its output and delete isolated graph vertices. Since syntactic degree never decreases along a wire, every remaining marked-dependent wire has degree one, and every conjunction has at most one such operand. A wire of degree zero depends on $Y$ alone and takes value one on the all-one $Y$-assignment.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:normal}
A useful disjunction cannot have one marked-dependent operand and one degree-zero operand. Consequently the dependent part consists of $|X|$ marked inputs, $M$ disjunctions of two dependent wires, and $K$ conjunctions with one dependent and one degree-zero operand.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Such a mixed disjunction would be true at $x=0,y=1$. Along a path to the output, every later conjunction has a degree-zero other operand, true at this assignment, and every disjunction preserves truth. The output would be true there, contradicting $f_G(0,1)=0$. A conjunction of two dependent operands would have degree two. These observations exhaust the possibilities.
\end{proof}

For a dependent wire $w$, distributivity gives the expansion
\[
 F_w(x,y)=\bigvee_{v\in X}\bigl(x_v\wedge\alpha_{w,v}(y)\bigr),
\]
where $\alpha_{w,v}$ is the disjunction, over directed paths from $x_v$ to $w$ in the dependent part, of the conjunction of the degree-zero multipliers along that path. A missing path contributes zero and an empty multiplier list contributes one. This is a finite path expansion, used as an identity rather than as a circuit construction. At the output $o$,
\[
 \alpha_{o,v}(y)=\bigvee_{u\in N(v)}y_u,                 \tag{\thesection.1}\label{eq:neighborhood}
\]
as follows by setting the marked inputs to the singleton $v$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:centers}
The circuit has $K\ge\vc(G)$ mixed conjunction gates.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For such a gate $g$, let $\operatorname{Src}(g)$ be the set of marked inputs connected to its dependent operand by paths containing no conjunction. Some gates may have an empty source set. Call $g$ relevant if it is the first conjunction on a path witnessing some edge $vu$: that is, a path from $x_v$ to the output whose multipliers are all true at the singleton $y=1_{\{u\}}$.

Every edge has such a witnessing path by \eqref{eq:neighborhood}, and it has a first conjunction: a path with none would make the output true when $y=0$. For a relevant $g$, if $\operatorname{Src}(g)=\{v\}$, choose $v$ as its center. Otherwise, following the same suffix path from any $v'\in\operatorname{Src}(g)$ shows that every neighbor $u$ witnessed through $g$ is a common neighbor of all these sources. Two distinct sources have at most one common neighbor, by the absence of a four-cycle. Since relevance gives at least one, that neighbor is unique; choose it as the center of $g$.

For every edge $vu$, the first conjunction of its witnessing path has center either $v$ or $u$. The centers of the relevant gates form a vertex cover, and there are at most $K$ of them.
\end{proof}

The wire reversal below is an instance of the classical transposition principle. \citet[p.~46]{JuknaBook} gives the exact OR-network count and its historical attributions. We include the read accounting because the degree-zero multipliers here are themselves Boolean circuits, and conjunctions remain in the transposed network. Isolated marked inputs have already been removed.

\begin{lemma}[Transposition with an exact read count]\label{lem:transpose}
Let $P_\vee$ be the number of degree-zero disjunction gates. There is a monotone circuit with outputs $\alpha_{o,v}$ for $v\in X$ and with at most
\[
 P_\vee+M-|X|+1
\]
disjunction gates.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Keep all degree-zero gates. Process the dependent wires in reverse order. Put $\beta_o=1$. For a wire $a\ne o$, form the disjunction of one term for each occurrence in which a later dependent gate reads it. If that reader $r$ is a disjunction, the term is $\beta_r$. If it is a conjunction with degree-zero multiplier $m_r$, the term is $\beta_r\wedge m_r$. The latter term needs at most one conjunction, which is irrelevant to the present count. Reverse induction shows that $\beta_a$ is the disjunction of the products of multipliers on paths from $a$ to the output. Therefore $\beta_{x_v}=\alpha_{o,v}$.

Let $\operatorname{reads}(a)$ count operand occurrences, so using the same wire twice counts twice. Every useful dependent wire other than the output has at least one read. Joining its terms requires at most $\operatorname{reads}(a)-1$ disjunctions. There are $2M+K$ read occurrences in total, and $|X|+M+K-1$ dependent wires other than the output. Thus the new disjunction count is
\[
 \sum_{a\ne o}\bigl(\operatorname{reads}(a)-1\bigr)
 =2M+K-(|X|+M+K-1)=M-|X|+1.
\]
Adding the $P_\vee$ degree-zero disjunctions proves the bound. Constants or duplicate terms may reduce it further.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:onesided}]
The neighborhoods $N(v)$ for distinct $v\in X$ have pairwise intersections of size at most one. Lemma~\ref{lem:orsums} applied to the transposed circuit gives
\[
 P_\vee+M-|X|+1\ \ge\ \sum_{v\in X}(|N(v)|-1)
 =|E|-|X|.
\]
Thus the original number $P_\vee+M$ of disjunctions is at least $|E|-1$. Lemma~\ref{lem:centers} gives at least $\vc(G)$ conjunctions, even before counting any degree-zero conjunctions. The lower bound follows. The star circuit from the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} has marked degree one: every star multiplies a marked linear sum by an unmarked variable, or a marked variable by an unmarked sum. It attains the bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:degreewitness}
If a monotone circuit beats $|E|+\vc(G)-1$ for a four-cycle-free bipartite graph, then after deleting unused gates its syntactic degree is at least two with respect to each side of the bipartition. In each orientation, some conjunction reads two positive-degree wires.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:onesided} to each choice of marked side. If every conjunction had a degree-zero operand, induction would keep every useful wire's degree at most one.
\end{proof}

\section{What supported zeros say about Boolean complexity}
Here we distinguish an output that is a supported zero on an input from a supported zero coefficient of a formal polynomial. The distinction is necessary even for a linear polynomial: $x-1$ has no zero coefficient, but evaluates to the old zero at $x=1$.

The map
\[
 R_0\hookrightarrow R\times\B,
 \quad\tau\longmapsto(0,0),\quad a\longmapsto(a,1)
\]
is an injective semiring homomorphism. Its two coordinates will be denoted $\pi$ and $\chi$. For a circuit over $R_0$, the first coordinate is a ring circuit and the second is its monotone shadow. Unary additive inverse, if present, acts trivially on the second coordinate.

For the following proposition, inputs to $(\F_2)_0$ are $\tau$ and $1$, representing false and true, and constants $\tau,e,1$ are allowed. Boolean circuits in this section may also use free constants zero and one. For a nonconstant graph function these constants can be removed by evaluating gates with constant operands, without increasing size. Read the answer by $\pi$; define $C_0(f)$ to be the minimum size when the \emph{final output} is never $e$ on Boolean inputs, and $C_*(f)$ without that condition. Intermediate outputs may be $e$ in both definitions. All sizes count the relevant binary gates; Boolean NOT gates count one. The unpublished Fable consultation already states this output qualifier and the factor-three comparison explicitly \citep[Q2, corollary]{FableConsult}; we restate and prove them to fix the model.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:complexity}
For every monotone Boolean function $f$,
\[
 \cmon(f)\le C_0(f)\le3\cmon(f),
 \qquad
 C_*(f)=\Theta(\cbool(f)).
\]
Reading the answer by $\chi$, instead of by $\pi$, always computes a monotone Boolean function.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The shadow of a final-output-zero-free circuit agrees with its ring value, since its only possible final values are $\tau$ and $1$. Taking the shadow therefore gives the first inequality. Conversely conjunction lifts as multiplication. Disjunction lifts on $\{\tau,1\}$ by
\[
 a\mathbin{\operatorname{OR}}b=a+b+ab,
\]
using one multiplication and two additions. Checking the four pairs shows its result is $\tau$ for two false inputs and $1$ otherwise. Replacing every monotone gate by these formulas gives the second inequality. The intermediate sum $1+1=e$ is allowed.

For unrestricted circuits, the same formula implements OR, multiplication implements AND, and $1+a$ implements NOT in the ring coordinate. Thus $C_*(f)\le3\cbool(f)$. Conversely addition in $\F_2$ is XOR and multiplication is AND. XOR has a constant-size AND/OR/NOT implementation, while both $e$ and $\tau$ map to the Boolean constant zero. Projecting and replacing gates therefore gives $\cbool(f)\le cC_*(f)$ for an absolute constant $c$, with the harmless constant-function cases treated directly. The last assertion follows because $\chi$ sends addition to OR and multiplication to AND.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The output condition over a general ring]\label{rem:generalring}
Let $R$ be any nonzero commutative unital ring. Encode each Boolean input by $\tau,1$, and allow free constants $\tau,1$. Require the final output to be $\tau$ for false and $1$ for true, and allow addition, multiplication and unary additive inverse, counting each gate once. The minimum size $C_{0,R}(f)$ for a monotone function then satisfies
\[
 \cmon(f)\le C_{0,R}(f)\le4\cmon(f).
\]
For the lower bound, take the shadow and delete inverse gates, whose shadows are identities. For the upper bound, AND is multiplication and OR is $a+b-ab$, using at most four gates. Checking the four Boolean input pairs gives precisely $\tau,1$ as the final results. Intermediate old zeros are allowed: for example, $1+1$ is the old zero in characteristic two. Thus this extends the output-level comparison, while the unrestricted $\Theta(\cbool)$ statement above remains specific to $(\F_2)_0$.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Why the output qualifier is essential]
If $e$ is forbidden at \emph{every} useful gate and every Boolean input, and constants are $\tau$ and $1$, the remaining nonzero shadows are monotone and true on the all-one input. Adding two such wires would produce $1+1=e$ there. Consequently every useful addition has a zero operand and can be deleted. The only resulting nonconstant functions are conjunctions of variables. The all-gates formulation of the monotone-equivalence assertion is therefore false.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[The precise consequence for clique]\label{cor:clique}
For every clique-function family to which the monotone lower bound of \citet[Theorem~3.9, p.~12]{AB} applies, final-output-zero-free $(\F_2)_0$ circuits obey the same lower bound up to constant factors. The family has polynomial-size unrestricted $(\F_2)_0$ circuits if and only if it has polynomial-size Boolean circuits.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:complexity}. The cited monotone lower bound is the only external input.
\end{proof}
This identifies the required comparison without proving a new nonuniform Boolean lower bound. A statement merely that the ratio of the two complexities is exponentially large does not imply that the smaller complexity is polynomial. Thus ``exponential savings'' must be specified as a reduction to polynomial size if it is used in an equivalence with membership in $\mathrm P/\mathrm{poly}$.

\subsection{Slice functions}
A $k$-slice function is zero at weights below $k$, one at weights above $k$, and arbitrary at weight $k$. It is monotone. The polynomial-overhead simulation is classical, attributed to \citet{Berkowitz} by \citet[Theorem~2.6 and Remark~2.7, pp.~57--58]{WegenerSlice}. Wegener proves the stronger overhead $O(n\min\{k,n+1-k,\log^2n\})$. We give a simpler cubic-overhead construction because it specifies exactly the output-zero condition used here.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:slice}
If an $n$-variable $k$-slice function has a Boolean circuit of size $s$, it has a monotone circuit of size $O(s+n^3)$. Its final supported zeros in the preceding circuit model can therefore be eliminated with polynomial overhead.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
First compute each wire and its complement together. By De Morgan's laws, an AND gate produces the positive output by AND and its complement by OR of the complementary operands; OR is dual, and NOT swaps the pair. This yields a circuit with at most $2s$ binary gates whose only negations are input literals.

On the exact weight-$k$ slice, $\neg x_i$ equals the monotone threshold $T_i$ asserting that at least $k$ of the other $n-1$ variables are true. Replace every negative input literal by $T_i$. Let the resulting monotone circuit be $g$. It agrees with the original function at weight $k$.

A threshold on $m$ inputs can be computed by the recurrence
\[
 T_{j,r}=T_{j-1,r}\vee(x_j\wedge T_{j-1,r-1}),
\]
with $T_{j,0}=1$, $T_{0,r}=0$ for $r>0$, omitting impossible indices. This uses $O(m^2)$ binary gates. Compute all $n$ functions $T_i$ and the thresholds $T_{n,k}$ and $T_{n,k+1}$ in $O(n^3)$ gates. Then
\[
 T_{n,k+1}\vee\bigl(T_{n,k}\wedge g\bigr)
\]
is zero below the slice, agrees with $g$ on it and is one above it. Boundary values $k=0,n$ use the same constant conventions. Proposition~\ref{prop:complexity} converts this monotone circuit into a final-output-zero-free one with constant-factor overhead.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Parity tests}
\begin{proposition}\label{prop:parity}
For bits $b_1,\ldots,b_m$, lift $0$ to $\tau$ and $1$ to $1\in(\F_2)_0$. Their sum is $\tau$ if all bits vanish, $e$ if a positive even number are one, and $1$ if an odd number are one. Thus an even-parity test passes exactly when the sum belongs to $\{\tau,e\}$, a Boolean semiring under the inherited operations, with its own multiplicative identity $e$. Its inclusion is not unital.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The ring coordinate of the sum is parity, while the support coordinate is the OR of all bits. These two values distinguish the three cases. The pair $\{\tau,e\}$ has $e+e=e$, $e^2=e$, additive identity $\tau$ and multiplicative identity $e$, so it is Boolean.
\end{proof}

\section{Two lifting problems and two independent losses of information}
This section answers which comparison follows solely from the coefficient and support homomorphisms.
There are homomorphisms
\[
 \N[M]\longrightarrow\Z_0[M]\longrightarrow\B[M],
\]
where a zero coefficient maps to $\tau$ and a positive coefficient maps to that positive old integer. The first map is injective and its image has no supported coefficient zeros. For $M=\N^n$, append the homomorphism $\B[M]\to Q_n$ that remembers only the monotone predicate generated by the monomials. Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is exactly the minimization of gate count over lifts of $f_G$ along this composite.

For comparison, effective sign coefficients form $\N[C_2\times M]$, with $C_2=\{1,\varepsilon\}$ and $\varepsilon^2=1$. A coefficient $(a^+,a^-)$ maps to the old integer $a^+-a^-$ when $a^++a^->0$ and to $\tau$ otherwise. This gives a surjective homomorphism to $\Z_0[M]$: any integer is a difference of two nonnegative integers, and an old zero is represented by $(1,1)$. Addition and multiplication preserve presence because dimensions add and multiply without cancellation; traces are additive and multiplicative. An associative effective lift of structure constants must in addition satisfy all associativity equations in this larger semiring.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:independentlosses}
Supported coefficient zeros and repeated-variable identification in $\B[\N^n]\to Q_n$ are independent phenomena. No nontrivial supported coefficient zero occurs in a lift from $\N[\N^n]$, even when an edge is represented only by higher powers. Conversely a supported coefficient zero can occur without repeated variables.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every occurring coefficient in the image of $\N[\N^n]$ is a positive integer. The monomial $x^2y$ therefore has no supported coefficient zero, although it and $xy$ have the same Boolean minimal support and different total degrees. Conversely $x-x$ in $\Z_0[x]$ has the supported coefficient zero at $x$, whose exponent is one. For effective coefficients, $1+\varepsilon$ gives a supported zero already at monoid degree zero. These examples establish both separations.
\end{proof}

What transfers is evaluation through homomorphisms, including the same gate-list image and the preservation of equations already satisfied by a lift. A solution to associativity equations need not have a small circuit, and the existence of a small circuit does not impose associativity on an unrelated multiplication table. The homomorphisms alone therefore give no equality between a dimension-lift defect and the cost of edges represented through Boolean idempotence.

\subsection{The canonical formal determinant}
The formal target also matters for the determinant claim in the unpublished translation notes. The following is a consequence of classical monotone permanent support bounds, not a new separation. \citet[Section~4.3, pp.~887--889]{JS} prove a stronger multiplication bound by their content method. We give an elementary exponential bound with a complete proof to specify exactly what is computed.

For a nonzero commutative unital ring $R$, let $\Delta_n^{\mathrm{can}}\in R_0[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]$ have precisely the permutation monomials as its occupied exponents, with coefficient $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ on $\prod_i x_{i,\sigma(i)}$. The coefficient is interpreted in $R$.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:canonicaldet}
For $n\ge3$, a circuit computing $\Delta_n^{\mathrm{can}}$ from variables and free scalar constants in $R_0$, using binary addition and multiplication and unary additive inverse, has at least
\[
 \binom{n}{\lfloor n/3\rfloor}
\]
binary gates. The bound holds over every such $R$, including characteristic two.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Apply the occupancy map $R_0[x]\to\B[x]$. An old scalar, even the old zero, maps to $1$, while $\tau$ maps to $0$; inverse gates become identities. The target is the formal Boolean permanent polynomial, whose exponents have not been identified by $x^2=x$. Delete inverse gates and zero branches and read the remaining circuit over $\N$, with each nonzero scalar replaced by $1$. Its output $Q$ has positive coefficients and exactly the permanent's monomial support. Its binary size has not increased.

Every useful gate polynomial $Q_g$ is homogeneous. Indeed, fix one parse occurrence of $g$ and all monomial choices outside it, giving a monomial context $m$ such that every monomial of $Q_gm$ occurs in the output. Positivity and the output degree $n$ force all monomials of $Q_g$ to have the same degree. They also force each such monomial to be a partial permutation. Degree-zero gates can be eliminated supportwise, since positive scalar multiplication changes no monomial support.

Take a parse tree for an output permutation monomial. Bypass addition steps and descend a product child whenever it has degree greater than $2n/3$. At the last product with degree greater than $2n/3$, both children have degree at most $2n/3$, and one has degree $d>n/3$. Choose this child occurrence. For $n\ge3$ it is a computation gate, and
\[
 n/3<d\le2n/3.
\]

For a fixed chosen gate $g$, one monomial context $m_g$ forces every monomial of $Q_g$ to use exactly the rows $I_g$ and columns $J_g$ absent from $m_g$. Both sets have size $d$. Every other possible context of $g$ must use their complements, since multiplying that context by any fixed monomial of $Q_g$ gives an output permutation. Hence the total number of permutations whose parses can be assigned to $g$ is at most $d!(n-d)!$. This bound counts all permutations respecting these two sets, and so remains valid for shared gates and repeated descriptions of a context.

Put $k=\lfloor n/3\rfloor$. Since $k\le d\le n-k$, we have $d!(n-d)!\le k!(n-k)!$. Assigning every output permutation one of its chosen gates, and writing $s$ for the number of binary gates, gives
\[
 n!\le s\,k!(n-k)!,
\]
which proves the claim.
\end{proof}

Projection to $R[x]$ can erase additional occupied monomials whose coefficients are old zeros. A small ring circuit for the determinant lifts gate by gate to $R_0$, but its lift may retain exactly such additional exponents and therefore fail to compute $\Delta_n^{\mathrm{can}}$. Proposition~\ref{prop:canonicaldet} concerns this specified formal element. It gives no lower bound for unrestricted Boolean circuits or for an arbitrary formal lift whose ring projection is the determinant.

\section{The remaining exact question}
The unrestricted question is the following: if $G$ is bipartite and has no four-cycle, must every $P\in\Sup(G)$ require at least $|E|+\vc(G)-1$ variable-input nonnegative arithmetic gates? The analogous question for every graph of girth at least five is the formulation attributed to L-meta-608; removing the triangle restriction gives the formulation attributed to L-meta-612. These questions remain undecided in this paper.

The obstruction can be stated without metaphor. A monomial whose support is an edge may have degree greater than two. Taking the degree-two component can delete the only witness for that edge. The polynomial $x_u^2x_v$ for a one-edge graph is the smallest example. Proposition~\ref{prop:missing} gives a lower bound in terms of the number of these missing quadratic witnesses, and Theorem~\ref{thm:twomissing} charges their full cost when at most two are missing. Theorem~\ref{thm:threemissing} extends the full count to at most three missing witnesses, including empty quadratic support. Proposition~\ref{prop:fouredgeboundary} settles the empty-quadratic case with four missing witnesses. For nonempty quadratic support and four missing witnesses, Theorem~\ref{thm:maxfour} settles maximal cover gain and Corollary~\ref{cor:fourresidualfinal} records the remaining lower-gain cases; the general four-or-more-missing-witness bound remains open. For marked degree at least two, the path expansion also has products of two dependent factors; replacing repeated marked variables by one can create new minimal edge witnesses. The transposed neighborhood calculation no longer has the linear form required by Lemma~\ref{lem:transpose}. Corollary~\ref{cor:degreewitness} proves that any counterexample in the bipartite case must encounter this obstruction on both sides.

\begin{example}[A discarded-gate charge that is false]\label{ex:chargefailure}
It would suffice to charge at least $r+\vc(G)-\vc(G_2)$ discarded gates, but that proposed inequality is false. Take four vertices $u,v,w,t$, four centers $a,b,c,d$, and four private leaves $\ell_a,\ell_b,\ell_c,\ell_d$. In $G_2$, join the centers respectively to $\{u,w\},\{u,t\},\{v,w\},\{v,t\}$, and join each center to its private leaf. Add $uv$ and $wt$ to obtain $G$. The old core is an eight-cycle. A cycle using one new edge has length at least five; one using both has length at least six. Thus $G$ has girth five. The four pendant edges certify $\vc(G_2)=4$, and together with the two new edges form a six-edge matching. The four centers together with $u,w$ cover $G$, so $\vc(G)=6$. There are twelve old edges and fourteen edges in all.

Put $A=u+w$, $B=u+t$, $C=v+w$, $D=v+t$. Compute
\[
 a(A+\ell_a)+b(B+\ell_b)+c(C+\ell_c)
 +(d+ABC)D+d\ell_d.
\]
The four clause sums cost four gates, the three pendant additions cost three, forming $ABC$ and adding $d$ costs three, the five remaining products cost five, and joining their outputs costs four. The total is nineteen, the star bound. Boolean distributivity gives $ABCD=uv\vee wt$, so the circuit computes $f_G$. Its formal quadratic part is exactly $H_{G_2}$. Extraction deletes only the two products forming $ABC$ and the addition $d+ABC$, leaving sixteen gates, one more than the optimal fifteen. Thus $r=2$ and the cover number drops by two, but only three gates disappear.

Folding the last pendant into $(d+ABC)(D+\ell_d)$ would save a gate, but accepts the independent input $\{u,w,\ell_d\}$. The missing charge in this example is therefore supplied by inefficiency in the retained quadratic circuit. Counting discarded gates alone cannot establish the desired universal bound.
\end{example}

The construction was explored in unpublished project notes beginning in November 2025, independently of \citet{FGJM}, whose preprint appeared on 19 November 2024. The first texts were produced by Gemini 2.5 Deep Think in the Gemini app's Deep Think mode from a conversation with Gemini 2.5 Pro. Versions were deposited on Zenodo under HI-AI from 6 November 2025 and later withdrawn. A GPT-5-series Pro model in ChatGPT Pro mode at reasoning effort ultra extracted the algebra in March 2026. GPT-5-series Pro models in the same mode and effort produced the April--July 2026 corpus, and Codex runs at reasoning effort ultra produced the August--September workbench. The circuit translation notes of 21--23 November 2026 were produced by Claude Opus 5.5 at effort max, with consultations by Claude Fable 5.2 at effort max and Claude Opus 5.5 at effort high. The circuit map was produced by Claude Opus 5.5 at effort high; its degree-one argument by Claude Opus 5.5 at effort max. These are cited only as unpublished project work.

The checks comprise independent derivations from statements, targeted proof review and finite exact computations, with their separate scopes recorded through the workbench; the reasoning-effort setting was not exposed and is not inferred.
